Remember when we used to just hop on a ferry to France after school, with a few quid in our pockets and a rucksack full of snacks? How could I forget? Those were the days. Right, so we’re still… hopelessly lost. I double-checked the route, honestly, but it seems like this satnav has a personal vendetta against me. Aye, well, relax, Liam. It's just a bit of a detour. This area… it looks familiar. Hang on… I think we need to go back to that roundabout we passed about ten minutes ago. There was a sign for Market Harborough, wasn’t there? There was! But the satnav told me to ignore it! It said it would be "a more efficient route." Efficient?!

Cor, this rain. Proper miserable, innit? Reminds me of that November back in ‘68. Remember that, Arthur? Flooded the whole of Costessey down by the river. Aye, vaguely. I was just a lad, mind. Mostly remember me mum fretting about the drains. Didn't fancy getting me boots wet, she didn’t. Still don’t, if I’m honest. This lot's coming down proper sideways. Honestly, it’s enough to cancel the bingo tonight. I was looking forward to it, too. A little bit of socializing, you know? Gets lonely, otherwise. And these are your favourite, Arthur – ginger nuts. Fresh from the oven. Ginger nuts, eh? Right then. You shouldn't 'ave bothered, Jean. Though, I reckon a biscuit or two might just chase away the gloom. Thanks. Lovely. Proper lovely. You still using that new oven, then? Seems to bake 'em a bit crisper. That oven! A right beast it is. Took me ages to work out where the timer button were. Doctor says… well, you know. . Though, a sliver… just a sliver wouldn't hurt, would it? Doctor always says something, doesn't he? Never says anything good. Remember when they told me I needed to cut down on the pork pies? Pork pies! That was a tragedy. Oh, Bernard. You and your pork pies. You haven’t changed a bit. Honestly, you'd think the world was ending. Well, they  were  a cornerstone of my diet! Just a small one each day, mind. It’s the principle of the thing, Jean. Being told what you can't 'ave. Gives you a right rebellious streak. Reckon he’s got a point, Jean. It’s the freedom, innit? The freedom to do what you want, when you want. That’s what’s been taken away. You two are hopeless. Sitting here lamenting the loss of your pork pies and rebellious streaks. It’s a bit dramatic, don’t you think? We’re lucky, really. We've got a roof over our heads, we've got each other.

Honestly, Chloe, I’m pulling my hair out. This Instagram thing…it’s just a black hole for time and barely any sales. I spent all day yesterday creating reels, editing them…and what? Three likes. Three! Right, okay, let's unpack that. Reels can be tricky. Are you focusing on the right hashtags? It's about finding the niche, isn’t it? Have you looked at what other smaller skincare brands are doing? Not the big corporations, the ones with a similar size and scale to Honest Skincare. I’ve had a  look , yeah. And they're all seemingly doing those silly dance trends, or showing off products in unrealistic lighting. I’m trying to be authentic, you know? Show the process, the ingredients…but it doesn’t seem to be clicking. Plus, the algorithm clearly hates me. Authenticity is brilliant, honestly. But you need to be  strategically  authentic. Think about visual appeal. Lighting is key! Even natural light makes a huge difference. And those dance trends… okay, they’re annoying, but sometimes a little bit of playful content can broaden your reach. It doesn't mean selling out, just experimenting. What about before and after photos? Honest results are powerfully persuasive. I’ve done a few. Sarah’s testimonial with the eczema – that one did really well. But getting people to send photos…it’s a hurdle. And then there's the legal stuff. Proof of consent and everything. It’s stressful. Absolutely. Legalities are important. And Sarah’s testimonial is a great example! Focus on those. Build on that. Another thought - are you thinking about Etsy at all? It has a built-in customer base looking for handmade and natural products. I’ve considered it. But the fees! And the competition! It feels like shouting into a hurricane. eBay’s a bit better, listing-wise, but… I just can’t seem to get the pricing right. People keep trying to haggle. Haggling is just part of online selling, I’m afraid! Maybe you need a slightly higher base price to allow for that. And don’t be afraid to stand your ground. You're selling high-quality, handmade skincare. It's not cheap, and people need to recognise the value in that. What about limited-edition sets? Creates a sense of urgency. Limited edition…that’s an idea. Christmas sets, maybe? I was thinking of doing a rosemary and orange scrub this year.

Honestly, John’s pronouncements on the telly yesterday… unbelievable. Talking about cutting back on social care again. As if there isn't enough suffering already. It's just… callous, isn't it? You're not wrong, Margaret. It’s all short-term thinking, as usual. They’re chasing headlines, not solutions. Social care is the bedrock of a decent society, and chipping away at it bit by bit… well, it’s predictable, I suppose, but still infuriating. Did you see that piece about the care home closures in Essex? Scandalous. I missed that one, sadly. My eyes glaze over after a bit, to be honest. Too much negativity. It just churns my stomach. You know, I was just thinking about Mrs. Abernathy, one of my former pupils. Such a bright girl, loved history. She's got dementia now, lives in one of these poorly-funded homes. Seeing her... it breaks your heart. Terrible, isn't it? It's not just the lack of funding, though. It's the staff turnover. Low wages, stressful conditions… you can’t expect people to provide quality care if they’re constantly feeling undervalued and overworked. Remember when we were worried about Sarah’s grandmother? Thankfully, the home she was in wasn't too bad. Yes, but even that wasn’t perfect. The meals were… bland, to say the least. And the activities! A sing-song every Tuesday. That’s hardly stimulating for someone who used to be a botanist, you know. I used to pop in, read to her sometimes. It was the least I could do. Keeps you going, doesn’t it, doing something? It does. Keeps you feeling connected. I miss teaching, you know. Not the marking – heavens no! – but the interaction with the students. Shaping young minds. It felt… purposeful. I know what you mean. Though I sometimes wonder if I made any difference at all. All those years, all that effort… did it really translate into anything tangible? I worry sometimes I just perpetuated a system. Don't be ridiculous, Margaret. You were brilliant. The kids loved you. Remember little Thomas, who couldn’t read a word when he joined Year 3? You worked wonders with him. He went on to get a degree in engineering! That’s hardly perpetuating a system, is it? That’s a life changed. Oh, Thomas. He always did have a spark. It's funny, the ones you really remember, isn’t it?

Speaker_1 said, pushing a stray curl behind her ear. "It's reached a point where I'm actively considering wearing layers indoors. Like, three jumpers and socks in December. Ridiculous." Seriously though, are you looking at those smart thermostats? My sister swears by hers. Apparently, you can control it from your phone and it learns your habits." Speaker_3 : "Oh, yes! Did you use nutmeg, Eleanor?" "Thank you, Chloe! Yes, a generous pinch. It’s all about the nutmeg. And the roasting the parsnips properly – you can’t just boil them. Making furniture just doesn't feel like  work  when you’re doing something you genuinely enjoy. Just means thinking about how to make sure I can afford to enjoy it for longer, you know?" He took a long sip of his wine. "Wouldn’t mind a bit of that parsnip mash myself, Chloe. Looks proper good." Mark: "Fifty-three! Crikey, you’re young! I’m nearly forty, and the thought of retirement feels… distant. I'm stuck in technical support, troubleshooting conveyor belts and pressure gauges. Exciting, right? Though, I did manage to pick up a new torque wrench the other week. Proper lovely piece of kit, really. Balanced weight, ergonomic handle… you’d appreciate it, Rhys, I reckon." Need to make sure everything's properly secured when I'm building those tables, you know?

Honestly, Mum, this is ridiculous. We've got three different forks, two different knives, and enough spoons to feed a small army, but none of them match! It’s making the roast look… chaotic. Chaotic's a strong word, love. It's family dinner, not a Michelin star restaurant. A bit eclectic, perhaps. Pass the gravy, would you? Eclectic? That's charity for it, lad! Your Dad's been promising to sort this out for years. Says it's "treasured memories." Meaning he keeps every chipped mug and bent fork he's ever owned. They bring back stories, though, don’t they, Brenda? This one , your Uncle George used this at his wedding. A good lad, George. Tragic what happened. George… aye. Headed for the mines straight outta school, he did. Hard life, that. Never saw him smile much after the accident. Should’ve stayed above ground, he should’ve. Grandpa, you don’t have to bring up the accident at dinner. It's a bit morbid, isn't it? Morbid? Life  is  morbid, lass. Just need to remember the good bits amongst the bad. Speaking of good bits, remember your Auntie Elsie's trifle? Now  that  was something to smile about. Elsie's trifles were legendary. Though your Dad swore she used to sneak a drop of sherry into the cream. Said it gave it a ‘certain something’. Dad! You used to raid the fruit bowl after she left, pretending you were checking for unripe peaches! I did no such thing! Just ensuring the quality control was up to scratch. Needed to make sure Elsie hadn't gone stingy with the raspberries. Right, of course. Quality control. So, are we ever going to talk about anything other than past glories and questionable desserts? I was thinking, we could have everyone over for a proper games night next weekend? Board games, maybe even charades? Games night, eh? Sounds lovely, pet. Though I'm warning you now, I’m ruthless at Scrabble. Ruthless! Don't worry, Brenda, I’ll be your wingman. I’m surprisingly good at finding obscure words. I haven't played Scrabble in years. Might be a bit rusty. But I’m always up for a laugh. Though, someone needs to remind me of the rules... Rules? Just make up your own, like they do down south. Always changing things, them southerners. Grandpa, you know you don’t mean that.

Honestly, this chicken's lovely. You really nailed the lemon and herb marinade, didn’t you? Mmm-hmm. Can I have more peas, please? In a minute, love. Just finishing my mouthful. So, about work… Mr. Harrison’s being a total nightmare again. Harrison? Who's Harrison? Is he a bad guy? He’s not a  bad  guy, just… difficult. He wants that Miller report finished by Friday. Friday! It's practically a miracle I got the Peterson proposal out on time this week. He's piling the pressure on, you know? I swear, he just enjoys watching people squirm. Can you tell him no? Like, a big, loud "No!" Oh, I'd love to, darling. But, unfortunately, my job depends on keeping him reasonably happy. It's a delicate dance. Just trying to juggle everything is exhausting. Thinking about it, though... this skiing holiday can’t come soon enough. Skiing! Will there be snow? Lots and lots of snow? Can I throw snowballs at you? Loads of snow, I hope! We're going to Austria, remember? The Alps. And yes, you can definitely throw snowballs at me. Plenty of snowball fights planned. Although, be warned, your mum’s a surprisingly fierce snowball target. I’ll be the best snowball thrower ever! Will there be hot chocolate? With marshmallows? Of course, there'll be hot chocolate with marshmallows! Mountains of it. We'll practically be living on hot chocolate for a week. Did you pack your favourite hat? The fluffy pink one? Yes! With the pompom! And my snow boots! Good girl. Right, peas then? So, no news on the flights being further delayed, I hope? I checked this morning, and everything seemed stable. Just need to confirm the ski hire. I was thinking we should pre-book that, especially for you, sweetheart. Things get snatched up quickly. Can I have a really big ski? Bigger than Daddy's! Well, probably not quite as big as your dad's. We need to make sure it’s the right size for you, safe and manageable. But we'll find a good one, don’t worry. What do you think about us taking those lessons? The little group ones they offer? Lessons? Will I fall over a lot? Possibly! Everyone falls over when they’re learning to ski. It’s part of the fun! The instructor will be there to help you up, and show you the best way to do it.

Honestly, Maths is just…  ugh . Mr. Davies just keeps piling it on. Quadratic equations! Who even  uses  quadratic equations in real life? Well, architects, probably. And engineers. You know, building things. It’s not  completely  useless, Liv. You’re just not thinking about it properly. Did you at least look at the extension problems? Looked? I stared at them. They stared back. I think one of them blinked. It felt like a personal attack. And then English! Mrs. Peterson is obsessed with analysing poetry. "What does the colour blue  symbolise  in this stanza?" I just wanted to say 'blue'? It's blue! You're impossible. You know, you’re actually pretty good at English when you apply yourself. You just get frustrated when it’s not straightforward. Remember last year’s Romeo and Juliet essay? You nailed that. Yeah, but that was… different. Something about dying lovers is inspiring, apparently. Food Tech today was interesting, though. We made those little sausage rolls. They were actually quite good! They were  amazing ! I’m definitely going to try and recreate them at home. Mum gave me a weird look when I kept talking about puff pastry, though. She's worried I’ll turn into a baker. You wouldn't be the worst thing to turn into! Better than a mathematician, definitely. So, what are you doing after this? Still planning on practicing your Spanish? I’m never going to be fluent. My brain just doesn’t work with conjugations. I am! I'm working on the past tenses. It’s tricky, yeah, but Señora Rodriguez says if I keep at it, I could even consider doing an exchange program. Imagine, a year in Spain! A year in Spain? Wow. Proper adventurous! I'd probably just spend the whole time complaining about the lack of decent tea. Seriously, you should do it. It'd look brilliant on your uni application. I know! That’s kind of the idea. What about you? Any thoughts on what you want to do after Sixth Form? You're still thinking about Graphic Design, right? That’s the plan. It’s just… stressful. Everyone's talking about uni, and jobs, and… it's a lot. I overheard my mum on the phone yesterday, talking about student loans. Made me feel slightly queasy. Tell me about it. My dad keeps saying I should just go into business – “Secure, stable salary, Chloe!”

Honestly, Mum, you'd  love  "Everything Everywhere All at Once." It's completely bonkers, but in a brilliant way. Like, a bagel creates a universe - a universe! - and it's all about family and regret and… well, a lot of things. A bagel, love? Creating a universe? Sounds a bit daft, doesn't it? I’m not sure I’d get the hang of all that. I prefer a nice, straightforward story, like "Brief Encounter." Now  that  was a film. Proper heartbreak. You know, a bit of quiet longing… not jumping between different dimensions. But that's the point! It's not quiet! It's a sensory overload in the best way. And the performances are incredible. Michelle Yeoh? Outstanding. You know, you always say you want to see something different, something that challenges you. This does! Different, yes. Challenging, perhaps. But I spent my life dealing with paperwork and raising children, love. I don't need my brain scrambled further by jumping bagels. What's it  really  about, though? Underneath all the… the whatchamacallit... the chaos. Okay, right. Okay. Underneath the chaos, it’s about a mother and daughter, Evelyn and Joy, and their relationship. Evelyn feels like she’s failed as a mother, always working, never really present. And Joy, her daughter, is struggling to connect with her, trying to tell her something important. The multiverse stuff is just a vehicle to explore that. A vehicle, eh? Like a motorcar? Well, I suppose that's a bit more understandable. Sounds a bit like me and your sister, Brenda, really. Always battling over whose turn it was to visit our mum. Though I doubt a bagel was involved. No, thankfully no bagels. Though, Brenda  does  have a way of sucking the joy out of any situation. Anyway, I was thinking we could all go see it next week. The Arts Cinema's showing it. We could get fish and chips afterwards. Fish and chips… now you’re talking! That's something I understand. But are you sure it’s not too… intense? I do get a bit flustered with all this newfangled film-making. Remember "Avatar"? All that blue! Gave me a headache for days. It's not  that  intense, Mum. They mix the action and the weirdness with a lot of humour. It’s genuinely funny, even with the existential dread. And it’s only about two hours. We can leave early if you’re not enjoying it.

Honestly, Mum, the traffic getting in was  awful . Took me nearly an hour and a half from Coventry. I swear, the M6 is just a perpetual car park these days. Oh, you’re lucky! Used to be worse, love. Back in my day, getting home after court was a nightmare. Rush hour was something else. Still is, I reckon, just a bit more… organized chaos now. Did you see they’re rebuilding that junction near Spaghetti Junction? Promises it’ll be better. Promises. Promises are cheap, Mum. You know that as well as I do. So, have you heard anything more about Auntie Carol’s knee? She sounded pretty down on the phone last week. Aye, poor Carol. Consultant says it's needing a proper op now. Reconstructive surgery, apparently. She's terrified of hospitals, you know she is. Keeps saying she'll just manage, but at her age… Well, it’s not ideal, is it? Her pension’s not exactly overflowing either, so the cost of everything… it's a worry. It is a worry. We should probably offer to help with some of the bills. I can definitely spare a bit. It's awful seeing family struggle like that. Reminds me of when Dad was off work with his back, how tight things were. He’d be furious if he heard you saying that, your father. He wouldn’t want anyone feeling sorry for him. Stubborn as an ox, that man was. Speaking of stubbornness, are you still thinking about that driving course? Yes, but it’s so expensive! Nearly £500 for a five-day intensive. I know it would improve my confidence, especially navigating London – I’m going to that conference next month – but it's a lot to swallow. Maybe I should just stick to public transport. Don’t be silly, love. Safety first. And you’re a good driver, just a bit… anxious, aren't you? Remember when you nearly drove into that lamppost when you were learning? Your father nearly had a heart attack! Oh god, don't remind me! He went on for hours about how dangerous driving was. He was always such a stickler for the rules, wasn't he? Probably why I'm so cautious now. You know, I was reading this fascinating legal thriller the other day. Really got me thinking about the complexities of the law. Law, eh? Well, I’ve seen a fair bit of it in my time, working at the court.

Honestly, the air quality’s improved a bit today, hasn’t it? Still not exactly fresh Norfolk air, but… manageable. Feels lighter than yesterday. Definitely. I was starting to feel like I was breathing soup. Though, I'm still sticking to my filtered water, thank you very much. Remember that documentary we watched about pollution here? Still gives me the shivers. Don’t remind me. Though, I was pleasantly surprised by the new research coming out of Tsinghua. They're actually really pushing for innovation in air purification tech. Maybe things will genuinely improve long-term. Fingers crossed. Anyway, back to slightly less apocalyptic topics… my office was a whirlwind this afternoon. Professor Chen’s paper got rejected again. Third time this year! Can you believe it? Poor bloke. What was the feedback this time? Same as always. “Lacks originality,” “Methodology questionable,” the usual academic jargon. He’s so disheartened. I tried to offer some constructive criticism, but he just stared blankly at me for a solid five minutes. Honestly felt like talking to a brick wall. Professor Chen is a lovely man, but let’s be honest, his research has been going downhill for a while. Maybe he needs a break, a sabbatical. Somewhere with…cleaner air. Possibly. I’ve suggested it to him, delicately of course. He just seems to think it’s a personal attack on his intellect. Right. Speaking of things that are frustrating, I still haven't managed to get a decent replacement for that silk scarf I accidentally spilled tea on. Remember that one? The blue and silver one? Vaguely. The one you cherished? It  was  rather lovely. Any luck online? That's the problem! Everything online is either incredibly cheap polyester or costs a small fortune. I was hoping to find something similar in that little market near the park tomorrow. You know, the one with the vintage fabrics? That's a good shout! I’ll come with you. We could make a morning of it. Grab some baozi from that little stall we like too. Oh, that would be perfect! I’ve also been meaning to get some new spices. The Sichuan peppercorns I bought last week were a complete disaster; tasted like sawdust. Typical. They’re so hit and miss here. Remember that amazing cumin I found last month? I'm hoping to recreate that lamb dish I was thinking about. Oh, please do!

Or… if not, we could use the living room and make it all twinkly and magical. What do you think?

Honestly, this salad is depressingly beige. Like, where's the excitement? The colour? I feel like I’m eating wallpaper paste. You're always moaning about the food, Livvy! It's lunchtime, it's free, and it fills you up. What more do you want? A Michelin star? Well, a  little  flavour wouldn't go amiss. I swear, they just throw a few lettuce leaves and some anaemic tomatoes on a plate. Remember that dodgy lasagne last week? I nearly choked. Don't remind me! My stomach hasn't forgiven them yet. Nkuku cleared his plate though, which says something, doesn't it? He'll eat anything. Proper bottomless pit, that one. He absolutely is. Right, changing subject. Are you still planning on going to that rooftop bar thing on Saturday? The one Liam's friend is sorting? Yeah, definitely. Apparently, the views are amazing. So long as it isn't raining, which, let’s be honest, is a massive ‘if’ this time of year. My mum’s already nagged me to wear something “sensible.” Sensible? Like what? A tweed suit? She keeps going on about "respectable young women." It's like I’m still ten years old. She’s just worried, I guess. Being a Filipina immigrant, she has this ingrained idea of how girls should behave. It’s… complicated. I get that. My nan's the same. Everything’s about reputation and doing what’s expected. It's exhausting sometimes. Anyway, what lecturers are driving you mad this term? Mine's history - Mr. Davies - he ambles through lectures like he's perpetually falling asleep. Oh,  definitely  Davies. Honestly, I'm half expecting him to start snoring mid-sentence. My worst is Professor Harding in psychology. She picks up on literally  everything . If you look at her the wrong way, she’ll give you an extra essay. Ooh, sounds terrifying. See, that's what I'm missing from psychology. I really should have given it a chance. But then I’d have to actually  pay attention . It's a good course, genuinely. But Harding… It requires dedication. Seriously, avoid eye contact. And don't breathe too loudly. Are you managing alright with your dissertation? That’s looming, isn’t it?

…and then the seagull just  snatched  it right out of her hand! Full-blown baguette heist, right there on Brighton beach. Honestly, Mum was fuming. She’d been looking forward to that sandwich all morning. Aye, that’s reet rotten! Seagulls, man, they’re proper thieves. Remember that time I was feeding pigeons in Newcastle and one came down and nipped my finger? Nearly drew blood! Seagulls are opportunistic scavengers. Their behaviour is entirely predictable from a biological perspective. It’s quite fascinating, really. Right, thanks for the biology lesson, James. Some of us were just enjoying a good laugh. Anyway, Brighton was… Brighton. Overcrowded, overpriced, but the pier was decent. You should have come, Anya. Naw, I'm alright, lad. Sunderland’s got its own charm, ken? Besides, I’ve been buried in corpora all summer. It’s like, a never-ending sea of words. Tidying up inconsistencies, making sure everything’s properly tagged… thrilling stuff, I know. Speaking of things needing careful management, how are you finding the corpus work, Anya? Still grappling with the nuances of lexical ambiguity, I presume? Don't even go there, James. It’s enough to drive a girl mad. You’d think a word’s meaning would be a bit more straightforward, wouldn’t ya? But no. One minute it's an adjective, the next it's a verb, and then suddenly it's referring to a historical artifact! Sounds delightful. Seriously, Anya, you need a holiday. Like, a  real  holiday. Not just staring at text files. What about Spain next year? We could go surfing. Spain sounds lovely, actually. But holiday money’s a bit tight at the moment. Mum’s been saying we should all go back to Whitby. Proper traditional seaside town, that is. Fish and chips on the beach... cannae beat it. Whitby... I recall a rather pleasant walk along the coastline there a few years back. The ruins of the abbey are quite impressive. Ruins are good. Fish and chips are even better. So, Whitby it is, then? A tentative vote for Whitby? Aye, I’d be up for Whitby. Though, I'm hoping they've not increased the price of the mushy peas again. Last time I went, they were practically highway robbery! You Brits and your obsession with mushy peas. It’s quite… peculiar. Have you two seen that new series on Netflix, "The Crown"? Oh, "The Crown"!

…and then young Timmy, bless his cotton socks, decided to smear his mashed potatoes all over the curtains! Honestly, some days… you just never knew what you were going to get. Cor blimey, that sounds a right kerfuffle, Barbara. Reminds me of little Kevin down the road. Used to be forever gettin' into scrapes, that one. Did he ever settle down, Kevin? Kevin’s running a ferret farm in Wiltshire, David. Apparently, it’s quite lucrative. Settled doesn’t quite cover it; he’s surrounded by hundreds of ferrets. More stable than some careers teachers have, I reckon. Speaking of careers, how’s that eBay selling going, Barbara? You said you were hoping to finally shift that old china cabinet. Oh, it's a nightmare, John! Nobody wants a perfectly good oak cabinet anymore. They all want flat-pack nonsense from Ikea. I’ve had three offers, all ridiculously low. One fellow offered me twenty quid! Twenty quid! It's worth at least a hundred and fifty, surely? A hundred and fifty? You're havin’ a laugh, Barbara. Things ain’t worth what they used to be. Still, if you need a bit o' spare dosh, might be worth takin' the twenty. Every little helps. David’s right to an extent, Barbara. The market’s flooded. Have you considered local Facebook Marketplace? Sometimes you get better luck with folk nearby appreciating quality craftsmanship. I’ve tried, John! It's just endless haggling. And people making ridiculous requests - "Can you deliver it for free?" "Can you take a picture of it from a different angle?" Honestly! Always someone tryin’ to get a bargain, innit? Remind me of my Uncle Arthur. Never paid a full price for anything. Could talk the hide off a donkey. Speaking of things changing… this election. What do you reckon, John? Don’t even start me, David. It’s a mess. Utter chaos. Nobody seems to know what they’re doing. My students are hopelessly cynical – hardly surprising, really. They look at the politicians and see… well, not exactly shining examples. Makes you long for the old days, doesn't it? When things seemed… simpler. Though I suppose they weren't, really. Remember that trip we did to Cornwall, John, years ago? Staying in that youth hostel? Ah, yes. Penzance. Rough around the edges, that hostel was. But the coastal path was magnificent. And the horses… remember all the wild ponies roaming around?

Honestly, the sheer volume of research on infant feeding is  astronomical . I swear, every study contradicts the last. One minute exclusive breastfeeding is the gold standard, the next it's formula supplementation for optimal growth. It's exhausting! Tell me about it! Before Leo arrived, I thought, "Breast or bottle, what's the big deal?". Now I get it. It’s a minefield of opinions. My mum keeps sending me articles about the benefits of almond milk in formula – almond milk! Almond milk? Seriously? Where’s she getting that from? That sounds like something you find on a conspiracy website, not in a reputable medical journal. I know! I showed it to Mark – he just looked at me like I’d sprouted a second head. He’s very pro-breastfeeding, bless him, but even  he  thinks it’s a bit much. It's just...it feels like everyone has an opinion. My nan keeps asking if I’m “trying hard enough” to breastfeed. Hard enough? It’s not a test, Nan! Oh, the pressure! My Aunt Carol keeps hinting that I should start solids early, apparently, it’s ‘essential for brain development’. Again, the research is conflicting. Some say wait until six months, some say four, some say… well, it’s ridiculous. Exactly! And it’s not just the medical stuff. It’s the judgement. You feel like if you even  consider  formula, people look at you like you've failed. "Oh, you're giving him formula? Are you sure he’s getting enough nutrients?" Like breastfeeding is the  only  way to do things right. It's so ingrained, isn't it? The societal pressure is immense. I had a colleague last week, she was practically in tears because she was struggling to latch and felt guilty for needing to supplement. I tried to reassure her, and point her towards some supportive resources, but you know it’s hard to shake that feeling. It really is. Leo’s been… a character, feeding-wise. He latches on for five minutes, falls asleep, and then squawks for more immediately after. It’s draining. And I feel like I’m constantly doubting myself. Am I producing enough? Is he getting enough? Is he happy? It sounds exhausting. Have you spoken to a lactation consultant? They can be surprisingly helpful. I've been liaising with one for a project we're doing on infant feeding support networks, and they’ve got some brilliant tips.

Oh, that's a right pain, isn’t it? They always say these things are going to make things easier, don't they? Never do. Digital systems... pah! Remember when they tried to bring in that electronic patient record thing back in the early 2000s? Absolute shambles that was. Tell me about it. I’ve been hearing similar complaints from the medical records team. Mark – that’s one of the clerks – was absolutely fuming yesterday. Said he was looking at three times the paperwork he was last week. This new Head of IT, Brenda, seems to think technology is the answer to everything. Doesn't understand the reality on the ground. Sounds stressful, Auntie Sarah. You need a holiday. Seriously. Anything exciting planned this weekend? I was thinking of heading down to Brighton, maybe. Bit of sun, bit of shopping… Brighton sounds lovely, darling. Though I'm quite happy puttering about the garden, to be honest. The roses are finally starting to bloom properly, and I’ve managed to get those weeds under control. Though the squirrels are still getting at the bird feeder. Absolute menace, those squirrels! They are, aren't they? Little furry bandits. I saw one the other day trying to bury a nut in the flower pot. Right next to my prize-winning petunias! Honestly, sometimes I think they do it on purpose. Speaking of the garden, I was thinking we could finally tackle that overgrown patch by the shed. It’s been on the list for ages. Need to get round to clearing it and maybe put in a little patio area. Somewhere to sit and have a glass of wine in the sun. A patio! That sounds amazing! Imagine, summertime drinks in the garden... I'm in! I can even help with the clearing, I don’t mind getting my hands dirty. I'll definitely lend a hand too. Though my back isn’t what it used to be. We’ll have to be sensible about it. Maybe break it down into smaller chunks over a couple of weekends. Sensible is key. And we need to make sure Geoff gets his act together and helps out too. He promised he'd prune the lavender weeks ago, and it’s practically touching the roof! Geoff... yes. He’s got a lot on with the new project at work, apparently. Big presentation next week. Nervous as a kitten, he is.

Speaker_1 finished, dramatically waving her hands. Speaker_2 : "Honestly! What’s the point then? It’s not Christmas if you can't stick sparkly things everywhere. My mum says she’s using dried orange slices this year instead. Sounds...beige.” Chloe: "Beige is the perfect word for it. Beige Christmas decorations. Ugh. I spent, like, twenty minutes trying to work out how many carrots Mr. Henderson needs to feed his rabbits. It was ridiculous." Chloe: “Rabbits! Seriously? That’s what he pulls out for a maths test? Speaking of band names, did you hear Ed Sheeran's playing at the Corn Exchange in December? My mum managed to get tickets!" Maisie: "No way! That’s amazing! I’m so jealous. Are you going with your family?" Chloe: “Yeah, my whole family.

Honestly, Arthur, you’ve gone quite mad with that rat. It's blinking! And it’s wearing a tiny waistcoat! Where did you even  find  such a thing? Found it at a car boot sale down in Wymondham, love. Just a quid it was! Needed a bit of tidying up, mind you. Sewed on a new button, gave it a good dusting. Bit of character it has, don’t you think? Makes a good listener, actually. Doesn't interrupt. A blinking rat in a waistcoat, Arthur? You haven’t lost the plot entirely, have you? Though, I must confess, it  is  rather charming in a peculiar sort of way. What's all the commotion then? I could hear you both from the hall. Arthur's showing off his new acquisition. And I was just saying, it's ridiculous! But, Matthew, would you like a cup of tea? I’ve put out biscuits. Shortbread, your favourite. Thank you, Margaret. Always a pleasure. So, the rat. Is this a new hobby? Puppet shows for the neighbourhood? Not puppet shows, no. More for… companionship, really. Gets a bit lonely, you know. Even with you two ’round, sometimes. And it’s good for my hands. Keeps 'em busy. I’ve been trying to get the hang of the handbells again, you see. Got the old ones out the loft. Oh, the handbells! That's lovely, Arthur. You used to ring them so beautifully at St. George’s. Remember, Matthew? He could play 'Greensleeves' without a mistake. I do indeed. Quite impressive, Arthur. Though, I must say, I haven’t heard them in years. Are you planning a performance? Thinking about it. Just a bit of practice for myself, mostly. Fingers aren't as nimble as they used to be, mind. And my eyes… not what they were. I need to get them checked, really. Been putting it off. Don’t you dare, Arthur! You know that new optician, 'Bright Eyes,' opened up on the High Street. Heard they're very good. We should book you an appointment. I'll do it tomorrow. You can't be fumbling about with those tiny bells and fiddling with that rat if you can't see properly. Margaret's right. Vision is crucial, especially at your age. And the rat needs a competent puppeteer, wouldn’t want it falling off the sofa. Alright, alright. You’re both nagging me.

...and then Professor Davies just went on about semiotics for  another  hour. Honestly, Mum, I’m starting to think he just enjoys hearing himself talk. I need a serious dose of anything  but  semiotics today. What are we doing after this? You said we were going to wander down towards the waterfront? Aye, lass. That’s the plan. A bit of a potter about, see what we can see. Remember when this place was just a dusty old builders' merchant? Not a fancy café with Venetian names and Italian pastries. God, I do! I used to come here with Dad when I was little, buying bits of wood for his DIY projects. It smelled of sawdust and cement, not vanilla and coffee. It’s mental how much Bolton’s changed, innit? Even this café… “Café Venice.” Bit much, isn’t it? They were trying to be clever, our Brenda and Tony, the owners. They’ve done a decent job, though, haven’t they? More interesting than a builders’ yard! Reckon they got inspired by one of those trips to Italy? My Margaret down the street went to Venice a few years back, came back raving about the gelato. Gelato sounds amazing. I’m starving, actually. Fancy sharing a pastry when we’re done here? That chocolate one looks lethal. Ooh, aye, that does look good. Although, I’m still craving a proper Eccles cake. They don’t do those here, do they? Shame. Venice doesn't exactly scream 'Lancashire delicacy'. Remember Mrs. Hargreaves’ Eccles cakes back in the day? Better than anything you could buy. Mrs. Hargreaves! You’re making me feel old! My nan used to get them from her every Saturday. Honestly, Mum, those were the days. So, waterfront and pastry? Are we just meandering or do you have a specific route in mind? I promised Liam I’d call him later to tell him where I am. Let’s just see where our feet take us, love. That’s the joy of it, isn’t it? We can head down Chorley New Road towards Smithy Square, and then loop around towards the river. There’s a little antique shop just off Victoria Square that you might like. They always have lovely bits and bobs. And they've got that little walkway along the Irwell now - much better than it used to be, all overgrown with weeds. They've cleaned it up proper.

…and then he just  looked  at me! Like, genuinely, no words. Just this bewildered expression. I swear, the waiter nearly dropped a plate. Honestly, Mark is something else. Oh my god, you’re joking! Mark really is a walking disaster. Remember that time he tried to order chips in Italian at that restaurant in Rome? Don't remind me! He was so convinced he was pronouncing it correctly. It was a whole ordeal. Anyway, enough about him. How's the project going? You seemed stressed last time we spoke. It’s…intense. We're launching a new training program for the entire department. So much moving of parts, so many egos to manage. It’s exhausting, to be honest. I'm fuelled entirely by peri-peri chicken and sheer willpower at this point. Hence, Nandos! What about you? Bupa must be busy with the new campaign, right? Yeah, it is. The healthy eating campaign is actually going really well, which is a nice change. We’re finally seeing some engagement on social media. It's mostly just Instagram-able salads, though. Want to hear a funny anecdote from yesterday? Do! I desperately need a distraction from spreadsheets. Okay, so we had a photoshoot for the campaign - all bright and airy and full of kale. And this one influencer, she insisted on having a personal blender on set to ‘perfect’ her smoothie between shots. Like, a full-sized blender. It was a ridiculously oversized thing! Then, halfway through, she spilled green smoothie  everywhere . All over the set, on the camera crew… it was chaos. No! Seriously? That’s brilliant! Influencers, honestly. I’m surprised they let her bring a blender in. They didn’t, initially! She just…showed up with it. Apparently, she “needs it for her brand.” It was peak influencer behaviour. Anyway, it brought everyone together, surprisingly. Even the normally stern head of marketing was laughing. See, there’s always a silver lining! Speaking of bringing people together, are you still thinking about that holiday to Greece in September? Absolutely! I’ve been looking at flights. Santorini looks incredible, but Mykonos seems a bit…overrated, maybe? Have you looked at anything? Briefly. Santorini is definitely on the list. I think we should also consider Naxos. It's a bit more relaxed, supposed to have really stunning beaches, and it's not as overrun with tourists. Plus, the food is supposed to be amazing.

…and honestly, the new landlord is just dreadful. They haven't fixed a single thing since they took over. The leaking gutter is still dripping all over Mrs. Peterson’s prize-winning roses. It’s absolutely appalling. Landlords, eh? Always a story there, aren't they? Reminds me of trying to buy a little plot of land in the Dordogne back in the 80s. Absolute nightmare. Bureaucrats breathing down your neck at every turn. You needed a different form for the soil analysis than you did for the water rights. Utter chaos. Sounds familiar! Though thankfully, my current property woes are slightly less…continental. Have you heard about Chichester Cathedral? The spire collapsed! Good heavens! No, I hadn't. Dreadful news. Extraordinary piece of engineering, that spire. They say it was down to a combination of factors, weather, age… and apparently, the architect, a chap called Porden, used a rather innovative, if ultimately flawed, method of construction. I read something about him. Some sort of spiral staircase built  inside  the spire, to help with stability. Ambitious, but evidently not enough. They’re having an open day and a photo exhibition focusing on its history and the restoration work, apparently. I was thinking of going. Excellent! There’s always something to learn from those sorts of events. Reminds me of when I was researching Philip II of Spain, you know, Philip of Spain and Mary Tudor? I spent a week in the Spanish archives in Simancas. Trust me, the level of detail they kept… astonishing. And completely overwhelming. Goodness! That’s incredible. What were you researching at the time? The influence of Tudor policies on Spanish maritime expansion. Rather dry, I admit, but the documents! You could feel the weight of history. And the sheer inefficiency! Mountains of paperwork for everything. It makes you appreciate the digital age, doesn’t it? Though…perhaps not entirely. Quite. Speaking of archives, I'm helping Michael with his book about the anarchist movement in Paris at the turn of the century. He’s been spending a  lot  of time at the British Library. He’s absolutely fascinated by the sheer number of pamphlets and posters they have. Anarchists, eh? Quite lively characters. We had a French visitor here a few years back, a rather ardent supporter of his ideals. He kept going on about the superiority of French property laws – surprisingly complex, you know, with all the ancient feudal rights still influencing things today.

Ugh, this is… okay. Not amazing. Auntie Mei's cooking is definitely a step up. Don't be such a drama queen, Liam. It's perfectly decent. Way better than the canteen slop we get at school, anyway. And Auntie Mei's busy, she's got, like, fifteen other people to feed tonight. Seriously, Liam. You’re always moaning about the food. Remember last Christmas when you said Grandma’s roast potatoes were “structurally unsound?” They  were ! They kept collapsing! Anyway, it’s just... I’m used to a certain standard. My mum’s a fantastic cook. My mum tries, bless her. Last week she attempted a lasagne. It tasted vaguely of cardboard and despair. I think we ordered pizza instead. Classic. You know, I was thinking about that horrifying Maths test we had yesterday. Mr. Davies is actively trying to break us, I swear. Tell me about it! I spent the whole lesson staring at question five, which was some ridiculous equation involving logarithms and… something about a Ferris wheel. Ferris wheels? Seriously? It was designed to be difficult, apparently. He said it was "diagnostic." Diagnostic of what? Our impending mental breakdowns? I think I saw Ethan crying in the corridor afterwards. Poor guy. He’s struggling with that whole advanced algebra thing. Ethan’s always been a bit of a mess, hasn't he? Remember that time he wore two different shoes to PE? Oh my god! The blue flip-flop and the bright red trainer! He just shrugged and said, "It adds character." He’s got a point though, doesn't he? Like, who cares about matching shoes when you’re facing a looming A-Level exam? Speaking of A-Levels... Have you guys figured out what you're actually doing? I’m still completely lost. I’m thinking History and English Lit, but I’m not sure. I’m sticking with Computer Science and Maths. Probably Physics too, I guess. My dad's pushing it on me. My mum wants me to do Law. Apparently, I have a “gift for arguing.” Which is just a polite way of saying I’m argumentative. I'm leaning towards Drama and Media Studies. Always been obsessed with film, you know? Plus, my drama teacher says I have "potential." Which is a slightly better compliment than "argumentative." Potential for what? Dramatic flailing? Shut up, Wembley! It’s potential for acting, obviously!

Pressure and deadlines and… grading. I’d rather just, you know, write about stuff. And watch YouTubers. Speaking of, have you seen that new one, ‘CosmicKate’? CosmicKate? Is she that astrophysics one? The one who explains black holes in, like, five minutes? She’s amazing! I’ve been following her for ages. I think she and Tom Holland would be the perfect couple. They're so cute together. Totally! Actually, thinking about jobs… maybe I should be an actor. Or a film director. No, wait… that requires  more  filming and editing. Ugh. What about something completely different? Remember how you used to play the clarinet? You were really good. Oh, blimey. That was ages ago. Mr. Henderson used to be on at me about ‘perfect duty’ and ‘finger placement’ and… it was stressful. Not exactly the pathway to a glamorous career, is it? Unless I become a professional busker, I suppose. You could teach! Like, clarinet lessons. Or music history. You're surprisingly knowledgeable, especially when you’re not moaning about Macbeth. Fair point. I do like music. But teaching… that means dealing with  children . Tiny, energetic, clarinet-smashing children.

A badger, eh? Blimey. We 'ad a fox gettin' into the bins a while back. Right nuisance, that were. Clever things, foxes, mind you. Always scramblin' about. Used to watch 'em from the window as a lad, down on the marshes. Aye, foxes are crafty. Badgers though… they’re somethin' else. Thickset little chaps, they are. Remember old Mr. Grimes down the road? Swore a badger dug a sett right under 'is shed. Said it was makin' the whole thing sink! Oh, that's a vivid image, Arthur! Grimes always did exaggerate. Though I must say, the wildlife round here  has  been more noticeable lately. I saw a pair of kingfishers down by the river the other day. Gorgeous! Such brilliant blue. It's the urban sprawl, isn’t it? Less space for them to go, so they're more likely to venture into gardens. I was reading an article about how the badger population in Norfolk has actually increased in recent years. It’s quite remarkable, really. Increased, you say? Well, I never! Used to be a bit of a rarity, seein' one. Back in the fifties… different world altogether. Everythin' was slower, quieter. Less traffic, less… commotion. Commotion! That’s the word for it. This new motorway they’re buildin’… monstrous thing. Ruinin’ the countryside, it is. Remember when we used to drive down to Great Yarmouth? Proper Sunday drive that was. Now it’s just a queue of lorries. Oh, Great Yarmouth! Brings back memories. That arcade with the penny pushers… spent a fortune there as a girl. And the smell of the sea! It was just… bliss. It  is  a shame about the motorway. I’m trying to use my car less, actually. Thinking about getting an electric bike. Much more environmentally friendly. Have you looked into those, Dad? Electric… bike? Sounds a bit… faffy, doesn't it? All that charging and batteries. Give me a good old petrol engine any day. My old Morris Minor – now  that  was a car. Reliable as anything. Though it did leak oil like a sieve, come to think of it. Oh, I remember your Morris Minor, Bernard! Always parked outside the Queen’s Head, dripping oil all over the pavement! Classic, that were. Never understand why you got rid of it, you didn’t. Needed the money, didn't I? Times were tough. Still… miss it, I do. Proper driver's car, it was.

Honestly, Arthur, look at this! I’m drowning in jumpers. Absolute drowning. I swear, every season I buy another one, thinking, ‘Right, sensible Sheila, you need something warm.’ And then…this. A mountain. Well, can’t be a bad thing, can it, Sheila? A warm lady’s a happy lady. Though I always say, too many jumpers and you’ll be lookin’ like a particularly fluffy sheep. You're terrible, Arthur! Honestly. Sheila, you could open a second-hand shop with that lot. I’m trying to clear out my kids' old school uniforms, too. Bit of a clear-out frenzy across the board, it seems. Remember when Marcus was at King Edward's? The uniform shirts! They just multiplied, didn't they? Never understood it. King Edward’s! Oh, good heavens. Fancy school, that. Did they really make them wear those ties with the little heraldic birds? Dreadful things. My little ones went to the village primary, much simpler. Though, between you and me, I always thought the headmistress had a thing for floral skirts. She had a new one practically every day. Floral skirts... reminds me of me mum. Always had a flower pattern somethin’ or other. Said it cheered people up. Didn’t always do it, mind. She could be sharp as tacks when she wanted to be. My daughter, Emily, she’s all about Twitter, you know. Absolutely glued to it. Apparently, there’s a real debate raging about the importance of Latin in schools these days. Can you imagine? People arguing about Latin! Tweeter? Is that like a little bird? Honestly, I don't understand these newfangled things. I used to get all my news from the Eastern Daily Press. Now, everyone's shouting at each other online. More like a flock of geese, innit? Squawkin’ and fightin’ over crumbs. I’ve seen a few posts about that health service, though. Not a pretty sight. Queue’s longer than a bleedin’ football pitch. Don’t even get me started on the NHS. I had to fight for weeks to get my mum an appointment with a rheumatologist. Weeks! And she’s in agony. Keeps saying she’d be better off going private, but she won’t. Thinks it’s a weakness. Well, you can't blame her. My sister’s got such bad arthritis, she can barely open a jar. The doctor just keeps telling her to take paracetamol.

"Around the World in Eighty Dishes? That sounds…ambitious, love. Seriously ambitious. Especially given we’ve got, what, three weeks until your cousin’s stag?" He leaned back on the well-worn sofa, nursing a mug of lukewarm tea. "Honestly, I think you're biting off more than you can chew. Remember the Great Yorkshire Pudding Incident of '18?" "Oh, shut up, Jamie! That was  one  slightly collapsed Yorkshire pudding! And it was Auntie Maureen’s fault, not mine. She put the oven on too high. This is different. This is about showcasing my, and our, culinary prowess. Besides, it's  Come Dine With Me , not a Michelin-starred restaurant." She wiped her muddy hands on a tea towel. "Right, next question: stag do theme. Any brilliant ideas?" "Well, you know Liam’s obsessed with that awful sitcom, 'Silicon Valley'." Jamie grinned. "Could do a tech-themed thing? Lots of awkward presentations, questionable networking…?" "Liam would  hate  that, he finds it excruciating. He’s been moaning about it for years! No, no, needs to be something… energetic. Something a bit ridiculous. Remember that time at university, when we all went to the medieval fair and ended up jousting with pool noodles?" "Vaguely. And I mostly remember ending up with a concussion. Please don't suggest jousting, Anya. His poor mum." "Alright, alright. Just thinking aloud. What about a ski trip? Somewhere cheap, like Bulgaria or somewhere?" "Bulgaria in…February? With this weather?" He gestured towards the snowy window. "You'll be needing to build an ark, not book flights. It’ll be like this for weeks yet. I'm bringing in the snow shovel again tomorrow, I reckon." "True. Snow’s a bugger, isn’t it? Still pretty though. Makes me wish we'd planned a proper winter holiday instead of constantly failing to book anything." She sighed, sinking onto the sofa next to him. "Remember that time we kept meaning to go to Iceland to see the Northern Lights? We never got around to it." "We were too busy arguing about whether to get the extended warranty on the campervan." He chuckled. "Priorities, eh?" "Aye, priorities. Right, holiday. Rule one: somewhere warm. Rule two: somewhere with a lot of sunshine. Rule three: somewhere we can actually afford considering the stag do and the Come Dine With Me extravaganza." "Sounds reasonable. Restricting it to somewhere warm immediately cuts out most of Europe.

"Oh, bless him. That's classic toddler behaviour, isn't it? Remember when my Sarah tried to paint the dog with yogurt? The poor thing looked like a fluffy, vanilla monster." "Aye, kids will be kids. Me mum used to say it were all learning, you see. Messing about, exploring. Though I’m not sure the dog appreciated it much.” He pauses, looking at the roast potatoes on his plate. "These are lovely, though, Annie. Proper golden like." "Thanks, Dad. I tried to follow your mum’s recipe, the one you always used to talk about. Did she have a secret ingredient, do you think?” “Well, she didn’t  say  it was a secret, now did she. But she always used a bit of goose fat. Just a knob, mind you. Enough to give 'em a bit of crispness. Most folks don’t bother these days, use oil instead.” "Goose fat, huh? Interesting. I’ve always used olive oil. Makes a big difference, does it?" "It does! I remember trying it once, because Arthur insisted, and they were magnificent. So much better than anything I’d done before. Very authentic.” "I was a bit nervous trying it. I thought it might make them…gamey?” “Not at all, luv. Just adds a bit o’ richness, see? It's a proper old-fashioned thing, though. My mum, she got hers from Farmer Giles down the road. Used to be a proper farm, he did, not like these places now. All concrete and sheds.” He sighs, a hint of melancholy in his voice. "It's tough, isn't it? Seeing those changes. It’s the same with so many places. Progress comes at a cost sometimes." "Don't I know it. When I was a girl, Harrow was full of orchards. You could pick your own apples in the autumn. Now it’s all high-rise flats and busy roads.” “We were just talking about the changing landscape in my environmental politics lecture today. Actually, it’s quite alarming the rate at which we're losing biodiversity in agricultural areas.” "Bio...what now? Sounds a bit fancy, that. All I know is, don’t seem to be many bumblebees about these days. Used to be they were buzzing all over the roses, you see. Now...a few, maybe. Not like they were." "That's a good indicator, Dad. Fewer pollinators means less food, eventually.

Honestly, Mum, this roast is incredible. You’ve really outdone yourself. Better than last Christmas, I reckon. Agreed! Though, last Christmas' Yorkshire puddings were a bit more…voluminous. These are lovely though, all fluffy and golden. You know, I tried to make them once. Disaster. They looked like deflated pancakes. Aye, Yorkshire puddings are a tricky beast. Too much fat, not enough heat, and you’re in trouble. It’s an art, lad, a proper art. Your dad was quite partial to a good Yorkshire, you know. Used to say they were the perfect vehicle for gravy. She's right, you know. Elsie's Yorkshire puddings were legendary. Used to soak up the gravy like a sponge. Waste not, want not, that was my mum's motto. Gravy… good gravy...used to be proper gravy back in me day. Not this stuff with cornflour. Real gravy, from the dripping. Smoked ham bones too. Nowt like it. Grandpa, you always say that about everything! It's always “back in your day” this and “nowt like it” that. But I do get your point, Mum’s gravy is definitely special. She uses a bit of red wine, apparently. Well, a girl’s got to have her secrets. It's a recipe passed down from my own mother, originally. And a splash of Worcestershire sauce, of course. Don't tell anyone! I won't breathe a word! So, Dad, how's the house renovation going? Last time you were talking about the leaky roof and the dodgy wiring. It's... slow. Very slow. Found damp in the downstairs bathroom, which wasn't on the original list. The builder keeps saying things are "more complicated than they seem." Which usually means more expensive. Oh, that's awful! That always happens, doesn’t it? It's like opening Pandora’s Box. Remember when I was renovating my flat? I thought I'd just replace the kitchen tiles... ended up having to rewire the entire apartment! Aye, it's a right palaver is house renovation. Should've left it alone, honestly. Your father's got a knack for finding trouble, that one. Hey! I'm just trying to make the place liveable again. It’s nearly fifty years old, after all. It’s got character! Character... draughts, more like. Used to be a good sturdy house. Built to last. Houses don't build 'em like they used to.

…and honestly, the feedback from the undergrads after that flipped classroom pilot was incredible. They said they actually  engaged  more with the material because they’d done the initial reading and problem-solving beforehand. Less time lecturing, more time genuinely discussing and challenging the concepts. Right. That’s the core of it, isn’t it? Moving from broadcasting to facilitating. It's the same principle I apply to SparkFlow. You can tell people  what  to do, but if you don't create the environment where they  want  to figure it out themselves, it’s just… noise. Remember that disastrous marketing campaign we launched in Q2? We told people to download the app. Total flop. Then we changed tactics - focused on showcasing real users getting results – suddenly, traction. Exactly! It’s like, authority doesn’t command respect anymore, at least not from this generation. It’s about credibility and transparency. What are you thinking for SparkFlow, then? Still pushing the AI-powered project management? Yeah, but refining the approach. We’re getting bogged down in the “AI is magic” narrative. It’s not about magic, it’s about efficiency and freeing up people’s creative energy. We need to highlight the tangible benefits - reduced burnout, better prioritisation, increased collaboration. I was watching this viral video last night, remember those 'oddly satisfying' things? Oh, the one with the perfectly stacked boxes? Yes! Exactly! It was a short animation of software automatically sorting tasks based on priority and deadlines, all visually engaging. The comments were insane - people saying they felt instantly more organised! It’s a simple concept, but the execution was brilliant. We need that level of accessible explanation. Forget technical jargon. Brilliant. You’re thinking about using that visual storytelling approach for SparkFlow’s onboarding? Rather than listing features? Precisely. And I was also pondering something related to university education, actually. Seeing how the flipped classroom worked for you got my gears turning. What if we created… a plugin for SparkFlow? Targeted specifically for university students. It could integrate with their VLE - Moodle, Blackboard, whatever. Automatically generate a task list based on the week’s readings and assignments, prioritize based on deadlines, and offer AI-suggested study groups based on shared interests and learning styles. That's...that's incredibly clever, actually. It tackles procrastination  and  isolation, both huge issues for university students. But the integration… that’s a chunky piece of development, isn't it?

Honestly, I’m knackered. This chicken curry needs  serious  attention. How was your day, Liv? You look like you’ve seen a ghost. Tell me about it. Mr. Henderson decided to change the entire scope of the Carter project  again . Mid-deadline. It’s just… infuriating. I swear, he enjoys watching us burn the midnight oil. Did you manage to get those extra shifts covered? Yep, got Sarah to do Saturday. She owes me one after I covered for her last month. But weekends are precious. We  need  a chilled one after this week. I’m thinking film night on Sunday, loads of snacks, total avoidance of anything remotely stressful. Sounds heavenly. I'm putting that in my diary now. Speaking of weekends, have you heard about that Halloween party down at The Black Swan? Apparently, it’s themed – Cornish folklore. Cornish? Really? That’s a bit specific, isn't it? Is it just, like, pasties and tin mines? Apparently, they’re going all out! Giant pasty sculptures, dramatic readings of Cornish legends… the whole shebang. I already RSVP’d. Fancy going? We could dress up as… I don’t know, Piskies? Piskies! Oh, Liv, you’re brilliant! I'm in. I'll probably go as a drowned sailor. Something tragic and vaguely Cornish. Though, I really need to review the Cornish folklore, don't want to accidentally insult their ancient spirits. Don’t worry, as long as you don’t start chanting ancient curses, we’ll be fine. Seriously though, work is completely draining me. I was thinking... remember we talked about that online project management course? Should I finally sign up? Absolutely. It would look amazing on your CV, and honestly, anything that lets you cope with Henderson's antics and keep the project on track would be a win. Five years from now, imagine! You’ll be running entire departments, delegating tasks, feeling like the boss! Bossy Liv, huh? That’s the dream. It's just... five years feels like a  long  time. Where do you see yourself in five years? Still battling mental health crises? Actually, I've been thinking a lot about it. I really love the nursing, don't get me wrong. But I’m also increasingly interested in specialised trauma care. Maybe a master's in that area? Possibly even working with veterans. There's a real need. That’s…amazing, actually. Seriously impressive. You’d be brilliant at that.

Honestly, Mum, I’m just drained. This project at work has been relentless. Deadlines are shifting every five minutes, and everyone's breathing down my neck. Oh, love. That sounds properly stressful. Production Controller, you say? Sounds important, though. You always were clever, weren't you? Even at school. Remember that time you built that amazing model of the solar system? That was forever ago. And it was mostly cardboard and tin foil, Mum. Not exactly NASA material. It's less about cleverness and more about firefighting these days. And trying to keep all the departments from ripping each other's throats out. Right you are, right you are. Teams, eh? Always a bit of a bother. I had a right one at the Women's Institute, trying to get everyone to agree on the bake sale theme. Ended up with three different themes and a whole load of upset people. Sounds chaotic. At least bake sales don’t affect quarterly profits. This contract is huge, Mum. If it goes south, it could be a real problem for the company. Now, now, don’t you get yourself all worried about that. They paid you a decent salary, didn’t they? You’re doing a good job. Just remember to breathe, love. Take a proper lunch break, even if it’s just ten minutes. I try. But it feels selfish when there's so much to do. Plus, Liam keeps saying I'm glued to my phone. He's got a point, I suppose. Liam, is it? Still going strong then? Good lad. Don’t let him walk all over you, though. You've got your own ambitions, haven’t you? Remember that postgraduate degree? You worked hard for that. I do. And I like my job, most of the time. It's just… the pressure. It’s not like my Gran used to tell me when I was little. "A problem shared is a problem halved," she’d say. Your Gran was a wise woman. Still is, bless her. We should pop round and see her next week. It's been ages. How’s her hip been? Actually, that's a really good idea. She’s been complaining about it again. I keep meaning to book a doctor's appointment for her, but you know how it is... things get in the way. Absolutely. It’s always something, isn’t it?

Honestly, this rain is  dreadful.  Reminds me of a Doncaster November, it does. At least the coffee’s decent. Oh, stop being so dramatic, Chloe. It’s just a bit of drizzle. And it’s France! We’re supposed to be soaking up the culture, not complaining about the weather. Did you see that article about the French cycling team? They’re looking strong for the Tour this year. Cycling? I’m more of a football lass, love. Proper football, not that fancy stuff. United’s been playing alright this season, though. Bit patchy, mind, but better than last year. What about you? Still obsessed with cricket? You know me. Always. They showed a decent match yesterday – England actually put up a fight. Speaking of fights, how’s your thesis going? You sounded stressed last time we spoke. Don’t even  start  about the thesis. It's arseovertip. Honestly, trying to translate 18th-century scientific texts… it's a nightmare! The language is so flowery and full of metaphors. It’s like they were trying to win a poetry competition, not explain gravity! I'm stuck on this one sentence; it keeps saying ‘the celestial sphere doth impart its influence…’ and I'm drawing a blank. Oh, that does sound difficult. "Doth impart?" Seriously? Right, let me have a go. Thinking aloud… 'doth impart' would be ‘bestows’ or ‘communicates,’ wouldn’t it? So, roughly, “the celestial sphere communicates its influence…” Is that close? We could try looking up phrases common at the time - a French equivalent to a thesaurus might help. Bestows! That’s brilliant, actually! You’re a genius, you are. I've been trying to brute-force it and just coming up with gibberish. See, that’s why I need you. My brain just goes fuzzy with these old words. It’s making me wish I'd studied something easier, like… underwater basket weaving. Underwater basket weaving? Chloe, you'd sink! Remember how you struggled with French in GCSE? You’d be lost without me to translate the menus! And, seriously, you’re doing amazing work. Actually contributing to our understanding of science history. That’s pretty cool. Easy for you to say, you’re studying Archaeology! Digging up old pots is a lot more straightforward than trying to decipher riddles written by blokes in wigs. Seriously, what  is  the scientific method even like back then? It feels like a lot of guesswork and praying for favourable results.

Honestly, I nearly jumped out of my skin this morning. Big one. Right there, on the curtain. Black, shiny…legs everywhere. Oh, spiders again, Diane? You'd think living in a house like you do, with all the cleaning you must do, they'd have nowhere to hide. That's what you'd think! But they breed like…well, like mice, don't they? And this wasn’t just any spider, Sarah. This was a Daddy Long Legs, the really scary sort. I felt like I needed a ladder to reach it. A ladder? Goodness! You are dramatic. They’re harmless, you know. Daddy Long Legs are practically vegetarian. Harmless to you maybe! I’ve read stories, Sarah. Stories about them being the most poisonous spiders in the world, just because they don't have fangs big enough to bite humans properly! It’s enough to give you the jitters. I had to get a newspaper and… well, you know. Don’t tell me. I really don't want to know. I had a little spider incident myself last week. Nothing nearly as dramatic, thankfully. Just a tiny one, practically invisible, spinning a web between the picture frames in the living room. I had to gently relocate it to the garden. Felt rather bad, actually. Garden’s full of them, I bet. They love damp places. Speaking of things in the house, I had a right fright with a mouse last Tuesday. Heard scratching in the walls in the kitchen, kept it up for hours. Thought I was going mad. Oh dear! Mice are dreadful. Did you get it caught? Nearly! I set a trap, and it ran straight over it. Clever little thing. I spent the rest of the afternoon chasing it around with a broom, like something out of a cartoon. Ended up cornering it in the bathroom and…well…let’s just say the house smelled rather unpleasant for a while. I can imagine. We’ve been lucky, haven't we? No mice in years. Just the occasional spider, as we’ve discussed. Though I did have a problem with pigeons nesting on the balcony last spring. That was a nightmare! Pigeons? Now that’s a nuisance. Flying in and out, leaving…well, you know. I had a robin in the shed once. Cute at first, but then it started bringing nesting materials everywhere - bits of string, paper, even my good gardening gloves!

“It's wonderful you're taking an interest, dear. Family history's a rabbit hole, isn't it? Once you start pulling, you never know what you’ll find! I’ve spent years tracing mine, thanks to having nothing much else to do in retirement. Bristol’s got a complicated history, you know. Lots of comings and goings." “Bristol, yes! My understanding is your grandmother was born there?” Sarah asked, taking a sip of the tea ANON had offered earlier. "My mum often mentioned a great-aunt who’d married a sailor and disappeared to Bristol. Never heard from again. Tragic, really.” “Ah, yes, Mary. Your great-great-aunt. She eloped with a ship’s cook, as far as I can tell. Scandalous at the time! My grandfather, her brother, never forgave her. Said she shamed the family. He was a strict man, my grandfather, Thomas. Worked in the docks. Tough life. He always regretted not going to America like so many others were at the time. Said it was a chance for a better life, but his loyalty kept him anchored to Bristol." “That’s fascinating. It’s amazing how those small family dramas ripple down through generations. It’s something I try to explain to my students when we study history – it’s not just kings and queens, it’s the everyday lives of ordinary people, and the decisions they make.” “Exactly! And those decisions affect everyone who comes after. You’re a teacher, you said? What do you teach?” “English Literature. Mostly Shakespeare and Victorian novels. It’s rewarding, although the marking… goodness, the marking!” Sarah chuckled. "It’s a constant battle to get them enthusiastic about Chaucer. I try to make it relatable, you know, find the humour, but some of them just glaze over." “Chaucer… I remember struggling with him myself! We didn’t have the resources they do now. Just a dusty textbook and a very severe headmaster. Education’s changed drastically. Though, I suspect, some things remain the same. The struggles of young people trying to find their place in the world.” "Absolutely. It's comforting, in a way, to know some things don't change. It  is  comforting, despite…everything.” She paused, the lightness fading slightly from her voice. “Speaking of changes, I’ve been trying to understand Mum’s illness better. It was so swift, wasn’t it? The initial diagnosis…it was like a punch to the gut.”

Honestly, it looks like a giant, colourful jellyfish drifting across. Do you think they ever get nervous up there, those balloon pilots? Nervous? Probably. But mostly exhilarated, I imagine. It’s a stunning view, isn't it? Takes a special kind of bravery, or perhaps just a very calm nature, to be suspended like that. Remember Uncle Barry’s disastrous attempt? Don't remind me. The sheep were  terrified . He swore the wind was actively trying to sabotage him. Landing in Farmer Giles' prize-winning pumpkin patch wasn’t exactly the graceful descent he’d envisioned. Graceful isn’t a word I’d associate with Barry. His attempt to charm Farmer Giles with a hastily-bought bunch of wilting daffodils didn’t help either. Though, I did feel a bit sorry for the sheep, they were genuinely traumatised. Poor things. Well, they recovered. Thankfully. Speaking of animals, have you seen any hares today? I was hoping for a glimpse. Not yet. Though, I did spot a kestrel hovering over that field earlier. Magnificent bird. Makes you realise how much wildlife we’re surrounded by, even right here in Norfolk. It's a welcome change from the grey concrete of the university, isn't it? Absolutely. It’s… grounding. All those deadlines and grant applications… sometimes it feels like I’m orbiting a planet of paperwork. By the way, did you manage to sort out the camping gear? We need to get that tent sorted before next month. Nearly. The tent is fine. It’s the sleeping bags I’m slightly dubious about. They’re a bit… well, let’s just say they’ve seen better days. I was thinking we might need to invest in a couple of new ones. Proper, warm ones. Considering how chilly it gets at night. Right. Another expense. We really need to be sensible with the budget. The conference in Edinburgh is going to hit us hard. Those flights alone... I know, I know. I’ve started looking at cheaper alternatives. Possibly the train? It would be slower, but… You know, looking at those power lines, it’s just… bizarre, isn’t it? How we’ve just integrated these massive structures into the landscape. They're everywhere. It is. A testament to our reliance on electricity, I suppose. Though, aesthetically, they're not exactly a selling point for the Norfolk countryside. You'd think with all the government subsidies for renewable energy, they'd bury them underground.

Right then, that was a proper set! Didn't think I’d be chasing after a ball at my age, mind you. Lovely day for it, though. Bit nippy, but lovely. It was! Definitely a good work-out. Though I'm feeling it in my legs already. You’re always so energetic, David. How do you do it? All those gyms to manage can’t be easy. It’s a lot, lass, it is. You wouldn’t believe the amount of drama you get in gyms. People arguing over treadmills, someone leaving a protein shaker in the cold storage...it's endless! But, you know, I enjoy it. Keeping people active, seeing them progress. What about you, Sarah? Still enjoying teaching languages? I am, mostly. It’s rewarding when you see a student finally grasp a concept they’ve been struggling with. This term, I've got a particularly enthusiastic group of beginners learning Spanish. They’re picking it up faster than I anticipated. Spanish, eh? Always wanted to learn Spanish. Reminds me of holidays in Spain when I was a lad. Proper sunshine we had. Mind you, the food wasn’t always the best. Yorkshire puddings are still the best, I reckon. Proper hearty food. I can't argue with that! Yorkshire puddings are amazing. We had a Spanish guest stay with us last summer, and she kept asking for puddings! We had to explain that they’re not really a Spanish thing. She was very confused. That's cracking! It’s funny how different cultures are, isn’t it? One of the things I often tell the trainers at the gyms is to be mindful of individual needs. Don’t push someone too hard, and always explain  why  you're asking them to do something. It’s a bit like teaching, isn’t it? Finding the right way to explain something until it clicks. Absolutely. I've been reading a lot about different learning styles lately – visual, auditory, kinesthetic… tailoring your coaching, or in my case teaching, to those styles makes a huge difference. It's fascinating, really. Did you know there's research suggesting that people learn languages best when they're emotionally engaged? So, incorporating games and role-plays is much more effective than just drilling grammar rules. Emotionally engaged, eh? That's clever. I hadn't thought of it like that. We try to create a friendly atmosphere in the gyms, but maybe we could be doing more to connect with people on a personal level.

Oh, Maureen, you’re killin’ me! Liam tryin’ to teach Gran maths? That’s rich! He's only just mastered it himself, isn’t he, love? Well, I thought I’d help. She seemed a bit bored, you know? And it's important to keep the brain ticking over. Ticking over? I’ve been tickin' over for ninety-two years, lad! I reckon I’ve heard enough numbers for one lifetime. Give me a good cup of tea and a bit of gossip any day. Aye, Maureen’s tales are far more entertainin’ than numbers. Remember that story she told us about the runaway goose, Hilda? Still makes me laugh. Hilda was a terror, that goose was. Escaped from Farmer Giles’ farm and ended up in the middle of the market, causin’ havoc. Nearly knocked over Mrs. Featherstonehaugh and her prize-winning pumpkins! Can we talk about something else? Like, what about dinner tonight? Are we having that casserole Mum was talking about? Aye, the lamb casserole’s on the menu tonight. Lovely and warm, just what Gran and Grandpa need. I'll start prepping it after I clear away these teacups. Speaking of which, Maureen, could you give us a hand? Your back’s stronger than mine these days. Always gettin’ asked to do things. Don’t I ever get a moment’s peace? But alright, alright, I'll lend a hand. Though my hands aren't what they used to be. Arthritis, you know. Like grippin’ rusty nails. Don’t you fret, lass. We’ll do it together. Two old hands are better than one shaky one. I could help too, Mum. I'm pretty good at loading the dishwasher. That'd be grand, Liam. Thank you, love. While you’re at it, could you check on the heating? It feels a bit chilly in here. These old houses, eh? Drafts everywhere. Chilly? It’s mild as a daisy in here! You youngsters are always complainin’ about the temperature. Back in my day, we were glad to have any heat at all! We burned coal, you know. Smelled somethin' awful it did! She's right, you know. We didn't have central heating until the 60s. Remember shivering through the winter, Maureen? Shiverin' and huddlin' 'round the fire, that’s right. And Ma would make us a hot water bottle filled with pinches of silver foil to keep our feet warm.

Speaker_1 said, her voice thick with a North Eastern lilt. She tapped the dashboard of the car impatiently, peering at the satnav. "Twenty-seven years! You're a legend, Brenda. Though, I reckon even Shakespeare would struggle with Ms. Henderson. Satnav being helpful, then?" "Aye, it's mostly alright. Says we need to take this turning onto… are you sure this is right, love? It looks suspiciously like a farmer's field." "Trust the satnav, Brenda. It's a marvel of modern technology, even if it did try and send me into Lake Windermere last Tuesday. Remember? I was swearing blind at it, weren't I?" “Aye, you were. Like a bairn deprived of its sweetie. Still, you’re right. We  are  running a bit late. The lads are bound to have already started setting up. Are you nervous about tonight? Big crowd expected, innit?” “A little, naturally. First proper gig back since… well, you know. Still feeling a bit stiff in the shoulder, but it's manageable. The doctor says rest, but how can a writer rest when he’s got new poetry begging to be shared?” "Doctor's orders are doctor's orders, love. Don't be pushing yourself too hard. Remember what happened last time you tried to be a hero and lifted that bag of wool for Agnes? Spent a week lookin’ like a crumpled newspaper.” “Don’t remind me! Agnes’s ‘specially dyed merino’ nearly did me in. Should have used a trolley. Anyway, the weather’s looking decent, thank goodness. Saw a kestrel hovering over the fields back there. Proper good sign.” "Aye, a kestrel's always a good omen. Though I’m still worried about this rain they were predicting. Ruins a ceilidh, rain does. Now, about your sister's wedding... Did you manage to book the ceilidh band?" "Almost. They have one Friday night open but if we move the wedding reception forward an hour, it’ll work. I was hoping you’d have an opinion on that.
