You’re always so good at arranging things.” “An hour? Hmm. It’s a bit of a faff for everyone, isn't it? But if it means getting a decent band, then fair enough. Just make sure your Auntie Maureen doesn't complain. She'll blame the change in time for everything from a bad harvest to the decline of the Roman Empire." "You know her too well.

"…and honestly, the lighting in that atrium was just  awful . Didn’t capture a single beam properly in my sketches. Ruined the whole mood,” Amelia sighed dramatically, stirring sugar into her latte. Daniel chuckled, already halfway through a bacon sandwich. “Dramatic as ever, Amelia. It was a bit gloomy, yes, but hardly a tragedy. Besides, you’ve got an eye for detail, that's what makes you good at this. Think about how we can  fix  it, not just complain about it." Amelia rolled her eyes playfully. “Easy for you to say, Mr. Practical. You probably love gloom and shadows. I’m thinking skylights, maybe some strategically placed reflective panels… definitely ditch the neon strip lighting, that’s an abomination." “Neon strip lighting  is  an abomination,” another voice piped in. This was Liam , a slightly older friend joining them at the table. “Speaking of abominations, did you see Chloe yesterday? She looked absolutely knackered. Said she’s drowning in paperwork at Beaumont & Blackwood. Apparently, old Mr. Beaumont keeps changing his mind about the library's shelving.” "Oh, poor Chloe!" Amelia exclaimed, her architectural concerns momentarily forgotten. "Is she alright? She seemed so confident when we were at uni.” Daniel nodded sympathetically. “She’s always been a bit of a perfectionist, bless her. Burns the candle at both ends. Honestly, Beaumont's a nightmare. I had a brief stint there a few years back. They suck the life out of you.” “I told her to stand her ground,” Liam continued, taking a sip of his coffee. “Reminded her she's a brilliant designer, not a filing clerk. I think she's feeling a bit undermined, you know? Like her input isn't valued.” “That’s dreadful,” Amelia agreed. “It's so important to have a supportive environment. Remember Professor Davies and that brief he used to go on about? The one about communal living? He always stressed the importance of consultancy – listening to the  people  who are going to live in the space. You can build the most technically perfect building, but if it doesn’t work for the users, it's a failure." "Exactly! It’s the heart of good design," Daniel added. "Which reminds me, I was thinking about that university project brief again. This concept of 'intentional community' - it's tougher than it seems to translate into a workable building. Balancing privacy and shared spaces… it’s tricky.” Liam leaned forward.

Honestly, the state of the A1 this morning. Absolute gridlock. I swear, they timed it perfectly to coincide with the school run and everyone rushing to work. Took me nearly an hour to get here. You wouldn't believe the weaving and bobbing. People just don’t have the patience anymore. Tell me about it! I came straight from work. It was a nightmare. Mrs. Higgins in accounts was complaining she was late for a meeting – again. She blames the cyclists, you know. Mrs. Higgins blames everything but her own lack of planning. Cyclists, squirrels, pigeons… the list goes on. Did you see that article in The Times about driving etiquette? Apparently, letting someone out is the most basic courtesy, and barely anyone does it anymore! It's true. Everyone's just so focused on getting somewhere first. I was behind someone this morning who just  hugged  the roundabout. No indication, no letting anyone merge. I wanted to honk! Oh, I know the feeling! But you shouldn't. It just escalates things. Remember what your grandfather always said? "A calm head and a polite wave will get you further than a horn and a raised fist." Honestly, Grandad was such a saint. He’d probably offer them a cup of tea if they cut him off! Speaking of which, this tea smells amazing. Thanks, Mum. You're welcome, darling. So, any news from Chloe? Has she confirmed about Saturday night? I really want us all to go to that new tapas place. "El Sol," isn't it? She said she’s pretty sure, but she's got to check with Liam. Apparently, his band has a last-minute rehearsal. Typical. They always seem to be scraping things together at the last minute. Men. Always leaving things to the wire. But I do hope she can make it. It would be lovely to all be together. It feels like ages since we’ve had a proper girls' night. Remember that disastrous karaoke night at "The Rusty Mug"? Oh God, Mum! Don't remind me! You attempting "Bohemian Rhapsody" was… something else. Honestly, the whole pub was staring. I was feeling confident! And it's a classic! Besides, at least I gave them something to talk about. Liam nearly choked on his pint. So, you and Liam, everything alright? You seem a little… quieter than usual. It’s nothing major, honestly. He’s just… been stressed with work.

Right, so I’ve had another look at this job description for the Digital Content Editor at Midlands Radio. It's… ambitious, isn’t it? They really want someone who can do everything. Video editing, social media strategy, podcast production… honestly, it’s a lot to pack into one person. Aye, it does look like a proper handful. But then most good jobs do, don’t they? They put all that in there to see how many people  actually  bother reading it and thinking about whether they can do it. You are brilliant at all those things though, aren't you? Honestly, I’m surprised you're even questioning it. It's just… it's not exactly what I'm used to. Teaching languages is very structured, very defined outcomes. This is… fluid. And the competition is bound to be fierce. Loads of journalists and media graduates will be after this. Well, you’ve got experience they won’t. You've worked with multicultural audiences, had to explain complex concepts in simple terms, thought about how to engage people with different learning styles... that's all transferable skills, love. Think about the podcast work you’ve already done. You’ve interviewed local artists, documented community projects… you practically  are  a content creator already! I know, I know. It’s just getting it down on paper. They want ‘demonstrable experience’ in each area. I’ve been wrestling with how to phrase my experience in the language lab as relevant to video editing, for example. I mean, I edited student projects, but it wasn't exactly Oscar-worthy stuff. Nobody's expecting Oscar-worthy, love. It’s about showing you understand the principles. Think about it – you had to ensure the audio was clear, the visuals were engaging, the pacing was right to keep people's attention. That’s all video editing, just… on a slightly smaller scale. Use the STAR method – Situation, Task, Action, Result. Describe the situation, what you needed to do, what you actually did, and what the result was. Right, STAR. Good reminder. Okay, let’s see… “During a project requiring students to present their language learning journey, I was tasked with editing their video submissions to ensure clarity and technical quality…” That sound a bit… robotic? A bit. Tone it down a touch. More like, “As part of a project where students recorded presentations about their language learning, I was responsible for editing the videos.

…and honestly, Sarah, the thought of another five years slinging software solutions just makes my stomach churn. It's lucrative, yes, incredibly so, but it feels…empty. Like building a beautiful, intricate clock that tells the wrong time. I understand completely, Mark. You’ve been saying variations of that for years, haven’t you? Remember that disastrous “motivational speaker” phase? Oh, God, don't remind me. I truly believed I could inspire people with… vaguely positive affirmations. Turns out, most people just wanted a free cup of coffee. But this feels different. This feels…grounded. Pottery. Actually creating something tangible, something beautiful. It  does  seem more "you," doesn't it? More aligned with that quiet creativity I’ve always admired. Building a business, though... that's a whole different beast from software. You’ve got the entrepreneurial drive, that's undeniable, but have you really considered the logistics? Marketing, sales, kiln maintenance... That's what I've been wrestling with. I’ve been researching kilns, obviously. Found a couple of reliable brands online, planning to get quotes. And I’ve been sketching out a business plan, though it’s laughably simplistic at the moment. Think: "Mark's Mudworks – bringing handcrafted ceramics to the Sunshine Coast." Catchy, right? It's a start. Needs refining, definitely. But the enthusiasm is wonderful. Have you thought about where you'd do it? Renting a studio space feels sensible, rather than trying to convert the shed here – lovely as it is. Absolutely. I looked at a few options in Mooloolaba. There’s a shared studio space with a couple of other artists. Seems ideal – shared equipment costs, built-in community, potential for collaboration. The rent's reasonable too, relatively speaking. What about the teaching aspect? You mentioned it earlier. That’s where you shine, truly. You’re a natural teacher, Mark, far more patient than you give yourself credit for. Classes, workshops… beginner’s pottery, glazing techniques. It’s a fantastic way to generate income  and  build a following. I can even help you advertise – I've got good connections with the local community centres; they're always looking for enrichment programs. That would be incredible, Sarah. Really. I'm feeling a bit… overwhelmed, if I'm honest. The thought of taking on this much responsibility, leaving behind a perfectly comfortable income… it’s daunting. It  is  daunting, but don’t let fear paralyse you. Remember the trip to Tuscany?

"Oh, come now, Arthur. It's only dreadful if you’re expecting Michelin-star cuisine. Back in my day, during the war, cabbage soup was a luxury! You’d be grateful for a bowl, you would." Agnes chuckled, a warm, Scottish sound. “Besides, I hear young Colin down the street is on some sort of intermittent fasting thing. Claims it’s working wonders.” "Colin, is it? Oh, the things they come up with. Finn here thrives on chaos and carbohydrates. Trying to get him to eat anything green is a battle of wills. He’s utterly convinced that broccoli resembles tiny, angry trees." She wiped potato from Finn’s cheek. "Tree! Tree!" “Speaking of young ones, did you hear about the schools? Absolutely dire, Sarah. Apparently, there’s a waiting list for every primary school in Cambridge. It’s scandalous! My granddaughter, Penelope, had to go to a school in Saffron Walden, miles away. Miles! Just dreadful for the poor girl’s commute.” "It's heartbreaking, isn't it? When I was teaching, classrooms were bursting at the seams, but nothing like this. And the housing, don’t even get me started. People crammed into these little terraced houses, and all the new builds are these ghastly boxes. No character at all." Agnes sighed, stirring her gravy. "It’s all down to this influx, isn’t it? Polish migration, Eastern European workers... Don’t misunderstand, I’m not saying they’re a bad thing, but the infrastructure just hasn't kept up." "It's a mess, Agnes. Honestly. We were looking at moving further out last year, but the prices were ridiculous. And you’re right about the schools. You practically need a second mortgage to get your child into a decent one. We’re lucky, for now, with the childminder. Keeps him happy and gives me a bit of space." Sarah looked tired. "Though, frankly, I'm starting to feel like a professional potato-wiper." “A worthy profession indeed! Do you know, Penelope sent me a picture of her fiancé the other day. He has a beard. A truly magnificent beard. Down to his chest, it was. She says he's quite the hipster." Arthur shook his head. "Beards! It's a phase, I tell you, a phase. Like those dreadful handlebar moustaches back in the sixties. Though, I must admit, I did briefly consider growing one myself when I was… oh, perhaps twenty-something."

Tell me about it, love. It's like a permanent background hum of anxiety, isn’t it? Remember when it all kicked off? We were having that barbecue at the cricket club, weren’t we? A perfectly lovely day, and then… the news started filtering through. People arguing, kids confused… it was a right mess. Absolutely. I remember your Geoff kept trying to mediate, bless him. He just wanted everyone to get along. I think he almost had a coronary that day, didn’t he? Though, to be fair, the pies were a bit dodgy that year. Remember Brenda's apple crumble was the only real saving grace? Oh, Brenda's crumble  always  saves the day. You know, it makes you think about school, doesn’t it? Being back at sixth form, agonizing over A-levels and sneaking cigarettes behind the gym. Remember old Mr. Harrison, the history teacher? A right stickler for detail. Oh my goodness, Mr. Harrison! He’d have you written up for breathing too loudly in his class. He used to say, "Silence is the cornerstone of intellect!" Honestly, the man! Speaking of school, has little Leo started crawling yet? Your daughter sent me that adorable video. He's a whirlwind! Just yesterday, he was attempting to scale the sofa like a tiny mountaineer. It's exhausting, but wonderful. It feels like yesterday I was dropping Sarah off at university. Time just flies. Sarah’s going to that summer music festival, you know, the one near Stratford? Oh yes, the Meadowbrook one! I saw an ad for it. Fancy her going to a music festival. She always did have an ear for music. Remember her practicing the piano for hours? You were always so supportive of her playing. She was good, too. Could pick up anything. It’s a shame she didn’t pursue it more seriously. It would have been nice for her to go to music college. But then, life gets in the way, doesn't it? What about you? Still juggling marketing and proofreading? It's keeping me busy, thankfully. I've got a couple of new clients, which is good. It's just… all the paperwork. Honestly, sometimes I think I spend more time filling out forms than actually doing the work. They’ve been messing about with the car park passes at the office again, too. You’d think they’d have sorted that out by now.

Aye, I hear ye, Hamish. It’s a right whirlwind, that platform. You've got to be careful, don’t ye? I mean, my job practically demands I engage, but it's a precarious balancing act. The PR team are always on my back to "join the conversation" on… well, everything. It's the speed of it, isn't it? Everything’s instant. And people react before they think. I had a student, bless her heart, last week. Posted a wee joke about… well, never mind the specifics. It was mildly controversial, a bit tongue-in-cheek, but it just exploded. She was getting barraged. Och, the poor lass! What did you advise her? I told her to take a breath, log off, and don't engage. Anything she said would just fuel the fire. Then, when she was calmer, we drafted a measured apology, acknowledging that the joke didn’t land well and explaining it wasn’t intended to cause offence. Thankfully, it diffused things, but it was a stressful couple of days. Makes you think twice about posting  anything . It does. I had a bit of a scare myself a few months ago. We launched a new sustainability initiative at the firm, right? Very proud of it. I tweeted about it, you know, clever hashtags and all that. Got a couple of responses praising it. Then, out of nowhere, someone accused us of greenwashing. Greenwashing, eh? The bane of modern corporate messaging. Exactly! And they were quite aggressive about it. Started digging into our past practices, finding minor inconsistencies, blowing them completely out of proportion. My heart nearly stopped. I spent a good hour crafting a response, backing up every claim with data and transparency reports. It was a nightmare. Took the entire PR team to manage the fallout. Jeez. Did it settle down? Eventually. But it showed me how quickly things can spiral. One single accusation, amplified by thousands of people, can do serious damage. I'm much more cautious now. More careful about what I share, and when. I’ve started scheduling my tweets now, letting them sit overnight before they go live, just to get a fresh perspective. A good tactic. I try to avoid using it for anything related to the university, mostly. It's far easier to focus on my teaching and the students. I do use Instagram, though. Just for wee pictures of the garden.

Honestly, I need a full body massage. This weekend was… intense. Three breakdowns, a medication adjustment, and a frankly bizarre incident involving a pigeon and a park bench. A pigeon and a park bench? Seriously? You work miracles, you do. What happened? Did the pigeon steal someone's sandwich? Worse. Apparently, a patient thought the pigeon was a government surveillance drone. Started trying to build a cage around it. Security had to intervene. It was… a lot. How was  your  weekend, then, Miss Project Coordinator Supreme? Don't tell me you just organised spreadsheets all day. Not  just  spreadsheets, no. We had the quarterly review on Friday, which was surprisingly smooth. Then Saturday was Liam’s birthday do. You know, the one you couldn’t make. I know, I know! And I felt terrible. But three patients needing crisis intervention takes precedence, sadly. Was it a good party? Did he get plastered? It was… chaotic. In a fun way. A lot of questionable dance moves, a bouncy castle – which was utterly ridiculous for a group of nearly thirty year olds – and a DJ who clearly thought he was performing at Glastonbury. I’m still finding glitter in my hair. A bouncy castle?! Oh, Liam. He’s lost it completely. Did Mark go? He did. And he spent most of the time arguing with Dave about the merits of vinyl versus streaming. It was a repeat performance from their debate last month, honestly. I swear, they could debate the temperature of a room for an hour and still disagree. Sounds about right. Speaking of arguments, are you still annoyed about me using the last of the oat milk? A little. Just a little. You know I need oat milk for my porridge every morning. It's the only thing that gets me functioning before 8am. Okay, fair. I’ll buy some tomorrow, I promise. Extra creamy one, to apologise. It’s just… I was making this amazing matcha latte, and I completely forgot. I was stressed about work, you know? I do know. But maybe invest in a spare carton, just as a contingency for when the pigeon-related emergencies arise. Solid advice. Hey, are you ordering pizza tonight? I'm starving. And I'm not dealing with cooking after that weekend. My brain feels like scrambled eggs. I was thinking about it, yeah. Do you fancy a veggie one? I’m trying to be a bit healthier.

Honestly, Mum, I'm still reeling from what Dad said earlier. About Aunt Carol and the voices. It was… unsettling. Well, he has been a bit… peculiar lately, hasn’t he, love? Since the retirement, it's like he's filled the void with…well, with worry and strange pronouncements. Wellington's given him a lot of time to think, I suppose. He's just concerned, really. Carol has always… been a sensitive soul. These 'voices', as you put it, she's had them for years. He's just noticing them more now, perhaps. The silence down there can play tricks on your mind. Sensitive? Dad implied she was talking to spirits, Dad! He was practically convinced she was channelling someone who’d died! It's not exactly a reassuring thing to hear at the dinner table, is it? Your father and his dramatics. He's always been a bit prone to exaggeration, haven't you, Arthur? Remember the time he swore the neighbour’s cat was a spy for the Russians? That was different! The cat  was  staring at me funny. And it  did  have a suspicious amount of glitter on its fur. Glitter? Dad, you're unbelievable. Anyway, back to the point - Uncle George’s visit. Has anyone heard from him? Is he actually sticking to the 18th as he said? I spoke to him yesterday. He's confirmed. He’s booked the train ticket, apparently. He said he’s looking forward to seeing us all - especially a decent roast. He’s been complaining about the cooking at that little B&B he's been using. Good, good. Least we’ll have some company. It gets rather quiet here, doesn’t it? Though, I still think he needs to be reminded about the stairs. He’s not as nimble as he used to be. We'll make sure he doesn't try any heroics. Speaking of things, I managed to pick up a new car! A little Fiat 500. It's bright red, you'll love it. It's much better on petrol than my old banger. Oh, darling, that's lovely! A red Fiat! Very you. Excellent decision. Where are you planning on driving it first? I was thinking of taking it down to visit Mum and Dad next weekend. Give them a proper chance to see it. And maybe encourage Dad to lay off the spirit talk. Just trying to keep abreast of events, that’s all.

Right then, Arthur. Another hour wrestling with this subjunctive. It’s enough to make a body weep, it is. Honestly, I’m starting to think I'm too old for this. Sixty-eight years on this earth, and I’m struggling with “si… entonces.” It’s mad, isn’t it? Now, now, Maureen. Don’t go getting yourself down. It’s a tricky language, Spanish. Always has been. Took my nephew, Simon, three years to get a decent grip, and he’s a whizz at languages, the lad. Years in Brussels, you know. Brussels, eh? They’re practically multilingual over there, aren't they? It seems so easy for some folk. I even tried one of them language learning apps, the Duolingo one. Felt like I was just repeating phrases like a parrot. No real understanding, just a load of brightly coloured owls telling me off for getting the gender of a table wrong! Oh, I know the one. My neighbour, Mrs. Davies, swears by it. Says it keeps her brain ticking. But she’s already fluent in French, so it’s a bit different for her, innit? You need a proper foundation, Maureen. Like when I was learning surveying. Need a solid base before you can build anything on it. And that’s what I'm missing! All this focusing on grammar and conjugation, and barely any conversational practice. I had an online tutor last week, a young lad from Madrid. I spent the entire session feeling like a right daftie. Couldn’t string two sentences together! He kept saying, "Mucho ánimo," which is lovely, but doesn't help me order a cafe con leche! “Mucho ánimo.” Good lad. You gotta remember, Maureen, learning a language is like learning to ride a bike. You’re gonna wobble, you’re gonna fall. The key's gettin' back on. Have you thought about joining a local conversation group? There's one runs at the community centre, Tuesdays. I looked into it. Mostly retirees who want to reminisce about holidays in Benidorm, I reckon. Not exactly immersive language practice. It's just as complicated when you think about places like Spain itself, isn't it? They’ve got Catalan, and Basque, and… all alongside Castillian. It's a linguistic minefield! Aye, that's true. Spain's a bit like Switzerland, in that regard. Always had multiple languages. My mate, Derek, he’s got a daughter living in Barcelona.

Right, so this is… a lot. Honestly, Dad, you’ve kept  everything . Old bank statements from 1998, menus from restaurants we’ve probably all forgotten existed… It’s classic Dad, isn't it? The man’s a walking archive. Though, I’m impressed with your organisational skills, even with this avalanche. You’ve got most of it in labelled boxes. Labelling doesn’t mean it's useful, does it? Look at this… a fax confirmation for a holiday booking in the Isle of Wight. 2003! We went to Cornwall that year, didn’t we? Probably. I’m trying to separate the essential from the… well, the historical. Let's focus on the banking stuff first. I see a few statements from NatWest, and some older ones from Barclays? Barclays. He was a loyal Barclays man. Still is, I think. Though I’ve convinced him to finally look at switching to online banking. Took a lot of persuading, I can tell you. He was terrified of being hacked! Perfectly understandable. Especially when you’ve been writing cheques your whole life. He’s a creature of habit. So, these statements – do you know if anything here is needed for tax purposes, or anything like that? Not likely. He retired five years ago, you know. Pension’s sorted, thankfully. Though, there's always some form or another needing signing, eh? Speaking of forms, have you scanned any of this yet? My scanner's on the blink. I’ve scanned the most important bank statements so far. Put them on a USB stick. It’s surprisingly satisfying, actually. Like digitally decluttering the world. You know, it’s almost like corpus linguistics – extracting relevant data from a massive body of text, only with bank statements and bills instead of novels. Corpus linguistics? You and your fancy words, eh? Teachin’ English, and bringin' linguistics into it. Still, makes sense, I suppose. All data, isn’t it? Exactly! Just a different kind of text. Though, much less exciting than analysing Shakespeare. Though, maybe I could analyze Dad's receipts. A fascinating study in impulsive biscuit purchases, no doubt. Don't you dare! Actually, speaking of things I'm impulsive about... did you see Kelly Brook in that new ad? Absolutely stunning. I might have. She's always been a classic. Anyway, back to the mountain of paper… Right, what about these airline tickets? Are these from the trip to Greece?

Honestly, this petrol price is ludicrous. Absolutely ludicrous. I swear, it's gone up another 5p since last week. Aye, tell me about it. I filled up back home, near the docks, and it nearly choked me. Five-oh-two a litre! Five-oh-two! You'd think they were selling liquid gold, not petrol. It feels like it. I did a quick comparison on the app - there's a Shell just down the road that’s significantly cheaper. We should've gone there. Should’ve, should've. You were in a rush to get to… what was it again? That meeting with Mr. Davies? Right. Important one. Progress report for the Henderson project. I needed to be sharp. Although, at this rate, I'll be taking the train just to save a few quid. Train’s just as bad, innit? Rail fares are through the roof. It's all a con, really. They just bleed us dry. You're not wrong. Thinking about it… remember that biker group we saw last summer on the A1? Those lads were right, weren't they? Saying petrol prices would eventually force everyone onto electric. Aye, they were. I remember. Big group, all leather and chrome. Reckon they were right, but I couldn’t see mesel’ going electric just yet. Too much faff. And where are they getting the juice from, eh? Probably burning even  more  coal somewhere. Valid point. The electric car thing needs a lot more thought, doesn't it? Logistics, the environmental impact of battery production… Still, it’s a long-term solution, I suppose. Long-term’s fair enough. I just can’t be bothered with all the charging bits and bobs. I like the freedom of just fillin’ up and going. Besides, what about up north? Charging points are scarcer than hen’s teeth! That's definitely an issue. Although, the government is supposedly rolling out more infrastructure. Speaking of which, did you see that article about the new speed cameras they’re installing on the A69? No! Where? Near Hexham? Honestly, they're always plonking 'em where you least expect it. You'll be catchin' someone out, alright. I try to stick to the speed limit, but it’s hard when everyone else is flyin’ past. I know what you mean. It’s frustrating. I tend to drive a little more defensively, just to be safe. Especially with the state of some drivers these days.

Dad! Seriously, can you not be chopping onions  right now ? I’m trying to visualise my forehand! It's all blurry, I can’t concentrate. Blurry? You were hitting serves like a rocket just an hour ago, Liam! A little onion isn’t going to dismantle your technique. And it’s shepherd’s pie, not just onions. Comfort food for a champion, eh? He’s got a point, love. It is a bit distracting clattering about like that when he’s trying to focus. Liam, darling, just take a breather. You don’t need to be drilling every single shot before dinner. Come and tell us about your lesson with Mr. Davies. Was it good? It was okay. He kept going on about my footwork again. He makes it sound like my feet are a separate entity from my body! "Liam, you need to  commit  to your movement!" It's like, yes, I know I'm moving, Mr. Davies! What more do you want? "Commit to your movement" is actually very sound advice, you know. It’s all about transfer of weight and balance. Think of it like this - when you’re running, you commit to the stride, right? Same principle. Exactly. And Mr. Davies isn’t wrong, you do sometimes seem a bit hesitant. Remember that match against Ethan last week? You were playing brilliantly, then you missed a couple of easy shots and your whole game seemed to fall apart. It was like you lost that commitment. That was different! Ethan’s a cheat. He calls the lines in his favour all the time. Oh, here we go. Blaming the opposition. A true champion finds a way to win, regardless of a few questionable line calls. It’s all part of the game, Liam. You need to develop that mental strength. Speaking of mental strength, I was reading about Carlos Alcaraz the other day. Did you see his match against Rune at Wimbledon? Absolutely incredible! The way he came back from being down two sets… phenomenal. He's only 20, can you imagine? Yeah, but he’s got a completely different game to me. He’s all about those ridiculous drop shots and forehand winners. I'm more… consistent, I guess. Consistent is good, lad! Solid fundamentals. Don't try to be something you're not. But you can learn from Alcaraz's resilience. He doesn’t get flustered easily.

Right, this is boss, Mum. Proper boss. You've outdone yourself this year. Though… these napkins are a bit weird, aren’t they? They look like… underpants. Honestly. They  do  a bit, don't they? Thought they were a laugh, trying to be a bit festive. Your Uncle Barry sent 'em. He's got a strange sense of humour, that one. Anyone want more sprouts? Please! And I love the napkins, actually. They're hilarious. University life is so… well, it’s not always this nice. Remember last Christmas Eve? We were all huddled in a tiny kitchen in a student house, eating cold pizza and listening to awful Christmas tunes. Aye, but you were happy, weren't you, love? That's the important thing. This spread here… this is the real deal. Still, reminds me, did you manage to get all your Christmas shopping done yet, Ellie? Nearly! Just need a gift for Liam. He's being impossible to buy for. Keeps saying he wants "experiences," which is just a fancy way of saying he doesn’t want anything. Experiences, eh? When I was your age, we were grateful for a pair of socks! Everything was so different back then. And the music! None of this modern rubbish. Give me a bit of Bing Crosby any day. Do you think they’ll have the Queen’s Speech on this year? I always watch it. They always do, Nan. It's tradition. Though I always fall asleep halfway through. So, Ellie, you said Liam’s friends… what do they call you? You mentioned some proper weird nicknames the other day. Oh, don't remind me! It’s all a bit silly. There’s "Sparkle Pony" and… and "Professor Plum." It started as a joke, you know, because I’m always going on about my essays. "Sparkle Pony"? Goodness me. You're a serious student, love, you don't need a nickname like that! Remember when you went to Florida last summer? That was a proper adventure. Were you nervous flying? The airport is always such a faff. Florida was amazing! The sun, the beaches… it felt like a different world. I'm thinking of trying to go back next year, maybe for a few weeks. Dad, you remember how we used to argue over the wishbone every Christmas? Remember who always got the bigger piece? Aye, I do. Your mum always managed to subtly manoeuvre it

Honestly, these are a bit pale, aren’t they, David? Not enough colour. Needs a good five minutes more, I reckon. Now, now, Brenda, don’t be a critic. They’re perfectly lovely. And plenty of gravy covering them. You’re always fussing. A bit of colour doesn’t make it taste better, you know. Grandpa, you're impossible! Mum's potatoes are always amazing. Maybe the oven’s just a bit off today. Everything seems to be taking longer. It is a bit off, I'll admit. It’s been making a funny noise lately. David, have you remembered to book that repair person? Not yet, love. Been a bit busy with the harvest reports. They're a nightmare this year, honestly. Prices are plummeting. You wouldn’t believe the stress. Oh, Grandpa, that sounds awful. Is it really that bad? Are you going to have to… you know…? Don't you worry your pretty little head about that, Elsie. We’ll manage. We always do. Just need to tighten the belt a bit. Which reminds me, Elsie, how’s that new project going at work? Still coordinating chaos? Pretty much! It’s the Davies account, remember? They’re ridiculously demanding. They want everything yesterday and then complain it's not exactly what they envisioned. I spent yesterday untangling a spreadsheet that looked like a Jackson Pollock painting. Sounds stressful, dear. Are you eating properly? You look a bit tired. I’m surviving on caffeine and sheer willpower, to be honest. But it’s good money, Mum. I’m putting some away for a flat, you know. Getting my own place is really the goal. Sensible girl. Foot on the ladder. That’s what it’s all about. Remember when I started out, Elsie? Barely had a shilling to my name. Worked on my uncle’s farm, dawn ‘til dusk. no holidays, no nothing. David, please. Elsie’s trying to tell us about her job. Though, honestly, it does sound like you’re working yourself too hard, love. Have you had that conversation with Mark yet? About… you know… Oh. Right. Mark. Not yet. It’s… complicated. He's been distant lately. Keeps saying he’s busy, but… Distant, eh? Young men are funny things. Always running around like headless chickens. Probably just a phase. Don’t be ridiculous, David. It could be more than a phase. Elsie, are you happy?

Honestly, I don't know why I bother making risotto. It’s a complete faff, isn’t it? And then it's either gluey or dry. Pizza sounds so much easier. It is easier. Absolutely. But a good risotto… a really good risotto… is worth the effort. You’re just not being patient enough, love. Remember that one at that Italian place in York? Spectacular. That was five years ago, David! And probably cost a week’s wages. I’m thinking minimal effort tonight. Plus, young Leo’s been nagging about pizza all day. Fair enough. Pizza it is. Although, the new Marks and Spencer pizzas… have you tried those new sourdough ones? They're not bad at all. Certainly a step up from their usual offering. I was in M&S earlier! Specifically for ingredients for, you know,  the risotto  I was initially attempting. They’ve really upped their game in the food department, haven't they? That halloumi… I got some. Planning on grilling it with the pizza. Good shout. Halloumi is always a winner. Did you see they had that special on the Spanish red? A fourteen-year-old Rioja for under fifteen quid. Incredible value. You and your wine! You’ll bankrupt us. Though, a fourteen-year-old Rioja  does  sound tempting… Right, Leo's home. Leo, darling, can you set the table, please? We're having pizza and grilled halloumi. Speaking of things that need setting, I have that appraisal next week. The Head of Department’s been hinting at increased responsibilities… more paperwork, naturally. Oh, David, that's brilliant news! Finally some recognition for all your hard work. Though, more paperwork does sound like a nightmare. Did you manage to finish that crossword today? The one from the Times? The clues were utterly fiendish. Nearly. Got stuck on 17 across. Something about… equine welfare? It was a particularly cruel clue. "Concern for horses' wellbeing" - six letters. "Welf..." It drove me mad. Welfare! Of course! I was thinking something completely different. You know, sometimes I wish I’d gone into equine therapy. It feels more fulfilling than transcribing endless legal documents. You’d be covered in mud and cat hair. Speaking of which, where’s Jasper? He’s usually glued to your feet. He’s… under the sofa, I think. He’s been acting strangely all day. Hiding, and just... staring. Probably contemplating the existential dread of being a fluffy orange cat.

Right, I’m officially declaring this a disaster. Look at this dress! It’s meant to be a sparkly silver, and it looks like…grey glitter on cheap fabric. Honestly! Relax, Beth. It ain't that bad. More of a, ya know, subtle shimmer. And you'll look lovely in it, love. What heels are you wearin' wi' it? Subtle shimmer? It's depressing, Liv! And I haven't  got  any heels. That's the whole point! I was hopin' to find some clanky ones at Primark. Something that makes my legs look a mile long. Not these flat, black, sensible things. Sensible's good, Beth! You'll be able to dance all night. I went for heels – proper stilettos, like, risking life and limb – and my feet are already screaming. See? Ooh, not good, Rach! Reminds me of that time I wore those ridiculous platforms to the Leeds festival. Never again. My ankles were swollen for a week. You look alright in that dress, though, Beth. Maybe a bit of lipstick will brighten it up? Aye, lipstick! And a good fake tan, eh, Beth? It'll really make the shimmer pop! I’m wearin' this velvet number, and I'm terrified I'll look like a giant plum. Velvet? Sounds lush, Maisie! I’m starting to think I should've just stayed home and worn my pyjamas. Why did I even bother coming? It’s always like this! Hours spent stressing over what to wear for a night that’ll probably involve most of us endin’ up on the floor. Now, now, don't be like that! We're goin' out to celebrate Sarah's birthday, right? She’ll be chuffed to see us all lookin’ half-decent. Besides, a couple of cocktails and you’ll be forgettin' all about the dress. Rach's right. Sarah's craved this night for weeks. We can't let her down, and we definitely can’t let her see us lookin’ like we’ve lost a fight with a fashion disaster. Think of the photos! Speaking of photos, is anyone else getting drunk on pre-drinks like me? My mum made a batch of rum punch. It's dangerous, but delicious. It tastes like sunshine and regret. Sunshine and regret is an excellent description! My nan’s made some elderflower cordial with gin. It’s surprisingly strong. I’ve already had three. Three?

Honestly, Mark, you were  raving  about the Regency period again last night. The embroidery! The social etiquette! It's lovely, I suppose, but don't you ever get tired of it? It’s a bit… intense. Intense? Come on, love. It’s escapism. A bit of ballast against the spreadsheet chaos of the week. Besides, imagine the party we could throw! A proper Regency ball. Think about the music, the gowns… I  am  thinking about the gowns. Think about the cost! And the sheer logistical nightmare of getting everyone into breeches and tailcoats. Not to mention sourcing a decent waltz orchestra. I’d need a whole team of event planners just to coordinate that. You’re always practical, aren't you? But that’s why I love you. Someone has to be. I'm the flights of fancy, you’re the… the grounding rod. But indulge me, just for a moment. Imagine the scene. Fairy lights strung across the garden, the scent of honeysuckle… Okay, okay, you’re painting a nice picture. Though I still think sourcing the right pianoforte would be a Herculean task. Still, going back to something a little less… elaborate... I was thinking about what Sarah was saying the other day, about spiritual awakenings. Sarah? From book club? What was she on about now? She was talking about finally feeling… connected. About believing she'd found her soulmate later in life. It rather got me thinking. Do you ever feel like you've had a truly profound spiritual experience, beyond the usual anxieties about work and remembering to pay the council tax? Profound... no, not really. I'm a bit too pragmatic for that, I think. I appreciate things, I appreciate  you , obviously, but I don't spend a lot of time pondering my soul. Foot and mouth disease of the mind, I call it. Charming. So, no yearning for a deeper meaning in the universe? No feeling like you're part of something larger than yourself? I find meaning in smaller things. A good cup of coffee, a well-configured network, the feeling of a warm duvet on a cold night. That’s enough for me. Don’t get me wrong, I’m glad Sarah's feeling happy and fulfilled. But I’m not sure I’m cut from the same cloth. It's interesting, isn't it? How different we are. You're so… grounded.

Honestly, Sarah, this whole Etsy thing is more stressful than managing a multinational account. I thought, 'little side hustle, lovely creative outlet.' It's…a lot. Especially the packaging. People  expect  things to arrive looking like they've been handled by white gloves. Tell me about it! My nan’s got a little crafts page on there too. She’s obsessed with crocheted hedgehogs. Says it’s keeping her brain ticking over. But the postage costs! She nearly had a heart attack when she realised how much it was to send a badger to Scotland. It’s the online marketplace, isn't it? It throws everything at you – marketing, photography, customer service… It's almost a second job. Though I must say, your knitted hats are gorgeous, Eleanor. Really unique. I've been eyeing up that cable knit one with the pom-pom. You’re sweet, Claire. It's just…I feel like I’m constantly battling algorithms and people complaining about the thread colour being  slightly  different from what they saw on the screen. It's petty. And the way people stereotype about small business owners… expecting handmade equals dirt cheap practically. Oh, I know! People think because you’re doing it “for fun” you should be practically giving it away. It's ridiculous, innit? It's the same with posting on socials. You’ve gotta be like, a social media guru on top of everything else. I tried helping Nan with hers. It was a disaster. She kept accidentally posting pictures of her cat instead of the hedgehogs. Bless her! You know, it’s funny, how regional accents seem to be viewed. I was at a conference last week, and a woman from up north was presenting. Honestly, some of the side-eye she got just for the way she spoke… it was awful. People just automatically make assumptions. Absolutely. It’s ingrained, isn’t it? Like Americans thinking anyone British speaks with a posh accent. I get it all the time. "Oh, you're British, you must have been to Eton!" It's exhausting trying to correct it. It's so lazy, yeah. Like, judging people’s intelligence based on how they talk. Remember that documentary we watched about gun violence in America? The way they talked about certain accents correlating with certain behaviours... terrifying. It’s a societal problem, isn’t it? That link between language and behaviour.

Right, this is a disaster. Absolutely a blooming disaster. What's up, Liv? You sound like you’ve just stubbed your toe on a badger. Worse, Finn. Much worse. Remember I said I was meeting Chloe and Ben for drinks tonight? Yeah? What happened? Did Ben finally reveal his secret collection of porcelain dolls? No, nothing that weird, thankfully. But Chloe's flatmate, that Emma… she’s apparently having a party. A  massive  party. And Chloe’s invited the whole lot of us. Okay… not a disaster. Sounds like a laugh, actually. A laugh? Finn, I’ve got a mountain of coursework due on Monday. A mountain! And I was planning on, you know,  actually  studying tonight. Plus, I still haven't sorted out that tax form thing. My mum's been on at me something fierce. Tax? Already? Feels a bit early for that, doesn’t it? I’m still avoiding it. Just pretending it doesn’t exist. Classic. Look, Liv, a bit of a break won’t kill you. You deserve it. Besides, Chloe’s parties are usually pretty good. Remember the one last month with the karaoke? Let’s not. My rendition of "Bohemian Rhapsody" still haunts my dreams. It was like a strangled cat trying to yodel. Oh, I remember that! It was… memorable. Memorable in a deeply embarrassing way. Right, so what do I do? Go and mingle with a hundred strangers while my dissertation writes itself? Mingle, have a couple of drinks, have a laugh. Then come back and bury yourself in books. Balance, Liv. It’s all about balance. And maybe sneak out early. Nobody will blame you. I’m totally in favour of the sneak-out-early plan. It’s the responsible student option. Besides, last time I went to one of Chloe’s parties, someone spilled a pint down my back. Never again. See? You both understand! But what about this tax thing? I’m proper lost. My mum keeps saying “just fill it in, love,” but she doesn't actually  explain  anything. I can have a look at it, if you want. My dad’s an accountant, so I've picked up a few pointers. It’s probably simpler than you think. It’s just all the jargon that throws people. Would you? Seriously? You’re a lifesaver, Finn. You’re speaking my language. Proper helpful. Back home, everyone just shouts at you about taxes.

Speaker_1 shivered, despite the warm Croatian evening. Speaker_2 , her mother, chuckled, swirling the wine in her glass. "Honestly, love, you'd think after all these years, you'd have learned to check the times online. You’re at uni, aren't you? They have apps for everything now.” Speaker_3 , Eliza's younger brother, grinned. “Yeah, Liz! Easy peasy. Google Maps, sorted.” "Aye, well, Google Maps decided to take me on a scenic route through some dodgy estate, that's what happened," Eliza retorted, playfully rolling her eyes. "Anyway, what about you, Dad? Did you manage to escape those spreadsheets and join us in paradise?" Speaker_4 , Eliza's father, let out a weary sigh, adjusting his tie. “Managed to, yes. Though paradise still requires checking emails, I'm afraid. This new automation project… it’s a mess. Half the spreadsheets are incompatible. Honestly, sometimes I wish I’d followed your mum's lead and become a midwife.” He glanced at Margaret. Margaret smiled gently. “It’s a rewarding job, David, but not for everyone. Seeing new life come into the world… there's nothing quite like it. Speaking of life, Liam, how's school going? Still torturing Mr. Harrison with your questions about Roman history?” Liam groaned. "He says I’m 'too inquisitive.' Like, isn't that a good thing? We're doing gladiators now, though. That’s pretty cool. I’m thinking about getting a tattoo of a gladiator helmet. What do you reckon, Eliza?” He looked at his sister expectantly. Eliza blinked. “A tattoo? Liam, you’re only fourteen! Your mum will kill you.” “Mum always says I should express myself,” Liam argued, mimicking Margaret’s tone. Margaret frowned. “I say you should express yourself  responsibly , Liam. A tattoo is a permanent decision. Think about it carefully. It’s not something you can just erase like a Facebook post… although I’m thinking about deactivating mine, actually. Too much negativity these days.” “Yeah, Nana's always on there complaining about the price of sausages at Tesco,” Eliza chimed in, earning a playful glare from Margaret. David cleared his throat. “Talking of supermarkets, have you noticed how drastically prices have gone up? Even here, in Croatia. It’s ridiculous. I was saying to Mr. Hawthorne at work – he’s a consultant, naturally – about how businesses are exploiting the current situation." “Hawthorne, eh?” Margaret raised an eyebrow. “London type, is he? All crisp suits and salary packages?”

Look at this! Remember this one, Arthur? Taken right on the cliffs near Land’s End. You were trying to take a selfie with the lighthouse, and nearly tumbled over! Near enough did, didn't I? Blasted wind, ya know. Strong enough to blow a bloke clean off 'is feet. Glorious view though, weren’t it? Proper postcard stuff. Shame about the picture being wonky. It's a great picture, honestly. Captured the wildness of the place. Did you manage to see any actual sun, though? I remember hearing the weather was dreadful during your stay. A bit spotty, but we had some lovely sunny patches. Enough to make the coast sparkle, that’s for sure. And the YHA was brilliant. So well-run, and the staff were just lovely. Volunteering was good, felt like we were actually  doing  something. Aye, the YHA was a treat. Met a right friendly bunch too. That young fella, Liam, he was a grafter, that one. Always lending a hand. Reminded me a bit of me brother, bless ‘im. Used to be a hard worker, 'e did. It's good you both found it fulfilling. I was a bit worried, honestly. Spending a week volunteering, it wasn't exactly your usual holiday. We needed something different, didn’t we? And it was a chance to see Cornwall properly. We didn't just stick to the coast, we even managed to get inland a bit. Remember that little village, Mousehole? Charming. Charming and rather steep! My knees weren’t thanking me for that climb, I can tell ya. Should’ve brought me walking stick. Nearly went a-tumblin' again, I did. You and gravity have never been friends, have you? Anyway, tell me more about the cycling. Did you manage to catch any of the race you were hoping to see? Just a glimpse, unfortunately. It was passing through St Ives while we were there. We got to see the peloton whizz by, but the crowds were absolutely massive. Couldn’t get anywhere near the finish line. Still exciting though! Proper speed they were goin', y’know. Blurs of colour. Couldn’t tell who was who. I was more interested in the pasties, to be honest. Had a four cheese one from a little shop – best I've tasted in years. Priorities, Arthur, priorities. So, what’s next on the agenda? Planning any more adventures? I was thinking, you mentioned Yorkshire… Oh, yes!

Honestly, ANON, this is incredible. You’ve really outdone yourself this time. Better than your Nan’s, and that's saying something. Aye, well, Nan's got years o' practice on me, hasn't she? Though, I reckon I'm gettin’ there. Took me ages to get the bechamel right this time. Nearly threw the whole thing out the window. It’s perfect. Seriously. You're a natural chef, ANON. I’m gonna be mooching off you for all my meals from now on. You could open a restaurant, you know. 'Anon's Amazing Italian,' or summat. Don't be ridiculous, Liam. Though...it  is  very good. So, ANON, you were saying something about a disastrous date the other night? You looked like you'd seen a ghost when you walked in. Oh, you have  no  idea. Right, so, he—let's call him 'Reginald'—he's a solicitor. Proper posh Cambridge sort. My cousin, Sarah, set us up. Said he was ‘a gentleman’ and ‘very stable.’ Stable like a wobbly tower of Jenga, more like. Reginald, eh? Sounds like a character. What happened? Did he turn out to be a secret tax evader? Worse, Liam. Much worse. He spent the entire evening talking about… bonsai trees. Like, detailed, intensely passionate explanations about pruning techniques and soil composition. I barely got a word in edgeways. No! Seriously? That’s… incredibly dull. Did you at least try to steer the conversation elsewhere? I tried! I genuinely did. Mentioned my job, asked about his family, even brought up the weather! He just… circled back to bonsai. Apparently, he’s judging a competition next month and needs someone to “appreciate the subtle nuances of the Variegated Japanese Maple.” I nearly choked on me wine. Oh man! That’s brutal. You've got to admit, that’s a story worth telling. You're a legend, ANON. It is! Poor you! It sounds like a social endurance test. So, no second date then? Absolutely not. I’d rather spend an evening wrestling a badger than listening to another lecture on bonsai pruning. Sarah’s convinced I’m being ‘too picky.’ She says I need to 'lower my standards.' Sarah needs to back off. Bonsai enthusiasm is a non-negotiable deal-breaker. Seriously. Absolutely. Lower your standards? Nonsense. You deserve someone who can hold a conversation about, I don’t know, something other than miniature trees. Speaking of standards… Liam, are you still seeing Chloe?

Honestly, the silence has been deafening! You’re back! Barcelona didn’t swallow you whole, then? Nope! Though there were moments I thought I might disappear into a tapas bar and never return. Barcelona was… incredible. Absolutely incredible. You wouldn't believe the architecture, the food… Tell me everything! Did you see the Sagrada Familia? I’ve been wanting to go for ages. My little sister is obsessed with Gaudi. Of course! It’s… wow. Pictures don't do it justice. It’s just… organic, you know? Like a giant, beautiful, slightly chaotic forest growing out of stone. And Park Güell was amazing, ridiculously touristy but amazing. I took, like, a million photos. Ugh, the tourists. I hate the crowds. So, Barcelona sorted out your travel itch, then? Paris still on the cards? We talked about doing that together, remember? Yeah, Paris is still the plan! We're definitely going to try and book something for October, I think. Flights are surprisingly reasonable if you book in advance. I was looking at a long weekend, maybe four days? We could hit the Louvre, obviously, and wander around Montmartre… Four days sounds perfect. I booked that new ‘Call the Midwife’ boxset from the library, we could have a cosy night in too, just to recover from all the sightseeing. Although, to be honest, I’m slightly exhausted just from  thinking  about all the planning. I had a crazy weekend on shift. Oh no, what happened? Anything major? You looked knackered when I left. Nothing  major , just the usual Friday night chaos. Two admissions with suspected overdoses - thankfully, both are doing okay now – and a really difficult patient who was incredibly distressed. It's draining, you know? You see so much sadness. I can only imagine. It must be so tough. You’re amazing, doing what you do. Seriously. I feel guilty complaining about being jet-lagged after a city break. Don't be! You deserve a break. Did you meet anyone cute over there? Don’t tell me you spent the entire time admiring buildings! There  was  one guy… at a little bar in the Gothic Quarter. We chatted for a while, he was from Valencia. Really friendly, clearly a local. But… nothing came of it. I was too busy sight-seeing to properly pursue anything! Plus, you know I'm terrible at flirting. Oh, don’t sell yourself short! You just need someone who appreciates your incredible ability to memorise historical facts about Catalan architecture.

…So, you said you were a teacher? That's a world away from what I do. Dealing with teenagers must be…an experience. An  experience  is putting it mildly, David. It's a constant, evolving, slightly chaotic, and occasionally rewarding experience. Fifteen years I've been at it, mostly secondary school. English Literature, mostly. It’s surprisingly fulfilling, you know? Seeing a child genuinely connect with a poem, or understand a complex theme… it’s really quite something. Though some days, I question my sanity. I can imagine. I find myself questioning my sanity regularly, but in a different way, I suspect. I’m in tech, primarily – building and scaling online marketplaces. It's all about algorithms and growth hacking and… well, a lot of jargon I barely understand myself half the time. My current project, though, is a platform connecting freelance artisans with buyers globally. Ethical sourcing, sustainability – that's the buzzword now, isn’t it? It is. Sounds fascinating, actually. Much more tangible than staring at spreadsheets all day, which was my previous job, before teaching. Shocking choice for a literature student, I know. Junior accounts manager at a logistics firm. Dorchester’s not exactly brimming with glamorous career options when you’re fresh out of university. Dorchester, right? Lovely little town. Family holidays when I was a kid. I grew up in London, obviously. It’s amazing how different the pace of life is. You must miss the countryside sometimes, though. I do, periodically. Although, to be honest, the countryside around Dorchester can get a bit… monotonous. Give me a lively market town any day. The Logistics job, though… that was soul-crushing. Just endless paperwork and feeling completely disconnected from anything meaningful. Then I saw an advert for a teaching assistant at the local comprehensive, and just thought, “Why not?” Best decision I ever made. What about you? What did you do  before  the tech world? It feels like everyone in that industry has a bizarre, pre-tech backstory. You’re not wrong! Mine's a bit… scattered. I tried law school, ended up dropping out after a year. Too much memorization, not enough… solving. Then I bussed tables in Soho for a while. Honestly, probably learned more about people and resilience from that than I ever did in a lecture hall. That’s where I met some investors, actually. They liked my hustle. They offered me seed funding for my first, very unsuccessful, online pet supplies business.

Honestly, Liam, I'm proper stressed about this house situation. It's gettin' to me, it really is. Still on about the washing up, then, lass? You know, a little scrubbin' never hurt anyone. It’s not just the washing up! It’s the whole lot! Finn leaves his gym kit lyin’ about like he owns the place, Maisie’s got a tower of dishes taller than me, and Ben… well, Ben just seems to think food magically cleans itself. It’s a tip! A right state, it is. I’m doin' more than my fair share, aren't I? You do your bit, aye. But you're a bit of a neat freak, love. You always have been. Remember when we were kids and you'd rearrange my Lego? That's different! That were Lego. This is our  living space . We're supposed to be adults, not a load of overgrown teenagers! I spent ages last weekend cleanin' the bathroom – scrubbin' the grout, everything! And Finn left hair everywhere again. Everywhere! Alright, alright, calm down. I'll have a word with them. Maybe a house meeting's in order. A proper sit-down, establish some ground rules. A house meeting? Will that even work? Last time we tried that, Ben just kept saying, “It’s chill, I’ll sort it later,” and then it never got sorted! He’s got a point, hasn’t he? 'Chill' is basically his motto. But we can't just let it carry on like this. It's not fair on you. Tell you what, I'll suggest a rota. Washing up, cleaning, weeding the little garden patch… Weeding? Seriously? Ben thinks a weed is anything green and out of place. He'd pull up all the flowers! We’ll have to supervise then. Look, maybe we make it a bit more… engaging. Like, whoever does the most chores gets to choose the takeaway on Friday? Now you're talkin'! That might actually motivate them. But what about Maisie? She's pretty hopeless. I reckon she’d ‘forget’ to do anything. We could pair her up with Finn. They could be the 'cleaning duo.' Finn's got the energy, Maisie's got… well, she’s got enthusiasm, at least. And Ben, we’ll make him do the bin duty. He can't argue with that. It's basic. Bin duty… that's brutal. He’ll hate it.

Right then, that’s the lot. My back's killing me, Arthur! Heavens, they load you up with things these days, don't they? Honestly, felt like I was carrying the weight of the world. Aye, seems that way, Margaret. You got everything on the list then? Did you manage to find them elderflower biscuits I were after? Let me see... milk, bread, eggs, potatoes, sausages… ah! Here they are. Elderflower biscuits, two packets. They were on special offer, you know. Saved us a bob or two. Did you now? Always good to get a bargain, ain't it? Them biscuits are a right treat, you know. Reminds me of my mum, she used to get ‘em for us when we were little. Used to sit by the fire, me and my brother, dunkin’ 'em in a cup o’ tea. Proper happy times, them were. Don't start reminiscing, Arthur! You’ll be at it all afternoon. Though, I do remember your mum. Lovely woman. Always smelled of lavender. You’ve got her eyes, you know. Lavender, eh? Never noticed that myself. More liked of a bit o' peat, if I’m honest, workin’ in the garden. What about them sausages? Are they the ones you usually get? The Cumberland ones, yes. Figured we'd have ‘em for supper tomorrow night. With mashed potatoes and gravy, of course. Can’t have Cumberland sausages without mashed potatoes and gravy! Right you are. Can’t argue with that. Though, I was thinkin’ maybe a bit of fried bread to go with ‘em? Just a little bit, mind. Don't want to go overboard. Arthur! You and your fried bread. You’ll be the death of me, you will. But alright, I suppose. A little bit won't hurt. Did you see that young lad in the Co-op? Bless him, struggling with a mountain of nappies and baby wipes. Aye, I saw him. Looked like he was about to drop the whole lot. Poor fella. Must be a handful, lookin' after a little one. Makes you think, don’t it? It does. It really does. All that responsibility. I remember when the children were little. It was a constant whirl. But lovely, of course. Wouldn't swap those years for anything. Though, a bit of peace and quiet now and then would have been nice! Aye, I can imagine. You done well, Margaret, you did.

Oh, aye, I bet! Poor Liam, trying to impart wisdom on that one. Gran doesn't need quadratic equations, pet, she needs a nice cup o’ tea and a sit down. He's a good lad, though, wanting to help. It wasn't  that  bad, Auntie Carol. I just thought… well, she’s been asking about calculations, like for her pension. I figured a bit of maths might be useful. Useful? Quadratic equations? What’s useful is knowing how many sugar cubes go in a pot o’ tea, and whether I can still manage to get the telly remote without needing Arthur to help. And your maths, lad, looked a right muddle! Aye, Liam. Stick to summat you know. Like which football team’s having a good run. That’s proper knowledge. Now, now, Arthur. Don't be dismissive. Liam’s just being thoughtful. Still, Gran’s right, sugar cubes and telly remote control are far more pressing matters today, aren't they? Right, who wants a biscuit? I’ve got ginger nuts, custard creams, and those chocolate ones young’un loves. Chocolate, please, Auntie Carol! Ginger nuts are fine for me, love. And a strong brew. Arthur here keeps forgetting to put the milk in. I do not! I just prefer it without. A man’s entitled to his preferences, aren't he? Always the same, you two. You've been arguing about tea for sixty years! Right, biscuits and tea sorted. Now, about the telly. I was thinking of putting on “Escape to the Country.” Gran seems to like a good bit of countryside. As long as they’re not showing those fancy houses in London. Give me a crumbling cottage in Yorkshire any day! Somewhere with a proper fire and a garden big enough to grow rhubarb. There’s a house on in North Yorkshire tonight, Gran. Near Thirsk. Stone walls and a big garden. Actually, it's got an orchard too. An orchard! Now you’re talking. What kind of fruit? Apples and pears, mostly. And some plum trees. You know what they say, an apple a day keeps the doctor away. Though I reckon a pint of bitter’s just as good, if not better. Honestly, Arthur! Right then, “Escape to the Country” it is. And afterwards, I was thinking we could play a game of dominoes. Unless anyone’s got better ideas? Dominoes sound good. I'm pretty good, you know.

Honestly, this NHS waiting list is ridiculous. I've been trying to get a check-up for months. Feels like they're just shuffling you around. Tell me about it, innit? My mum’s been waitin’ for a specialist appointment for ages. She’s gettin’ right on at me to sort it, but what can I do? It’s a right mess, the whole system. I've been lookin' at those online health tests, you know, the ones that send you a kit. Yeah, I saw an ad for one. Pretty pricey though, weren't they? Is it worth it? Seems like a bit of a gamble, doesn't it? Like, if it flags something dodgy, what do you do then? I've considered it. My Nan was saying she just ordered one – a full blood work thing. Said she's feeling a bit run down. She’s always been one for taking preventative measures, my Nan. Reminds me of her constantly saying, "a stitch in time saves nine!”. Bit old-fashioned, that one. It’s a tricky one. They can give you peace of mind, but also cause unnecessary anxiety if you're already feeling a bit worried. Plus, you still have to get the results interpreted by a proper doctor. My mate, Dan, did one and everything came back ‘slightly elevated’ for some random thing. He spent a week obsessing over it before he spoke to his GP who told him it was probably just because he'd had a curry the night before. Right, that’s exactly what I was thinkin’! It's a bit like those fitbit things. I got one last year, thought I'd finally get in shape. Ended up just stressin’ over whether I’d hit my step count. I was walkin' round the block five times a night just to get to ten thousand. Mad, innit? Absolute madness. It’s the dopamine hit, isn’t it? The instant gratification of a little badge popping up on your screen. It’s manipulative. Speaking of technology, have you seen the new Samsung foldable? The adverts are insane. The what now? Honestly, I'm happy with my old phone. It does everything I need it to. These fancy gadgets just seem like a way for companies to get more money out of you. They break down quicker too, I reckon. I’m with you on that.

Speaker_1, said, scrolling through her phone. Speaker_2, , her mum, looked up from a crossword puzzle spread across her lap. "Fancy olives, are we, love? Bit posh for a Tuesday, aren't we? Just get the regular ones. And don’t forget milk. We’re down to the dregs." Speaker_3, , Eliza's younger brother, piped up from the floor where he was engrossed in a football video game. "And crisps! Definitely need crisps. Salt and vinegar, the proper ones, not that cheese and onion rubbish." Speaker_4, , Eliza's dad, who’d been silently reading a newspaper, lowered it slowly. "Right, let's try and stay focused. We’ve got a shopping list to build, not order a banquet. And Liam, turn that racket down a bit, will you? It's giving me a headache." He had a distinctly London accent, a source of much amusement for Eliza growing up. Eliza grinned. "Alright, alright, Dad. No lavish spread. But the olives make sandwiches better. Seriously. So, bread, milk, olives... what else?" Margaret sighed good-naturedly. "Don't forget the washing powder. We're running low. And I need some more bath bombs. My skin’s been playing up." "Bath bombs?" Liam scoffed. "You're like a grandma, Mum." "Keep your opinions to yourself," Margaret retorted, playfully glaring at him. “And David, did you remember to get that fly spray? The one Sarah recommended? There’s been a right swarm of bluebottles lately. Buzzing about everywhere." David frowned. "Sarah's repellent? I bought some. It's in the shed, I think. Though, honestly, they seem immune to everything. Remember that huge spider in the bathroom last week? Gave me a proper fright." "Oh, don’t remind me," Eliza shuddered. "I nearly screamed the place down. I got a bite on my ankle, I think. It's itching like mad." She showed her leg. "Proper angry looking, innit?" Margaret examined it with a practiced eye. "Hm, could be a mosquito. Try some cream. We’ve got hydrocortisone in the cupboard, that usually does the trick. Or a cold compress. That helps too.” "I've got some of that insect bite stuff from Boots," David offered. “Stronger than the cream, right? Might be worth a try.” Liam, momentarily pausing his game, asked, “What about those electric zappers? Do they actually work?” “They’re a waste of money, love,” Margaret said dismissively. "They attract everything  except  the ones you actually want to kill.

Ugh, P.E. was  brutal  today. Mrs. Davies made us do suicides five times! Five! I swear, my legs are gonna fall off. No way! Really? Ours was alright. Just a bit of volleyball. Although, Liam  did  spike the ball into Mr. Harrison's face. No! Seriously? Did he get in trouble? Mr. Harrison’s got a face like thunder. Apparently not. Mr. Harrison just sort of… rubbed his face and muttered something about needing new glasses. Liam's a menace, you know. Total chaos agent. He always is. Remember when he swapped all the sugar and salt in the science lab? Don't remind me! Mr. Peterson nearly had a meltdown when he tried to make tea. It was everywhere! Pink, sugary salt water. Legend. Speaking of science, I'm totally lost on this photosynthesis thing. Like, I get the basic idea, but the equations... forget it. Oh! I think I kinda understand it. It’s basically plants eating sunlight, right? And turning it into, like, sugar fuel. Wanna me explain it properly? Please! You're better at science than me. I'm pretty sure I'm gonna fail the test. It's the same test as Ethan's, isn't it? He’s stressing  hard . Yeah, same one. He was going on about it all lunch. Apparently, he's watching that 'Science with Sam' YouTuber to cram. You know, the one with the ridiculous hair? Oh, him. He's awful! Like, I appreciate the effort, but he’s so… energetic. It’s overwhelming. I prefer 'Cosmic Kate'. She explains stuff so clearly. Have you seen her video on cellular respiration? Cosmic Kate's good, yeah. I follow her. I’m trying to get my Instagram followers up though. It’s so hard. Everyone’s got, like, thousands. I know, right? I'm stuck at 237. I posted a really good selfie the other day, with that filter that makes your eyes look like actual stars, but barely anyone liked it. Maybe you need a theme? Like, aesthetic or something. Or post more regularly. I saw Sophie’s feed, it's all pastel colours and perfectly arranged stationary. It’s ridiculously pretty, but I’d never be able to keep up. That’s the thing! I don’t  want  to have a perfectly curated feed. I just want people to see my… well, my life, I guess. My slightly chaotic, slightly embarrassing, everyday life.

"Aye, it's proper beastly, this cold. Feels like me chest's full o’ wool. You reckon it's just a cold, Liam? Or should I be gettin' checked out?" "It sounds like a cold, Maisie. Though you’ve been looking pretty peaky. Do you have a temperature?” “Nah, not really. Just achy and proper bunged up. And I keep coughin' up…well, never you mind. I’m fair knackered, to be honest. I was hopin' to get some decent work done today, lookin’ into that AI facial recognition thing for the project.” "Right. That  would  be a lot to deal with when you're feeling like this. You rest, love. I'll order in something. Thought we could have that Lloyd Grossman curry kit we got last week. Remember? The one with the questionable instructions?” "Oh, aye! That one! The one where it tried to convince us it was gourmet cooking. Still, beats nothin', I suppose. Though last time, I swear that Madras mix-up gave me a funny tummy. Could’ve been food poisoning, actually..." "Food poisoning likely, yes. Though it was probably the extra chilli you added. Remember, everything in moderation, even spice!" "Seriously though, have you had your flu jab this year? And your Covid boosters?” “Aye, aye. Flu jab in October, Covid boosters religiously. Mum would have me ears if I didn't. She'd be on to me every five minutes, wouldn't she? “Maisie, are you vaccinated? Are you washing your hands? Are you wearing a mask?” It’s a full-time job just dodging her." "Sounds familiar. My mum's the same. Always worrying about germs. Actually, there was a fascinating article I read the other day about how AI can now analyze subtle changes in facial expressions to detect illness… even before symptoms manifest. It's a bit creepy, really." “Creepy, aye. But then again, it could be useful in hospitals. Early detection, faster treatment, all that. Imagine, a camera in a waiting room recognising someone's got a fever before they even know it themselves.” "Precisely. Though the ethical implications are huge. Consent, privacy… Who gets access to that data? It's a real minefield. It’s feeding into my PhD research, actually. I'm looking at the societal impact of mass-scale body language recognition." "Blimey, that sounds complex. Does it mean cameras will be watchin’ everyone, all the time?

Honestly, David, you’re being deliberately difficult. “Quaff”? Really? It’s barely a word! It's in the dictionary, Eleanor. Perfectly valid. And it scores me a good 23 points, doesn't it? Your turn, Mum. You’re looking rather pensive. Are you planning a tactical masterpiece? Tactical masterpiece? Don’t be ridiculous, David. I'm assessing the available tiles. Honestly, the modern obsession with points… when I was headmistress, we focused more on the joy of language, the nuance. Not simply maximising a score. The joy of language needs funding, Margaret. Can’t pay the bills with joy. Though, I confess, I do enjoy a good Scrabble. Used to use it in Latin lessons, you know. Testing vocabulary. "Aqua" was always a favourite. Latin lessons! Grandpa, you're dating yourself. I had to google “aqua” just last week. So, Mum, what are you playing? You’ve been staring at those vowels for five minutes. I’m thinking… “Aerie.” It's a bit… pedestrian, perhaps, compared to your “quaff,” David. But it connects, and it opens up options. And it’s a perfectly respectable word. "Aerie," clever. Eight points. Alright, I need to think. This is tougher than I thought. Reminds me, did you manage to get to the butcher’s today, Eleanor? The queue was absolutely monstrous. Absolute gridlock at the Arndale. Couldn’t even get near the place. Don’t remind me! I abandoned the attempt. Honestly, you’d think they were giving away gold bars. Ended up having to go to that little supermarket on the corner. Quality wasn't fantastic, but at least I got something. You and I need to plan to order online next time, it saved us so much hassle last Christmas. Online butcher? Good heavens. Back in my day, you simply endured the queue. Built character, it did. Taught patience. You're romanticising slightly, Arthur. It was often freezing cold, and Mrs. Henderson always hogged the best cuts. Speaking of hogging, I was just reading an article in  Record Collector  magazine. Apparently, there's a vinyl resurgence. People are paying ridiculous amounts for obscure 80s synth-pop. Really? You know I used to be  obsessed  with synth-pop! Bow Wow Wow, The Human League… I had all the singles. I should dig those out. Should I post a picture of my collection on Facebook? Eleanor, dear, do you need to broadcast your vinyl collection to the entire internet?

Blimey, that's a good cuppa, that is. My throat was drier than the Mendip Hills in August. Nearly finished clearing that patch of brambles, you know. Nasty things, brambles. Proper determined to cling on. Aye, they are that. Determined, just like some of the things I’ve dealt with in the antique trade. Though, bless my soul, these working party tasks are a bit more straightforward than haggling with Parisian collectors. Did you manage to wrestle those roots out, then? They’re a devil to shift. Not entirely. A few stubborn ones are mocking me still. I’ll get ‘em tomorrow. This TME thing is surprisingly… demanding, isn’t it? I thought it'd be a bit of light gardening. Light gardening! Oh, Arthur. You’ve got a proper optimistic view of things, haven’t you? My back's singing a mournful tune. Still, it's good to be doing something, isn’t it? Keeps the cobwebs off the brain. You were saying earlier about your work… printing systems, wasn’t it? Sounds terribly clever. Never quite understood the technical side of things myself, always preferred the aesthetics, you see. Well, clever's a bit strong, Penelope. More… persistent, perhaps. Years of persuading people that my electro-photographic process was the future. It wasn't an easy sell at first. Trying to convince publishers that they could copy pages faster and cheaper... rather revolutionary, you see. Revolutionary! Like finding a Georgian snuff box disguised as a later imitation. That’s a good day, that is. So, where did you do most of your demonstrating? Germany, primarily. Dusseldorf, Frankfurt, Hamburg... for years I lived out of suitcases. Exhibitions were the key. You had to  show  people. Publish and be damned, my motto. The Germans, they appreciated the precision. The efficiency. They’re not easily swayed by fancy words. You had to prove it. We had a particularly good showing in '78 at the Frankfurt Book Fair. Remember that? Frankfurt… vaguely. I was rather occupied with sourcing a set of Regency silver dessert spoons at the time, if I recall correctly. Always a drama getting those through customs, you know. But tell me more about Germany. Was it… lonely? Lonely at times, yes. But stimulating. I met some fascinating people. Brilliant engineers, ruthless businessmen, eccentric artists... You learn a lot about yourself when you’re miles from home, surrounded by people who don’t necessarily understand your accent.

Honestly, Dad, English Lit is killing me. Mr. Davies is obsessed with analysing every single comma. It's all about interpretation, isn’t it? Like, what’s the  point ? Well, lass, that's a bit like asking what the point of a scenic route is, isn’t it? It's about appreciating the details. Understanding  why  the author used that comma, or that particular word. It’s about unlocking their meaning. But some of it just feels… pretentious. He was droning on about the semiotics of Virginia Woolf’s garden shed yesterday. A garden shed! Woolf was a clever one, your Virginia. And everything has meaning if you look hard enough. Think about the etymology of words, for example. Ever wondered where ‘quinoa’ came from? Quinoa? Seriously? We’re talking Woolf and you’re going into ancient grains? Well, it’s a good example. It's from the Quechua language of the Andes. So, a word all the way from South America ending up on our plates in Cornwall. Pretty fascinating, that. Makes you think about how language evolves and travels, doesn't it? I suppose. Still, I’m thinking about uni courses. I’m leaning towards Linguistics. Proper studying of language, rather than just… dissecting novels. Linguistics is brilliant, love. York has a good department, you know. Or maybe Manchester? Less travelling for your mum. Have you looked at their phonetics courses? That'd be right up your street. The way different accents shape the same words… Yeah, I’ve been browsing. It’s just… philosophy keeps popping up. Everyone’s saying I should do a philosophy module. Apparently, it’s good for critical thinking. Philosophy is good. But it can get a bit… removed from the real world, can’t it? Like, arguing about the existence of unicorns when there’s a perfectly good bacon butty waiting. Exactly! Though, I did read this really interesting thing about determinism and free will. It’s messed with my head a bit. Determinism, eh? That’s a tricky one. Reminds me of that time I saw a stagecoach race, years ago. Absolutely bonkers. Driver was muttering about fate and the horses’ destiny. Then one of his horses tripped over a badger and they came last! Showed him, didn't it? Badger interference! Clearly, free will wins. Are we nearly at that service station yet? I need a toilet and a proper coffee.

Right then, that’ll be about done, I reckon. Smells lovely, this does. Proper roast potatoes, you've got there, ANON. Not like that pale stuff you get in some places. Aye, I've been watchin' 'em like a hawk. Don't want 'em burnin'. My nan's recipe, this is. She could do roast potatoes like nobody else. Proper crispy on the outside, fluffy inside. Can’t get that nowadays, can you? They look alright to me. Better than anything I've managed to cook in weeks, that’s for sure. Just beans on toast most nights, that’s me. Beans on toast!
