At your age, lad? You need proper nourishment. You'll be all skin and bones. Your mum not keepin' an eye on you? Nah, Mum’s fine. She's got her own things to worry about. Besides, it's cheap. Gotta keep the bills paid, you know. That’s true enough. It’s a bleedin’ nightmare, isn't it? Everything’s gone up. Even a tin of tomatoes feels like a luxury now. Nan used to stretch a pound for a week, she did. She was a resourceful woman, your nan. Knew how to make everything last. Used to mend socks 'til they were inside out! I remember, used to go round there for tea. Proper Yorkshire puddings, too. Not these thin excuses you get nowadays. Puddings? You making Yorkshire puddings too, ANON? Trying to! First time for everything, isn’t it? It’s a tricky one, apparently. Got to put the batter in just as the meat’s coming out of the oven, or else they'll be flat as a pancake. Don't you worry about it, lass. It’s all about the heat. Hot fat in the pan, that’s the key. Reminds me of me mum. She'd get the oil sizzlin' something fierce. Sounds like a fire hazard, that does. A little bit of sizzle never hurt nobody. Speaking of families... how's young Liam doing? Your brother, right? He’s alright, thanks for asking. Starting his apprenticeship next month. Electrician, he is. Seems happy enough, which is a relief. Worried about him, mind you. It's hard work, proper hard. Good for him. Proper trade, that. Keeps you busy. Aye, and gives him a future, which is more than I can say for some. What about you, Dan? Still managing at the building site?

…and honestly, the conjugations for the subjunctive mood in Spanish are just  brutal . I swear, every student I've spoken to this week has been fighting a silent war with ‘hubiera’. Subjunctive, eh? Sounds fancy. Makes my shift at The Crown seem pretty straightforward, doesn’t it? Though, arguing with Barry about the correct way to pour a pint of Guinness… that can get pretty complex. He’s convinced it's all about the angle. Barry sounds like a character. I imagine a lot of character comes with the bartending job? You seem to enjoy it, though. You always look… relaxed, even when the place is packed. Yeah, I do alright. Pays the bills, keeps me active. Plus, I get to hear all sorts of stories. You wouldn't believe some of the proposals I've witnessed. Last Tuesday, a bloke got down on one knee right in front of the dartboard. Classic Birmingham. What about you? Still loving teaching languages? Mostly. Some days are tougher than others. This term feels particularly draining. Lots of teenagers who think TikTok is a legitimate substitute for grammar lessons. But then you get a student who suddenly clicks, who finally “gets” the subjunctive, and it makes it all worthwhile. Speaking of teenage angst, are you still playing football? I remember you mentioning it last time. Still trying to. The knees aren't what they used to be, mind. Trying to stretch them out a bit, but it's a constant battle. We’re in a league with a few teams from Solihull now. Proper competitive, actually. Sarah’s been nagging me to get a proper physio, you know? To avoid crippling myself. Sarah sounds like a good influence. How’s she doing? Still training for the marathon? She is. Absolutely relentless, that woman. Training schedule is more demanding than my boss's. Speaking of relentless… I need to get my driving test booked. Been putting it off for ages. It's ridiculous, I'm nearly 25! Oh, that’s important. Living in Birmingham without a car… you’re pretty limited. Why haven't you done it yet? Just… procrastination, I guess. It’s the theory test that gets me. Keeps failing miserably. All the hazard perception stuff messes with my head. Trying to spot potential accidents when I'm already stressed about the multiple-choice questions. It’s a vicious cycle. I completely understand.

Honestly, Arthur, you’ve been circling the biscuits tin like a sparrow for the last ten minutes! We’re going to be terribly late for break time at the community centre if you don’t settle down. And for heaven's sake, stop fiddling with that watering can! Just admiring the fuchsias, Doreen. Lovely colour, innit? Reminds me of the ones my Nan used to have back in Costessey. Though hers were always a bit patchier, truth be told. And well, a biscuit would be nice. A digestive, if you’ve got any. Running late already? I thought you two were the masters of leisurely schedules. What’s all the commotion? And Doreen, are those biscuits I smell? Glorious. Peter, you wouldn't believe it. Arthur’s been mesmerised by the flowers and, predictably, demanding biscuits. We're meant to be at the community centre by eleven, helping Fiona set up for the donation box drive. Donation box, eh? For Gambia, wasn’t it? Lovely country, Gambia. Always wanted to go. Shame about the driving though. Seems a bit mad, doesn't it? All those mopeds and donkeys on the roads…couldn’t manage it, I reckon. You’d need nerves of steel, Arthur, I’ll grant you that. I read a report about their road infrastructure – or lack thereof. It wouldn't suit you, all that chaos. Still, a worthy cause, eh? Sending those garden tools for the farmers. Fiona's doing a cracking job organizing it. She is. I was just thinking, Peter, we really ought to make a proper banner for the box. Something eye-catching. People are always rushing past. Maybe something with a picture of a smiling child? Good idea, Doreen. I could probably get something printed fairly cheaply. I still have contacts from when I ran my business, you know. What about something like, "Help Us Grow a Better Future in Gambia"? A bit cliché, perhaps, but it gets the point across. Sounds a bit... fancy, doesn’t it? Maybe just something simple? "Donations for Gambia," that'll do. And a picture of a lovely geranium, if you can manage it. Geraniums do well, you know. Less fussy than fuchsias. Arthur, geraniums aren’t exactly representative of the Gambian climate. We need to appeal to people’s generosity, not their gardening preferences. Perhaps a picture of the crops they’re trying to grow? Millet, I think it was?

Honestly, I spent like, three hours last night scrolling through TikTok. Three! It's a black hole, I swear. Tell me about it. I tried to limit myself to just checking emails before bed, and ended up watching a guy build miniature furniture for hamsters. Don't ask. Hamster furniture? Seriously? That’s… oddly specific. Is this a new trend? Should I be starting a hamster furniture business? Don’t you dare, Liam. We’ll be drowning in tiny sofas and miniature dining tables. Anyway, has anyone seen that new horror film, "The Whispering Pines"? Apparently, it’s genuinely terrifying. Oh my god, I’ve heard about it! Sarah from work said she didn't sleep for two nights after watching it. I'm a bit scared to even look it up. I'm always up for a scary movie. But only if we have loads of snacks! Popcorn, chocolate, maybe even some of Mum's brownies... Brownies! Now you’re talking my language. We need a proper feast. Want to order pizza? I’m feeling a pepperoni and mushroom. Pizza sounds amazing. But let's not forget about the leftovers from dinner. We’ve practically got a fridge full of that chicken curry. Speaking of, wasn't there a sale on mango chutney at the supermarket yesterday? I meant to grab some. You and your chutney obsession, Chloe! It’s delicious, but seriously. There's like, a whole shelf dedicated to it in your pantry. It’s an essential! You can’t truly appreciate a good chicken curry without mango chutney. Anyway, what’s everyone been up to this week besides doomscrolling on TikTok? Did you hear back from Jake about that concert? No, still nothing. I’m starting to think he’s forgotten all about it. It’s so frustrating! I was really looking forward to seeing that band. Give him a chance, Freya. He’s probably just busy. Although… …he  has  been awfully quiet lately. Liam! Don't start. Freya doesn't need your romantic commentary. She's got enough to deal with. Honestly, it's just a bit annoying. I don't want to seem clingy, but a simple text back would be nice. Don't worry, you’re not clingy. Just send him a casual text. Something like, "Hey, just checking in, hope you're well!" Nothing intense. Agreement. Casual is key. Remember that disaster with the grand romantic gesture I tried with Emily?

Cor, that was a right lovely cuppa, Margaret. Proper strong, it was. Best I’ve had all week. Though me knees are creakin’ somethin’ awful now. All this sittin’ you see. You always say that, Arthur! And they’re not  that  bad today. A bit of a walk will do them good. Shame about the rain, mind. Aye, a right gloomy look it’s got. Looks like it'll open up any minute. Should've brought me anorak, should have. Anorak! Don't be daft, Derek. It's hardly a blizzard. A bit of drizzle never hurt anyone. It's just – getting home… getting home’s the bother. What's wrong with getting home, Arthur? The bus comes every half hour, doesn't it? It  did . That's the thing, innit? They changed the route last month. Said it was for “efficiency reasons." Efficiency! They’ve made it twice as long to get back to Costessey. And the walk to the new stop… it’s a killer. They do love a re-organisation, don’t they? The council, I mean. Always meddling where they shouldn’t. Remember when they changed the traffic lights on Magdalen Street? Nearly caused a riot! Oh, Derek, you and your Magdalen Street stories. You told me that three times already this afternoon! It wasn't  that  bad. No, but it’s the same principle! They don’t think about folk like us, do they? Folk who ain’t got cars zoomin' about. Speaking of cars… did you see young Tom Wilkins drive past earlier? In that new Jag? Blimey. Show-off, he always was. Never understood what all the fuss was about with them fancy foreign things. Give me a good old Vauxhall Viva any day. Reliable. Now  that  was a car. Oh, Derek, you and cars! You're forever reminiscing about old Vivas and Fords. It's like talking to a museum. Well, they  were  proper cars! Not all this plastic and bells and whistles you get now. These modern ones, you can barely get your head under the bonnet to have a look. Absolutely. No character. No soul. Just… complicated. Heard tell they've got computers controlling everything now. Computers! In a car! Madness, I tell you. Are we going to talk about cars all afternoon? Arthur’s worried about getting home, remember? We need a solution. I was thinkin'... perhaps Margaret could give me a lift?

…and honestly, the traffic has been horrendous. I thought getting away from Birkenhead on a Friday afternoon was bad, but this… this is a whole new level. Are you two alright back there? Dad, you haven't fallen asleep again, have you? No, no, just… contemplating the sheer volume of lorries. It’s quite overwhelming, isn't it? Reminds me of the oil rigs, actually. Massive logistics operations. Though, admittedly, fewer biscuit crumbs. Don’t you start comparing motorway traffic to oil rigs, Michael. It's bad enough as it is. And I’m perfectly fine, thank you very much. Just enjoying a bit of the scenery. Though, all I’m seeing is grey concrete and flashing brake lights. Well, look on the bright side, we’re getting closer to your new place, Maureen! It's bound to have more than concrete. Gardens, hopefully? A decent kitchen? Less opportunity to observe the nation’s driving habits? Gardens are definitely on the list. I'm dreaming of roses, you know? Proper, blowsy, rambling roses. This flat just didn't allow for that. And a proper kitchen! A space where I can actually  bake  without knocking things over. I’ve missed baking. Remember that Victoria sponge you made for Emily’s wedding, Maureen? That was a masterpiece. Practically disappeared within minutes. Oh, don’t remind me! It was the only thing I was remotely proud of doing in the last few years, truth be told. Teaching was… well, it was teaching. It wore me down. I needed somewhere that felt like home. Somewhere with light. You deserve it, Mum. And the house  is  lovely. Bigger than you initially thought, right? And the garden is proper big. I saw pictures, it's got space for a greenhouse, even. It does, it really does. But moving… it’s daunting. All the boxes and the sorting. And the car! Oh, the car. I’m dreading getting it there. It's a beast, isn't it? That Rover. It's a classic, Maureen. A proper workhorse. Though, I do worry about those suspension springs. They have been sounding a bit… rumbly. Definitely needs a service. Dad, when was the last time you actually had it checked properly? Honestly? Ages. Years, probably. Been meaning to… you know how it is. Life got in the way. Fewer planning applications to deal with these days means fewer excuses to pop down to the garage, I suppose.

Honestly, Mum, I’m still gutted about the bike. Like, properly gutted. I was actually thinking of posting about it - you know, just to raise awareness. Maybe someone saw something. Darling, you shouldn't waste your energy engaging with that negativity online. It’ll just attract trolls. And besides… you don't need to. I have some really good news. Really? What? You’re joking, right? Please tell me it’s not another one of your…optimistic surprises. Remember the 'worm farm' you tried to set up in the garden? Very funny. This is a  genuinely  good surprise. The police called this morning. They recovered your bike! No way! Seriously? Where was it? Who took it? Well, they found it abandoned down by the seafront, near the pier. Turns out, some kids, local lads, nicked it as a bit of a laugh. They were showing off to their friends, apparently. The police caught them this afternoon. Not a very clever idea, was it? Showing off! That's awful! They could have hurt themselves, or someone else. And what about  my  bike?! Is it…okay? Any damage? It’s a bit scuffed, a few scrapes on the handlebars and a slightly bent mudguard, but nothing major. They said they’ll have it cleaned and polished for you, and it'll be ready for collection tomorrow morning at the station. I’ve already arranged it. Oh my god, Mum, you're the best! Thank you so much! I can’t believe it! I've been so worried I'd have to save up for ages to get a new one. College is expensive enough as it is. Don’t mention it, love. I know how much that bike means to you. You practically live on it! I’m just glad they found it. It’s a relief. Although… knowing you, you'll probably be posting about  that  all over Instagram now. Probably! A before and after! #BikeRescue #Blessed #HastingsCycling. And I'll tag the police, to say thank you. They were pretty helpful, apparently. Just be mindful of what you post, alright? Don't want to get anyone into trouble or make things worse. Speaking of which, how’s the college application going? Have you sent off the personal statement yet? Almost! I’m just tweaking the last paragraph. It’s harder than I thought, actually. Trying to make myself sound…impressive. It feels a bit fake, you know?

Right, that's it! I’m officially declaring war on Trans-Siberian Railway routes! Honestly, who designs these things? It's utterly impossible to connect them! Bit dramatic, Rhys? It’s just Ticket to Ride. And you’ve massively overextended yourself trying to claim all of Russia. You're leaving gaps everywhere. It's classic Rhys. Wild ambition, followed by spectacular collapse. Just like that time he tried to build a badger sett in the garden. That was a  very  ambitious badger sett, Gareth. And it would have been magnificent had the soil not been so…uncooperative. Besides, this is different! This is about strategic dominance! Strategic dominance over a cardboard railway network? You’re a strange bunch, you are. Still, reminds me of trying to get funding for the community centre back in the day. Constant battling for scraps. Now  that  was strategic dominance. Remember the council meeting in ‘98? Pure theatre. Theatre and a lot of shouting, Dai! And me ending up making everyone tea to diffuse the tension. Speaking of, anyone want another cuppa? I’m making some Welsh cakes too. They need to cool down a bit. Oh, Welsh cakes! That would be lovely, Bronwen. Thanks. Rhys, stop grumbling and try connecting to Scandinavia. It’s much less contested. Scandinavia doesn't have the  gravitas  of Russia. It’s all fjords and smiling Vikings. No real strategic weight. You're equating railway routes with geopolitical power, Rhys. It’s a board game. It's a  metaphor , Gareth! A metaphor for global dominance! And I'm losing! You’re just suffering from over-ambition, darling. Like the badger sett. Listen, did you manage to get those train tickets sorted for the return journey? The 3:15 from Hereford? Yes, they're booked. Though the journey’s proving to be less of a delightful scenic route and more of a sardine can experience. Apparently, families are travelling everywhere now. Families are  always  travelling everywhere, Rhys. Especially during school holidays. You’ll be lucky if you can find a seat next to a toddler who  isn’t  covered in sticky sweets. Don’t listen to Dai, he’s always been a bit grumpy on trains. Here, have a cake. It might sweeten the journey. They're still a bit warm, mind you. Lots of cinnamon in these ones. Cinnamon…and a hint of…raisins? Bronwen, you shouldn't have. Raisins are an abomination.

Eleanor Ben chuckled, adjusting his glasses. "Desperately? You’ve got three wood, two brick, and a thriving ore mine. You're practically a medieval industrialist, El. I'm the one struggling here with a paltry five brick and no sheep to speak of." Ben "That's because you’re being overly strategic, darling. Sometimes you just need to grab what you can, be opportunistic. Remember that time we played Scrabble and you spent fifteen minutes planning a triple word score that was ultimately blocked by my 'quill'?" She grinned, eyes sparkling. "Don’t overthink it!" Eleanor Ben sighed dramatically. "That  was  a devastating blow. And a perfectly reasonable strategy! Quill was just... luck. But you're right. I’m probably overthinking this whole thing." He rolled the dice. "Seven. Lovely. Robber goes on your ore mine, dearest. Serves you right for your industrial dominance." Ben Eleanor feigned horror. "My ore mine! Cruel! Absolutely cruel! You know my dad practically drilled into me the importance of resource management when I was a child, practically force-feeding me economics textbooks. This feels like a personal attack on my upbringing." Eleanor “It’s just a game, Eleanor," Ben said, smiling. "Although, I do wonder, do you think your dad’s lectures unintentionally moulded you into the cleverest negotiator I know? About everything, not just board games. I’ve never met anyone who can talk their way out of a parking ticket with such conviction.” Ben Eleanor laughed. “It’s a skill, isn’t it? Learned over years of Norfolk farmers trying to convince me to buy their produce for a less-than-fair price. They’re a tough crowd, you know. Anyway, back to Catan. Speaking of negotiating and resources… it strikes me how much of this game mirrors actual global trade, doesn’t it? All these little settlements, vying for limited resources… it's a microcosm of the real world." Eleanor "Absolutely," Ben agreed. "And the robber? A very apt metaphor for geopolitical instability. Or excessively enthusiastic customs officials, depending on your point of view.” He paused, taking a sip of his beer. “It's interesting, though, how different drinking cultures influence how we approach these things. My mates back in London, we’d play board games fuelled by pints of bitter, arguing intensely about the optimal tile placement, then forgetting why we were arguing five minutes later. It was all much more… chaotic.”

Honestly, the bins were the final straw. Three different colours, different days, different rules! It’s like a logistical nightmare. I spent twenty minutes yesterday trying to decipher the council website. Welcome to suburban life, Liam. Kerrie’s been battling them for ages. Remember when she tried to argue about the size of the recycling bin? Apparently, they don’t care if you're a postgraduate with a degree in organizational psychology. Oh, don't I know it! Cardiff Council are just as bad. Honestly, the younger generation, relying on spreadsheets and websites. Back in my day, you just knocked on the council worker's door and had a nice chat, didn’t you? Sorted everything out with a cup of tea and a biscuit. Now it's all automated nonsense. Progress, right? Though I miss the simpler times. So, the moving stuff... how's the furniture situation? Are you keeping the chaise lounge? I still think it's brilliant. I'm selling it, actually. Too big for the new place. It'll look ridiculous in a flat. Plus, it’s a nightmare to move. Speaking of moving, Kerrie, have you managed to sort out the white goods? Fridge, washer, tumble dryer... all that jazz. Buying those things is always a headache, isn't it? I’ve been looking at those new induction hobs – apparently, they're brilliant. But they're a bit pricey. Remember that dodgy washing machine I bought from Currys? Burst a pipe and flooded the downstairs! Cost me a fortune to fix. Oh yeah! The Great Washing Machine Flood of '18. Still gives me nightmares. Did you ever check the warranty? Warranty? Don't be daft! I was lucky to get it working again at all. Speaking of things that go wrong, has anyone seen the news about that hospital waiting list? Absolutely scandalous. My niece, bless her heart, is waiting for a knee replacement. Been on the list for nearly a year! It’s terrifying. I’m seriously considering getting private health insurance. It's a ridiculous amount of money, but… you just don't know what's going to happen. My mum's been having those weird skin rashes, and she's been putting off going to the doctor. Honestly, it's a postcode lottery. Yeah, it's awful. My mate’s sister needed an emergency operation and had to wait three days on a trolley.

Honestly, Mum, this traffic is mental. I swear, it hasn’t moved an inch for the last five minutes. Are you sure we couldn't have just gotten an Uber? Absolutely not, Liam. Your grandfather would haunt me. He loved this Volvo, you know. Said it was the only thing that could navigate London without losing its mind. And we’re saving money. Ubers are a luxury. Besides, I like driving. Yeah, but it’s stressful! Some of these people are proper aggressive. Did you see that bloke in the van flashing his lights at me just now? Like I was doing something wrong! London drivers, darling. A unique breed. Just ignore them. You’ll learn. Road rage won’t get you anywhere, believe me. I dealt with far worse when I was your age cycling everywhere. Easy for you to say, you’re behind the wheel. Speaking of which, are you sticking to the speed limit? I'm convinced you’re creeping along. I am perfectly adhering to the posted limits, thank you very much. I’m not about to get a ticket. Unlike some people who were speeding last week… Don't remind me. I paid that fine, Mum. It’s gone. And it was just a tiny bit over, honestly. A tiny bit can be a significant bit, Liam. Anyway, are you still enjoying the TLS? You were saying last week you found some interesting articles. Yeah, it’s pretty good actually. They had a really fascinating piece on the future of publishing – digital versus print. Bit depressing if you think about it. People are just glued to their phones, proper abandoning books. It is a concern. I see it every day at work. Submissions are down, print sales are… well, they’re not flourishing. But there’s still something irreplaceable about the physicality of a book, wouldn't you agree? The smell, the feel… it’s an experience. Totally. I love the smell of old books, especially. My grandad always had piles of them in his study. Though, the convenience of a Kindle is hard to beat, I can’t lie. Convenience isn’t everything, darling. It lacks soul. Remember that trip we took to France last summer? That tiny bookshop in Avignon? The owner was a character, completely resistant to e-readers. Said they were soulless rectangles. Yeah, he was brilliant! Totally stuck in his ways.

…and then the seagull just  snatched  it right out of his hand! Right out his hand, Liam! A full sausage roll! He was stood there, mouth open, lookin’ like a right lemon. Aye, that’s brilliant, Chloe! Poor Uncle Derek. He's so particular about his sausage rolls too, isn't he? Always wants the pastry just so. Typical Derek. Honestly, the drama he makes over a bit of pastry. Remember that time he sent the curry back at that Indian restaurant? Said it was ‘too orange’. Too orange? Seriously? He's a legend, our Derek. Never change, Uncle D. Okay, okay, let's hear  my  holiday story then. Prepare yourselves. Picture this: Cappadocia, hot air balloons, sunrise... postcard perfect, right? Right, go on then, what happened? Don't leave us hangin'! Well, I’d finally managed to get a decent selfie with a balloon in the background – you know, Insta-worthy – and as I was scrolling through to find a filter, a goat decided to eat my croissant. Right in front of my face. A goat ate your croissant? Seriously? I'm not makin' it up! It was a proper, brazen goat. Just strolled up, nicked the croissant from my hand, and munched away like it was nothin’. I panicked and dropped my phone! Luckily, it was okay. But the croissant… gone. Oh, that’s gold! Only you, Elly, could have a goat steal your breakfast in Turkey. You looked a right picture, I bet. You should've used it for a story! "A girl, a croissant, and a hungry goat." Could be a book title. See? That's why you're still a student, Elly. You’re too easily distracted by goats and croissants. I'm balancing spreadsheets all day, keeping accounts in order, and  you’re  getting mugged by livestock. Hey! It's an enriching cultural experience! Plus, it was better than what Liam did. Oi! What's that supposed to mean? Remember that "romantic" boat trip you took Sarah? Oh, don't remind me. The one where you were trying to impress the girl, and you accidentally steered the boat straight into a flock of ducks? Right, alright, it was a slight navigational error! And the ducks were fine! They just quacked a bit. It was a  moment . A moment of sheer panic, more like! I saw your face, Liam. White as a sheet. Proper embarrassing, that was.

…and honestly, Alistair, battling a blizzard in a tent hardly sounds like relaxing. It sounds terrifying! I mean, I appreciate the romantic notion of being utterly connected to nature, but a flooded tent at -5 degrees isn’t exactly conducive to inner peace, is it? Now, now, Moira. Don't get your knickers in a twist. It’s not  always  a blizzard, you know. And "utterly connected" is the thing, isn't it? That's the point. There’s a… a stillness you find out there, when you’re stripped bare of all the modern nonsense. No telly, no internet, just the wind and the snow – and hopefully a good sleeping bag. Aye, Dad’s got a point. It's not about  enjoying  the discomfort, Moira. It’s about learning to manage it, to become resilient. It's like... mental yoga, really. You’re testing yourself, learning your limits. And the rewards, when you get through it… they're unparalleled. Waking up to a sunrise over a snow-covered glen… you can’t buy that kind of feeling. Mental yoga, is it? Right then. I think I'll stick to actual yoga, thank you very much. And I’d rather buy a sunrise, honestly. Perhaps a particularly vibrant print. Less likely to involve frostbite. Seriously, Alistair, you’re pushing seventy. Shouldn’t you be sticking to gentle rambles and birdwatching? Birdwatching's lovely, Moira, but it lacks a certain… challenge. And pushing seventy doesn't mean I'm suddenly incapable of a bit of adventure. It means I’ve earned the right to have a bit of adventure! Besides, I’m careful. I always check the weather, tell someone where I'm going… I'm not completely mad, you know. He’s meticulous, Moira. Absolutely meticulous. He researches the area, knows the route like the back of his hand, packs enough emergency gear to survive a small apocalypse. He's more prepared than half the people I know who just pop down to the shops. Apocalypse gear while wild camping? That sounds like a recipe for attracting unwanted attention from the local wildlife. Are you sure you're not trying to lure Bigfoot out? Bigfoot! Good one, Moira! No, just sensible precautions. You wouldn't want to be caught short with a broken ankle and no way to signal for help. Remember that time you fell hiking in the Lake District, Moira?

Right, that was brilliant. Honestly, I haven’t felt that relaxed in ages. That little detour through the countryside was a good call. Aye, weren't it? Needed a bit o' green after that concrete jungle o' London, didn't we? Though, I still think we shoulda stopped for a proper pasty. Cornwall’s practically on the way home! Liv, we’ve been driving for eight hours. My stomach would have staged a full-scale revolt if I’d added a pasty to the equation. Besides, we have that lovely roast planned for tonight. Remember? Your mum's been promising that beef wellington for weeks. Oh, aye, the Wellington. You know I always secretly hope she burns it. Just a bit. For the drama. You’re awful. She puts so much effort in. And it's genuinely delicious. Speaking of delicious, did you finish ‘The Secret History’ yet? I was asking you about it on the phone, and you just mumbled something about deadlines. Sorry, sorry! Deadlines are brutal this week. Loads of new data coming in. But yeah, I finished it last night. Absolutely breathtaking. Donna Tartt is a genius, isn't she? The prose... and the characters. All those impossibly privileged, morally ambiguous students… I thought so too! The atmosphere she creates is just incredible. That sense of brooding, impending doom… it really clung to you, didn't it? I keep thinking about Henry Julian. Such a fascinating, unreliable narrator. Aye, he was. And the whole Greek mythology woven in… absolutely clever. Did you catch the symbolism with Dionysus? I was reading an article about it this morning, explaining how it related to their whole group dynamic and their descent into… well, everything. I picked up on bits and pieces, but I'll have to look that up. I tend to just absorb the feeling of the story, rather than dissect it academically. Which is probably why I’m an engineer and you’re a corpus administrator! Cheeky! Someone's feeling superior 'cos they've got a fancy postgraduate degree. Not superior, just… different. Although, on the subject of different, have you heard about that new Fellini retrospective at the BFI? I was thinking we could go next weekend. Fellini? Oh, right. The Italian director? '8 ½'? 'La Dolce Vita'? I’ve  heard  of them. Didn’t do much studyin’ him at uni mind. We were all about the contemporary British stuff, weren’t we?

Right, so Captain Awesome has landed his spaceship… but it’s a bit wobbly, isn't it, Leo? And Princess Sparkle needs to rescue him. He needs a stronger base, Mum! Like… like a pyramid! A sparkly pyramid! With rainbow bricks! A sparkly rainbow pyramid. I like your thinking, Rosie! That’s brilliant. See, Leo? Rosie’s got the engineering skills already. Now, where’s that instruction booklet for the spaceship? I’m trying to remember if we have a blue cone for the engine… I used the blue cone for the antenna on the sparkly pyramid! It's for Captain Awesome's secret messages. Of course you did. Very resourceful. Right then. We were talking, weren't we, about that funny phrase Mrs. Higgins used today? Remember? About the… sparkly unicorn? Not quite, love. She said, "Don't put all your eggs in one basket." Have you heard that before? Yeah! Dad says it when I have loads of Pokemon to trade and I give them all to one friend. Exactly! It means don’t rely on just one thing. It’s an old saying. My granny used to say it all the time. She had a chickens! Real ones, not just in a picture. She’d be scattering corn around the garden, and she’d say it if I tried to put all the corn in one spot, rather than spreading it. Did Granny have a typewriter? She did! A big, clunky one. It made such a satisfying  clack-clack  noise. I used to love watching her type letters. Sometimes she’d let me peck at the keys, but I made such a mess! Do you know what a typewriter is, Rosie? No. Like a computer? A bit like a… very old computer. Before computers, people used typewriters. It's no where near as easy as using Excel, you know. Imagine trying to edit a document on a typewriter! It was all about correcting fluid, and Tipp-Ex. Can we play PlayStation now? Please?! Hold your horses, Leo! We're having a lovely chat. Besides, I've got to finish marking those essays on the Roman Empire. Blimey, they’ve got some misunderstandings. One boy thought Hadrian’s Wall was to keep  the Romans  out! Silly! Romans were  in  the wall! Exactly! See, Rosie understands. You're going to be a brilliant historian one day. We need to teach you Excel, though.

Aye, well, I was sorting through the garden shed this morning. Mud, you know, clings. And it was easier to just chuck on this than change. Don’t fuss, Margaret. It's just an old shirt. At least I’m here, aren’t I? Smelled lovely when you walked in. This coffee’s champion, by the way. Strong as anything. It is good, Margaret. You’ve definitely stepped up your game. Though the marmalade… a bit too chunky for my liking. I prefer a smoother preserve. Reminds me of that farm we drove past on the way here, actually. Remember that one, just outside Guiseley? All those apple trees, laden down with fruit? Aye, I saw it. Looked like an absolute paradise. I often wonder, do they have those pick-your-own days anymore? Seems like everything’s getting so corporate, all this farming. Used to be proper little family affairs. Reminds you of those deserted medieval villages, doesn't it? You know, the ones they find when they're building estates. Empty, silent, swallowed by the fields. Remarkable, isn’t it? All that history, just under our feet. I read a fascinating article about the Weald in Kent. Used to be teeming with iron production, then it just… vanished. Like a mirage. Speaking of vanishing things, have you driven down Bingley Road lately? It's an absolute nightmare. Roadworks everywhere! They’ve ripped up half the street. Don’t remind me! I had to detour all the way round yesterday. It added nearly twenty minutes to my journey. What are they even  doing ? Seems like they've been digging the same hole for six months. It’s like they're building a new Roman Empire, one pothole at a time! Still, at least it gives the builders something to do. Indeed. I was thinking about making some of your lovely plum jam again, Margaret. Do you remember when we tried to make elderflower cordial? That was a disaster, wasn't it? Tasted like… well, I can't quite put my finger on it. Something medicinal. Oh, don't remind me! That was a foul concoction. We nearly threw the whole lot away. I’ve been trying to grow herbs in the garden, you know. Basil, rosemary… it’s a constant battle against the slugs. Slugs. The bane of every gardener’s existence. You know, I worry about my Aunt Mildred.

Honestly, Janice, this year has flown by. Feels like Christmas was just around the corner, and now we’re talking about New Year's Eve already. Tell me about it, David! Where has it gone? I’m absolutely knackered. That flu bug's been going around the ward like wildfire. I swear, I'm spending half my shift handing out paracetamol. Are you having a quiet New Year’s, then? Hey, you two! Yeah, it’s crazy how fast time goes. We were just discussing that at work - deadlines looming, trying to get everything tied up before the break. I'm going to Hannah's. She’s doing a massive potluck – apparently, there’s a vegan paella! A vegan paella? Blimey! Sounds a bit ambitious, doesn't it? You'll need an army of chefs just to get the rice right. Exactly! But Hannah's got this thing about trying new recipes. Anyway, what about you two? Any big plans? Just a quiet one, I think. A nice roast dinner, a bit of telly, maybe a few fireworks on the telly if it’s raining. Don’t fancy battling the crowds at the pub. How's your mum doing, Janice? Still managing with the arthritis medication? She is, thankfully. Dr. Patel’s adjusted the dosage slightly, seems to be helping. She's been quite clever, sticking to those gentle stretches he showed her. Although, she's moaning that the cream she’s using for the itching is smelling something awful! Keeps saying she smells like a lavender farm exploded. Oh, poor thing! Have you tried that Eucerin cream? My friend used it for eczema – she said it was brilliant, and unscented. That’s a good shout, Chloe. I'll mention it to her. She's terribly stubborn though, always says she doesn’t want to bother me. I tell her, “Mum, you  are  me in a few years, so don’t be daft!” That's solid logic, Janice. You have to be firm with them. Speaking of bothered, I've been trying to help my sister, Susan, with her Facebook. Utter chaos! She keeps posting pictures of her cat, Winston, wearing tiny hats. Winston in hats? I need to see this! Facebook is a minefield for older relatives. They just don’t grasp the concept of privacy. My grandma once accidentally shared a picture of her dentures with everyone! Oh, bless!

Honestly, this algorithm is driving me mad. It’s meant to be identifying trends in consumer sentiment, right? But it keeps flagging “slightly damp dog” as a major negative comment about the new biscuit range. Seriously! I've spent the last three hours trying to debug it, and I'm starting to think it's developed a vendetta against canines. Slightly damp dog? Oh, you’re pulling my leg. No way. That’s brilliant, though. Exactly the kind of ridiculous thing that can happen with AI. Sounds like you need a break, love. You look properly stressed. You’ve been glued to that laptop all week, haven’t you? Tell me about it. Postgraduate life is not the glamorous whirlwind of intellectual stimulation everyone pretends it is. It's mostly staring at lines of code and questioning my life choices. Though, the money  is  decent, thankfully. Rent in London isn’t cheap, you know? No kidding. My flatshare is… well, let's just say the shared fridge is a source of constant tension. So, what's the biscuit company? Are you secretly trying to sabotage their marketing campaign? No, nothing like that. They’re a big one, though. Sort of old-fashioned, proper British biscuits. Honestly, their target audience seems to be pensioners. Which might be why my algorithm is so obsessed with dogs – apparently, that's a key demographic for biscuit enthusiasts. Only in England! Speaking of old-fashioned things, did you see that "Great British Baking Show" finale? Absolutely gutted for Paul. He was robbed! Oh my god, yes! I was screaming at the screen. That cardamom krumble was a masterpiece. It's genuinely criminal they didn’t give it to him. I mean, the judge’s comments about it being "a little bit too complex"?! What are they even judging? I know! It just feels like they wanted a predictable winner. Anyway, enough about soggy bottoms and complicated pastries. How's your family? Has your mum started dropping hints about me settling down yet? Don't even go there. She's been asking about your "career progression" – apparently, a copywriter isn't quite the stable path she envisioned for you. Though, to be fair, she does admire your independence. And recently she's been going on about Uncle David’s grandson – apparently he’s a “lovely young man studying something very serious at Cambridge”. Oh, the horror! Serious studies.

Honestly, Fiona, I’m feeling it in my back. This transcription work is killing me. I swear, I spend more time hunched over a keyboard than standing upright. I really need to get back into Pilates. Remember that class we took, ages ago? Pilates, eh? That’s a memory. I vaguely remember you complaining about the instructor’s relentless positivity. Me, I’m actually feeling pretty good. Been doing those morning walks around the park. Keeps the mind clear, you know? Edinburgh's crisp air does wonders. You both sound far too energetic for a Sunday afternoon. Honestly, a good lie-down and a biscuit is my idea of exercise these days. Though, I suppose putting words on paper is  sort of  a workout for the brain... And the eyes. Oh, the strain on the eyes! A biscuit wouldn’t go amiss, Mum. But I’m serious. I need to move. I’m stiff as a board. And I keep seeing these articles about the importance of core strength for older women – apparently it prevents falls and all sorts! Don't start projecting that onto me, Eleanor. I’m hardly ancient. Though, I’ll admit, climbing Arthur’s Seat is getting slightly more… challenging than it used to be. Challenging? You’re just getting soft, David! Still, it’s lovely you're out walking. Keeps you connected to the city. I miss proper fresh air, sometimes. Living in London... it's just… grey. And expensive. Don’t even  mention  expensive. Have you seen the prices of houses around here lately? It’s insane! We were looking at that little semi-detached in Ealing – three bedrooms, garden – and it's listed for almost half a million! Half a million! For something that needs a complete overhaul. It’s ridiculous. Absolutely ridiculous. Edinburgh's climbing too, of course, but not at that rate. You could still get something decent, a flat with a view, for that money. Though, a house… that’s pushing it. Honestly, it’s heartbreaking. My generation – we bought houses for a pittance compared to this. You both work hard, you deserve security. Are you seriously considering moving, Eleanor? We're toying with the idea, Mum. Just toying. The commute is dreadful, the cost of living is squeezing us dry... It's tempting to move somewhere smaller, more affordable. Somewhere with a little more… peace. But leaving London… it’s a big decision.

Honestly, it’s breathtaking, isn’t it? You’d never think you were in a city, just… swallowed whole by nature. Aye, it’s grand, that it is. Bit breezy though, innit? Me hands are startin’ to ache already. I should’ve brought thicker gloves. You always do say that. Are you alright? You seem a bit… quieter than usual. Still stressed about the new corpus tagging protocol? Aye, still a bit bothered, to be fair. It's not exactly rocket science, but the sheer volume is a nightmare. They've gone and added, like, a whole new sub-category for slang used  specifically  within online gaming communities. Gaming slang! Honestly! You try tagging "noob" in a thousand different contexts. I spent three hours yesterday just debating whether a "pwned" instance was ironic or genuine. Only you would get into that level of detail. It sounds… intense. Engineering has its own complexities, you know. I’m wrestling with drainage solutions for a new sustainable housing project. Trying to balance environmental impact with affordability – it's a constant battle. Drainage? Right. Sounds… practical. Less philosophical than deciphering teenage internet lingo, anyway. Heard anything new about the Budget? Seems like everyone's panicking about it. It's pretty grim, isn’t it? Especially for young people. My dad’s absolutely livid. He’s been hammering away at spreadsheets, trying to figure out how the proposed VAT increase will impact his business. It's small, a carpentry workshop he runs, but every little bit counts. Me mam’s frettin’ too. Her energy bills are already through the roof. She’s started coverin’ the windows with that bubble wrap stuff – proper lookin’ like a spaceship, she does. Said she’s givin’ up on summer holidays this year. Bubble wrap? Wow. That’s… resourceful. Though I can’t say it’s exactly aesthetically pleasing. Actually, speaking of frivolous… have you seen the price of theatre tickets lately? Oh, don’t even start! I was lookin’ at tickets for  Wicked  last week. Just for a single seat, midweek! It cost more than me rent! Exactly! Utter madness. I was thinking about seeing  Hamilton  when it's back in London. Reckon it’s worth the splurge?  Hamilton ? You know I'm a sucker for a good musical. But the price…  Hamilton , eh? Fancy. You’ve been saving up, haven't you? A bit. Freelance engineering doesn’t exactly scream "consistent income", you know.

Right, alright. That's… bold, Karl. Very bold. Like a Smurf exploded. You’re sure you’ve got the right shade for the shed? Remember Maureen said it was 'duck egg', not 'Smurf blast', yeah? Calm down, Kev. It's a work in progress. Duck egg is terribly beige. I needed a little… life. And Maureen knows nothing about colour. Honestly. Besides, I’m experimenting. You know I like to push boundaries. It’s… artistic license. Artistic license? You're painting a garden shed, Karl, not directing a Shakespeare production! Remember that play you were involved in, what was it, 'As You Like It'? Didn't go down a storm, did it? Audiences preferred the Rovers Return, I hear. That was… an experience, yes. The director had… eccentric ideas about woodland nymphs. And the set design was atrocious. I told him, I said, "A single fern doesn't constitute a forest, Clive!" But no, he insisted on a plastic badger. A plastic badger! A plastic badger! I’ll give him that, that’s pure gold. Speaking of gold, fancy a punt on the Grand National? I know a fella… Absolutely not. Money doesn't buy happiness, Kev. It buys expensive paint, which then needs applying to garden sheds. Besides, I'm trying to focus on… well, on making this look vaguely presentable before Anon notices. He's got a bee in his bonnet about the state of the backyard, doesn't he? Keeps muttering about 'kerb appeal'. Kerb appeal? He's living in a back yard, Karl! Who’s looking at the kerb?! Although, I did see a listing for a place down the road, proper fancy, got a patio and everything. Three-bed, too. Must be costing a packet. Everything does these days. It's madness. All this urban development. They’re ripping up entire neighbourhoods. It's not progress, it’s vandalism. Remember that little antique shop on Smithdown Road? Gone. Just a block of luxury flats now. Aye, that place was good. Got a right bargain on a vintage record player there once. Thought I'd finally get around to playing all me dad’s old Elvis vinyl. Never did, mind. Too busy driving folks about. See? That’s what I mean. Memories lost. Items discarded. Speaking of discarded, do you still have that toolbox I borrowed last summer? The one with the adjustable wrench? Oh, aye. Still got it.

Blimey, this is a lot less… dramatic than the mountains were this morning, innit? Just… fields. Endless fields. And cows. So many cows. Yes, darling. Poland is rather… agrarian. It's a lovely, gentle green, though, isn’t it? A change from the sheer rock faces. Though I do miss the views. Gentle is one word for it. Boring is another. Are you sure you’re alright, though, Eleanor? You’ve been awfully quiet since we passed through that little village. Oh, perfectly alright, Chloe. Just… contemplating. This trip, you know? It feels rather monumental, doesn’t it? Years I've spent surrounded by… things. And now, just this campervan and you. It’s rather freeing, actually. A little frightening, maybe. Frightening good, I hope! Think of all the horrifying piles of junk you've got rid of! Honestly, I didn’t think you’d manage to clear out that much. Your house was practically a historical site. It was. And so much of it was nonsense. Sentimental rubbish, mostly. That collection of ceramic thimbles… honestly. Who needs a hundred ceramic thimbles? Your Aunt Mildred, apparently. Remember her insisting you’d be a renowned collector? Don’t remind me. She also insisted I'd be a barrister. Cambridge Graduate, you know, clever girl, should be arguing cases in court! It never quite worked out, did it? Hence the TEFL and now… this. Hey, there's nothing wrong with a bit of TEFL. Besides, you’re a brilliant teacher. My students in Bury would adore you. They'd love your posh accent! Though, you know, forgetting your vowels gets a bit tiring after a while. I try to soften it for them. Don't want to intimidate the poor dears. How are things back home, by the way? Still seeing… Liam? Nah, finished last month. Turns out he wasn’t quite as keen on the whole ‘travelling the world’ thing as I thought. Said he didn't want to leave his nan. Typical. Still, I’m alright. Honestly, it's a relief, to be honest. Gives me more time for, you know, adventure. Like this! Excellent. Freedom is a wonderful thing. Though adventure does come at a cost, doesn't it? The petrol alone is bleeding me dry. Have you looked at the bank balance recently? Briefly. Let’s just say we’re living frugally. Found a little supermarket back there, though.

Are we nearly there yet, Dad? My back’s killin’ me. This journey feels like it's gone on forever. Nearly, love. Just gotta get off at the Fulwood junction. Fifteen minutes, tops. You've been moanin' about your back since St Anne's. You’re tougher than you let on, aren’t ya? You’re probably just fiddling with your phone too much, Poppy. All that scrolling isn’t good for your posture. It’s not just the phone, Zuzana! It's a combination of everything. The car, the sea air, probably the existential dread of A-Level physics. You know. Standard teenager stuff. Physics, eh? Should've stuck with English, like your mum always said. Less brain-bending. By the way, did you ever finish that book you were reading? The one about the Viking woman? Aye, I did. It were brilliant! Proper twisty and dark, right up my street. Reminded me a bit of those stories Gran used to tell us about the Pendle witches. All that Lancashire folklore. Oh, I remember those! Your dad used to tell them too, didn't he, Michael? A bit dramatically, I might add. I just liked to add a bit of flair! Kept you kids entertained. Remember that one about the clog-wearing ghost that haunted the mill? Yeah, and you used to make us all hide under the covers! It was terrifying. I still have nightmares sometimes! It’s funny how memories resurface, isn't it? I was thinking about Kosice the other day, about my grandmother's garden. She grew the most incredible roses. It feels like a lifetime ago. Moving house again, though, Mum. It’s just… a lot. When are we ever gonna unpack properly? We will, love. Rome wasn’t built in a day. Besides, we’ve got the new supermarket to check out first. Heard good things about that Aldi that's just opened on the edge of Preston. Might be cheaper than Tesco. That’s what I’m hoping! The prices on the fruit and vegetables have been ridiculous lately. And all this disruption with the train strikes… it’s making everything so much harder. Tell me about it! I missed half a day of revision last week because the trains were cancelled. Exam season's stressful  enough  without that. Do you think they'll postpone them, though, with all the strikes?

Honestly, Mam, you’ve appeared like a blooming apparition! I wasn’t expecting you today. Thought you were still holed up in Kendal with all those boxes. Well, I got a bit… overwhelmed, dear. All those memories surfacing. Each receipt, each postcard… it’s like reliving half a century. Your niece, Bethany, helped a bit, but there’s just  so much . I thought a change of scenery would do me good. And I knew you were free today. Your brother, Thomas, was a dear, he drove me over. Gran! You’re here! I thought you were going to be buried under piles of old photographs forever! What are you doing in Thirsk? Can you finally teach me to knit? Hello, love. Buried is a bit dramatic, isn’t it? And knitting… well, I might attempt it. But first, a cup of tea and a sit down. You look like you’ve been running a marathon. He has, practically. He's been trying to build a "self-watering plant system" using old Lego and a repurposed hamster wheel. It’s… unconventional. Honestly, the ingenuity of youngsters these days! It’s not unconventional, it's innovative! It’s using resourcefulness to solve a problem! And it’s almost working. Just need to figure out the flow rate. Gran, do you think a small pump would help? A pump, you say? Back in my day, we used a watering can and a bit of elbow grease. Simpler times. Though, I do admire your ambition, dear. It’s a shame your grandfather didn’t live to see this. He used to say I had a ‘head for figures’, and he’d have loved a bit of engineering. He would have, wouldn’t he? He'd have probably built a whole robotic farm out of biscuit tins. Speaking of things from the past, Mam, did you find any… interesting relics in the sorting? Anything embarrassing for Thomas? Oh, quite a few things. Let’s just say his teenage fashion choices were… questionable. And there was a rather unflattering photo of him in a school play, dressed as a particularly grumpy badger. A badger?! Seriously? Can I see? Please? Oh, stop it, you. You’ll be wanting to put it on social media. Honestly, the internet and these phones… I don’t know how you youngsters manage. It's all so fleeting. It  is  rather dizzying, isn’t it?

Right, so… this is a bit slow, innit? I thought a new M2 chip would be, like, lightning fast. Feels like I’m back on my old Pentium 3. Yeah, it’s noticeable. What are you running, exactly? Background processes eating it up? You gotta close all that chrome nonsense, mate. Seriously, ten tabs open? Are you having a laugh? Bit dusty around the vents, isn't it? Might be overheating. Remember when my grandad's telly kept cutting out? Turns out it just needed a good hoover around the back. Old tech, all prone to that. Dust? Seriously? I've barely touched it. And yeah, I know about the Chrome thing, alright? I was just… researching. You know, for work. Found some amazing fonts. Researching fonts? At three in the afternoon on a Tuesday? Sounds legit. Look, let’s run a diagnostics test. I downloaded this thing, CrystalDiskInfo, it’ll check the drive health. Could be a dodgy SSD too. Speaking of dodgy, did you hear about old Mrs. Higgins next door? Apparently, her cat, Winston, climbed a tree and wouldn't come down. Fire brigade had to be called! Proper kerfuffle. Blimey! Winston’s always been a bit of a drama queen. Remember when he chased my nan up the garden path? Nearly gave her a heart attack. Good thing she was doing that Pilates class, reckons it kept her fit enough. I should probably get back to that. My stomach's been looking a bit... cushion-y, lately. Pilates? You? Right. Listen, let's focus. CrystalDiskInfo says everything's looking good on the drive. Maybe it's the RAM? You only went with 8GB, didn't you? That's… ambitious for what you do. It was the cheapest option! Money doesn’t grow on trees, you know. Besides, I’m an artworker, not a video editor! You could get some of that stuff online, you know. My cousin in Cyprus does that. Sells retro consoles and games. Proper bargains. You could even get hold of a Sega Dreamcast! Remember those? Dreamcast! Now you're talking! I used to spend all my pocket money on those. Man, those were the days. Unlike this laptop. Hold on, hold on. I’ve got an idea. Check Task Manager, see what's consuming the most CPU. It’s likely some background process you forgot about. Or maybe something weird running after you installed that software for the new fonts.

Aye, it's proper nice isn't it? Much better than that awful place down the street with the fluorescent lighting. I reckon they'll do well. So, how's the TEFL work going? Still mostly online, then? Mostly. One student in Krakow, a delightful chap from Saudi Arabia, very keen to improve his business English. Otherwise, it’s a scattering of lessons. It’s… enough to keep the wolf from the door, but not exactly fulfilling, is it? It’s not quite the academic life I envisioned, you know? Remember all those postgraduate seminars in Cambridge? Now I'm explaining the difference between 'there,' 'their,' and 'they're' to teenagers. Life throws you curveballs, doesn't it? Still, you're good at it, Sarah. You always were a natural teacher. It's just... a shame you didn't pursue it properly. "Properly" being the operative word. The whole… situation with my father and the estate… it complicated things, didn't it? Took away any real sense of direction. And then... the rest. Don’t beat yourself up about it, Sarah. It was a long time ago. And you're doing okay now, really. You're here, aren't you? In Poland. Living your life. Finding little joys. Like this bistro. It's true. Poland has been surprisingly… therapeutic. It's far enough removed from everything, to almost… reinvent myself, perhaps? Though reinventing feels a bit grandiose, doesn’t it? Perhaps just a slight… adjustment. I reckon Tarnow suits you. You always were a bit of a dreamer. Remember when we were kids, and you were convinced you’d be a famous archaeologist, uncovering lost cities? Oh, goodness. I was obsessed with Indiana Jones. I even tried to dig up the garden with a spoon, convinced I'd find Roman coins. My mother was not amused. Do you ever think about those childhood dreams, Emily? What you wanted to be? Sometimes. I wanted to be a vet. Then when I started my teacher training, I thought I'd open my own language school, you know, something really bespoke. But… life kind of gets in the way, doesn't it? Especially with rent and bills these days. I’m trying to get the fitness together, though. Signing up for a Zumba class next week. Zumba! Good for you! I’ve been… well, walking. Mostly. The park is lovely, but it's hardly a vibrant fitness regime.

Honestly, Dad, the ticket prices for the Steam Fair this year are ridiculous! Thirty quid for a day out? It's gone up so much. Remember when it was fifteen? Thirty quid ain't bad, love. Think about what you'd pay for a day at Disneyland. At least you’re seeing real engines, not cartoon characters. And it's a good cause, innit? The Dorset Steam Fair always donates to charity. It is a lovely event, David. I went last year with Mrs. Higgins from the care home. She absolutely adored the stationary engines. But I agree, the cost is creeping up. I suppose everything is these days. Are you going, Chloe? Yeah, Mum. I was thinking of going with Liam. We wanted to see the vintage tractors, especially. But I'm trying to be sensible with my student loan at the moment. Liam says we could share a ticket, but I don't know if they let you do that. Can’t rightly say, Chloe. Always best to ask. They usually have a good info booth near the main entrance. Speaking of entrances, did they improve access for folks with disabilities this year? Remember last time, it was a right struggle getting Mrs. Peterson up that muddy bank. That's a very good point, David. I’ll have to check. The care home has several residents who'd like to go, but only if it's accessible. They really enjoy the atmosphere, you know, the music and the smells. It brings back memories. That's so sweet. I hope they can manage. Maybe they could hire a mobility scooter? Bournemouth often has those services. Right, Bournemouth’s a bit pricey to hire one, though, isn't it? Speaking of prices, have you seen the houses around here lately? Absolutely extortionate! I wouldn’t put a foot in the door for anything less than a million these days. Remember when you could get a decent sized house in Winton for twenty-five grand? Don’t remind me, David! It's madness. I’m thinking about downsizing, actually. My little bungalow in Harlow is getting a bit too much to look after on my own. It's got a lovely garden for the cats, but moving all this furniture... it's a nightmare. Oh, Mum, that's a big decision! Where were you thinking of moving? Closer to Bournemouth? Possibly. Somewhere a bit smaller, with easy access to the shops.

Aye, lass, I know that feel well. Spent a lifetime accumulating things, only to be faced with the prospect of movin' 'em all again. It’s… overwhelming. But Thirsk's a lovely spot, isn't it? Much better than that draughty old place in Kendal. Thirsk is gorgeous, Elsie. And a flat is much easier to manage than a big house, especially as you get older. You’ll be able to potter about so much more easily. I’m still trying to convince David to downsize, but he's got the hoarding gene, that one. He insists he needs all those old train timetables from the 60s! Train timetables? Seriously? Who even  uses  train timetables these days? You can just look it up on Twitter. Don’t be too quick to dismiss them, Finn. David finds a certain comfort in tangible history. And Twitter? Honestly, it's a cesspool of misinformation and vitriol these days. I tried to engage in a conversation about the latest play at the York Theatre Royal the other day and… well, let’s just say it didn't end well. Oh, don’t even start me on Twitter. It’s a breeding ground for dreadful arguments. I stick to Facebook, mostly posting pictures of my class. They’re much more sensible, generally. At least, until exam season hits. Exams... I remember those days. Though my worries were more about passin' than what they’re learning now. Seems like there’s a lot of fuss about not a lot these days. Schools are rubbish, anyway. Pointless homework. They keep changing the curriculum. It’s all just… complicated. Year 10 mocks are next week, though.  That's  stressful. See, Finn? That’s a good reason to cut back on the Twitter. Focus on your mocks. Thinking about it, speaking of stressful, how are things going with the church fete? You’re in charge, aren't you, Elsie? Aye, I am. And it’s a nightmare! Got no volunteers for the cake stall, and Mrs. Higginbottom's rhubarb crumble is apparently "too tart" for the judges. Honestly, the etiquette around village competitions these days... it’s appalling! They're disputing the jam label size! Oh, Elsie, you’re a saint. You’re dealing with the very heart of Yorkshire eccentricity! I could help with the cake stall, actually. I make a decent Victoria sponge. And I bet I can wrangle Mrs. Higginbottom’s rhubarb recipe down a bit.

Honestly, it’s everywhere, isn’t it? Minecraft. Poppy, darling, put down the chocolate bunny for a minute. We’re talking. But it’s Easter chocolate! Can I have another bite? It’s brilliant, Mum! You can build anything! We built a giant castle last week. And a rollercoaster! I’m sure it's very clever, Leo, but spending all day in front of a screen isn't the healthiest thing, is it? Speaking of healthy things... have you both booked your dentist appointments? Mine's next Tuesday. Dreadful, really. Dentist is scary! Well, it's important, sweetheart. Tiny little niggle at the moment, just a check-up. Leo, you’re due in a couple of weeks, aren't you? Yeah, but I don’t want to go. Last time they poked me! They didn’t poke you, love, they were just checking. Remember? And they gave you a sticker. Maybe we should get your hearing checked too, while we're at it. You've been a bit quiet lately. Why? My ears are fine! Just a thought. It’s been a busy few months with school and everything. Right, birthdays! Remind me, Poppy, when's Auntie Emily's birthday? April 27th! That’s right. And Leo’s, as you know, is just a week after - May 4th. Crazy how they’re both born so close together. Your Grandma loves it, says it's like having a double dose of birthday joy. I wish my birthday was with someone cool. Like Monet. Monet? The painter? Yeah! He painted really cool water lilies. I learnt about him in art. He did, didn’t he? Very famous. More famous than being nine, darling. Anyway, we need to think about birthday parties. Leo, any ideas? Can we have a Maths-themed party? With numbers as decorations? And cake shaped like a giant equation! A Maths-themed party... that's a first. Poppy, what about you? Anything you want? More chocolate? Maybe! Or a school trip to the zoo! We’re learning about animals. A zoo trip sounds lovely. We’ll have to look into that. Though, between school trips and birthday parties, I think I need a holiday! Honestly, the school trip to the science museum next month is going to be mayhem. Twenty-five Year 4s, all excited about explosions... Can we make radishes explode? Like in the volcano experiment? Definitely not, Leo.

Speaker_1 exclaimed, throwing her hands up in the air with a laugh. "Honestly, you're a miracle worker, Liv. Some people are just determined to be grumpy. So, how did the rest of the day go then? Did you manage to get through that particularly tricky referral?" "Ugh, don’t even get me started on Mr. Davies. He’s got aphasia, right? Post-stroke. But his family are… intense. They want him chatting about the weather and quoting Shakespeare by next week. I tried to explain the realistic timescale, but the daughter practically accused me of not trying hard enough." “That’s awful. Families can be so difficult. You have to tread so carefully, don’t you? They're grieving and scared, and they often project that onto your abilities. Did you at least get to spend some time just with Mr. Davies?” "Yeah, a bit. We looked at old photos of his pet rabbit, Flopsy. He managed to point and grunt happily at the picture. Little victories, right? But it's exhausting emotionally. Speaking of exhausting, this place is a tip! Honestly, Mum's been here, and it looks like a bomb’s gone off." "Tell me about it! I forgot how much chaos one woman can create when left unsupervised with a vacuum cleaner and a penchant for rearranging furniture. Did she at least manage to start on the washing?" "Nope. She mostly rearranged the cushions. And insisted on showing me her prize-winning marrows. Which, let's be honest, look like they’re about to burst.” Speaker_1 shuddered dramatically. “We need to tackle this mess before anyone else arrives. Are you up for Operation Declutter? Pizza and cheesy films afterwards as recompense?" “Absolutely. My brain needs a serious unwinding after dealing with Mrs. Peterson today. She insists her husband's memory loss is caused by faulty Wi-Fi. You try reasoning with that!" Speaker_2 chuckled. "Seriously though, I'm happy to help. It's good to be back, Liv. It feels like ages." "It has! Feels like just yesterday we were sneaking out to the Ashford cinema to see that awful rom-com with Hugh Grant. Remember we swore we’d never tell Mum we were even interested in that kind of film?" "Oh god, yes! 'Four Weddings and a Funeral'! And the sneaking! We had to climb over the fence because we were late. So mortifying when we got caught."

Sailing, you say? Good heavens, David, that's quite the perk! Lectures all at sea with your oral surgeon? Absolutely absurd! I remember when the NHS actually  felt … generous. These days, getting a decent appointment feels like winning the lottery. It was a different world, wasn't it, Arthur? You could practically name your own terms. I mean, free sailing! It felt almost… decadent. Though, the lectures were definitely a bit… unorthodox. Trying to explain root canals while the boat pitched and rolled – not ideal for anyone’s concentration. Prague, though, has been a revelation. Booked flights for a song last month. You should come along, Eleanor. Prague sounds lovely! I’ve always wanted to go. The architecture, isn't it just stunning? All those bridges and the castle... I read something about astronomical clocks the other day, too. Though getting tickets for performances there can be a nightmare, can't it? Remember that fiasco last year with the Royal Ballet in London? We were  sure  we'd got tickets, only to arrive and find they’d been double-booked. Double-booking is a national sport these days, isn't it? Speaking of securing things, have you lot heard about the jive event? They’re holding it at the old barn down by the river. Apparently, they’re converting it into a proper events space. Wedding receptions, workshops, that sort of thing. It's amazing what they're doing with it. Yes, the barn! Brilliant idea. Used to be just rotting away, didn’t it? A real blight on the landscape. Good on them! About time something positive happened there. It’s all part of the…rebranding, isn't it? This whole effort to spruce up the town. It is, isn't it? It's a shame what happened to it though. Remember when the square was bustling? All the independent shops and the weekly market. Now it's just chain stores and betting shops. Absolute truth, Eleanor. It was a proper market town then. The architecture, too. They ripped out so many of the original buildings in the fifties and sixties. Just awful, characterless blocks. It didn't need updating, it needed  preserving . That’s what I've always said! They demolished the old Victorian library to build that horrific concrete monstrosity. A truly senseless act. We've got to fight to retain what character we have left. So, what about the solar farm application last night?

Honestly, this sunshine is doing wonders for my mood. It’s a world away from drizzly Dorchester, isn't it? Though, I do miss a proper English cuppa sometimes. This stuff's… fine, but it lacks a certain  oomph . It's alright, isn’t it? Getting used to it. And the birdsong! It’s absolutely bonkers here. Not a robin in sight. More like… peacocks, apparently, further inland. Right, let’s get back to this moving image case study thing. I’ve been having a bit of a think about how to make it really sing, you know? Not just a bunch of clips tacked together. Absolutely. It needs a narrative, doesn't it? A real 'hook'. We talked about using short films to illustrate different communication strategies – good, bad, and downright disastrous. But how do we make it engaging for teachers themselves? They're busy, they’re marking, they're dealing with… well,  everything . Exactly. That's the challenge. I was thinking, maybe split it into scenarios. Like, "The Misunderstood Email," or "The Meeting That Didn’t Go Quite Right." Short, sharp, and relatable. Then, after each scenario, have a short analytical piece, highlighting what  could  have been done differently, with some actionable advice. What do you reckon? I like that. The scenarios are clever. But we need to ensure the advice is genuinely helpful, not just… textbook stuff. Remember Mrs. Higgins from my last school? She would roll her eyes at anything that sounded remotely theoretical. Keen to get practical, she was. Right, practicality is key. Keep it grounded. Perhaps model it on common classroom situations - parent-teacher conferences, dealing with difficult students, even collaborating with other teachers. And we could incorporate some social networking aspects, too. The way communication has evolved online… it’s a whole new minefield. Oh, absolutely! The online aspect is crucial. I've been reading some fascinating research on how even seemingly innocuous comments on social media can escalate into full-blown conflicts. Teachers need to be equipped to deal with that. It's not something they necessarily covered in their initial training. I know. And the speed of it all! A misunderstood post can go viral in minutes. Imagine the fallout for a school. I was thinking, we could create a module specifically on digital communication etiquette, targeted at teachers and even parents. Brilliant! We could even get some student input. Interview some older students about their experiences with online communication – what they find confusing, what they wish adults understood.

That was lovely, wasn't it? The air’s clear after that rain. Smells properly of salt and… well, just sea, really. It was. Though I think I’ve got a bit too much sun already. My nose is tingling. We really need to invest in proper hats. We do. Though you look rather dashing without one. All windswept and academic. Reminds me of those photos of you on that research trip to the Hebrides. Wild hair, intense gaze… studying barnacles, I believe? Don’t remind me. Barnacles were significantly less charismatic than I’d hoped. Still, fascinating creatures, actually. The way they cement themselves so stubbornly... Perhaps a metaphor for life in academia. Absolutely. So, did you hear back from Sarah about the coastal erosion workshop? She seemed really keen. I did! She’s in. Apparently, her department is finally taking climate change seriously and has allocated some funding. Can you believe it? She was practically bouncing when she told me. Said she owes you a huge thank you for suggesting it in the first place. Good! About time. I mean, it's obvious, isn't it? The coastline is changing everywhere. Did she mention what aspect she's focusing on? She’s looking at the impact of rising sea levels on the local fishing industry. It’s a really practical angle, and she’s already been talking to some of the older fishermen in Lyme Regis. Apparently, they’ve seen some drastic changes in the last twenty years. Lost entire fishing grounds, they say. That’s heartbreaking. It's hard to imagine growing up without the sea, isn't it? My grandfather used to take me crabbing down at Southend. We’d spend hours, armed with string and bits of bacon rind, hoping to catch something. My dad used to do the same. Though he insisted on using live worms. Said bacon rind was “far too refined” for crabs. He'd always tell me stories about the tides, the currents... how the sea was a living, breathing thing. My grandfather was more interested in the architecture of the piers. He'd quiz me on the engineering – the piles, the support beams… completely oblivious to the crabs scuttling beneath our feet. He was an engineer, you know. Always looking for the structures, the fixed points. Maybe that's why he never got particularly close to the sea, in a feeling kind of way.

Ugh, this show's lighting is  awful . It's really washing out everyone’s outfits. Look at Anya, honestly, that dress looks drab under these lights. Drab? Aye, maybe. But she's workin' it, lass! It's a classic silhouette, innit? That kind of simple elegance never goes out of fashion. Proper timeless. You lot down south are all about the flashy, neon colours and things layered over things. Give me a well-cut dress any day. Hold on, Yorkshire Rose! Don't start the regional fashion war. I  like  neon. It's fun! And layering is an art form. She’s not exactly setting the world alight with Anya's dress, though. It's a bit…safe. Like she’s trying too hard to blend in. Exactly! It’s predictable. And the shoes? Beige heels with that dress? Criminal! It’s a palate cleanser after all the vibrant colours we’ve seen on the red carpet this year. Remember Dua Lipa at the Grammys? Now  that  was fashion. Dua Lipa? Fancy! I saw a bit of it on the telly. All glitter and feathers, weren't it? Looked a bit much for me, to be honest. Give me somethin' I can wear to a wedding, not a disco. My gran used to say, "If you’ve got nuthin' to hide, you don't need sequins.” Wise woman, my gran. That’s brilliant! Your gran sounds amazing. But that’s the beauty of fashion, isn’t it? Expression! You can be comfortable and classic, or you can go completely over the top. Anya’s playing it  too  safe. It’s like she used a fashion template. And the hair! So boring. A sleek straight style just doesn’t do anything for her face. A bit of texture, some waves… something. It's all very… corporate. She’s probably got a stylist tellin' her what to wear. Happens, doesn't it? They want you to look “approachable” and "relatable." It's a load of rubbish, really. People can tell when you’re tryin’ too hard. Like when shops try to sell you those jumpsuits that are supposed to look effortless. You look like you've been wrestled into them. True! The effortless look is the hardest to pull off. It takes a lot of deliberate effort. I’m actually thinking of trying a corset trend I saw. Bit daring for me, I suppose, but I’m going to a club next weekend.

Honestly, Mum, Mr. Davies just  doesn't  get it. He marked down my photo of the pier for ‘lack of composition’. Lack of composition! It's a moody, atmospheric shot! The grey sky, the reflections… it’s supposed to be melancholy! Melancholy is good, love. Shows you're thinking. But I suppose he’s got a particular idea of what ‘composition’ entails. What else did you do today? Anything exciting at college? College was…college. We dissected a frog. Pretty grim. And then we had that lecture on post-structuralism. I swear, Professor Harding just enjoys watching us suffer. I think he speaks a different language. Sounds about right. Post-structuralism. Makes my head spin just thinking about it. Remember when I tried to read Derrida? Gave up after three pages. Stick to photography, then. You’re clearly better at that. Thanks. It’s just…sometimes I feel like I’m not good enough. Not good enough for Davies, not good enough for college, not even good enough to take a decent photo of a seagull. Don’t be daft. You’re incredibly talented. That photo of Grandma’s garden last summer? Absolutely stunning. Captures her perfectly, the way the sunlight hit her face… you have an eye, Elsie. A real eye. It's more than just pointing and clicking, you understand light and feeling. You always say that. Because it’s true! Now, tell me more about that pier photo. What were you  feeling  when you took it? Forget about Davies and his ‘composition.’ What did  you  see? I don’t know… sadness, I guess. It felt like Hastings was feeling sad that day. All grey and…empty. Everyone was huddled up, shielding themselves from the wind. Like the pier itself was tired, waiting for summer. That's beautiful, Elsie. See? You  do  get it. Try explaining that to Mr. Davies. Maybe he’ll see it then. Speaking of feeling things, work was awful today. Mrs. Henderson called in sick with a migraine, which I completely understand, but then the phones were ringing off the hook and Mr. Finch was giving me grief about something ridiculous. Honestly, sometimes I feel like I'm going to scream. That’s rough, Mum. Mr. Finch is always a nightmare. Should you tell him how you feel? Easier said than done, love. He's one of those people who thrives on making others uncomfortable.

Honestly, Derek, this application form is a nightmare. "Previous employment history – detailing responsibilities and quantifiable achievements." Quantifiable achievements! What quantifiable achievements does one accrue when looking after little Timmy and Maisie? Did I quantify the impact of calming Maisie’s tantrum after a particularly upsetting episode of Peppa Pig? I think not! Aye, it’s all a bit much, innit? They never made you write things like that when I was a young lad. A handshake and a promise were enough. You’d get a job down at the market, and if you were a good sort, you kept it. These days… modern life, eh? Fancy a digestive, love? You're right, Brenda. These forms are a ridiculous exercise in bureaucratic hoops. They’re designed to filter people out, not find good candidates. I'm marking essays at the moment, and you'd think the kids would at least  try  to put a sentence together. Honestly, the grammar… it’s like they’ve completely abandoned any notion of proper English. It’s the children, Derek! All this screen time. They’re losing their ability to communicate properly. Remember little Chloe, the one who bit every single child who came near her? Her mother blamed the iPad! Cheeky little tyke, Chloe. Though biting’s not the best behaviour, is it? We had a robin build a nest in the shed last year. Lovely sight, watching 'em feed the chicks. Little blighters were chirping something fierce. Reminded me of your Chloe, actually. Speaking of wildlife, I saw a cockerel strutting around my garden this morning. Bright red comb, the whole nine yards. Absolutely brilliant. My neighbour, Mrs. Higgins, is furious. Says it's disturbing the peace. She’s got a very precise idea of what constitutes peace. A cockerel! How lovely! I wish I had something like that. Just a bit of life. It’s all so… quiet here since I retired. Too quiet. I miss the little ones. Remember your birthday next month, Brenda?
