Thought I’d get you that little bird feeder you were looking at. Saw a right pretty one down at the garden centre. Though the workmanship was appalling, mind you. The little hooks were bendin’ already. Shabby workmanship everywhere you look these days. I’ve been trying to get into 3D printing. It’s fascinating, really. I’m planning on designing a little birdhouse for Mrs. Higgins' garden.

…and so, I’ve booked her flight. It's all quite sudden, really. Just a few weeks ago, I was thinking about another quiet Christmas, and now… well, now I’m getting Anya. Anya. That's wonderful, Eleanor. Truly. It's been too long since we’ve seen her. How did she react when you told her? Oh, she was overjoyed, Malcolm. Absolutely beaming. Said she was desperate to get away from the… the relentless heat, mostly. But also, she admitted, a bit lonely. The job she has is demanding, and she doesn't have a huge circle of friends there. She’s been quite brave, really, going it alone in Sydney. Brave is the word. Leaving your family, starting a new life across the world... it takes a certain kind of strength. And Brighton! She’ll love it here. It's not the bustling metropolis of Sydney, of course, but it's got a charm, doesn’t it? A relaxed feel. It does. Though I'm concerned about the adjustment. The weather, for a start. And the pace of life. She’s used to everything being open late, shops and restaurants… here, everything shuts down practically at nine. We’ll adapt. We always do. And I’m sure we can find things for her to do. Perhaps look into that pottery class she mentioned? Remember she used to love working with clay? Yes, that’s clever, Malcolm! I completely forgot about that. It would be something she could enjoy, something creative to do. But… …it’s the practicalities, you see. The flat… it's cramped, isn't it? For three of us? It's cosy, Eleanor. And we've managed perfectly well for years. We can certainly make room for her. We’ll rearrange the living room, maybe. Your sewing corner can live in the spare bedroom for a while. But what about… finances? It’s been… difficult, as you know. My pension barely covers the bills. Bringing Anya in… it's a huge responsibility. I don't want to be a burden to her. Don’t talk like that, Eleanor. You’re not a burden. And she's your daughter. She  wants  to be here. We’ll manage. I've got a bit of savings, you know, from my teaching days. We can certainly stretch it a bit. And honestly, having her here will be… a joy. More than worth any financial worry.

…and honestly, Dad, I still can’t quite wrap my head around it. The Scottish referendum result. So close! It feels like the entire country held its breath. Aye, it did. A nail-biter, that’s what it was. Though I must confess, watching from down here in Brighton, it felt a little… distant. Like we were spectators at someone else’s drama. Doesn’t affect us directly, does it? Though the ripple effects… well, who knows. Well, politically? Economically? It's bound to. And the arguments were so compelling on both sides. I had a particularly animated discussion with a student earlier – a young lass from Glasgow, fiercely pro-independence. She presented a brilliantly argued case, you know? Made me question my own assumptions. Young people have a passion for these things, don't they? Good for them. Reminds me a bit of the arguments surrounding the EU back in the day. Still, glad it’s settled, in a way. Uncertainty's a rum thing. Speaking of settling, how did that interview go for you last week? The one at King's College? Oh, the interview... It was… interesting. They seemed very keen on research experience, more so than I anticipated. They grilled me on my recent paper about post-structuralism and Victorian literature for a solid twenty minutes. Felt like an interrogation! Twenty minutes! Blimey. Sounds intense. Were you feeling confident afterwards? I’m not entirely sure. I thought I presented my ideas clearly, but they kept pushing, probing. The Senior Lecturer, Dr. Ainsworth, he was particularly… searching. Keeps a very straight face, that one. Difficult to gauge if you're impressing him or not. Ainsworth, eh? Sharp as a tack, that man. Was he the one who recruited your colleague, Davies, a few years back? Yes, that’s him. Davies always said Ainsworth has a peculiar way of ensuring only the toughest candidates survive. He practically told me it was a weeding-out process. It’s just... I really want this position. It would be a great step up. I understand. It's important. You deserve it. You've put in the work, son. Don’t let a few pointed questions knock your confidence. Now, have you heard anything back? Not yet. They said they’d be in touch by the end of the week. It’s agonizing waiting! My daughter, Sophie, keeps asking me if I got the job.

Right, so you’re telling me that cardboard box is  vital  for the mousetrap game? Honestly, Penelope, you're getting far too carried away with the engineering. It's supposed to be fun, not a structural physics experiment! Don't be absurd, David. It’s about the  suspension of disbelief , darling! We need to create the illusion of a proper mousetrap chamber. Ollie will be far more impressed with a decent prop. Besides, Leo's already got the cheese secured. Gorgeously pungent cheddar, I might add. Guys, the cheddar smells amazing, but can we move this conversation along? I'm trying to research escape room design. This mousetrap thing is only tangential. Tangential? It's  the  game! I've been practicing my ninja-like movements so I can grab the cheese without setting it off. Think I'll go for the crouch-and-sprint approach. All this talk of cheese! Honestly, you all are ridiculous. Penelope, you and your elaborate games. David, always the pragmatist. And the boys… well, the boys are being the boys. Anyone want a biscuit? I’ve got ginger snaps. Yes, please, Margaret. Ginger snaps sound perfect. Penelope, back to the vital cardboard box... are we talking double-layered corrugated, or single? Because that makes a rather significant difference to structural integrity, you know. Good heavens, David! Don't start with the structural integrity! Single-layered is perfectly adequate. Just needs a bit of tape. Reminds me of that time I was working in Boston for three months. They take their packaging  very  seriously over there. Everything is triple-sealed. You couldn't get a cracker open without a crowbar. Boston, huh? What were you doing? Researching Anglo-Saxon poetry manuscripts, actually. A fascinating project, though the weather was abominable. Drizzly, grey, and relentlessly damp. Not unlike a London November, I suppose, but somehow... more pervasive. And the portions! The American portions are  enormous . I swear, I gained five pounds just looking at the menus. My cousin lives in LA. They eat everything in massive portions. He says the kids are obsessed with sugar. Like,  really  obsessed. It’s true. I read a study about it. The rates of childhood obesity are higher in the States than here. It’s quite distressing. And the marketing aimed at children… it’s relentless. Well, they do advertise sugary cereal with cartoon characters waving at you. It’s a calculated strategy.

Honestly, darling, you wouldn’t  believe  the fabrics they had! It was like stepping into a silk dream. You’re back! Sounds promising. Let me guess, you raided another Suzhou silk shop? You know my credit card is weeping already. A little bit. But it wasn’t just silk! I found this gorgeous linen, perfect for a summer dress – light and breathable, absolutely ideal for this heat. And… …this! What is  this ? It’s… shimmering. What is it even made of? I’m not entirely sure! The seller just called it "cloud weave." Apparently, it's a local specialty. It feels like… like holding a captured sunset. It's incredibly soft, and just look at the colours. . Wow. It is beautiful. Seriously stunning. So, what are you thinking of making with it? A top? A skirt? I was thinking a long, flowing skirt. Something I can wear to those conferences, you know? Something a bit more… elegant than my usual jeans and sensible blouse. I’m tired of blending in. Blending in is your superpower, love. Don't lose it. Remember that disastrous attempt at a sequined jacket you made last year? Nearly blinded Mrs. Chen with the reflection. That was  one  jacket, and it was a valuable lesson in not attempting to bedazzle everything within a five-mile radius. Besides, I've improved. I’ve been watching those YouTube tutorials, remember? Precision is key. Precision and restraint, I hope. What about the linen? You said it was good for a summer dress? Absolutely! I found a pattern online – it’s a simple A-line shape, but with these beautiful little cap sleeves. I was thinking maybe a pale blue, with little embroidered flowers around the neckline. Something easy to wear, but still… me. Sounds lovely. Practical, you, with a dash of charm. Are you going to have those alterations done again? You know Mrs. Zhang's pricing is surprisingly reasonable. Yes! I swear, getting things fitted properly here is such a godsend. Last time I tried to alter something myself… well, let's just say it looked like a very enthusiastic octopus had been involved. A vivid description. So, roughly how much did this… cloud weave… set you back? Don’t tell me you cleared out the entire shop. Oh, nothing outrageous. About 300 yuan. It’s the linings and buttons that add up. I got some beautiful mother-of-pearl buttons.

I’m tellin’ ye, Mary, it was ridiculous. I nearly threw the remote through the telly. Sheehan was rock solid! Him and Porter, they were workin' overtime there in the scrum. Alright, Liam, deep breaths. It was a tough match. England played well, you have to give them that. At least Oisin enjoyed it, didn't you, love? Yeah! It was brilliant! Especially when Farish scored. And that tackle by Earl! Wow! Did you see it, Grandpa Moira? Indeed I did, Oisin. A very robust tackle. Though I always preferred a bit of finesse myself. My boys, when they were at school, they played rugby. Jimmy was a prop, a sturdy lad, and wee Angus, a scrum-half, quick as a flash! We used to go to every match. Aye, well, it’s good to see you’re enjoyin' it, son. You’ll be runnin’ about on the pitch yourself before long. They’re big on rugby in school these days, aren’t they? Yeah, Mr. Davies makes us do it every Tuesday. It’s hard work, but it’s fun. I'm not very good though. I keep dropping the ball. Don't worry about that, darling. Practice makes perfect. Liam’s going to teach you some tricks, aren’t you? Absolutely. I’ll show ye how to pass like a pro. After he’s off to bed, though. He's gettin’ awfully quiet. I’m not tired. Yes, you are, love. You’ve been bouncing around like a little rabbit since that try. Time for your pajamas and a story. Stories are important, you know. They fill the imagination. I used to read them Gaelic fairy tales to my grandchildren. Do you know any Irish stories, Liam? I do, Moira, I do. Loads. I’ll have to tell Oisin a few before he nods off. Though, right now, I'm thinkin’ about that last penalty… honestly! Liam! Focus on the present, will you? Let's sign those birthday cards for Auntie Sheila. She’s turning seventy, can you believe it? We need to get them posted tomorrow. Right, right. Cards. Good woman, Sheila. Another year older. She'll be demanding a rematch next time, no doubt. Can we look at the stars after I'm in bed, Grandpa Moira? Of course, dear. If the clouds behave. I have my telescope set up in the garden. We can try to find the Plough and Orion.

Honestly, it’s just… overwhelming. All this paperwork. I thought being a Language Research Administrator would involve more actual language research and less battling with conveyancing lawyers. Tell me about it. Coordinating fieldwork grants is a nightmare. Mountains of forms. But hey, at least we're in a nice building for it, right? This Printing House is pretty impressive. It is. Beats the tiny office I had back in Lincoln, that's for sure. Though, I’m starting to think moving out of London was a bigger financial gamble than I initially realised. House prices here are bonkers. Cambridge is always going to be pricey. Did you manage to find a place with a garden? You were going on about wanting somewhere your… potential… future… little ones could play. Potential future little ones. You make it sound like I’ve announced it! No, no garden. A tiny balcony. But it’s sunny, at least. And closer to my sister, which is the main thing. Speaking of, Sarah's just bought a ridiculous amount of baby clothes. So many little knitted hats! Oh, good for her! Is she struggling to decide on names? My mum’s been giving her a list. Some are… questionable, to put it kindly. "Percival"? Really, Mum? Percival! Oh, that  is  dreadful. Sarah’s leaning towards something a bit more modern. Willow, maybe? Or Finn. She’s showing me everything, obviously, tempting me with the adorable factor. I'm starting to feel a vague pressure. Like I should be thinking about it. Don’t let her – or my mum – pressure you! It’s completely your timeline. I’m still thinking about which university to send my future kids to, let alone whether they'll even  be  kids. True. You're so busy bouncing around the world for your fieldwork. You were telling me about that trip to the Basque Country, wasn't it? How's your Basque improving? Slowly! It's so frustrating. It’s a fascinating language, but the verb conjugations… oh my goodness. I’m resorting to flashcards again. I feel like a student all over again. Do you ever feel that way, slogging through administrative tasks? Like you’re forgetting your Linguistics degree? Absolutely. Sometimes I just stare at a spreadsheet and think, "I should be analysing syntactic structures, not reconciling expense reports!" But then, someone needs to keep the research wheels turning, right? And actually, I’ve been thinking about dusting off my German.

…and then the robin just  stared  at me, right? Like I'd personally insulted his family. Absolute cheek, the little blighter. You're winding us up, aren't you, Dan? Proper winding us up! Robins aren’t that dramatic, are they? He’s pulling your leg, Liam. Dan always exaggerates. Though, I do find bird behaviour fascinating. Ever read anything on avian linguistics? It's incredible how they communicate. Avian linguistics? You’re learning stuff now, are you? Thought you were just teaching people how to conjugate verbs, Tom. Well, there’s a crossover, isn’t there? Understanding patterns, structure… it’s all communication. Besides, it's not all conjugation. I'm trying to steer people away from just reciting textbook phrases and getting them comfortable  using  the language. Proper shout out to that, Tom. My younger cousin, he just parrots what he hears. Makes him sound like a broken record. Proper embarrassing when me mum’s going on about her prize-winning marrows. Marrows? Seriously, Liam? You haven’t told us about this. She’s got competitive marrows? Yeah, it’s a whole thing. Village fete, best in show, the whole shebang. She’s dead proud. Anyway, speaking of competitions… fancy a bit of grappling later? Got that new Thai boxing instructional DVD. Thinking of giving it a whirl. Grappling? You, Liam? Last time you tried MMA, you ended up with a black eye and a bruised ego. That was one time! And George was a cheat, he had a proper advantage, being built like a brick shithouse. Just need a bit of practice, you know? Gotta learn to protect yourself. You never know when you might need it. True words, mate. Especially these days. Though I reckon a good spade and a couple of raspberry canes would be a better form of self-defence for a gardener. More practical, innit? I’m with Dan on this one. A spade is far more useful. Speaking of useful, anyone seen that old acoustic I had? The Yamaha? Thought I left it here last time... Nah, didn't see it. You’re always forgetting where you put things. Probably chucked it in a box with your linguistics books. Could be. Or maybe you've sold it already. You were on about clearing out some space for a new computer, weren't you? Heard you trying to flog something else on eBay the other day – don’t tell me it was me nan’s teapot.

Honestly, I don't know why I even bother trying to make a healthy dinner on a weeknight. It's always a battle getting anyone to appreciate it. Hey, I appreciate it! And you’ve been working incredibly hard all day. Don't sell yourself short. What is it tonight? Something with lentils, I bet? You know me too well. Lentil shepherd's pie. At least it’s got vegetables. Speaking of hard work… I’m really starting to resent that commute. The M1 is a parking lot these days. Tell me about it. I spent two and a half hours in traffic yesterday. Two and a half! It completely wiped me out. I nearly fell asleep during that conference call with Mr. Henderson. Two and a half?! That's brutal. Do you think it’s always going to be like that? I was thinking about looking into getting a better car, something… more comfortable for the commute. A better car? Really? That’s a big expense, isn’t it? What are you thinking? Well, something with decent fuel economy, obviously. And maybe heated seats. My back is killing me after a day at the office and then battling motorway traffic. I was looking at those newer Skoda Octavias. They seem reasonably priced and pretty reliable. Octavia's are good. Solid choice. But… seriously? We're trying to save for a deposit, remember? That holiday to Italy we talked about? A new car would set us back  ages . I know, I know. It’s just… the thought of another winter spent frozen and miserable in the Astra… it’s bleak. And the Astra’s getting a bit long in the tooth, isn’t it? The last service cost a fortune, and I’m worried about things breaking. It’s just maintenance for now. We can cope. Think of the extra money we'd have for the holiday. Sun, pasta, gelato… You're tempting me. But seriously, you’ve heard about those electric cars, haven't you? The charging infrastructure is improving, and with the government grants… it could be a viable option in the long run. Less fuel, less maintenance... Electric’s a possibility, definitely. But the upfront cost is still pretty hefty, isn't it? And range anxiety is a real thing. Imagine being stranded on the M1 with a flat battery! My dad had a hybrid for a while, and he complained about how much he had to think about charging it.

Oh, Maureen, you’re killin’ me! Liam tryin’ to teach Gran maths? That’s rich! He's only just mastered it himself, isn’t he, love? It weren’t like that, Auntie Brenda. I was just tryin’ to help. She seemed bored. And it’s important to understand, you know? In case you need it later. Need it later? At me age? Laddie, the only equations I need involve figuring out how many biscuits are left in the tin! And I can do that perfectly well, thank you very much. She’s got you there, Liam. She's sharper than a tack, that one. Remember when she outsmarted old Mr. Davies at the bingo, eh, Maureen? Okay, okay, Gran. I get it. Maths isn’t exactly your passion. But it's important for future generations! Now, now, no need for arguments. It's lovely to see you trying to engage with yer grandma. That's what counts. We need to make sure they’re comfortable, both of them. Grandad, are you alright? You seem a bit quiet. Just admiring the wallpaper, Brenda. Reminds me of the one we had in our first little flat on Stanley Street. Bit faded now, this one, but still… brings back memories. Used to be somethin' fierce used to go on in that flat! Don’t you start reminiscing about your scandalous youth now, Arthur! Some things are best left forgotten! Remember Mrs. Higgins? Mrs. Higgins? Oh, she was a character, wasn't she? Always had a rumour about summat. Right, enough with the reminiscing! We’ve got a few things to sort out. Liam, you’re on dishwashing duty tonight, yeah? After all that explaining to Gran. And Maureen, could you pop down to the shops tomorrow morning? I'm running low on teabags, and we need some fresh scones for elevenses. Dishwashing  again ? It’s always me! You got involved in the maths lesson, didn’t you? That’s gotta earn you some chores. Besides, your dad’s got that dinner party on Saturday, so you’ll be helping with that. Restin’ on your laurels, you are. Scones, you say? With proper clotted cream and jam? Absolutely, Gran. The best clotted cream and jam you can get. And a nice cup o' tea, mind. Yorkshire Tea, none of that fancy stuff. Yorkshire Tea it is then. Grandad, I’m going to put the kettle on.

Right, so, pirates! Leo, you were saying you wanted to build a pirate ship? Out of cardboard boxes? Yes! A  really  big one! With cannons! And a flag! Can we have a parrot, Mummy? A real one? A  roar ing parrot! Like in the story! A roaring parrot, eh? That might be a bit tricky, darling. Real parrots are quite noisy and require a lot of looking after. Maybe we can make a parrot out of felt? We could do that during our stop motion animation project. Stop motion? Like Wallace and Gromit? Exactly! We can make our own pirate adventure! You two can be the pirates, I can be… the ship’s cook! Or maybe a fearsome sea captain! I want to be the captain! I’ll shout, "Avast ye!" and make everyone walk the plank! Very good, Captain. Just remember, we don't  actually  make people walk the plank! It's just pretend. Now, who’s hungry? I’ve made some pirate’s bounty – fruit skewers. Yes, please! Are there grapes? I like grapes! Me too! Can we have chocolate coins after? For treasure? Of course! Chocolate coins for treasure. Although, speaking of treasure, do you remember we're going to Stratford-upon-Avon next week for Shakespeare week? Stratford? Is that where Shakespeare lived? The man who wrote about Romeo and Juliet? That’s him! We'll see his house, and the Globe Theatre…well, a reconstruction of it. It’s going to be brilliant! We'll even see a play! Will there be swords? And shouting? Probably! Shakespeare liked dramatic scenes. Although, it's not  all  action. It's about stories and words and… magic! Magic! Like a wizard? Can we see a wizard? Not exactly a wizard, darling, but Shakespeare’s words have a kind of magic to them. They can make you laugh, and cry, and think really hard. And speaking of magic… remember that circus workshop we booked? The circus! In a  real  circus tent! With acrobats! That's right! It's next Saturday. They’re doing a magic workshop and another with stop-motion animation. Apparently, they use actual circus props. Imagine making a stop-motion film with a juggling ball! Wow! Can I learn to juggle? And be an acrobat? We’ll see, sweetheart. It’s a workshop, so you’ll learn some basic skills. But even just watching the professionals is going to be amazing.

...and honestly, the sheer disbelief on the policeman's face! I’d explained – repeatedly – that the flares were for safety. Safety! In international waters! Apparently, waving around bright red pyrotechnics near the port of Jeddah was considered… suspicious. Oh, Arthur, you always did find a way to attract attention. Sail Jeddah to Cyprus? That's quite a trip for a Sunday afternoon, isn't it? It seemed like a grand idea at the time. Needed a challenge, you know. After years of pulling teeth, a bit of open water felt… liberating. Though, being hauled in by the Saudi police wasn't part of the plan. They didn't quite appreciate the concept of recreational sailing. Recreational sailing? In Saudi Arabia? That sounds… ambitious. I taught in Riyadh for a few years myself, back in the late seventies. The restrictions were quite something, even then. Did you at least manage a good view of the Red Sea? Of course! And a rather stern lecture on cultural sensitivities. Let’s just say I learned a valuable lesson about needing proper permits for practically  everything . Clive, you were teaching in Riyadh then, weren’t you? What was that like? It was… unusual. Wonderful for the students, certainly. Eager to learn, genuinely interested. But the social restrictions… you couldn't even buy a decent bottle of sherry. Desperation led to some creative sourcing, I must confess! Remember old Mrs. Henderson smuggling brandy in her knitting? Mrs. Henderson! Good heavens, I'd almost forgotten about her smuggling exploits. I used to have a student who swore she saw Mrs. Henderson attempting to pass off Eau de Cologne as something a bit stronger to a group of visiting dignitaries. She was a character, that woman. But seriously, Clive, wasn't it fascinating seeing the blend of traditional values and a growing desire for Western education? My sister taught in Dhahran, and she said the women were particularly keen. Absolutely. The women were remarkable. Intelligent, driven… and often thirsting for something beyond the confines of their daily lives. It was a privilege to work with them, even with the limitations. A rather dramatic career choice, considering your father’s assessment of your… temperament.” "Don't you start, Giles.

…and then the algorithm just  completely  misinterpreted the sentiment analysis. We were trying to push our new range of historical fiction, and it flagged every mention of "war" and "death" as overwhelmingly positive! Honestly, I thought my boss was going to have a heart attack. Oh, that's awful, but brilliant! It's exactly what we’re talking about in the linguistics department, isn’t it? How easily context gets lost in automated language analysis. It’s almost comical, the disconnect sometimes. You’d think with all the advancements… You guys talking about AI gone wrong? I had something similar happen the other day. I was inputting data for the upcoming exhibition catalogue, and the system accidentally changed "Queen Anne’s Lace" to "Queen Ants’ Lace." Explained it to my manager, and he just stared at me. Apparently, that's a sensitive topic because of a disagreement about the botanical accuracy in an earlier edition. Queen Ants’ Lace?! That’s even better than the war-equals-positive thing! Honestly, it feels like we’re fighting a losing battle sometimes, trying to teach these systems nuance. They latch onto keywords and completely miss the bigger picture. Precisely! I’m coordinating a study right now looking at different regional dialect shifts and how they're being perceived – or, more accurately,  misinterpreted  – by machine translation software. The subtle changes in vowel sounds that are perfectly normal in, say, Essex, get flagged as errors. It’s ridiculous. It reinforces these outdated, standardised notions of “correct” English. It's frustrating, isn’t it? My project's about making catalogues accessible, which means understandable to everyone. But the software sometimes throws in these incredibly formal, almost archaic phrases. Like, instead of saying "this painting depicts a farmer," it'll say, "a rural agriculturalist is portrayed in this artistic rendering." Who  talks  like that? No one! Exactly. And it's meant to make things easier, right? Streamline communication? It often feels like it's adding layers of unnecessary complexity. I’m trying to convince my team to build a feedback loop, get users to specifically flag these weird translations, but… you know how it is. Budget, deadlines… I do. It’s the classic battle. We produce this amazing data showing the problem, and then it’s, “But how does that impact the bottom line?” It’s infuriating! We need people to appreciate that linguistic diversity isn’t some esoteric academic issue; it's vital for genuine communication.

"…and honestly, that new Adidas template is just awful, innit? Looks like a rejected Playstation game skin," Anya declared, gesturing emphatically at the muted television screen showing a blurry image of a footballer in a bright green and purple kit. A half-eaten bag of crisps lay beside her on the sofa. Liam chuckled, pushing his glasses up his nose. "A bit harsh, don't you think? I mean, it's certainly… bold. It’s trying to be modern, you know? Reflect the dynamism of the game." He took a sip of his tea. “Though I agree, the colour palette’s a bit much. Reminds me of those glow-in-the-dark bowling balls." Anya scoffed, her Geordie accent thickening with her disapproval. “Dynamism? It looks like someone threw darts at a colour chart! You can barely see the numbers, never mind the players! Remember when strips were just, like, solid colours? Proper like, navy or black? Simple, effective.” “Simple, effective, and boring," Liam countered, leaning back. "That's the problem with design these days, isn't it? Everything's gotta be 'innovative' and 'disruptive'. Sometimes, you just want a classic. Like a Birmingham City blue. Can’t go wrong with that.” "Aye, well, you'd say that, wouldn't ye? Always defending your team’s dodgy choices,” Anya teased, grinning. "Speaking of dodgy, did you see that sponsorship deal Everton got? That cryptocurrency company? What a disaster waiting to happen, that is. They're practically begging for bankruptcy." Liam nodded somberly. “It’s a worrying trend, isn't it? These sports sponsorships getting increasingly… questionable. It’s all about the money, plain and simple. Forget about genuine connection with the fans, or ethical considerations. It’s just about getting the highest bidder.” “Exactly! Remember when it was just used to be a betting company or a local car dealership? Now it’s all crypto and dodgy insurance schemes. How much more are they gonna squeeze out of the game before it becomes unwatchable?” Anya rummaged through her bag and pulled out her phone. "Speaking of squeezing, I'm proper peckish. Fancy a McDonald's? I’m craving a McNugget." "A McNugget? You're going to pick a McDonald's over a perfectly good cup of tea?” Liam asked, feigning outrage. “It’s nearly eight o’clock!” “Tea’s grand, but nuggets are calling to me, Liam. They’re practically begging.

Honestly, love, that traffic this morning was a nightmare. Sat nav sent me down a road barely wide enough for a wheelbarrow! I swear, these things are out to get you. Could’ve walked faster. Speaking of which, I grabbed a sandwich from Tesco on the way over. Their meal deals are the only saving grace. Meal deals are brilliant. I always get a sandwich, crisps and a fizzy drink. Honestly, Mrs. Davies is  killing  me with these practice subjunctive tests. It's all "If I were…" blah blah blah. Who even  talks  like that? I know, right? It's so…pretentious. Mr. Patel's explaining cell structures is… abstract, to put it nicely. He keeps using these weird analogies. Like, the mitochondria is the 'powerhouse' – okay, fine. But then he compared the Golgi apparatus to a tiny, incredibly efficient postal service. What even  is  that? Don't remind me! It was like she actually understood how to explain iambic pentameter without making everyone’s eyes glaze over.

Honestly, Mum, it’s mad, isn't it? Like, this whole religion thing. Everyone’s got an opinion. Even Liam at school was going on about Scientology. Said his uncle's in it, or  was  in it, I’m not sure. Apparently, it’s, like, a cult. Well, Liam’s uncle probably just didn’t like it. Doesn’t mean it’s a cult. There are different paths, love. It's about finding something that helps you understand the world, doesn't it? And helps you be a good person. Remember what Gran always said? "A good heart is all that matters, darling." "Pa!" But even Gran had her things. All that stuff about the nuns, and confession. It feels…weird. Like you’re just telling someone your secrets so they can…judge you, I guess. Is that what it's for? It's about absolution, love. Seeking forgiveness, and trying to be better. It’s a tradition, a comforting ritual for some. Not everyone’s cup of tea, naturally. And I’ll admit, the whole secrecy around the nuns was a bit…intimidating, even for me as a kid. You never really knew what they thought. It’s just…a bit like  The Matrix , isn’t it? Everyone’s plugging in, believing the same thing, and they don't even question it. What if it's all made up? What if the priests and nuns are just…actors? Oh, you and your films. It’s not quite as dramatic as  The Matrix , is it? People genuinely believe what they believe. They find meaning in it. And questioning is good, darling. Questioning is  healthy . Don't just accept things because someone tells you to. But be respectful too. I am being respectful! I'm just…contemplating. Liam was saying they brainwash people in Scientology. Make them cut off their families. That's not respectful. Liam says a lot of things, doesn't he? And some of them are…exaggerated. It’s probably true there’s a lot of pressure in some groups, to conform to their beliefs. It's all about control, isn't it? Happens in all sorts of things, not just religion. School, even. Cliques and peer pressure. Yeah, true. But it still feels a bit…dodgy. Like someone's trying to sell you something. Like they’re got a secret they’re keeping. Sometimes religion  is  used to manipulate people, I won’t deny that.

Some are doing amazing historical snippets, book reviews… even explaining Dewey Decimal System in a fun way. It’s a surprisingly good engagement tool. Dewey Decimal on TikTok? Now  that’s  a challenge. Imagine the hashtags! #DeweyDoesTikTok #LibraryLife. It’s too brilliant, really. But seriously, I'm still hesitant. The whole algorithm thing feels… manipulative. Like it's designed to suck you in. It is. It’s absolutely designed to suck you in. It’s a designed addiction, isn't it? Like a cleverly disguised fruit machine. But the Salford University marketing team are pushing us to use social media more. They reckon it’ll attract more students. They even had a whole training session on Instagram Reels. Reels! Oh, goodness. I attempted one showing off our rare book collection. It ended with me accidentally knocking over a stack of digitised Victorian pamphlets. The director wasn't impressed. Apparently, "historic preservation" doesn't sit well with shaky camera work and upbeat pop music. Oh, Brenda, you’re a legend! I can just picture it. I tried a Facebook Live tour of the local history archive once. It was dreadful. My microphone kept cutting out, and my hair looked like a bird had built a nest in it. See? It's not all smooth content creation and viral hits. It's a bit embarrassing, isn't it? I mean, we’re librarians. We're supposed to be the guardians of knowledge, not dancing awkwardly in front of a camera. Exactly! There’s a certain dignity to maintaining silence and order. Although, I will admit, I did have a little bit of fun trying to convince my colleagues that we should start a library mascot account.

“Right, David. So, circling back to the tape recordings – are we still intending to use those from the focus groups? I’m just having second thoughts about extracting solely quotes for the business case. It feels rather… impersonal, doesn’t it? Especially given the sensitive nature of what we're proposing." “Aye, I understand your reservations, Eleanor. But the board wanted concrete examples of patient and family needs. The recordings – meticulously transcribed, naturally – seemed the most direct way to show that. It felt less speculative than just citing statistical data, don't you think? Though, I’m open to tweaking the approach. What are you suggesting instead?" “Perhaps a more narrative approach? Weaving the themes that emerged from the focus groups – the overwhelming need for dignity, the isolation felt by carers, the difficulty accessing timely pain management - into a more flowing description. Supported, naturally, by the statistics. Less ‘quote, quote, quote’ and more ‘this is what our research consistently showed us, and these are some of the heartfelt stories that illuminated that.’" “That sounds…marginally less sterile. Alright, let's adjust the plan. Sarah in marketing can manage that. Now, on the consultation process itself. We've got the initial letters out to local councillors and community groups, haven't we? Any feedback yet?" “A trickle. Mostly inquiries about parking, ironically. And one rather pointed question from Councillor Davies about why Tunbridge Wells, of all places, was chosen. He reminded me rather sharply of the transport links, or rather, the  lack  thereof for those in more rural areas of West Kent. The geography, as you know, is challenging.” “Davies, eh? Always a stirrer. We knew we’d get that. Look, the rationale is clear. We’ve done the GIS mapping – three postcode sectors are significantly underserved for end-of-life care. Tunbridge Wells is central. It's accessible, within a reasonable distance. And the land we’ve provisionally secured… the views are rather splendid, actually. It'll be a calming environment." “The views  are  lovely, yes. But we need to proactively address Davies’ concerns. Perhaps a shuttle service from key transport hubs? Or a partnership with local taxi firms offering discounted rates for patients and families? We need to demonstrate we’re considering accessibility for  everyone ." “Good points. I’ll task Mark with looking into transport solutions. Now, let’s move onto the business case. We need to tighten the projections for local health service usage.

Oh, look at this! Remember this holiday to Cornwall, Liam? You insisted on wearing that ridiculous bucket hat! Cor, that was ages ago wasn't it? Must have been… '98? Goodness, you look young, love. And I was definitely sporting a questionable fashion choice. Still, the cream teas were brilliant, weren’t they? Speaking of brilliant, how was that interview, Chloe? You were quiet earlier. It was… okay. Honestly, a bit nerve-wracking. It was for that marketing agency, 'Bright Ideas'. They seemed to like my portfolio, but the interviewer was a bit intense. Lots of questions about campaign metrics and KPIs. It’s just… I’m not sure I'm ready for all that, you know? KPIs? Goodness, things have changed since I was applying for jobs! Just be yourself, darling. They wouldn’t have asked you for an interview if they didn’t see something in you. You’re brilliant at what you do. Remember that campaign you did for the local animal shelter? That was fantastic! Your mum’s right, Chloe. Don’t let them intimidate you. They’re probably just trying to see how you handle pressure. Did you mention your experience with social media advertising? That’s gold dust these days. Yeah, I did. I talked about managing their Instagram and Facebook, and how I increased engagement by forty percent in a couple of months. But he kept drilling me on analytics... like, the precise bounce rate on different landing pages. I just…spaced out a bit. Well, that’s something you can always learn. Don't let one interview knock your confidence. Tell you what, whilst this sauce simmers - remember Auntie Brenda's recipe? Always loved this lasagne – let's have a good chat about it. Distract you. Auntie Brenda’s lasagne! A legend, that woman. Though I always thought she put a bit too much nutmeg in it. Remember how she used to claim it was her secret ingredient? That’s true. It was… intense. Speaking of intense, did you see what Sarah posted on Instagram? She's off to Royal Ascot! All dressed up with the fancy hats and everything. Oh, bless her! Spending her inheritance, likely. Always had a penchant for flash. Actually, reminds me of your Great-Aunt Mabel. Remember I told you about her – she once tried to convince the local vicar to let her wear a tiara to church.

Honestly, Chloe, you’re tellin' me  The Ring  is scary? Like, a video tape? That's just…fashioned, innit? A right bit of clever marketing, more like. Fashioned? Seriously, Beth? It’s iconic! The whole concept – this malevolent spirit trapped in technology, slowly creeping into your life… the well, the hair… it's properly unsettling. And Samara’s face! Aye, the hair’s a laugh, I’ll give ya that. Looked like somethin' outta a fancy dress box. But creepy video tape? Nah. I’ve seen scarier things at a farmer’s market on a Saturday mornin'. Oh, and what, cows giving you nightmares? You’re being deliberately obtuse. Think about the atmosphere! The constant rain, the isolating house… it builds tension brilliantly. What's  your  pick for genuinely scary, then? Let’s hear it. Right then.  The Babadook . Now  that's  proper scary. Okay, I’ll give you that one. It’s psychologically unsettling, definitely. Less about jump scares and more about… the creeping dread of a mother’s mental health and a child's fear. Good choice. Aye, exactly! It messes wi' yer head, doesn’t it? It’s not just about a monster. It’s about grief and loneliness and how that can manifest. That’s what makes it truly terrifying. You can almost feel the woman's desperation. Definitely. It was cleverly done. Although, I still think some of the classics hold up. Have you ever watched  Hereditary ? Oh, god, no. I tried. Got about twenty minutes in and needed a strong cuppa and my mum on the phone. Too much… head-shaking, weird stuff. It did nowt for me. Too artsy, not enough… you know, proper scares. “Proper scares?” So, what constitutes a “proper scare” in Yorkshire, then? Chainsaws? Gory murders? No, no. Not necessarily. Just somethin’ that makes you stop breathin’ for a minute, then keeps creepin’ under your skin for hours after. Somethin' with atmosphere, like you said.  The Descent , that’s a good one. Claustrophobia mixed with genuinely terrifying creatures. Yes!  The Descent  is brilliant. Those tunnels were the stuff of nightmares. And the creatures… they were genuinely frightening. I love how they used the darkness and the limited visibility to build suspense. See? Now you’re talkin’! What about  Sinister ? The little drawings… and the super 8 films… proper gave me the heebie-jeebies when I saw that for the first time.

Right, Grandpa. So, I've been looking at this new iPad. The old one is just… well, it’s struggling to keep up with the kids’ games, bless them. Thought it might be nice for you too, for video calls with Sarah and the little ones. An iPad, you say? Fancy that. Never seen much point in them things, honestly. Seems a bit frivolous. Remember when a telephone was a luxury? This modern world…it’s rushed. I know, I know. But it's not frivolous when it lets you see your great-grandchildren’s faces whenever you want. And you could even look up those cricket scores you’re always moaning about! Cricket scores, hmm? Well, now you mention it…holds the memory of some good afternoons at New Road. Still, all this online business, it worries me. Someone’s always trying to get at you, isn't there? That grandson of yours, Michael, keeps telling me about phishing and scams. He's right to warn you. So, I was thinking, I could set it up for you, show you the ropes. We’d put lots of safety features on it. And I'll be here to help if you get stuck. You're a good girl, Eleanor. Always looking out. Though I still don't understand why people buy everything online these days. Just had a look at that armchair you wanted, the one from that website… ridiculous price! It's true, it  is  pricey. I’m trying to find something similar. I was actually thinking about Airbnb. Remember how we talked about going to Cornwall? Cornwall… lovely place. Used to take Margaret there every summer. Good fish and chips. Exactly! I was browsing, and there’s this charming little cottage near St Ives, perfect for a week. Pretty reasonable, actually. But it's all so… impersonal. Booking online, you don't get the feel of the place. No, you don't. Used to be you’d go into a little village, find a B&B, chat with the landlady. Get a proper home-cooked breakfast. These businesses…they're all about the pound, aren't they? That’s what I feel too. Speaking of food, have you ordered your pizza for tomorrow night? Mrs. Peterson said she’s got a really good deal on. Pizza? Oh, yes. Pepperoni, as always. Though I confess, the youngsters keep trying to get me to try pineapple.

…and then the llama  actually  spat at me! Right in the face! Absolute deluge, I tell you. Ruined the picture I was trying to get of the Andes. Utterly ridiculous. A llama? Seriously, Hamish? You, the Communications Manager, brought down by a South American ungulate? That's brilliant! I never thought you'd have it in you to be photo-bombed by a llama, of all things. Well, I’m not sure 'have it in me' really applies when a spit of llama goo is involved, Alistair. It wasn’t exactly a chosen pastime. And it wasn't just a wee dribble, it was a full-on, projectile display of llama displeasure. The guide just stood there, shaking his head. Said they don't often do that to tourists. I felt… violated. Violated by a llama. Only you, Hamish. Still, sounds like a cracking experience, even if covered in llama saliva. Better than staring at another grey Edinburgh building, eh? Speaking of cracking experiences, have you finished “The Secret History” yet? I let you borrow it last month. Aye, finished it last week. Tartan Noir said it was a masterpiece, and he wasn’t wrong. Absolutely captivating. The atmosphere, the characters… Muriel Spark would be proud. Though, God, those students were a terrifying bunch. Did you know Donna Tartt based the group on her own experience at Bennington College? I did! Fascinating, isn't it? The way fiction bleeds into reality. It's what makes a truly great book, wouldn’t you say? Gives it a weight, a resonance. I’m halfway through “Circe” by Madeline Miller now. Have you read it? No, not yet. I've heard good things, though. Greek mythology retold, right? Sounds right up your street. You always did have a soft spot for the classics. Remember when you tried to convince Mrs. MacIntyre that Homer was actually a feminist icon? Oh, the look on her face! Utter bewilderment. It was glorious. I maintain that Odysseus's manipulation of Penelope is a commentary on patriarchal structures, albeit a rather bleak one. It's all about perspective, Hamish. Aye, perspective. Though I’d argue Mrs. MacIntyre's perspective was somewhat more grounded in reality. So, “Circe” – is it worth the hype? Considering the llama debacle, my standards for entertainment are currently quite low. I need something… serious. Something to cleanse the palate, you know. Seriously? It's incredible.

Honestly, love, that "demonstrates a proactive approach to problem-solving" bit… it sounds a bit… try-hard, doesn’t it? Mum! I thought it was good! It’s what they want, isn't it? They specifically asked for examples of initiative. I’ve already explained how I redesigned the ventilation system in the student union at uni – that was proactive! Of course, the ventilation system was brilliant. You always were clever with those technical bits. But this… this application is for a junior architect role at a firm that designs  homes , darling. Not university buildings. They're not looking for a genius redesign of airflow. They want someone who can collaborate, someone approachable. I  am  approachable! And I can collaborate. This just… I want to show them I'm capable, you know? There's so much competition. Everyone’s got their Masters these days. Of course, you're capable. Don't you worry about that. You've got a brilliant mind, you really do. It's just… sometimes you get so caught up in showing off your cleverness, you forget to let them see the  you  underneath. Read it aloud, love. Start from the top. "To the Hiring Manager, I am writing to express my keen interest in the Junior Architect position advertised on…” See? Perfectly professional. It’s the rest of it… "My postgraduate studies at UCL equipped me with a robust theoretical framework and an extensive skillset in sustainable design…" Right. Stop. Theoretical framework? Honestly, darling, they don't want to hear about frameworks. They want to hear about how you’d draw a nice, cosy kitchen. Think about what they're actually  doing . Look at their website again. I did look at their website. They mostly do extensions and renovations. Classic suburban homes. I know. It just… feels simplistic. I’m trained to think about energy efficiency and… and complex spatial arrangements. And that’s wonderful! But you don’t need to shout it from the rooftops on a job application. Think about this: remember Mrs. Henderson down the road? The one with the leaky roof and the wonky extension? Vaguely. Wasn't she a nightmare? Always complaining about the builders. Exactly! You spent a whole afternoon helping her sort out a temporary solution while she waited for the insurance company. You used your knowledge to figure out what was wrong, and you explained it to her in a way she understood.

"Cheek is right, Arthur. Cheek and a half. They'll bleed you dry, won’t they? Always have, always will. Remember when they tried to tax the pigeons? Mad as a box o' frogs, that was." "Pigeons! Aye, I remember. Old Mrs. Higgins nearly had a fit. Said it was a conspiracy against the working class. Bless her heart, she was a character." "She certainly was, Arthur. A force of nature, that woman. And you're right about the council, Arthur. It's just… relentless. They don’t seem to understand a lot of folks are struggling like, really struggling. My niece, Carol, she's got two kids and works two jobs and  still  is behind on her rent. It’s awful." "Tell me about it. This modern world... too much pressure, ain't it? Back in our day, a man could work a decent job, provide for his family, and have a bit left over for a pint down the pub." "Aye. A man's word was his bond, too. You shook hands on something, it was done. Now it’s all contracts and clauses and loopholes." He pauses, taking a sip of his tea. "Remember old Reg Bailey's garage? Used to get your car serviced for a fiver. Honest work, that. Not like these fancy garages now, charging you an arm and a leg for something simple." “Oh, Reg Bailey! Lovely man. Used to give me a lift home sometimes when I was looking after little Timmy and Emily. He always had Werther's Originals in his pocket. Remember those, Arthur?” "Of course I do! What a treat they were. You don't see kids with sweets like that anymore, do you? All fizzy drinks and crisps, full of nonsense." "Speak o' the devil, did you hear about young Daniel? Got himself a new motor, 'e did. A bright red sports car. Says 'e needed something to show off to the girls." "Show off? Daniel? Typical boy! Though, I must say, he does look rather dashing. Still, a flashy car isn't everything, is it? He needs to think about his future, about saving for a house. Prices are outrageous now, aren’t they?" “Outrageous! It’s a disgrace. Trying to buy a house these days... it’s like winning the lottery. My grandaughter, Sarah, with her degree in… well, something fancy… she’s still living with her parents.

…and honestly, the fire escape stairs are absolutely knackered. They’re rusting through, and I swear one of the treads wobbled when I was up there last week checking the emergency lighting. We need to get that sorted ASAP, Fiona. It's a liability. Absolutely, Mark. Safety is paramount. I'll put a request in with the board immediately. But, funding, you know? We're all stretched. Did you check with The Bloom Collective about sharing the cost? They use the space quite a lot, and their photography workshops generate a decent income for us. I did pop my head round, but Sarah just said they're tight as well after investing in new studio lighting. Said they'd consider it for the next budget cycle, which is… helpful. Lovely, even. Meaning nothing will happen for six months. Typical. Right. Well, let's focus on what  can  happen. The gardening club are buzzing about the opportunity to use the rooftop space. Apparently, they’ve got a decent following on Instagram and are promising a 'bring your own bird feeder' day. A bird feeder day? Seriously? On the roof? I’m picturing pigeons descending like a feathered plague. And who's going to clear up the mess? They’ve assured me they’ll handle the clean-up. And it's good publicity, Mark. Attracts people. We need to be thinking about generating income, you know. The leaky roof downstairs hasn’t fixed itself, and that new furniture for the meeting room is looking tempting, isn't it? Remember how grumpy everyone was last week sitting on those wobbly chairs? Don't remind me. It was like a game of musical chairs with a high risk of injury. That new modular system from ErgoFlex? The one you showed me? That’d be brilliant, but it’s pricey. It is. But think of the flexibility! We could configure it for workshops, meetings, even a small exhibition. And speaking of workshops, have you heard back from the aromatherapy group about next quarter’s bookings? They usually bring in a good chunk. Yeah, they're confirmed for Tuesdays. They're also keen to move their storage boxes out of the back room – they’re saying it's getting damp. Which, surprise surprise, it is. It needs a proper dehumidifier, doesn’t it? I’ve been band-aid fixing it with those little silica gel packets. Silica gel packets?

Honestly, Bryn, you’ve outdone yourself. This lamb is… incredible! Better than anything we had in Cardiff last month. Absolutely brilliant, Dad! Seriously, I haven’t tasted lamb cooked like this in ages. What’s the secret? A little bit of rosemary, a touch of garlic, slow roasting, and a whole lot of love. My nan used to make a similar one, well, a  version  of it. Hers was more… rustic. Involved a lot of flour dust and near-kitchen fires. It's lovely, Rhys, really. Though, I suspect your nan’s rustic approach involved a lot more flavour too! Everything's just so comforting. It feels a million miles away from marking Year 8 sats papers. Aye, good food always does the trick, doesn't it? Warms you right through. Reminds me of Singapore, actually. My mum used to try and replicate Welsh dishes out there. Terrible results, most of them! Sweet chilli sauce on a Welsh Rarebit? You’d think she was mad. Oh, your mother, Dai! Bless her heart. She tried. Remember that attempt at Bara Brith she made? It was harder than a brick! We used it as a doorstop for a week. See? Family recipes are all about tradition, and sometimes, sticking to what you know! I'm sticking with the rosemary and garlic, thank you very much. So, Rhys, what are you up to these days? Still working on that historical linguistics project? Last I heard, you were buried in old Welsh manuscripts. It’s going well, actually. I’ve found some fascinating connections between Old Welsh and Cornish… things that predate the Norman Conquest and were previously unrecognised. It’s a bit dry for holiday conversation, I know. Don't be silly, Rhys! It sounds fascinating. Any chance you can translate some of it for me? I'm always keen to pick up a few phrases. Although my Welsh is limited to "Shwmae" and "Croeso." Don’t go trying to impress Bryn with your limited Welsh, Sarah! He’ll tell you it's atrocious. Fair enough! But it’s the effort that counts, isn’t it? Rhys, are you planning on presenting your findings anywhere soon? I’m hoping to get a paper published next year. There's a conference in Aberystwyth in the spring - I’m thinking of submitting. Aberystwyth! Nice. Fancy a weekend trip, then? Rhys, you could give a talk, and we could all go for a proper sea air walk.

"Aye, they're right cheeky round Brighton, aren't they? Like feathered little bandits. You were having a lovely time then, though, weren’t you? That trip sounded cracking." "It was brilliant, actually. The weather was surprisingly good. Better than I expected, honestly. Though, witnessing you being mugged by a seagull… that was a highlight. Brighton's a bit… hectic though, isn't it? Not exactly my cup of tea. Too much neon and overpriced fish and chips." "Hectic is the word! But I liked it. Loud, colourful, full of weirdness. Reminds me a bit of a carnival. Better than that, uh… what was it, Stamford? Where your Aunt Penelope lives? That felt proper dull, like stepping back in time." "Stamford is historic! And Penelope likes things… orderly. It’s a charming village, genuinely. Different vibe to Brighton, that’s all. Speaking of vibes, are you still planning on coming down for Dad’s birthday next month? We're having a barbecue at his place." "Aye, of course! Wouldn’t miss it. Though I’m dreading those quizzes your Dad puts on. He’s got a weird obsession with obscure trivia. Last year was all about Victorian railway gauges. Who even knows that?!" "He’s a walking encyclopedia. It's his superpower. And it  will  be railway-related this year, I guarantee it. So, are you seeing anyone at the moment, by the way? Still chatting to Liam?" "Nah, Liam's a lost cause. He still thinks 'Geordie Shore' is highbrow television. Managed to cut ties a few weeks back. Proper relief, to be honest. What about you? Anything exciting happening with… what’s her name… Chloe?" "Chloe’s good. We're actually looking at booking a trip to Italy in the spring. Tuscany, maybe. Lots of vineyards, good food… the usual." “Ooh, Italy! That sounds dreamy. You’ll have to send pictures. I'm craving a proper Italian now. This car journey's making me peckish. Fancy grabbing a takeaway when we get back?" "Definitely. What are you in the mood for? Thai? Indian?" "Let’s go for a chippy. Proper fish and chips, with lots of salt and vinegar. Need something familiar after all that posh Italian talk! Speaking of which, did you see that advert for the new Volvo? The one with the little girl and the dog?" "The emotional one? Yeah. Clever marketing. Makes you feel all warm and fuzzy, pretending their cars are just incredibly caring, not necessarily incredibly reliable."

…and then young Thomas, bless him, he just burst out crying! Right there at the table, during the buffet! Can you imagine? Auntie Maggie nearly choked on her vol-au-vent. Oh, poor Thomas. Losing his Nan like that, it must be incredibly difficult. It’s funny, isn't it, how grief just erupts at the most unexpected moments? My nephew, Liam, he hasn't said a word since his grandfather passed, but you can tell he's absolutely heartbroken. Just quiet, you know? Aye, quiet’s often worse, innit? My sister, Doreen, she's been a whirlwind ever since. Cleaning, organising, bossing everyone about. Says she’s just “keeping busy,” but I reckon she's trying to avoid feeling anything at all. It's a coping mechanism, I suppose. Definitely. My sister, Sarah, after Dad went, she threw herself into gardening. Became obsessed with roses, the poor thing. We all grieve differently, don't we? The funeral’s next week, isn't it? Are you managing alright with the arrangements? It’s a palaver, honestly. Trying to please everyone. Doreen wants a string quartet, and Liam, he insists on a specific Elvis song. Said Nan always loved Elvis. I'm just trying to keep the peace, you know? And coordinating with the crematorium... it’s a lot. It wouldn't be half as bad if I hadn’t been battling this back pain, to be honest. Oh, I’m so sorry to hear that. Are you still seeing the osteopath? That appointment I mentioned last time - how did that go? Well, he gave me some new exercises, but it’s hurting something fierce. He says it’s probably a slipped disc. Wants to send me for an MRI, but getting a referral from the GP is proving tricky. They’re all so busy! I need it though, I can barely bend down to dust anymore. It’s terrible for my work, you know? I understand completely. It's a nightmare navigating the NHS. My own knee’s been playing up, I’ve been on a waiting list for months for a consultation. Just keeps getting pushed back. It's infuriating! Speaking of being on your feet, how’s your boss, Mr. Henderson, treating you these days? Still on about trimming the fat, is he? Don't even get me started. He’s got this new obsession with healthy eating, hasn’t he?

"Sounds familiar, love. Marketing can be brutal. Remember that website redesign I did for 'Bumbles Honey'? They wanted a minimalist, cutting-edge design, but their target market were still pensioners who liked pictures of bees in floral hats. The conflict alone…" “Bees in floral hats? That’s brilliant, Mum! Did you tell them no?” "Of course not, Liam! You don't tell a client 'no'. You subtly guide them, gently suggest…it’s a delicate dance. Anyway, it eventually got done, but it wasn't pretty. What about you, Ben? Still at the warehouse then?" "Still there, Sarah, still there. Though, I did have a decent day today. We finally got the new automated sorting system up and running. It's reduced errors by about 15%, which is fantastic. The manager’s breathing down my neck for more improvements, naturally, but at least it’s progress.” He pauses. "Though, I'm worried about redundancies, you know? With the automation…" “Redundancies? Does that mean people lose their jobs?” "Essentially, yeah, Ethan. It means the company needs fewer people to do the same amount of work." "It’s a difficult situation, Ben. Technology marches on, doesn’t it? At least you were involved in the implementation, that’s something to put on your CV if things do change.” "Speaking of CVs, Dad, remember when you did that summer job at the car wash when you were my age? You said you almost got fired for polishing a Ferrari with a sponge!" "Don't remind me, Liam! It was a learning experience, that’s for sure. Mr. Henderson, the owner, was a very particular man. He specifically said  microfibre cloths only  for the Italians. I was distracted by the radio and…well, you know. He was practically apoplectic. I lasted about two weeks." "Oh, that’s a classic! You were always a disaster with cars, weren't you? Remember that time you tried to fix the brakes on my old Rover? It ended with me pushing it halfway down the High Street." "That was different! The Rover was a  lost cause . It was practically held together with duct tape and wishful thinking." "Did you ever go skiing, Dad? Mrs. Davies in my class went to Austria last week and sent pictures of the snow." "I did, Ethan, years ago. Once, just once. A corporate team-building exercise. It was…not my thing. I spent most of the time trying not to fall over and narrowly avoiding collisions with other skiers.

Oh my goodness, look at this! Remember this trip to Norfolk? You managed to capture Bernard, the badger, mid-sneeze! It’s truly spectacular. Bernard! Of course! Good heavens, I’d almost forgotten about Bernard. He wasn't exactly thrilled to be photographed, was he? Nearly took a chunk out of my boot. You were fearless, though. Just pointing your camera at a grumpy badger. Well, someone had to document the momentous occasion. You were too busy apologizing. Honestly, you apologize to  everything . Remember when you apologized to a pigeon for accidentally stepping near it? It looked rather distressed, didn’t it? It was hopping about dramatically. Can't just leave a pigeon in distress, can you? Anyway, this is a decent shot. The light was awful, though. I should have adjusted the aperture, really. You were learning then. Your photography skills have definitely improved since. Remember those blurry attempts at photographing the sunrise over the Broads? They looked like impressionist paintings, albeit very bad ones. Don't remind me! I was so determined to get that perfect shot. Ended up with nothing but a series of orange blobs. It's funny, isn't it? How engrossed you get when you’re trying to capture something. Like that trip to Japan last year. You were obsessed with capturing the cherry blossoms. Obsessed is putting it mildly! I was on a mission. Every single blog post, every leaflet, mentioned the ephemeral beauty of the sakura. I felt a responsibility to photograph it properly. Did you ever get tired of me yelling “Stop! Quick! Blossom!” every five minutes? A little, perhaps. But the results were worth it. Those photos you took in Kyoto… they're incredible. The way you captured the light filtering through the branches… absolutely stunning. Better than anything I managed. I think you really found your photographic voice there. I think being surrounded by such beauty helped. And the food! The food was photographic in itself. Remember that tiny ramen shop we stumbled upon? The steam rising from the bowl, the vibrant colors of the ingredients… Absolutely. You developed a real eye for detail. You've always been artistically inclined, of course, but Japan just… unlocked something in you. It’s almost a shame we're not going back next spring. I know. I miss it terribly. I've been thinking about taking a Japanese language course online. Even just knowing a few basic phrases would make a huge difference.

…and then the waves just  slapped  me! Honestly, Chloe, I swear I swallowed half the Irish Sea. Worth it though, right? Skinny dipping at night under the stars… it was magical. Blimey, you are mad! Proper mad! Ireland, eh? I went a couple of years back. Dublin's alright, bit touristy. But the countryside… stunning. Did you get to see any of the cliffs? Moher, that sort of thing? Ooh, Moher is incredible. I’ve got photos – honestly, it’s like another planet. Speaking of photos, have you guys seen that new app, “Memora”? It automatically creates little slideshows with music from your photos, really clever. I used it to make a reel of the café’s renovations, had loads of views. Memora, you say? Sounds a bit… fussy, doesn't it? I'm a simple man. Give me a good ol' Instagram filter and a sunset and I’m happy. I did a fair bit of travelling myself recently, before I landed this gig here. Went back to Tassie – Tasmania, for you lot – for a bit. Beautiful, rugged. Bit of everything. Tasmania! I’ve always wanted to go. It looks so… untouched. Proper bushland, yeah? Anyway, back to Ireland. Honestly, the craic was brilliant. I met this bloke, Liam, playing the tin whistle in a pub… Don't tell me you’re bringing home another Liam, Chloe! Remember what happened with Brendan? He was a lovely man! And this Liam was different. He was… intense. Anyway, it steered the conversation into a rather bizarre tangent. We ended up debating the practicality of surviving a zombie apocalypse in rural Ireland. Oh, god. Of course you did. You and Liam, planning your escape route from the undead. Did you factor in sheep? Because there's a  lot  of sheep. Sheep are good cover! Distract the zombies with fluffy goodness. I'd prioritise finding somewhere with a good water source though. That’s key. You can’t fight zombies on an empty stomach, you know. Right, sensible. Proper sensible. Although, thinking about it, if the world ended, I’d grab my poetry books first. What’s the point of surviving if you can’t have a bit of Eliot, eh? Seriously, stop being dramatic, Tom! Someone needs to know how to bake bread. Speaking of which, I've been trying to recreate my nan's challah recipe. It’s driving me insane. It’s been passed down for generations, but the instructions are just… vague.

"Aye, right mess that must've been! What did you do, Liam? Just stand there, lookin' daft?” “Not exactly daft, but… surprised. I'd just mentioned I was researching sentiment analysis of social media reactions to travel restrictions. You know, for my PhD. Apparently, referencing ‘border enforcement’ and ‘algorithmic bias’ in casual conversation is a red flag now.” He chuckles, a slightly weary sound. “They asked a  lot  of questions. About my funding, my research, my intentions… the works.” "Algorithm bias, eh? Sounds a bit fancy even for you. Grew up in Birmingham, you did, not Silicon Valley. Did you tell 'em you were from Brum?” “Briefly. It didn't seem to improve the situation. They clearly thought I was building some sort of automated deportation system or something. Honestly, it’s ridiculous. Cambridge is supposed to be a haven for ideas.” "Aye, well, the world's gerrin' a bit uptight, innit? Remember when we used to sneak into Alton Towers when we were kids? No ID, no nothin'. We'd just climb over the fence." “Don’t remind me! My mum would have killed me if she'd known. Those were simpler times. Though I’m not sure climbing fences to get into theme parks is quite equivalent to… searching for loopholes in border control algorithms.” "Exactly! Still, same principle - a bit of rebellious spirit, a bit of gettin' away with it. You shoulda told 'em you were off to see the Nemesis." “That would have been a convincing argument, wouldn't it? 'I'm researching rapid adrenaline response in humans using a highly controlled, albeit thrilling, environment!'” "Exactly! See? You’re a clever lad, you are. Still, seriously, that’s a bit mental. You're just doin' research. What are you playing these days, anyway? Something less likely to trigger national security, I hope." "Trying to avoid anything that looks remotely tactical. Actually, I've been pretty obsessed with Stardew Valley. Surprisingly relaxing, considering the current state of the world." "Stardew Valley? The farm one? You? I thought you were all about dystopian simulators and fighting robots!" “I  am ! But sometimes, escaping to a pixelated farm and growing virtual pumpkins is exactly what I need. It's soothing. Much better than pondering the existential dread of algorithmic surveillance.” He gestures to the peanuts. "Want some more? I think they're starting to run low." "Aye, give us a few more.

Honestly, this batter is spot on. Best chips I’ve had in ages. You’re quiet, Penelope. Enjoying yours? Yes, it’s…fine, Sarah. Just a bit preoccupied, I suppose. So, you're really sticking with the rowing, then? I thought you'd given up after that disastrous first attempt on the Cam. Disastrous is putting it mildly! I ended up backwards, tangled in the ropes, and pretty sure I accidentally splashed a swan. But no, I’m going back. The instructor, David, is really patient. He says I have potential. Can you imagine? Me, a rower! Never thought I’d say that. It’s just…intimidating. All those lean, muscular types gliding along. I look like a bewildered hippopotamus. Oh, you're exaggerating. You're perfectly capable. You’re a whiz at kayaking, aren’t you? Remember that weekend in Wales? You were fearless, tackling those rapids. That was different! Kayaking's more…me. Less reliant on teamwork, less chance of looking entirely foolish in front of everyone. Though, I did capsize once… into a rather unpleasant patch of reeds. Proper scratchy. But rowing… it’s a whole team effort. And getting the technique right is proving a nightmare. It takes time. Everything does. Speaking of outdoors activities… I need to buy some proper waterproof trousers. The rain here is relentless. I’ve been tutoring poor little Emily all last week, and I swear I was damp through my cardigan by lunchtime. Absolutely. I ended up looking like a drowned rat last week after a walking meet with the historical society. Ended up buying one of those fancy breathable ones. Expensive, but worth it. You know, speaking of family, I did finally manage to meet up with Cousin Liam last month. Liam? Your dad’s niece? The one who lives in Australia? After all these years? The very same! It was… odd, actually. We're only distantly related, but there was this instant connection. We spent hours just chatting, discovering all the shared quirks we inherited from Great Aunt Agnes. You remember her, the one who collected ceramic cats? Vaguely. She was a character. So, Liam? What’s he like? He's lovely. A marine biologist. Absolutely fascinating life. He even showed me some pictures of the coral reefs he studies. It was wonderful to finally put a face to the name, you know? It feels like a missing piece of the family puzzle has finally clicked into place.

Right, so, I’m  still  not getting this Morse code. It’s like… dots and dashes, yeah, but how do you actually  remember  what they all mean? Mr. Davies is making us learn it for some random project. Honestly, who even uses Morse code anymore? Well, lass, it's good for the brain, isn't it? Keeps ya sharp. Your grandad used to be able to tap it out faster than you can send a text. Used to use it on the farm, back in the day. Difficult getting a signal sometimes, you see. Think of it like a code, a puzzle. There’s patterns, like wi’ texting. Not as many emojis, mind. Easy for you to say! You’re practically a history book. Remember when you tried to teach me to play the recorder? That was a disaster. I was pinging out a noise that sounded like a distressed seagull. Aye, you weren't keen on that were ya? This is different. This is about patterns and memory. Like… rememberin' where we parked the car after food shopping last week? That was a challenge, eh? Don't remind me. I’m convinced Vodafone has it out for me. Signal’s been dreadful all week. I missed a text from Chloe about results day plans. Nearly gave me a heart attack, thinkin' she’d said something about my grades already. Results day… that’ll be a good’un. Nerves gonna be through the roof, I reckon. Still, you've worked hard. Remember all those late nights, copyin’ notes, surrounded by stationery? Piles of pens, highlighters... it was like a colourful battlefield in your room. It  was ! And I'd love a new set. Proper proper good ones though, not those cheap ones from Amazon. I need something that writes well. Maybe I'll check eBay, see if I can find some vintage fountain pens. Something a bit different. eBay's good for a bargain. Just watch out for dodgy sellers. Remember that glass water bottle you ordered? Said it was brand new, turned up cracked! Had to send it back. Speaking of which, I need to order some more veg. We're runnin' low on everything. Proper roast dinner needs some good root vegetables. Definitely. Mum’s been trying to get me to eat more vegetables. She keeps going on about brain food. Says it’ll help me remember Morse code.

Blimey, it’s good to be back in a proper living room, innit? This place is a palace compared to student halls. Liam's mum really does go all out with the cushions. Tell me about it! I was starting to think I’d forgotten what a real sofa felt like. And yes, Mrs. Davies is obsessed. Seriously, where does she  find  them? So, exams over then? You look like you’ve aged about ten years. Over, thank goodness. Finished last week. Management Science was brutal. Absolutely brutal. I spent half of it staring at the ceiling, wishing I was anywhere else. You? How’d your coding go? Went alright, yeah. Touch wood. Think I finally cracked that loop issue, thanks to a late-night YouTube tutorial. You wouldn't believe how many London accents there are in the coding world. This guy was from Brixton, explaining algorithms! Proper mad, that. Reminds me of that time I tried to build a website back in sixth form. Ended up deleting the whole thing halfway through. Total disaster. Thinking about applying for that internship at Sterling now, though. Networking event last week seemed promising. Sterling, nice! Sounds serious. You going for the financial analyst role? Honestly, man, you’re gonna be snapping up jobs left, right and centre. You’ve always been brighter than me with numbers. Speaking of jobs… I’m finally thinking about pulling the trigger on that Japan thing. Japan?! Seriously? You’re actually going? I thought that was just a dream you had. Nah, it’s happening! Got a placement with that tech firm in Tokyo. Three months, contract work - sounds amazing. Bit nerve-wracking, obviously. I mean, Japan! I’ve always wanted to go, you know? The culture, the food... Wicked! Tokyo… mad. Always seemed proper futuristic whenever I saw it on telly. You gonna live there? Yeah, they're providing accommodation. Tiny apartment, I’m guessing, but it's central. I’ve been brushing up on my Japanese, but I’m still pretty hopeless. You know, I can order a beer, maybe. That’s about it. That’ll get you started. You should hit up Shibuya Crossing. That's gotta be on your list. Absolutely bonkers. Proper sensory overload. I saw a documentary about it once. Massive screens, millions of people… Definitely! And I want to try proper ramen. Not the instant stuff, but the real deal.

Oh, look at this! Remember this one? Taken at Buckfast Abbey last month. Honestly, ANON, you were practically beaming! You looked so peaceful, just sitting by the river. I was, wasn’t I? That was a lovely day. The gardens were particularly gorgeous. I'm glad we went. It felt… restorative. Though, I'm still slightly unnerved by all those monks. Are they  ever  smiling? Monks never smile! That’s the whole point, isn't it? Serious business, that's what it is. Running a brewery and all. Did you try the cider, young lady? Properly good cider, that. Strong, mind you. I did try some, Grandad. A small one! Didn't want to be weaving down the drive. It was surprisingly good, though. Better than I expected. He was trying to convince me to buy a crate, wasn’t he, Arthur? Said it would be perfect for Christmas. I told him I didn’t have room in my shed! Between the gardening equipment and… well, everything! A little Christmas cheer never hurt anyone, Penelope. Especially at our age. Speaking of age... I saw David Cameron’s name in the paper again. Still gallivanting around, avoiding taxes, I suppose. Disgraceful, it is. Absolutely disgraceful. All those politicians... Don't even get me started, Grandad. It's just infuriating. Trying to hide millions while ordinary people are struggling to pay their bills. Makes you want to… well. I’ll stop there. It does, sweetheart. It really does. Though, what  can  we do about it? Apart from shaking our heads and voting, of course. Are you all set for the local elections? Got your postal vote in? Yes, I sent mine off last week. It’s so important to vote, isn't it? Even if it feels like it doesn’t make a difference sometimes. It  does  make a difference! Every single vote counts. I’ve been voting since before you were born, young lady. And I’ve seen a few things change. Though not always for the better, mind you. My old Morris Minor...that was reliable! Wouldn't change for anything. Honestly, Arthur, your Morris Minor was a menace! It used to belch smoke and rattle like a box of loose bolts. Remember when it broke down on the M5? We were stranded for hours! A minor hiccup! Nothing a bit of elbow grease couldn't fix. Nowadays, these modern cars… all computers and plastic.

Honestly, Mum, Dad, it's  so  good to see you! You both look… tan! Belgium agreed with you. It did, love, it certainly did. A bit of a change from London, wasn't it, Brenda? Absolutely, George. Just breathing in the air felt different. Though, I have to say, cycling through Bruges was… an experience. Bruges, right? You sent me some lovely pictures. Was it as picturesque as it looks online? Even more so, love. Like something out of a fairytale. But the cobbled streets… the bike almost had a mind of its own! Nearly ended up in a canal, I did. Oh, Dad! You nearly gave me a heart attack with that text. Should've stuck to walking, maybe? He was determined to cycle everywhere. Said it was the best way to see the markets. And the frites, of course! We ate  so  many frites. Speaking of food, what was your favourite thing you ate? Seriously, I need a recommendation. I’m trying to branch out from just pizza and pasta. Moules frites, definitely. Proper Belgian mussels, cooked in white wine and cream. Magnificent. And the waffles, oh, the waffles. Fresh and crispy, with proper Belgian chocolate. Don't forget the speculoos biscuits, love! We brought back a whole tin. They're in the bag – I thought you'd like some. And the chocolate…Neuhaus, Leonidas... so much better than what you can get here. Amazing! Thank you, Mum. Seriously, you two always bring back the best treats. So, how was the SAT NAV? You mentioned it was a bit temperamental? Temperamental is an understatement! That TomTom nearly led us into a farmer's field twice. And once, it swore we could drive through a pedestrian zone. I told it, "You're having a laugh, aren't you?" Didn't seem to register.
