Speaker_3 : "Penicillin’s a devil, that is. Gives me the shivers just thinking about it. Nearly knocked me off my feet last time they gave it to me at the clinic. Made me feel like I’d swallowed a bag of bricks." Speaker_4 : "Brick, Agnes? You're forgetting your skiing days! Remember that time you slid down that snowy bank in Austria? Nearly broke your arm, you did! We laughed ourselves silly." He chuckled, a low rumble in his chest. Eleanor: "Skiing! Oh, don't remind me. My knees haven't forgiven me for that trip. Though Mark did insist on getting a new set of tyres for the Land Rover. Said it was essential, particularly with the winter coming. Cost a fortune, naturally, but he’s convinced it’s for safety." Doreen: "Always the practical one, your Mark. He's a good lad. Speaking of fortunes, my Brenda down the street says they're thinking of getting a new car altogether. Says her Fiesta's on its last legs. Needs a new MOT and everything else. Costs more to fix than it's worth, she reckons." Agnes: "New car? Fancy! I'd rather stick to my slippers and a good cup of tea. Got a lovely letter from Elsie today, you know. She’s doing alright at the bingo, apparently. Won twenty pounds last week! Said she misses our chats something awful.” Eleanor: “Elsie! Wonderful! I must call her. I’ve been so caught up with this… this constant feeling of being unwell. It’s impacting everything. I even cancelled my lunch with Susan last week. Susan’s been a lifeline with work, you know? Always there with a word of advice." Arthur: "You need a bit of something different, love. That acupuncture your daughter Sarah was telling me about? Might do you some good. Gets right down to the root of the problem, she says.” Doreen: "Acupuncture? Ooh, that sounds a bit… prickly, doesn't it? I'm more of a cupping person myself. Saw a lovely article about it in the magazine.

Right then, you two. I know this is a bit… heavy, but I think it’s important you know about it. We were talking about the pictures your grandpa showed you, the ones of ships, weren't we? Yes, Nana. Were those pirate ships? Not quite, love. These ships were used a really, really long time ago, and they weren't carrying treasure. They were carrying people. Lots and lots of people. Not by choice, mind you. Where were they going? They were being taken, a very long way, across the ocean, to places like America. It's called the slave trade. People from Africa – strong, clever people – were captured and forced to work for other people. Forced? That's nasty. It was terribly nasty, darling. Absolutely awful. They weren’t allowed to choose what they did, or where they lived, or who they married. They were treated like... like things, not people. They had to work very hard, often on big farms, growing things like sugar and cotton. Why did people do that? Why would they take people away? That’s a very good question, and it’s complicated. Some people wanted things like sugar and cotton, and they didn’t want to pay people fairly to grow it. So, they thought they could get it for free by exploiting other people. It was about power and greed, really. It was wrong. Terribly, terribly wrong. Was it a long time ago? Yes, a very long time ago. But it wasn’t that long ago, really. It ended a bit over one hundred and fifty years ago. People fought very hard to stop it. People called abolitionists. Brave souls who believed everyone should be free. What’s "abolish"? It means to get rid of something bad, to make it stop. Like, to get rid of slavery, to abolish it. It took years and years of fighting. Did you know, there were wars because of slavery too? Wars? Yes, a big one called the American Civil War. It was fought partly because some states wanted to keep slavery, and other states didn't. It was very sad and complicated, with lots of fighting and people getting hurt. And even after slavery was abolished, it took a long time for people to be treated equally. Did the people who were taken away, did they ever go home? Some did, eventually. But many didn't.

Honestly, the state of the news these days! It’s enough to give you grey hairs, isn’t it, Brenda? Tell me about it, David. Absolutely dreadful. Though, I must say, I did find that documentary on the ospreys fascinating last night. Did you see it? The chicks are almost ready to fledge. Ospreys? No, sorry! I was glued to 'Succession' – the finale was  epic . Seriously, the twists and turns… you have to watch it, Auntie Brenda. 'Succession'? Is that one of those terribly dramatic things? I prefer something a bit more… wholesome, dear. Like 'Call the Midwife'. Now  that’s  a show. Wholesome is all well and good, Brenda, but sometimes you need a bit of intrigue and backstabbing, don't you? 'Succession' is brilliant. Though, I'm still clinging to the hope that Shiv ended up with Tom. They're perfect for each other, dysfunctional as they are. Backstabbing… reminds me of Mrs. Higgins next door. Always whispering about poor Elsie’s prize-winning roses. Said they weren't  quite  right, they did. Always had a bee in her bonnet, that one. Elsie's roses  are  spectacular, Arthur! Mrs. Higgins just couldn't stand that someone else was winning. Speaking of winning, did you all see what happened at Wimbledon? Absolutely thrilling! Yes! Alcaraz was incredible. My Twitter feed was exploding with his shots. Honestly, the precision! It's mind-blowing to watch. Wimbledon’s always a lovely distraction, isn’t it? Reminds me of holidays we used to have in Bournemouth. David, you remember those seaside trips? Building sandcastles… Of course, I do, love. Remember the ice cream? That awful, neon-orange stuff they used to sell? Made your teeth ache just looking at it. You lot and your memories! Makes me feel ancient. I was just thinking about a holiday I took to Greece a few years back. The beaches were unbelievable – white sand, turquoise water… Greece? Wow! I’ve always wanted to go. I'm trying to save up for a trip to Italy next year. Rome, Florence, Venice… the whole shebang. Italy's lovely, dear. Though be careful of the pickpockets. My cousin, Doreen, lost her purse in Florence last year. Heartbreaking. Pickpockets… reminds me of that awful incident in Brighton. Years ago, of course. Dizzying crowd, you know. Lost my wallet. Never did get it back. Arthur, you’ve lost your wallet more times than I can count!

Right, nearly done. Honestly, this dishwasher is a blessing and a curse. It does the washing, but creates a mountain of stuff to put away. Mummy, can we read about Harry Potter now? Please? Just a tick, sweetheart, nearly finished. Daddy’s just about to start telling us about… who was it? George Stevenson? Aye! George! Trains! Vroom, vroom! Exactly! Now, be quiet for a moment, both of you, and let Daddy explain. He gets very passionate about trains, you know. Is he going to make train noises again? Possibly. He's got that George Stephenson impression he does. Prepare yourselves. Speaker_2 & 3: What did George Stephenson do, Mummy? Well, he was a very clever man, darling. He's famous for inventing, or rather, perfecting, the steam locomotive. You know, the engine that pulls trains? Before him, trains were a bit… clunky. Like a very grumpy duck? A bit like a grumpy duck, yes! They were unreliable and slow. George Stephenson figured out how to make them much, much better. He built the first public railway in England, the Stockton and Darlington Railway, in 1825. Really? That long ago? Yes, a very long time ago! Can you imagine a world without trains? It would take ages to travel anywhere! Vroom! Zoom! To Grandma’s! Can we go on a real train soon, Mummy? Of course, love. We can look at the train timetable tonight. Now, Daddy, your turn to explain the brilliant bits, I think. Explain! Explain! Right then! Now, George Stephenson… ...wasn't just about making trains  go . That’s important, mind you,  very  important. But it was about making ‘em go  safely  and  reliably . He came up with this thing called a flanged wheel! A what? A flanged wheel. See, normally, a wheel just spins on an axle, right? But on a train track, it tends to wander a bit. So, he added these little… ridges, these flanges, on the inside of the wheel. They sit against the sides of the rails and keep the train on the right line! Clever, eh? That’s why they didn’t fall off the tracks all the time, son. Rest of the early engines, they were bouncing about like… like a rabbit in a box! That’s a lovely image, darling. He also designed the Rocket, didn't he? Which was incredibly fast for its time. Aye, the Rocket! Won the Rainhill Trials in 1829.

Speaker_1 exclaimed, gesturing wildly with a wooden spoon. Flour dusted his cheek. Speaker_2 , patiently kneading dough, chuckled. "Liam, calm down. It's Words With Friends. Not the UN Security Council. You’re getting yourself worked up over a six-letter word." Speaker_3 , meticulously chopping vegetables, added, "Honestly, you're obsessed. I barely even touch the app anymore. Too stressful. I’m trying to focus on getting The Daily Grind properly ready for Christmas. It’s manic." Speaker_4 , leaning against the counter with a mug of tea, drawled, "Tell me about it. Santa's coming early to this place. We’re already runnin’ out of oat milk. Christmas chaos is a real thing, eh?" Liam scrubbed a hand through his hair, leaving a white streak. "But it’s just… unfair! I was building a strategy! A  perfect  strategy! And he throws in quixotic just to mess with me. It's like he  wants  me to lose." Chloe shot him a playful look. "Maybe he just likes big words, Liam. Some people do. By the way," she added, turning back to the dough, "I was thinking of incorporating some saffron into the bread this week. Do you reckon people would be into it?" “Saffron bread? Sounds fancy,” Priya mused. "You know, I was reading about these supper clubs popping up, mostly in Shoreditch. People are  paying  to go to someone’s house and have a home-cooked meal. Sounds potentially lucrative, doesn’t it? Maybe you could do one, Chloe. Your baking is insane.” "That's a thought," Chloe considered, easing the dough onto a floured surface. "It'd be a lot of work, though. Getting all the insurance and licenses sorted…" Liam perked up. "Speaking of licences, my cousin, Ben, got himself into a right state. Apparently, he’s opened a little vintage shop online, but he hasn't registered as a business yet. HMRC are sniffing around. Said he needs to pay VAT and all that jazz." Finn grimaced. “Yeah, that’s a messy situation. Friends of mine back home had similar trouble. It’s just… paperwork, you know? Keeps you up at night, thinkin’ about it.” "He's been trying to avoid it," Liam continued, shaking his head. "Says it’s too complicated. He’s panicking. I told him he needs to contact a solicitor, but he’s ragging against the idea because of the cost." Chloe sighed. "Poor Ben. Legal stuff is such a nightmare.

Honestly, this Thai green curry is  amazing . You have to try it sometime, Sarah. It's from that little place on Histon Road. Best I’ve had outside of Thailand, seriously. Oh, really? I've been meaning to try them. I’m always a bit wary of takeaways though, you know? Sometimes they’re just… greasy. My kids are notorious for complaining about anything that isn’t beige. Beige! That's a really good description of a lot of kids’ palates. Anya's phase is currently ketchup-only. It’s exhausting. But this place, it’s different. They use fresh ingredients, you can really taste it. Anya did try some the other day, just a tiny bit, and…surprisingly, she liked the mango sticky rice! Baby steps. How are Leo and Emily getting on, by the way? Still at primary school? They are, yes. Leo’s just become obsessed with Minecraft. Utterly and completely. I swear he dreams in pixels. Emily wants to be a dancer. Stage school auditions are next month – I’m starting to panic! They're expensive, aren't they? Oh, immensely. I’ve looked into it a little bit for Anya. Though, she’s showing more interest in coding, which is, thankfully, a little less… flamboyant. And cheaper! Did you see that robotics workshop they're offering at the community centre? It might be something Leo would enjoy. A robotics workshop? Really? I'll definitely look into that. He’d probably be all over that. It’s good to find things that aren’t just screen-based, isn’t it? I'm trying to encourage him to get outside more. Though, convincing a ten-year-old boy that sunshine is enjoyable is a monumental task. Tell me about it! Anya’s the same. I try to get her out for walks in the fields near Grantchester. It's so peaceful there. What about you? Do you have any hobbies, outside of battling Minecraft and stage school auditions? You’re cracking me up. Well, I used to enjoy painting, quite a lot actually. I did a watercolour course a few years back. But finding the time is the killer. After work, school runs, dinner… painting just gets pushed to the bottom of the pile. I did manage to dust off my brushes last month, though. Just a quick landscape. Felt surprisingly therapeutic. That’s wonderful! It's so important to make time for yourself, isn't it?

Are we nearly there yet? My feet are killing me. And honestly, Mum, did we  need  three different types of muslin cloths? Three! It's just… excessive. Darling, you never know with a baby, do you? You need a stash. And this Mothercare’s got the softest ones. You’ll appreciate having them when you’re elbow-deep in… well, you’ll see. Besides, it wasn't  just  muslin. You were eyeing that little knitted elephant. I was appreciating its aesthetic, not planning on purloining it. Honestly, you two act like I’m about to be a mum myself. Sixth form’s hard enough without adding nappies and sleepless nights! Aye, lass, you'll be alright. Remember your Auntie Maureen trying to convince me to buy a baby monitor that played whale song? Whale song! For a tiny human! We laughed that one for years. Headed straight into traffic now, though. Slowing down a bit, eh? Traffic’s always dreadful around Preston at this time. It’s a nightmare. Thinking about it...remember that survey they did on the house? The one Mr. Henderson did? He said the foundations were…solid. Solid like a rock, apparently. Dad was getting panicky about subsidence. He wanted to rip up the entire garden. Honestly, he gets worked up about everything. Is the bathroom renovation still happening next month? I told you I need to study in peace, that sound of drilling will drive me insane. Aye, booked it all in. They’re starting with the downstairs toilet first, least disruptive that way. After that, the spare bedroom and then finally the bathroom itself. It’ll be a right old mess for a while. Speaking of mess, remember when you were little, and you used to cover yourself in my Mum’s baking flour? Looked like a little snowman! Yeah, I remember. You were always taking photos. You’ve got a million pictures of me being a sticky, flour-covered menace. Do you think they'll do a good job with the renovation? I'm worried about them messing things up, especially the skirting boards. The company has excellent reviews, sweetheart. We vetted them thoroughly. And Dad’s fussing over them constantly. He'll be breathing down their necks. Remember that awful blankie you had as a child? The one with the little teddy bears? Don't remind me! It smelled like old gym socks and despair.

Honestly, this 'Cosmic Crusaders' thing has taken over your life, Isla. You've barely looked up from that screen all week! Christmas is next week, and all you're talking about is leveling up your space elf. It’s not  just  a space elf, Mum. It's Captain Lyra Nova, and she's vital to our raid team. And it’s Strategic Thinking, okay? It's about planning, predicting, adaptation. It's practically psychology! She’s got a point, Carol. Think of it as tactical resource management. It’s not that different from project planning, really. I used similar principles in my dissertation. Project planning? Honestly, Ben, you're enabling her. She needs fresh air, sunshine, and maybe a Christmas crafting session instead of battling pixelated aliens. Remember last year's disastrous attempt at gingerbread houses? They weren’t disastrous! They just... lacked structural integrity. And there’s no sun in Surrey in December! We're practically encased in perpetual twilight. Anyway, the raid is tonight, and we're going for the Zenith Crystal. It’s a huge deal. Zenith Crystal? Sounds impressive. What’s the reward? A new plasma rifle and a seriously cool skin for Lyra. Think electric blue and shimmering silver. It's the envy of the whole server. Plus, if we succeed, we unlock the new Mars expansion. Mars? Good heavens! Where does this end? You know, when I was your age, Christmas meant carol singing and building snowmen, not conquering imaginary planets. I used to dream of travelling, though. Remember that trip to Liverpool? Seeing the docks, the Albert Dock… You told me about that, Aunt Carol. It sounds brilliant. I’d loved to see it sometime. I’ve been so bogged down in job hunting, I haven't really had time to think about travel. It's a struggle, you know? Everyone expects you to have a five-year plan the minute you graduate. Tell me about it! Everyone keeps asking me what I’m going to  do  after A-Levels. Like I have a clue! I mean, I'm interested in astrophysics, but the competition is fierce. And have you seen the tuition fees now? It's outrageous. That’s true. University is a different world altogether to when I went. The cost is horrific. I remember working part-time at the Woolworths to help with my student loan. It wasn’t glamorous, but it taught me the value of a pound.

Right, so, iron is  obviously  crucial in Minecraft, isn’t it? You need it for tools, for armour… basically everything. But did you know that Netherite, which is like, the ultimate metal, is actually forged by combining Ancient Debris with Gold? Gold is shiny! Like my glitter glue! Netherite’s purple! Daddy showed me! You gotta find really deep down. It's dangerous! Yes, darling, it is. Very dangerous. Which reminds me, are you two taking your vitamins today? Or are you going to be bouncing off the walls all afternoon? Vitamins are yucky. Mine taste like orange! I like orange. They’re just little superheroes, saving you from getting poorly. Now, back to Minecraft. See, iron is good, but it’s a bit…common, isn’t it? Like cotton. Useful, everyone has it, but not exactly glamorous. Cotton’s for teddy bears! Exactly! And silk is like… Netherite! Rare, beautiful, and really, really precious. It takes a lot of effort to get it, doesn’t it? Silkworms are weird. Did you know, in the old legends, silkworms weren't  always  silkworms? Oh? What do you mean, love? Where did you hear that? From Nana! She told me a story. She said, long, long ago, silkworms were baby dragons! Small ones, obviously. They spun silk instead of fire because they were too shy to breathe fire. Baby dragons! That's cool! Well, that’s quite a story! A baby dragon… spinning silk… I like it. It’s much better than the stuff they tell you at school. That’s a proper legend. You've got a very vivid imagination, haven't you? So, shy baby dragons… weaving beautiful silk… They’d need valuable resources to build their nests, wouldn't they? Perhaps diamonds? Maybe emeralds! For shiny decorations! And… and cobblestone! For strong walls! And wool! Lots and lots of wool, like a big fluffy cloud! Wool… interesting. Wool is like the opposite of Netherite, isn't it? Common, readily available, but still important. Keeps you warm. It’s good to appreciate the common things, too. Back to the dragons… so, these shy, silk-spinning dragons, they lived in secret, hiding from the bigger, fire-breathing dragons. What kind of danger did they face? The big dragons got angry if they heard the little silk dragons humming! They thought the humming was making fun of them! So the silk dragons had to be  very  quiet.

Honestly, Liam, I'm proper fed up. Another assignment due Monday. Archaeology, who even  needs  to know about ancient pottery shards?! You say that now, but you were obsessed with that Roman villa dig last term. Remember how excited you were about finding that… what was it? A broken tile with a fingerprint? Aye, well, a broken tile's a bit different than a mountain of shattered pottery. It’s just… soul-destroying, innit? Makes you question everything. Think I should just chuck it all in and become a guitar tech or summat. A guitar tech? Seriously? Last time you held a guitar, you nearly took my eye out with the tuning peg. That was one time! And I was trying to learn 'Wonderwall' – a monumental task for anyone, let alone someone with two left hands. But still, proper music, like. Instead of… Neolithic baking techniques. Alright, alright. Music’s good. You could join a band, then. There's that open mic night at The Rusty Mug next week. You could read out your poetry. Don’t you dare. My poetry is for private consumption only, thank you very much. Besides, I’d be mortified. Speaking of mortified... did you hear about what happened down at the community centre? You mean… the thing with Mr. Davies? Yeah. Terrible. Absolutely terrible. I still can't believe it. It’s just… gut-wrenching, isn't it? The thought of someone doing that to a child. Makes you proper angry. And scared, to be honest. You hear these things and you think, how can anyone be capable of that? I don't know. I really don't. My mum always said… you just can't trust anyone. Which is a bleak outlook, I know. But… it’s hard not to think that now. It is. Makes you want to wrap everyone up in cotton wool. My little cousin, Sophie… I’d be terrified to let her out of my sight. Gets proper hold of you, doesn’t it? It does. It’s a good job his dodgy guv’nor got caught. Honestly, the interviewing on the news was proper uncomfortable to watch. Aye, it were. But hopefully, it helps. Shifting gears a bit, though… have you been practicing with your guitar lately? You were sounding pretty good last week, remember? You were almost nailed that solo from "Smells Like Teen Spirit." Yeah, I've been messing about a bit.

Ugh, I’m so bored already. Half-term’s only just started and I’ve already scrolled through TikTok twice. Tell me about it. My mum’s threatening to make me help weed the garden. Like, seriously? It’s supposed to be a relax-y week. Your mums are relentless. My dad's trying to drag me to the Science Museum. Apparently, there’s a new robotics exhibition. Sounds… thrilling. Robotics? Nah, I'd rather watch paint dry. I'm trying to visualise Montenegro, actually. Remember we were talking about that holiday? Photos online are amazing - the mountains, the coastline... Yeah! Montenegro! We need to actually  do  something about that. My dad says it's financially tricky right now, you know? Everything's so expensive. It is. My mum mentioned the same thing. But imagine, hiking in those mountains! Think we could convince our parents to at least look at package deals? My EPQ research is actually loosely related – I'm looking at sustainable tourism and the impact on developing nations. Seriously? That’s actually pretty cool. What's your project specifically? It's about ecotourism in the Balkans and whether it can genuinely benefit local communities or if it just ends up exploiting them. Loads of research into poverty, fairness, the whole deal. It’s ironically helping me justify a holiday! See? Everything's connected! My grandad was talking about how things were in Wembley when he was a kid – completely different. Poverty was much more visible, you know? It's easy to forget how much things have changed, even though there’s still loads of inequality around. It’s insane, isn't it? Like, you read about it in history, but it's another thing entirely to hear it from someone who actually lived it. Speaking of history, are you guys still stressed about that Ancient Rome essay? Mr. Harrison is brutal. Don't even go there! I'm drowning in primary sources. I’m thinking of just claiming I'm vegetarian now because it feels less stressful than arguing about whether or not Roman emperors enjoyed roast boar. Good tactic. I'm slightly more invested in the roast boar debate, if I’m honest. Although, I did have a weird dream last night about juggling olives. Juggling olives? What's that even about? Were there Roman soldiers involved? No! It was just me, in my kitchen, desperately trying to juggle olives while wearing a colander on my head.

Honestly, this kitchen is a disgrace. Seriously. Half the cupboards are hanging off, and someone left a mouldy avocado in the fridge  again . It's like living in a student hovel. Cor, you’re right about that. It's a bit rough, innit? Not exactly the Ritz, is it? At least the kettle works. That’s the main thing, really. And the bins get emptied... eventually. You Brits and your flat anxieties are fascinating. In my family, if the kitchen wasn’t chaotic, we’d have worried something was wrong. Sustained order is a sign of trouble, apparently. You talking about the mouldy avocado again, Liv? Because I swear it wasn't me this time. I threw out, like, three of those last week. This time it was definitely Ben from three doors down. Saw him sneaking in here earlier. Typical! Ben’s always been a menace. Honestly, I’m starting to think about applying for a different flat next year. Somewhere with, you know, actual working appliances. And maybe a dishwasher. Is that too much to ask? A dishwasher would be lovely! Though, then you'd have to  load  it, wouldn’t you? Still better than washing up after someone’s left a science experiment festering in the fridge. Speaking of which, have you lot seen my oat milk? I swear someone's been nicking it. Perhaps it's a targeted oat milk heist. A sophisticated operation. I’ll keep an eye out for any suspicious activity involving dairy alternatives. By the way, has anyone heard from Priya's mum? She said she might send some samosas. Nah, haven't heard anything. My mum called earlier, though. Apparently, Liam's been getting into trouble again. Liam? Your cousin? What’s he done this time? Surely he hasn't robbed another sweet shop? Worse, actually. He tried to… dye the family dog blue. Oh, bless his heart! That’s mental! Why blue, though? Apparently, it was for a TikTok video. He wanted to make it go viral. My mum was not impressed. She’s grounded him for a month. The yearning for internet fame... it's a powerful motivator. My auntie tried to start a YouTube channel teaching people how to braid their hair. It lasted about three videos. The lighting was atrocious. Honestly, families. They're a constant source of entertainment. My dad keeps trying to convince me to come home for Sunday roast.

Oh, children. A chaotic blessing, aren't they? Sounds about right. Christmas with the grandkids is always a bit… frenetic. Reminds me of when my own were little. You were a whirlwind, Amelia, always getting into something. Remember that year you tried to decorate the cat with tinsel? Oh, goodness, yes! Mum nearly had a heart attack! It was  glitter  everywhere, too. Everything was sparkly. I thought it was the most wonderful thing in the world. But you know, it's funny, those memories, they just… warm you, don’t they? Even the slightly stressful ones. How's your Christmas looking, Brenda? Are you seeing the family in Cardiff? I am, thankfully. Flying down on the 23rd. Bit of a hassle these days, the airport security, but it's worth it to be with them. My son, David, and his wife, Fiona, are hosting. They’re making a big effort this year. Apparently, Fiona’s decided to tackle a traditional Welsh Christmas dinner. Oh, brilliant! What does that entail? I'm always fascinated by regional Christmas traditions. Well, she’s attempting a Bara Brith – that’s a fruit loaf, very dark and sticky – and she’s got a whole turkey stuffed with sausages and leeks. Honestly, the aromas alone will be intoxicating. The kids are, predictably, more interested in the presents, but I'm looking forward to the food. What about you? Still in Totnes this year? Yep, staying put. Mark’s parents are coming down to visit. We're having a pretty low-key affair this year, to be honest. After the chaos of last Christmas, we decided to streamline things. One tree, minimal decorations, and definitely no questionable Father Christmas impersonations from the children! It's all about relaxing and enjoying the peace. Although, teaching English to teenagers does leave me a little frayed around the edges. Teaching, eh? Still enjoying it? It must be rewarding, in its own way. I remember you talking about wanting to teach abroad, years ago. Did you ever consider it properly? I did, for a while. There was a stint with a placement in Vietnam that sounded incredible, but the logistics were a nightmare, and Mark wasn't really up for it at that point. Now… well, with little Leo, it feels even less practical. Besides, Totnes is lovely, and I’m making a real difference to these kids. They're bright, but some really need a bit of extra support.

Right, nearly there then. Feels a bit strange, doesn't it? Seeing you after two whole years. Time flies, eh? Feels like five minutes since you were last scrumping apples from Mrs. Higgins' tree. Don't remind me! She used to chase us with a broom like we were criminals. Glad I’m not doing that now, teaching eager learners about the perfect past tense. It's a lot less stressful than evading Mrs. Higgins. Though, marking essays  can  be its own kind of torture. Teaching, eh? Still at that little language school in London? You seem to like it. You always were good with people. Better than me, anyway. Dealing with disgruntled customers all day takes a toll, you know. Yeah, it's alright. Pays the bills. It's… fulfilling, in a quiet kind of way. Thinking about the Brighton move though. That’s something else entirely. You reckon Crayford will change  that  much in another two years, with us gone? Change? Crayford's already changed. Remember when the old bakery was there, the one with the incredible sourdough? Gone. Replaced by another bloody phone shop. They’re popping up like mushrooms, these phone shops. Seems everyone needs a new one every six months. Speaking of phones, did you remember to download that parking app I sent you? Need it for Brighton. Those parking meters are a nightmare. Nearly forgot! Just doing it now. You wouldn’t believe the drama I had with my license photo. It looks like I'm staring directly into the abyss. Apparently, having a ‘slightly melancholic’ expression isn’t ideal for official documentation. Oh, you and your expressions. Always been a bit moody, haven’t you? Speaking of needing things… I’ve been under the weather this week. Proper chesty. Doctor says it’s just a bug, but it knocked me for six. Had to take a couple of days off work. The manager wasn't impressed. Said customer service can't stop for sniffles and coughs. As if empathy goes out the window when you're feeling rough! That's awful, Dad. You should rest properly. Brighton’s going to be good for you, though. Fresh air, the sea... Remember how Dad used to say the sea air cured everything? Aye, your grandfather. Always swore by it. Though his definition of “fresh air” often involved a pint in the pub overlooking the harbour. Still, it  is  a change.

Honestly, that meeting with the alumni was brutal. They wanted to fund a baroque lute department. A baroque lute department, Elara! Who even  plays  those anymore? A baroque lute department? Seriously? You'd think they'd be more interested in something…relevant. Did you manage to steer them towards the coding club at least? I tried, believe me. I layered it with the argument about future-proofing the university, about equipping students with skills the modern world demands. They nodded along politely, then brought it back to the lute. Apparently, Lord Ashworth is a passionate enthusiast. Apparently, passionate enthusiasts wield enormous amounts of money. Ah, the classic Ashworth manoeuvre. So, public relations is always a delicate dance, isn’t it? I had a slightly less dramatic, but equally tedious, meeting with the student union about the new sustainability initiative. Let me guess, they want more vegan options in the cafeteria  and  a complete overhaul of the recycling system by next Tuesday? Pretty much. Though this time, they also want me to personally lead a protest against fast fashion. Apparently, lecturing on Victorian literature doesn’t automatically qualify me as an environmental activist. They're reaching. Look, tell them you'll support it conceptually, point them towards the environmental society, and then subtly mention the budget constraints. Standard deflection tactics. Exactly what I did. It's exhausting, though, trying to manage everyone’s expectations. Speaking of exhausting, I spent the afternoon wrestling with that ridiculous online shopping cart. The dress I wanted was out of stock in my size, then mysteriously reappeared, then disappeared again. It was a digital cat-and-mouse game. Online shopping… the bane of my existence. I tried to order some new speakers for the study. Seven different websites, three different models, and still not sure if they'll even sound any better than what I have. Why don't you just go to Richer Sounds? It's much less stressful. And you can actually  hear  them before you buy them. You're right. I always forget about Richer Sounds. I get so bogged down in the details online. Anyway, while I was procrastinating on speaker research, I stumbled across this brilliant new band – ‘Spectral Bloom.’ Have you heard of them? Spectral Bloom? The name rings a bell... vaguely. What kind of music are they? It's... hard to describe. Kind of dream-pop, but with this really interesting electronic undercurrent.

Honestly, David, I’m getting quite frustrated with this bean bag cover. The ribbing just…doesn’t want to behave. It's all wonky on one side. Wonky ribbing? Sounds serious. Is it a catastrophic wonk, or a… manageable wonk? We still have time, supper needs to be on the table in about an hour. A manageable wonk, I suppose. But it’s intensely irritating. I’ve ripped it out three times now. I was so pleased with the colour – that dusty rose I picked up at the market – and now it’s just stressing me out. I’m starting to think I should just buy one. Mass-produced, perfect ribbing. The shame! Don't be silly. You’re brilliant at knitting. It’s just a bit of stubborn yarn. Remember that incredibly complicated Fair Isle sweater you made for Mum? This is nothing compared to that. Besides, a handmade bean bag has so much more character. You’re being awfully encouraging. Is there a reason for this sudden burst of positivity? Are you planning on announcing you're finally tackling the patio? No, no patio announcements. Just genuinely trying to prevent a full-blown knitting crisis. It was a good choice of colour, though. Really suits the living room. Speaking of which… have you had a proper look at that shower curtain I got? The…lime green and turquoise monstrosity? Yes, I have. And I’m still reeling. Monstrosity? I thought it was rather…bold. A little splash of colour in the bathroom. The magnolia was getting monotonous. Bold isn't the word I'd use. It’s aggressively vibrant. It's like being assaulted by a tropical fruit salad every time I shower. And it clashes horribly with the towels. It does clash with the towels. Admittedly. But I thought we could get some new towels! Something to complement the… vibrancy. Maybe a deep indigo? Deep indigo wouldn't even help! It’d just create a completely different, equally questionable colour scheme. Honestly, David, you and your decorating choices sometimes baffle me. Remember that wallpaper you insisted on in the hallway? Let's not revisit the floral explosion, please. We agreed to never speak of the sunflower wallpaper again. This is different! This is a shower curtain. A small piece of fabric. A very large, very brightly coloured piece of fabric that dominates the entire bathroom. This needs a bit more salt, I think.

Honestly, Arthur, you're being wilfully obtuse. It's not a conspiracy, it's just… inconvenient. That's all. Inconvenient? Doreen, the postman didn't deliver my pension book again today! Inconvenient is a bit of a weak word for that, wouldn't you say? It’s a blimming disgrace, it is. Been waiting for that for a fortnight now. Right, let's try to de-escalate this. What exactly happened with the pension book, Arthur? And Doreen, what ‘inconvenience’ are you talking about? You've been simmering all afternoon. It's the council, Charles. The new online portal. They're pushing everyone onto it, saying it's more efficient. Efficient for whom, I'd like to know? Certainly not for people like us. I spent two hours on the phone yesterday just trying to update my address, and the system just kept kicking me off. Two hours, Charles! I could have knitted a whole scarf in that time. They're trying to get rid of us, you know. Old people. No longer needed. Costs too much to keep us around. It’s plain as day. Arthur, that's ridiculous. That’s paranoia talking. The council is trying to modernise. It’s not a personal attack. It’s… bureaucracy, unfortunately. And sometimes it's badly implemented, I'll grant you that. Doreen, did they offer any alternatives? Alternatives? They said I could go to the council offices and get it sorted in person. Which is miles away, and the buses are a nightmare on Tuesdays. It’s designed to make it difficult, Charles, mark my words. Designed! See? She’s right. They don’t want us going anywhere. They want us stuck at home, forgotten. Like… like forgotten prisoners. Okay, Arthur. Let's not get carried away. Look, I’ll call the council tomorrow. I know a chap on the local authority, used to play cricket with him. I’ll see if he can intervene on your behalf, Arthur. Get them to look into the pension book. It's just a matter of getting someone to push the right buttons, you see? Really, Charles? Would you do that? That would be lovely. I'm not very good on computers, you know. Never been. Always preferred a pen and paper. Everything’s so… fleeting now. All digital, no substance. Substance. Exactly. They’re taking away all the substance, leaving us with nothing but… pixels.

Honestly, Sarah, you're right to be exasperated. It's all a bit much, isn’t it? Christmas creeping in earlier and earlier every year. I felt a bit of a twitch when they started putting the decorations out at work last week. A twitch! You’re such a grump, Auntie Carol! But I get it. It’s overwhelming. I tried to do some online shopping for presents last night, felt like I was wading through a sea of tinsel and ‘best festive offers.’ It’s exhausting just  thinking  about it. Now, now, girls. Don't start complaining about the wonder of consumerism. It keeps people employed, doesn't it? Though I will admit, even I felt a bit pressured when I saw the Boxing Day sales already advertised. Absolute madness. Did you manage to get those mince pies, Sarah? Oh, yes, I got the ones from Sainsbury's. They’re alright, though not as good as mum used to make. Remember those, Carol? With the little star sprinkles? Oh, heaven yes, Brenda! I've tried replicating them, you know, but it’s never quite the same. The pastry was always the key. A touch of lard, apparently, is what made all the difference. And a generous grating of nutmeg. Lard? Auntie Carol, that sounds…complicated. I'm sticking to shop-bought, thank you very much. I’ve got that copywriting project to finish, and I haven’t even started thinking about Christmas cards yet. The brief is dreadful, too. It’s for a…a badger-themed toilet roll. A badger-themed toilet roll? Seriously? You’re pulling my leg. I wish I was! Apparently, it's all about "rustic charm" and "natural comfort." I'm trying to make badgers sound appealing for wiping your…you know. Oh, dear. That  is  dreadful. You could quit and come work at the hospital with Carol! We’re always short-staffed. Just need to pass the training, mind. It’s intense, but rewarding. Don’t tempt her, Brenda! Though, she’d be brilliant. She’s got a good head on her shoulders, Lucy. Much better than some of the youngsters we get now. Barely able to boil an egg, some of 'em. Don't go comparing Lucy to the current crop, Carol. Every generation’s got its challenges. Remember when  we  were young? The flares? The questionable music? Questionable music? Dad, you listened to Queen!

Lovely morning, isn’t it, Eleanor? Bit dusty, but lovely nonetheless. Still getting used to the air, you know. Bushey was… well, Bushey wasn't exactly known for its dust. More drizzle, really. It is beautiful, Bernard. Absolutely. And yes, the air is different. Cleaner, in some ways, though the dust is a novelty. It’s so strange being surrounded by orange groves. Reminds me a little of holidaying in Spain as a child, but...different. Are you finding it easy to settle in, then? It’s quite a leap from Bushey, I imagine. A leap? Eleanor, dear, it's a chasm! Bushey was… predictable. Comfortable. Perfectly mundane. This… this is adventure. Though adventure does come with its challenges. The bureaucracy, for one. Trying to sort out residency? Don’t even get me started. It’s like navigating a maze designed by a particularly grumpy octopus. I can imagine. The paperwork here can be… robust. Do you have any advice for me? I’m starting the process this week. Anything I should be particularly mindful of? Be prepared to be patient. Immensely patient. And bring multiple copies of everything. At least five. They'll find a reason to ask for more. And learn a few basic Turkish phrases. Even "hello" and "thank you" go a long way. The officials, bless their hearts, appreciate the effort. Good tip, thank you. I’ve been trying to learn a bit. It's proving trickier than I anticipated. The grammar…! A beast, isn't it? I’ve been dabbling myself. Tried ordering a coffee the other day entirely in Turkish. The poor barista looked terrified. Ended up with a Turkish delight instead. Delicious, mind you, but not what I wanted. That’s a brilliant story! It’s so easy to make mistakes. I nearly asked for a goat at the market last week instead of mangoes. My pronunciation needs some work. A goat! Splendid! See? You’re already embracing the culture. We mustn't be afraid to look foolish. It's part of the fun. Have you been to Famagusta yet? The ghost town, I mean. Not yet. I've heard it’s incredibly poignant. A bit melancholy, perhaps. Poignant is a good word. It truly is. Standing there, looking at those abandoned hotels and shops... it's a reminder of how quickly history can change. I went a few weeks ago. Took a little tour.

Honestly, it’s getting worse, isn't it? I could taste it on the breeze just walking from the metro. Feels like I've inhaled a coal factory. Tell me about it. I was lecturing on Dickens this morning, ironically enough, and kept thinking of London smog. Except this is… different. Thicker, somehow. And it doesn’t smell of coal, it’s just… gritty. Exactly! It’s almost sweet, that underlying acrid smell. Disgusting, really. I was looking at some air quality reports online earlier. The PM2.5 levels are still well above anything acceptable. Back home, we'd shut the city down. Don't remind me. I did try to explain it to some of the students. They just looked at me, bewildered. They're used to it. It's just... background noise, apparently. That's what worries me most. The normalization of this. It’s unsettling, definitely. Remember when we first arrived? We were shocked. Now… well, we’re still shocked, but we’ve adapted. We wear masks more. We buy air purifiers. But it’s not right, is it? It shouldn’t be a lifestyle choice, having clean air. No, it absolutely shouldn’t. Honestly, I'm starting to consider moving. Not permanently, God no - I love teaching here, I love the students, and the research opportunities are fantastic - but perhaps taking a sabbatical back in Norwich for a few months each year. Just to breathe properly. That’s… sensible. I hadn't thought about it. My mom's been saying I look peaky lately, and I suppose she has a point. My runs have definitely suffered. My lungs feel like they're coated in sand. You  do  look a little pale. Though, let’s be honest, you always were a bit… pale. But seriously, it’s affecting us. And what about the cats? Their breathing seems more laboured lately. Good point. Mittens definitely seems less energetic. Right, masks it is then, tonight. Do we have any replacements? I think mine’s past its best. I think so. There are a few in the cupboard. So, apart from existential dread and respiratory concerns… how was your day? Any breakthroughs with the Chalmers thesis supervision? Chalmers is being Chalmers. Still convinced his theoretical framework can justify anything. I swear, the boy could argue that the sky is purple and somehow make it sound academically rigorous. He’s trying to incorporate Lacan into his analysis of… competitive bread baking.

Honestly, John, you’d think after all these years, you’d know not to put the baking tray directly on the gas hob! It’s smoking something awful. Sorry, love. Got distracted by this article about the local council’s new parking scheme. Utter madness, if you ask me. Smells like burning... what  is  that, anyway? It  was  meant to be a béchamel sauce for the cauliflower cheese. Now it mostly smells like burnt milk and regret. I’m going to have to start again. Honestly, sometimes I wonder how we’ve managed this long. Woah! Bit of a fire going on in here, isn't there? Everything alright? Mum, you look stressed. Just a minor culinary disaster, darling. Your dad decided to conduct an impromptu metal experiment on the gas hob. I was warming up a bit of bread, that's all. Don’t exaggerate, Deborah. Warming up bread with a baking tray on the burner? Bit unorthodox, Dad. Anyway, smells interesting. What are we having? Well,  were  having cauliflower cheese and sausages. Now, it’s looking more like sausages and… potentially, something else entirely. I'll see if I can salvage this béchamel. Did you have a good day, love? It was okay. Had a slightly chaotic morning. Client wanted a complete rewrite of a blog post, like, an hour before it was due to go live. Typical. I’m glad to be home. Any chance of a cuppa before dinner? Of course, sweetheart. John, could you put the kettle on? Just… please, stand well clear of the hob. Right you are. So, Deborah, what were you working on besides frantic blog post rescues? Anything exciting? Not really. Mostly just trying to convince people that using exclamation marks excessively doesn't make their marketing copy more engaging. It just makes it look desperate. Amen to that. Some people… Honestly. Remember that ad campaign for the garden centre last year? Every sentence had three exclamation points! It was madness. I do! "Fantastic plants! Wonderful prices! Hurry in today!!!" Gave me a headache just looking at it. Exactly! Speaking of headaches, I saw a photo from Aunt Carol's holiday in Spain on Facebook. She's got that same pose she always does, leaning against a wall, with a slightly pained expression. Oh, Carol. She’s the Queen of the Forced Holiday Smile. Remember that one from the Lake District, where she's clearly freezing, but beaming at the camera next to a very damp-looking sheep?

Right, so, if this is remotely accurate, the new 7 bus route actually goes  past  the Press bookshop now. Remember how we used to have to walk all the way around? Aye, reet! That's champion, that is. I’ve been grievin’ about that for months. Takes an age to get there, especially in this weather. You reckon it’ll be reliable though? Cambridge bus services…  sigh . That's the million-dollar question, isn’t it? The council’s plastered all over Facebook claiming it’s a ‘game-changer’ for residents, but we’ll see. They said the guided busway would be a game-changer too, and look at that – constantly delayed. Aye, tell me about it. Remember poor Bethany from the office? She missed a whole day's work because of that thing last November. Absolute chaos. Speaking of chaos, did you see that lass protesting outside the Senate House yesterday? The one chained to the willow tree? I did! Bit dramatic, wasn’t she? Something about divestment from fossil fuels? The University's got a reputation to maintain, you know. Can't be having people hanging off trees, disrupting everything. I can understand her point though, to be fair. It’s tough when you’re seein’ what’s happening to the planet. Makes you wonder what the point is in gettin' a fancy degree and all that if we’re all goin' to be underwater in, like, twenty years. Well, that's rather bleak, isn't it? But I do appreciate the passion. Cambridge certainly has a long history of student activism. Though, let’s be honest, a lot of it is performative. More for the Instagram likes than actual meaningful change. Maybe. But a bit o’passion is better than no passion, eh? Anyway, what were you saying about the bookshop? I'm needing a fresh copy o' 'The Northern Lights' – my mum's been badgering me to read it again. Right. Well, with the bus route, it’s suddenly perfectly accessible. It’s much better than trying to park anywhere near Trumpington Street. You know, speaking of accessibility... It still strikes me how different our uni experiences were, despite both being on the ‘top’ tier. How so? Sunderland Uni's not exactly the Sorbonne, but it weren’t all bad. Decent IT facilities, friendly lecturers… Of course, it wasn't. But the  atmosphere , you know? Cambridge felt… intense.

Honestly, the portion sizes here are ridiculous! I swear, this chicken Caesar salad could feed a small family. I’m going to be rolling myself out of here. Tell me about it! They clearly cater to a very particular clientele who feel the need to feel  seen  by the amount of food on their plate. It’s all a bit much, isn’t it? Though, I did sneak a photo of the dessert menu – it looks divine. It is lovely, isn’t it? A change from beans on toast for me, that’s for sure. Though, beans on toast has its place, you know. Simple pleasures. You wouldn’t think I’d appreciate a fancy lunch after… well, after all these years. After retiring, you mean? It's only been a few months, Mum! Don’t act like it’s a lifetime! And you  should  appreciate it. You deserve it. You dedicated your life to maths. Poor little Timmy telling Mrs. O’Malley he couldn’t possibly multiply seven by eight because it “felt wrong.” Honestly! Priceless. I remember you telling me about that. You probably single-handedly rescued his grade. Speaking of rescued, how’s Liam settling in? He seemed a bit…reserved when I last spoke to him. He's good, dear, he’s good. Still a bit quiet, mind you. Moving is a big upheaval even for a young man. He misses Dublin, naturally. The craic, he calls it. Trying to explain ‘craic’ to his tutor was a challenge, let me tell you. She kept asking if it was a typo! Oh, bless her. “The craic was mighty” is a phrase that’s going to be utterly lost on most people here. You'll have to teach  her  Irish culture, Mum! Maybe a session on Irish proverbs? That would be brilliant. Seriously. It would be amazing to learn more. You always had the best stories, Auntie Bridie. Remember that one about the leprechaun and the lost sheep? Ah, that was a good one. My grandmother used to tell it. Said it kept the children away from the bog. Though I suspect it was more to do with keeping them out of trouble than warding off mythical creatures! Honestly, it's fascinating how language shapes those stories. The rhythm, the alliteration… it's all so poetic. It makes me think about my work sometimes – taking these dry legal documents and trying to make them readable, accessible.

"Look at that thing! Still feels like it shouldn’t be there, doesn't it? Like a giant, silvery mushroom sprouting from the riverbank." "It does. A bit…overwhelming, really. Though, I suppose it's iconic now. More iconic than, say, the Woolwich Ferry, which, let’s be honest, isn’t exactly drawing tourists from across the globe.” “No, it’s not. Though, I do appreciate a reliable ferry. Simpler times, eh? You know, I was reading about the history of the Thames, actually. Fascinating stuff. All these mills and the trade…it’s hard to imagine the modern city growing from that." “It is. And look, the Cutty Sark is just visible over there. You know, we really should take the kids. They’ve been promising to go for months now. Though, getting there without a car is always an adventure.” "A monumental adventure! We're like explorers navigating the urban jungle. Public transport, the DLR…it's a commitment, isn't it? Still beating a car, though, wouldn’t you agree? The cost, the parking… the sheer  stress  of it all." "Absolutely. I’m quite proud of our car-free existence, actually. Gives the kids a bit more…perspective, I think. Forces them to rely on something other than ‘Dad will just drive me there.’" "True, true. Speaking of relying on things…I was trying to convert some American measurements for a cake recipe the other day. ‘One cup’… what  is  a cup, really? It’s such an imprecise unit! Why can't they just use millilitres like the rest of the world?" "Don't even get me started on the American system. It’s utterly chaotic. A cup! It feels like something out of a children’s storybook. Trying to bake anything from an American recipe is a constant source of anxiety. And don't get me started on Fahrenheit! I almost set the kitchen on fire last winter trying to understand oven temperatures." "Almost! That’s precisely my concern. It's madness. Reminds me, we need to book that holiday. I was looking at Cornwall again... somewhere with proper beaches, proper cream teas... and hopefully, a kitchen with metric measurements." "Cornwall's lovely. The kids would adore it. Though, it needs to be soon. It feels like forever since we had a proper family holiday. Something more than just a weekend away in Brighton." "Do you think they even  remember  what a proper holiday is like?"

Honestly, Mum, this rain is just relentless. It’s been chucking it down all morning. Sports Day is going to be a mud bath, isn't it? Well, love, you can’t control the weather, can you? Little Leo will still enjoy racing, even if he’s covered in mud. At least it’s not freezing cold. Remember that year at Ollie's school, the wind was howling and everyone was shivering? Don't remind me! Mia cried the whole way home because her ribbons kept blowing off. Honestly, kids and the unpredictability of life, eh? At least you can wear a bobble hat. It's just Leo’s been so excited. He keeps talking about winning the egg and spoon race. He even practiced with Barney last night. Barney? Let me guess, the bear you made him at Build-a-Bear? Yep. He’s got one paw slightly wonky, but Leo insists he’s “super speedy.” It’s adorable. I’m trying to teach him not to take every cuddly toy everywhere, but it’s a losing battle. He'd get distraught. I know exactly how you feel. Chloe still carries Mr. Snuggles around, even though she’s practically eight! It’s endearing, but sometimes you just want them to grow up a bit, you know? I'm trying to convince her he's for "emergencies only" now. They cling to those things, don't they? It's a comfort. Remember when you were little, Lila - you wouldn't go anywhere without Penelope the penguin? Oh god, Penelope! I’d completely forgotten about her. Mum, you kept her in a special box when I wasn't using her. I was so convinced she'd run away if I left her out too long. Kids are the same. Actually, speaking of convincing, I’ve been trying to convince Thomas to properly use the toilet, you know? Potty training is a nightmare. One minute he's going great guns, the next he's regressing back to accidents everywhere! Oh, the drama! Leo had his phases too. Remember when he'd only poo in the bath? It was absolute chaos! Children. They keep you on your toes, don’t they? Speaking of chaos… did you see the state of my freezer after I tried to defrost it? An absolute disaster. Ice everywhere! I might have to buy a new one. Those fancy frost-free ones look brilliant, but they're probably extortionate.

…and honestly, Sarah, I’m feeling really quite restless. This house-sitting is lovely, don't get me wrong. The view's incredible, the pool is a delight, but…it’s amplified what I was already feeling, you know? Just a bit… stagnant. Stagnant? You, stagnant? The man who launched three businesses in ten years? You're being dramatic, Liam. It’s a holiday, well, a house-sitting arrangement. Give it a rest. But, I get it. I do. This quiet is… different from our usual bustle. It's more than just the quiet. It's… I need a project. Something to sink my teeth into. Thinking about scaling 'EcoBloom' internationally finally feels… achievable. But the logistics... the funding…it's a lot. EcoBloom is brilliant, Liam. You should absolutely pursue it. But let's not bite off more than we can chew, shall we? Remember the aquaponics venture? Still got a slightly damp shed full of equipment, haven’t you? A painful reminder. Point taken. But this is different. There's real demand for sustainable gardening solutions, especially in places like California. I was thinking, maybe connecting with that investor I met at the conference in Berlin? Klaus Richter? He seemed genuinely interested. Klaus Richter? The one with the…rather intense handshake? Right. Well, nurture that connection. Have you looked at crowdfunding? It could be a good way to test the water and build some early support. It's on the list. What about you? You seem awfully content just folding socks, my dear. Are you truly happy teaching Year 4s about the water cycle indefinitely? Don't be cheeky. I enjoy my job, Liam. The children are wonderful, chaotic bundles of energy. But… you’re right. There’s this nagging feeling. I've been thinking about the online teaching certification. Remember how we talked about it years ago? Vaguely. Something about homeschooling options and a bit of extra income? More than that. It'd give me more flexibility. Maybe I could develop my own curriculum, teach internationally. Perhaps even offer support to children with learning difficulties, tutoring online. I’d love to feel like I’m doing something… more impactful. That sounds fantastic, love. Really. I’d support that wholeheartedly. We could even look at how EcoBloom could incorporate educational resources - gardening programs for schools, something like that. A symbiotic relationship! You and your symbiosis! Always thinking about the big picture.

Honestly, the way you lot say "butter." It’s like… utter. Like you’re struggling to get the word out! It's a Yorkshire thing, innit? We just pronounce it properly. Proper? You’re sayin’  our  accents are wrong? I reckon it sounds a bit, well, a bit… shouty, love. Like you're always arguin' with someone. She’s got a point, El. My Nan used to say, “Don't be arguin' like a Yorkshire lass!” Even though she was from Wigan. Go figger that one out. It's just the way we talk! We’re direct. And passionate about our tea. Speaking of passion, did you all see that new Pokémon Snap game trailer? It looks mental! Mental is right! I've been waiting for ages! I'm gonna need a new Nintendo Switch, though. Mine's seen better days. Anyone fancy popping to Game later? Nah, I'm working tomorrow. Need my beauty sleep, reet? Plus, I'm knackered from chasing spreadsheets all day. Audit & Accounts is a right laugh, let me tell you. Sounds thrilling. I’m knee-deep in essays on post-structuralism. That's  real  fun. Remember that camping trip we did when we were like, fifteen? Absolute chaos that was. Oh god, yeah! Remember when Liam’s tent collapsed in the middle of the night and he ended up covered in mud? And Dad nearly had a heart attack trying to build it again? And Mum kept yelling about squirrels eating all the After-Eights! She was proper stressed about those chocolates. Aye, memories. I used to be terrified of birds back then. Still am, to be honest. Fight or flight, innit? Just scream and run. Speaking of running and tech, has anyone got a Fitbit? I keep meaning to get one but I’m not sure if they're any good. I’d like to track my steps, but I don’t want to be constantly nagged by a wristband. My mum's got one. She's obsessed. It dictates her entire life now. Apparently, she walked six miles yesterday just to get her step count up. It's a bit mad. My cousin got one. Reckons it’s really helpful for motivation. Though she also complained it was constantly telling her to “move more” when she was literally just sat trying to balance the books. It’s like, the technology’s there, but sometimes it just makes things more stressful.

Never! Blimey, Sarah, you know how I feel about them Man U lot. Always gettin’ the benefit of the doubt. Always. Fifty years I've been watchin' football, and it never changes. Oh, Arthur, don't get yourself worked up. It’s just a game. Though, I have to admit, that  was  a dodgy call. Though, I was quite enjoying the excitement, even if my team lost. Did you catch that lovely goal Chelsea scored earlier? Actually, Mum, it was quite a significant tactical decision that led to that goal. The midfield rotation allowed… Right, right, let's not get too technical, Chloe. Dad’s got enough to process with the penalty decision. He’s clearly still fuming. Fuming’s the word, David. Fumin’! And it’s all politics, isn't it? They favour the big clubs. They do. Makes a fella wonder what it’s all about. Speaking of politics... I saw on the telly… Arthur, darling, please! We're having a lovely dinner. Let's stick to lighter topics. Chloe made that delicious shepherd’s pie. Remember how you used to complain when I made it, Arthur, and said mine was too bland? Well, it  was  a bit bland, wasn't it, love? Needed a bit more rosemary, a bit more pepper. Still, it’s a good pie. Don’t get me wrong. You always put your heart into it. I tried to follow Grandma’s recipe, but I tweaked it a bit. Added a touch of Worcestershire sauce, and a smoked paprika for depth. It’s interesting how culinary traditions evolve, isn’t it? Each generation adding their own… Chloe, you’re starting to sound like your lectures! Although, it  is  a really good pie. Seriously. Much better than the takeaway we had last week. Takeaway’s fine for a treat now and then. But nothing beats a home-cooked meal, especially when Chloe's put in the effort. Now, about that party for Margaret’s 80th… Have we decided on a theme yet? I was thinking 1940s, something a bit nostalgic. 1940s? Blimey. I was a lad then! Rationing and all that. Not sure that’s a particularly cheerful theme, is it? It could be done well, Dad. Vintage posters, wartime music… Restricting it to just rationing would be a bit grim. We could focus on the fashion and the music, the sense of community spirit. I quite like the 1940s idea, actually.

Honestly, I don't know what to do anymore. This whole… thing… is just overwhelming. Still feelin' like chuckin' it all in, then, Elara? You've been mopin' about it for a week. Mopin' is a strong word. Just… contemplating. Seriously contemplating. It’s just not for me, Liv. All those lectures, the readings… I can't absorb it. I’m just staring into space, pretending I'm listening. But you were so excited about this course! Archaeology? Diggin' up old bones and stuff? You used to play Indiana Jones in your garden back 'ome, remember? With your grandad's walking stick? Yeah, well, my grandad's walking stick didn’t require me to write a 5,000-word dissertation on Roman pottery shards. It was more about escaping the seagulls, mostly. Falmouth was… simpler. So, runnin’ back to Falmouth is the plan then? Back to the seagulls and Cornish pasties? Because that’s not exactly a long-term career solution, El. I don't know! Maybe. Sometimes I think it wasn't meant to be. Maybe I should’ve listened to my mum and done something… practical. Like hairdressing. Hairdressing? You? Trying to tame anyone’s hair would be an absolute disaster. Remember that time you tried to braid Daisy's hair at that beach party? She cried for an hour. Okay, point taken. I'm not exactly blessed with a steady hand. But still... everything’s so expensive. I feel like I'm just hemorrhaging money on something that isn’t even working. My student loan… it’s terrifying. Tell me about it! My Gran keeps askin' me when I'm gonna start earnin' some decent money. Like, I'm nineteen, Gran! It’s not exactly a sprint! But look, you haven't even finished the first term. Talk to your tutor. Explain how you’re feelin’. They have advisors. I know, I know. I just… I’m scared of looking like a failure, you know? Like I’ve made the wrong decision. Failure? Nah. Takin' a break isn’t failure, Elara. It’s figuring out what you  do  want. Speaking of names... did you ever find out why your mum chose "Elara"? It's a bit fancy for Falmouth, isn’t it? Actually, no. I’ve asked, but she always just gives me some vague, dreamy look and says something about stars. My dad threatened to call me Tiffany once.

Honestly, the risotto was absolutely divine. I haven’t had risotto this good since that little Italian place in Rome! Did you manage to finish yours, Liv? You were eyeing it up like it was the last meal on earth. I know, right? It was incredible. And yes, I did finish it. Every last grain. I was starving after that conference call this morning. Seriously, Mr. Davies just drones on and on about synergy. Synergy! Who even  uses  that word in real life? Typical Davies. He’s probably got a PowerPoint dedicated solely to synergy. So, tell me everything about this Project Coordinator life. Sounds impressive, by the way. Is it all colour-coded spreadsheets and aggressive email chains? Pretty much, yeah. Though, today was particularly stressful. We're launching a new sustainability campaign, which is, on paper, amazing. But getting everyone on board… convincing the marketing team that reducing plastic packaging isn’t ‘bad for branding’… it’s been a battle. Oh, I can imagine. So many people terrified of change. My job isn’t  quite  as chaotic, but Pearson’s new social media strategy is already driving me up the wall. They’re obsessed with TikTok dances, and I’m supposed to convince uni students that textbook rentals are ‘trendy’. It's... a stretch. Textbook rentals and TikTok dances. The modern world. What’s Sarah up to these days? Last I heard she was backpacking through Southeast Asia. She’s still there! She just sent me a postcard from Thailand. Apparently, she’s learned to scuba dive and is thinking of extending her trip for another six months. Lucky her. Makes me realize how stuck I am, doesn't it? All this marketing and spreadsheets... Don't say that! You’re brilliant at what you do. It’s just… sometimes I wonder if we should have done something completely different. Remember when we talked about opening a vintage shop? Oh my god, yes! "Retro Revival" or something equally cheesy. That was  the  dream. Imagine, surrounded by beautiful old clothes and quirky furniture. No more PowerPoint presentations. No more synergy. Actually, I’ve been thinking about that again lately. This project management thing is fine, but it's not… fulfilling. I feel like I'm just facilitating other people's dreams, not chasing my own. So, are you thinking about… leaving? That's a big decision. I don't know.

Honestly, Gran, Amazon's just… better. Faster delivery, bigger choice. It's the obvious one, innit? Obvious, is it, lad? Obvious to who? You youngsters and yer instant gratification. Back in my day, if you wanted somethin', you’d go to the shops. Actually  go . Get a feel for it, talk to the shopkeeper. There’s a proper thing lost there, I reckon. But Gran, that takes ages! I need this new graphics card for my computer by the weekend. I’m trying to finish the level design for that game I've been telling you about. Going to the shops to find one? Forget it. There's one shop in York sells computers, and they’d be sold out anyway. Right, a game, is it? All this digital nonsense. Still, good to be keeping yer mind active, I supose. But just 'cause it’s quick doesn't make it better. I had a look on Amazon for a new teapot the other week. Ended up with one that looked nothin' like the picture. All speckled and a funny colour. Sent it back, of course, but it was a right faff. Yeah, that happens. But customer service on Amazon is usually pretty good, isn't it? Easy returns. Ebay's worse for that. Ebay… now there's a story. I bought a supposedly antique brooch off Ebay. Said it was Victorian, silver, genuine gemstones. Looked lovely in the photo. When it arrived? Plastic beads, plated metal, and smelled strongly of lavender potpourri. Lavender potpourri! On a Victorian brooch! Oh, Gran! That's brilliant! You shoulda posted a review! I did, lad! A scathing one. Took ‘em a while to acknowledge it, then they offered me… a tenner back. A tenner! I told 'em I'd rather keep the brooch and use it as a doorstop. At least it’d have some purpose then. See, that's why you should stick to Amazon. They've got stricter sellers. Ebay's a bit of a wild west. It does, doesn't it? Still, there’s somethin’ to be said for a good bargain. I got a set of vintage buttons on Ebay once, for next to nowt. Proper mother-of-pearl, they were. Beautiful. You just have to be careful. Read the small print, look at the seller's feedback… a bit like life, really. True. I check the reviews too. Always. But Amazon Prime… it’s just too convenient.

Honestly, it's lovely here, Anon. Really relaxing after a week chasing deadlines. Though, a little… lived-in, isn't it? Lived-in is a polite way of putting it, love. It’s got character, that's what I say. Been accumulating character for… well, longer than I care to remember. Did you have a good journey up from Lewisham? The trains are a nightmare, you know. It was alright. A bit delayed, but nothing major. Thanks for having me, though. It's nice to get out of the flat. It’s starting to feel a bit… suffocating. Especially with the rain we’ve been having. Rain? Always rain in England, isn’t there? You'd think after sixty-odd years, I'd be used to it. Still, a bit of sunshine would be a treat. You look tired, though, love. Working too hard? A little, yeah. This new project at work is… intense. It's a huge production run for a new client, and everything has to be absolutely perfect. They're incredibly demanding. Logistical nightmares, honestly. I'm coordinating everything from raw materials to shipping, and every step has to be meticulously planned. They want daily updates, spreadsheets for days… it's exhausting. Sounds like a right palaver. Back in my day, things were simpler. Much simpler. You didn't have all these fancy systems and reports. A handshake and a promise was all you needed. I wish it were still like that, Anon. Honestly. But precision and accountability are key these days. It's about mitigating risk and ensuring quality control. Quality control… used to be called 'doing a good job'. And you got paid for it. Now it's a department. A whole department! What happened to pride in your work? It's still there, I think. It’s just… formalized. And there's a lot more pressure. I’m thinking about taking a yoga class, actually. Something to de-stress. Yoga? Is that that stretching business? Sounds a bit… new agey for me. Why not just have a cup of tea and a sit-down? Works wonders for me. You and your tea. It's more than that, Anon. It's about mindfulness, breathing... connecting with yourself. You should try it. Me? Connect with myself? I know myself well enough, thank you very much. Spent a long time getting to know myself, haven’t I? Had plenty of time.

"Poor thing. Osteopaths at Christmas! That sounds grim. Honestly, though, flying on Christmas Day… are you  sure  about that, Liam? It sounds intensely stressful." "Nah, it's alright, Chloe. The flights are practically empty. Everyone else is stuck on the roads, battling the elements. Dad booked it ages ago, said he got a ridiculous deal. Plus, being in Sydney for Christmas… sun, beach, my nan's pavlova...it's the dream, innit?" He grinned, a flash of white teeth. "Pavlova? Right, so you're abandoning all British traditions then? No Boxing Day sales?" Amelia, the café owner, raised an eyebrow playfully, sipping her cider. "I'm sticking with my usual – a catastrophic failure to finish the Christmas shopping and frantically buying discounted chocolate on December 26th." "Crikey, you blokes and your Boxing Day sales! It's all a bit much, isn’t it? We just do a barbie. Simple as that. No stress, just sunshine and snags. Speaking of which, I'm worried about getting enough decent sausages this year. The supermarkets around here… well, let’s just say quality control isn’t their strong suit." Ben, the Australian barista, meticulously cleaned his glasses. "A barbie does sound amazing. Chloe sighs. "Though, to be fair, a British roast is pretty good too. I've been experimenting with a new cranberry and port reduction this year. I’m also attempting a gingerbread yule log - wish me luck.” "Ooh, a yule log! You’re proper fancy, you are. Mum would be proud. Reminds me, we saw something awful on the way back from Tesco yesterday." "Oh lord, what now? Please don’t tell me it’s another Christmas light casualty. Mrs. Henderson’s inflatable Santa nearly decapitated a postman last year." "Worse, actually. It was a deer. Roadkill. Right by the A4. Poor thing. Proper mangled.” Liam shuddered slightly. "Oh, Liam! That’s awful. They’re so majestic, you know? It’s heartbreaking to see." "Yeah, it's a tough one. We've got a fair few deer round on the outskirts of Perth too. They can be cheeky little blighters, wandering onto the roads, especially at dusk. Foxes too, don’t get me started on the foxes. They’re practically running the joint out there." "Speaking of foxes, I saw a massive one in my garden last week. Bold as brass! Just casually digging up my prize-winning petunias. Absolute menace. Makes you wonder what they're even doing out so late."

Right, so, are we actually moving anytime soon, or are we just going to sit here and analyse the acoustics of Cambridge for the next hour? I swear, every voice here sounds so…posh. Posh? Come on, Liv. It’s just different. You’re used to Brum accents, aren’t you? There's a subtlety to it. It’s not like they’re all layered in honey and speaking through monocles. I think she has a point, actually. It's definitely…cleaner. Less grit. Makes me feel like I’m waiting for a butler to offer me cucumber sandwiches. Exactly, Finn! You get it. Liam's just defending it because he’s been living here for a few months now and is slowly morphing into one of them. That’s ridiculous! I’m just appreciating linguistic variation. Though, I have to admit, I did accidentally say “queue” the other day instead of “line.” Felt like a complete impostor. Oh, that was gold, Liam. Pure gold. Remember when you ordered a "biscuit" at that American coffee shop and they gave you a dog treat? Don't remind me! The look on the barista's face… Anyway, are we settled on getting back to Birmingham tomorrow? Yeah, tomorrow’s fine. I just need to double-check the final proof on this article before I completely switch off my brain. It’s about the resurgence of Doc Martens, surprisingly. Seriously? Doc Martens? That's what you spend your days writing about? Hey, someone's gotta do it! It's research for my authentic lived experience, okay? Plus, they're making a comeback, it's fascinating. What about you, Finn? Still wrestling with that dragon in your game? Pretty much. We’re trying to get the AI to behave slightly less… murderous. Apparently, having a dragon that instantly incinerates any NPC is not conducive to good gameplay. Go figure. Sounds stressful. You need a break. Hence, this trip. So, about getting back, I was thinking we could leave around lunchtime. Gives us time to grab some decent grub on the way. Lunchtime's good. But about the car... Liam, are you  sure  this thing is reliable enough for a three-hour drive? It sounds like a washing machine full of angry squirrels when you start it. It's fine! It’s a classic Mini. They’re built to last, you know. It just…characterful.

Honestly, you wouldn’t believe the state of the sound system in the music room today. Crackling like a bonfire! How are we supposed to properly appreciate Mozart with that racket going on? I know, right? It was awful. Mrs. Davies was practically apologising after every scale. I mean, I get it, it's old, but still. I’m starting to think she's deliberately trying to sabotage our performance for the upcoming concert. Sabotage? Bit dramatic, isn’t it? It’s probably just faulty wiring. Still, it’s really annoying when you’re trying to concentrate on the phrasing. I kept getting distracted by the buzzing. Did you guys hear about that new Arctic Monkeys track, though? Apparently, it’s leaked. No way! Seriously? Where? I've been starving for new Arctic Monkeys. Their last album was a bit… safe, wasn't it? Found it! Someone posted a link on Reddit. It's a bit rough, obviously, but it’s got that classic Alex Turner lyrical swagger. Very lo-fi, almost a bit shoegaze-y, you know? Woah, you’re right. It’s completely different. Not what I was expecting. It's got a weird, hypnotic quality. Proper good though. Much better than that bland stuff they put out last time. See, I told you! I'm proper buzzing about it, that's what I'm saying. It sounds like they've gone back to their roots a bit, scrapped the whole polished pop thing. Remember when we were obsessed with ‘Favourite Worst Nightmare’ back in Year 10? Man, those were the days! We used to play that album on repeat on the bus. Mr. Henderson nearly had a stroke. He kept telling us to turn it down, but we just cranked it up louder. Classic. Do you reckon they'll do a whole album in that style? Or is it just a one-off experimental track? I’m hoping for an album, definitely. It feels like… it feels like they’re experimenting with some of those physics concepts we were learning in class today, you know? Physics? What are you on about now, Slough? No, seriously! Think about it. The distortion, the layering… it’s almost like they’re visualizing wave interference. Like, multiple sound waves crashing together and creating different frequencies. It's not perfect, obviously, but there's a deliberate manipulation of sound that's reminiscent of how waves behave.

Right, so, Balanceability. Honestly, it’s a nightmare sometimes. Leo was practically launching himself off the curb today, convinced he was going to win the Tour de France. I almost fell over! Daddy caught me! I did too! But I went really fast! Vroom! You did, darling. Very fast. But remember what we talked about – looking where you’re going and being careful. It’s not a race, it’s about learning to balance. Like anything, learning takes time. Remember when you were learning to read, Elara? I did! It was hard at first. Miss Davies had to show me the sounds again and again. Miss Harding lets me look at the picture books even when I can’t read! That’s lovely, isn't it? They’re both brilliant teachers. Speaking of brilliant, did you hear about Sophie’s new house? Apparently, they’re renovating it completely. A  swimming pool , can you imagine? A swimming pool! With sharks? No, darling, no sharks. Probably just…water. Though, your dad would probably try to build a manmade waterfall, wouldn't he? He would! And then we’d all fall in! Don't dive in the deep end! It's dangerous! Like Miss Harding said! Exactly! Very sensible. We had a little chat at school today about water safety, and it turns out a lot of children don't understand how deep water can be, or how to float properly. It’s quite worrying.
