Their assessments are showing a real need for more practical water safety education. Assessments? Are they giving grown-ups assessments now? Not quite, love. It's about the school assessing the children’s understanding. It helps them decide what to teach next. Like… it’s the same as with your Balanceability. They want to see where you’re at so they can help you improve. I got a star sticker today! For listening! That’s fantastic, sweetheart! That’s brilliant news! Well done, you. You’ve been listening so well lately. That’s succeeding, isn't it? Doing something you set your mind to, even if it’s hard. Like learning to tie my shoelaces. That was  really  hard. It was! But you kept practicing, and now you’re brilliant at it. It’s the same with learning anything. Speaking of learning, did you know it’s National Cat Day in Japan today? Apparently, they celebrate it with cat-shaped pastries.

Honestly, I’m just… drained. This project at work has been relentless. Production targets are insane, and Mark, my manager, is breathing down my neck about everything. It’s like he thinks I'm deliberately sabotaging things. Aye, sounds a right nightmare, love. Mark, eh? Sounds like a proper control freak. My Dave at work's similar - always wants to know exactly what I'm doing, every five minutes. Gives you the heebie-jeebies, doesn’t it? But, you know, sometimes a bit of pressure can be a good thing, can’t it? Keeps you on yer toes. Easy for you to say, you're used to the Yorkshire grit! It's just constant, unrelenting stress. I haven’t been to the gym in two weeks. Two weeks, Bronte! I'm turning into a sofa-shaped blob. Remember how we used to go every Saturday morning? Pilates and then brunch? Oh, those were the days, weren't they? Proper good laugh. We should get back into it. Fresh air and a good stretch’ll do you the world of good. I’ve been trying to get back into running, myself. Bit slow going, though. My knees aren't what they used to be. Got a bit wonky after that fell during that charity race last year. A wonky knee! You’re so clumsy, Bronte. Still, the charity race was a great thing to do. Speaking of feeling drained... I had a disastrous date last night. Oh? Do tell. Was he a right daft lad? Don't hold back - I love a good disastrous date story. He was... pretentious. Utterly pretentious. He spent the entire evening talking about his "passion for artisanal cheese" and quoting obscure poetry. I nearly choked on my risotto trying not to roll my eyes. And he kept calling me "Darling," which is  never  a good sign. Artisanal cheese, eh? Honestly, some people… You’re better off without him, lass. Don't waste yer time on lads who think they're above everyone else. You deserve someone who makes you laugh, someone you can just relax with. Like, someone who doesn’t judge you for liking a good cuppa. Exactly! And he judged my tea! Said it was "too…robust." Can you believe it? I nearly walked out then and there. It’s just… I’m getting a bit tired of dating in general. It's all so much effort.

Aye, that was champion, Auntie Maggie! Best Domino's we’ve had in a while. Extra pepperoni was a good shout. Glad you think so, lad. Your uncle George was moaning about it being too much cheese last week, you know. Said it was slippin' off. Honestly, some folks! I told him, “George, it’s pizza, not a five-star ballet!” Now, Maggie, don’t tell tales! It  was  a bit much. Though I can’t deny this is proper good. Best pizza’s better than no pizza, eh, lad? You’re always saying that, Uncle George. You'd eat cardboard if someone put a bit of tomato sauce on it. He’s not entirely wrong though, is he? He’s got a simple palate, our George. Still, it’s lovely to have a bit of a laugh and a Domino’s after the drive, innit? Did you see young Bethany’s new car, George? She’s gone and bought a wee hatchback, bright pink it is! Pink? Pink?! Bethany? She’s got more sense than that! Looks like a giant sweet. She’ll be attractin' every lad in town. Reckon she’s learnt nothin’ from her poor choices in blokes, has she? She’s always been a bit daft, to be honest. Remember when she tried to dye her hair blue and it came out green? Aye, and blamed it on the shampoo! She’s a character, our Bethany. Though I do wonder what she'll do with all that money. Fancy car, though. Wonder if she'll give us a lift next time we’re going to see your cousin, Sarah? Doubtful. She’ll be showin’ it off to all her friends. Speaking of showin’ off…did you hear about Cyril Hargrave? Got himself a new extension…on the garage! Cyril Hargrave? He's got more money than sense, hasn't he? What's he even got to put in a bigger garage? Probably more sheep, knowing Cyril. Keeps gettin’ bigger, that flock of his. Though he's lookin' a bit peaky lately. Said he was struggling to get a decent haircut. A decent haircut? Cyril? He looks like a dandelion gone to seed. Needs a good shearing, more than a haircut, he does. Reminds me, Maggie, you said you’d look at booking me in for a trim next week. My ears are startin' to tickle. Aye, I will, love.

Right, that’s tha sorted. Strong enough for us then, eh? Honestly, this Cambridge water's a bit… bland. Not like back home, where the tap water tastes proper o’ minerals. It does lack a bit, doesn't it? I did try filtering it, but I’m not sure it made much difference. These carrots are looking good though. Did you manage to find decent ones at the market? Aye, they were grand. Proper knobbly, you know? I love a knobbly carrot. All that uniformity they get in the supermarkets… it’s a bit depressing, isn't it? Like they’ve sucked all the character out o’ them. You and your vegetables. It's endearing, really. I was just reading an article about the environmental impact of perfectly shaped produce. Apparently, a huge amount gets rejected before it even reaches the shops. See! Exactly! Waste, pure waste. Give us a wonky carrot any day. Saves the planet, tastes better… what’s not to like? We should start a campaign – “Embrace the Knobbly!” – it'd catch on, I reckon. I think you might be right. I’ll add it to my list of potential thesis topics. “The Socio-Economic and Environmental Impact of Carrot Aesthetics.” Catchy, right? You’re taking that a bit far aren't ye? But aye, it's brilliant. So, did you hear about the rumours surrounding Millie Bobby Brown and that actor, what’s his name… the one from that gritty gangster film. Ah, Jamie? Jamie Campbell Bower? Yeah, there's been a bit of chatter. Seems a bit random, doesn’t it? I always thought Millie had a more… indie vibe. Aye, well, everyone's got their type, haven't they? I reckon she’s got good taste. He’s a good looker, even with that… peculiar face he’s got. Reminds me of someone from one of those historical dramas. You know, speaking of actors, I saw that article about Daniel Radcliffe trying to open a pub in New York. Apparently, it's failing miserably. No! Seriously? Daniel Radcliffe? He's got to be shrewd. He's made a fortune from Harry Potter. What’s gone wrong? Apparently, the concept was… ambitious. Something about artisanal sausages and craft beer with obscure names. Turns out, New Yorkers just want a decent pint and a burger. Honestly, some folk just don’t understand the basics, do they? A good pub needs laughter, a friendly face behind the bar, and proper chips.

Right! “Sloth.” Anyone? Come on, it’s a good one! Sloth... hmm. Slowpoke? Absolutely not, Elen! Slowpoke isn't a word. You’re trying to trip us up already, Rhys! Strategic slothfulness? Strategic slothfulness! I love it! That’s brilliant, Gethin! Definitely counts. Your go, Nia. Don't let us down. See? It  is  a good word. And I was right to start with, the principles were sound! Though I suppose 'sluggish' might have been easier… Oh, and Gethin, you nearly broke the rules there! You have to  define  it, not just use a synonym! I was expanding the meaning! Elevating the vocabulary! Besides, a little creative interpretation is what makes Articulate fun, isn't it? Now, now, boys. Let’s stick to the rules, shall we? My poor old memory isn’t what it used to be, and I need a fair game. Besides, remembering the rules  is  part of the fun, isn’t it, Mairwen? Absolutely, Dai! And Rhys, be careful you don’t start bending the rules just because you’re losing. You always were a clever one, trying to find loopholes! Remember that time at Uncle Gareth's birthday, when you declared "rhubarb crumble" was technically a type of footwear because it has a crust? Oh, dear! That was a low point, wasn’t it? But it was technically correct! The crust  was  like a sole! Honestly, you all exaggerate. It was ridiculous, Rhys. Utterly ridiculous. You nearly caused a family argument over dessert! It was a brilliant argument! And fuelled by a lot of lovely crumble. Speaking of which, anyone fancy a second helping after this round? Focus, Gethin! Focus! “Quagmire.” This is a tricky one. Swamp? Bog? Close, but no. Think… deep, sticky… problematic. Difficult situation? Yes! Exactly, Mairwen! Brilliant! Your go. Dai, you’re awfully quiet. You’ve been staring into space. Are you alright? Just remembering my own days teaching, you know? Used to play Articulate all the time with the children. They loved it. A good way to encourage vocabulary, and teamwork. Though they certainly had a different perspective on what constituted a "word." Once, little Megan declared a "sparkle" was a perfectly acceptable noun. Oh, children! They do say the most wonderful things. You know, I had a little boy in my class last year who insisted that "happy" was an adjective, a verb,  and  a noun. Admirable ambition. I wish I’d had that kind of conviction.

“Honestly, you’re making this far more difficult than it needs to be. It’s just Rummy, not advanced calculus!” “But Sarah, the  potential  for strategy! The bluffing! The precarious balancing act of holding onto just the right cards… It's thrilling!” He slams down a card with unnecessary flourish. “Seven of Diamonds! Take that!” “He’s just showing off, Sarah. As always. Don't let him bait you into a long game. Remember last time? We were playing for three hours and he kept changing the rules as he went along.” "I did no such thing! I was simply  adapting  the rules to enhance the challenge!" He throws a playful glare at Idris. "You’re just salty because I won.” “Boys, boys. Stop bickering like a pair of… well, like a pair of brothers. Gwyn, be nice. And Idris, leave your brother to have his fun.” She picks up her own hand of cards. "Now, let's see... I've got a sneaky feeling I'm about to go out.” "See? Bronwen understands. It's supposed to be a bit of silly fun, not a doctoral thesis on card game theory, Gwyn. And Idris, you're hogging all the tea.” "Just enjoying a quiet moment before the inevitable Welsh card-playing chaos erupts. Besides, it’s a lovely cuppa. Mum's brew always is." He takes a long sip. “Remember that time Dad tried to teach us Cribbage? He kept getting the points wrong, and then he’d accuse  us  of cheating.” “Oh, goodness! He did! And he’d get so red in the face! 'It’s a perfectly legitimate score!' he’d bellow. 'You’re just trying to confuse me!'" “He was hopeless at anything strategic, your father. Wonderful at fixing tractors, though. A different kind of strategy, that one. Knowing which bolt to tighten, when to apply more pressure…” She pauses, considering. "Speaking of pressure, I need to pop down to the shops tomorrow for some more biscuits. Anyone want anything specific?" “Chocolate Hobnobs, definitely! And maybe some of those shortbread fingers? They go lovely with tea.” "Anything chocolatey, really. My sugar levels are perilously low." "Just don't buy those weird cheese and onion crisps again, Mum. Rhys  insists  on them, and they make the whole cottage smell like a badger's sett." "They’re a delicacy, Gwyn! You just don’t appreciate a good savoury snack."

Honestly, this new series on Netflix, "Chronicles of Atheria," is totally gripping. Have you guys seen it? A little. Mum keeps going on about it. Dragons and elves and…stuff. Not really my thing, to be honest. Still obsessed with "Space Explorers," though. Season four just dropped. Dragons and elves? Seriously, Chloe? You're missing out! It's properly complex. The political intrigue, the magic system… it’s brilliant. Even my dad’s into it. The special effects are decent, I’ll give it that. Though, a bit generic, perhaps? Reminds me of some of the simulations we run in the Navy, actually, just with more…fantasy. I tried watching it, but I got distracted. Kept thinking about my shift at Primark tomorrow. Saturday's always manic. Honestly, I’m so tired. Should’ve called in sick. You can’t! They’ll notice! Remember what happened to Liam last month? He pretended to have a dodgy tummy and they gave him extra shifts to make up for it. I know, I know! Just venting. Anyway, uni applications are stressing me out. I’m still undecided between Art History and… well, anything else, really. Art History? Really? That sounds amazing! I'm so glad I applied for Astrophysics. It's terrifying, obviously, but exciting. St Andrews are looking pretty good. St Andrews! Wow, ambitious! I'm still deciding between Surrey and Kingston. Accountant training is a long game, you know? Apprenticeships are the way to go. I’m with Crane & Finch now, pretty good experience. Got a decent bonus this year, too. Apprenticeships are smart. Less debt, put you straight into work. Navy's a bit different, obviously. Officer training is pretty intensive. But you get a lot out of it. Travel, skills...and they pay you while you learn. See, that’s what I want! Something practical. Care work isn't exactly thrilling, but it's rewarding. I helped Mrs. Henderson get her mobility back, it was proper heartwarming. Though, dealing with families can be… draining. Honestly, sometimes I feel like I'm juggling ten different personalities. That sounds tough, Mia. Sending good vibes your way! Speaking of draining, Grandma’s been under the weather again. She's got that cough that won't shift. It’s worrying everyone. Oh no! Poor Grandma. Has she seen the doctor? Hopefully, it's just a nasty cold. Christmas will be sad if she’s really unwell.

Speaker_1 said, pushing a stray piece of roast potato around her plate. The aroma of the cooked dinner still hung pleasantly in the air, softening the intensity of her words. Speaker_2 sighed, swirling the wine in her glass. “Gran, you say that about everything. It’s a perfectly safe route if you’re careful. And quicker than driving, especially with the parking charges nowadays.” “Safe? Quicker? It's a hazard, darlin'! I’d rather sit in traffic than risk a broken hip. Besides, the bus is lovely. You get a nice view and someone else does the driving. Much more civilized, innit?” Margaret chuckled, adjusting her floral-patterned cardigan. Speaker_3 perked up from his position on the sofa, where he'd been half-heartedly watching a nature documentary. “The bus? It’s packed, Gran. You end up standing the whole way, and the driver's got the music up loud. Not much fun, is it?” “Well, at least I’m getting somewhere!” Margaret retorted playfully. "Unlike some people I know, glued to the telly all day.” She gave Ben a good-natured nudge with her elbow. Chloe laughed. “Alright, alright. Honestly, though, Gran, think about it. Cycling’s good exercise. You need to get out more.” “I  do  get out more! I go shopping, don’t I? And I walked to the post office just this morning. Trekking, practically, in this weather.” Margaret made a theatrical shiver. “And walking is lovely. That’s the thing, isn’t it? A proper stroll, taking in the sights. You don’t get that whizzing past on a bike.” Ben finally abandoned the nature show. “Remember Uncle Barry trying to cycle to Brighton? He ended up with a puncture halfway down and had to hitch a lift back. Said it was the worst day of his life.” Margaret burst out laughing. "Oh, bless Barry! He wouldn't know a puncture from a penguin! Always relying on me to sort him out. Still, a good story, that. Speaking of travelling, I was thinking… we should plan a little day trip somewhere soon. Somewhere with a nice cup of tea and a good scone.” “That sounds lovely, Gran,” Chloe agreed. "Where did you have in mind?" “Well,” Margaret pondered, tapping her chin. “I saw an advert for a garden centre in Suffolk. Apparently, they have a fantastic café. And a little gift shop. So we could browse the plants, have a cuppa, a bit of a wander… would that be alright?”

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork involved in transcribing interviews with speakers of less common dialects can be  bonkers . You wouldn't believe the inconsistencies, even within a single speaker! Have you encountered anything like that in your role, Amelia? Oh, absolutely, Chloe. It's a constant battle. Though perhaps not to the same extent as, say, tracking down speakers of Cornish today. We're currently running a project looking at dialectal variation in East Anglian farming communities – you get some wonderfully layered constructions, but getting accurate transcripts… well, it’s a test of patience, let me tell you. It’s fascinating, though. Do you do a lot of field work? Fascinating indeed. The subtleties lost in print, swallowed by standardization… that’s what always saddened me. Fieldwork? No, not in my younger days. I taught linguistics at this very university for forty years, you know. Oswestry lad, through and through. Shropshire. Quiet place. But the university offered a world. Forty years! Incredible! What did you specialize in, Professor…? Davies. Arthur Davies. Historical linguistics was my passion. Tracing the evolution of words, seeing how languages subtly shift and change over centuries… it’s like unearthing a hidden history. Though I did get rather tangled up in Basque at one point. Utterly fascinating, that language. Completely isolated. Basque is amazing, isn’t it? It absolutely blows my mind that it’s a linguistic island in Europe. We had a researcher come through last year trying to definitively link it to something, anything, but it remains stubbornly resistant. It’s a proper head-scratcher for language researchers. Are you familiar with the controversy around its origins? Of course. The endless speculation. Some proposed links to Iberian, others to Caucasian languages... all ultimately unproven. But its structure, the agglutination, the verbal system… remarkable. I spent a sabbatical in Spain trying to get a handle on it. Beautiful country, of course. Madrid's a vibrant place. Though, you know, I'm more of a coastal man myself. San Sebastián was a highlight. Fantastic food. Spain is lovely. I spent a summer volunteering in Seville a few years ago. The architecture is just stunning! I’d love to get to the Basque Country though. It seems so… untouched, somehow. That’s exactly it! It feels like a different world. It's worlds away from London, isn't it? I lived there for six years for my postgraduate studies – a completely different energy.

Honestly, Liam, you’d think with all those qualifications you’ve got, you’d be able to fill in a simple Facebook form! It asked for five words to describe you, and you were stuck for fifteen minutes! It’s harder than you think, Chloe! It’s a terrifying amount of self-reflection prompted by a social media platform. And what five words  adequately  capture a nuanced human being? Besides, it’s a bit silly, isn’t it? This whole ice bucket challenge thing, for example. Don't be a grump, Liam. It's for a good cause! And the videos are hilarious. Remember Uncle Dave dumping the ice water over poor Mrs. Higgins? She deserves a medal for her bravery. I know, I know, it's for Motor Neurone Disease. It’s just… I feel like we're constantly bombarded with these online awareness campaigns. It feels performative sometimes. Oh, come off it! It raises awareness, gets people donating, and it’s a bit of fun. Mum's doing it next week with the WI, apparently. She’s already badgering Aunt Susan to nominate her. Speaking of Mum, did you see she’s finally decided to volunteer at the local animal shelter? About time, innit? She's always saying she wants to do something worthwhile. That’s brilliant, actually. She’ll be amazing with the animals. It's nice to see her finding something that makes her happy. Remember when she used to talk about adopting a rescue dog? Oh my god, yes! She wanted a Great Dane, didn’t she? Said it would guard the house. Dad nearly had a heart attack. He did! He said a Great Dane would need its own postcode. Anyway, what about you, Liam? Still teaching those students the intricacies of the English language? Sounds dreadfully dull. It's not dull! It’s rewarding, actually. Seeing them progress, overcome challenges… you wouldn't believe some of the things they struggle with. One student from Korea asked me if it was true that all British people drank tea all day long. "Do you drink tea ALL the time?" Exactly! It's funny the perceptions people have. Speaking of perceptions, you two still working in Bedford? Don’t tell me you’ve both escaped to London. Nope. Bedford’s alright. The recruitment market’s surprisingly busy, you know. Trying to find someone who can actually type faster than they can scroll through TikTok is a challenge.

Honestly, this coffee machine is a menace. It's either spitting hot water everywhere or producing something that tastes vaguely of burnt toast. I'm starting to miss instant. You're exaggerating, love. It's a bit temperamental, that’s all. Needs a bit of a talking to, like everything in life. A bit of coaxing. Aye, coaxing. Everything these days needs coaxing. The world, the government… even a simple coffee machine. Speaking of things needing coaxing, have you two had a chance to look into those removal quotes? I have, Mum. And it’s…eye-watering. Storing everything for six months while we find a permanent place isn't cheap either. I got one for over £3,000 just for the removal! Three grand! Blimey. That’s… significant. Did you ask about smaller, phased removals? Maybe taking a few boxes ourselves, spreading it out over a few weekends? I did mention it, but they said it would be more complicated and increase the risk of damage. They wanted a one shot deal. Well, damage isn’t going to do us any good, is it? We have Agnes’ antique teapot, you know. Honestly, these companies, they just see the pound signs. Politicians are no different, are they? Here we go. Politics already. What sparked that, Mum? Just thinking about it. This Labour leadership thing… it's awfully… safe, isn’t it? Everyone’s talking about electability, pragmatism… where’s the idealism? The fire? Don't even get me started. It's all focus groups and soundbites. Brings back memories of the oil industry, actually. Endless meetings, all designed to minimize risk, avoid any disruption. No one wanted to take a chance on anything new. It’s a bit depressing, isn't it? Like… the world’s getting a bit beige. Everything's about incremental change and avoiding upsetting anyone. Exactly! When did we stop trying to change things for the better? Remember when we used to hold those political rallies in Dublin? We’d be shouting about social justice, equality… We truly believed we could make a difference. Aye, you were a force of nature, Mary. Always knew exactly what to say, right to the heart of it. Me, I was more comfortable behind the spreadsheets, making sure the numbers added up to support your ideas. You were the practical one, Dad. The grounding force. Someone needed to keep your feet on the earth while Mum was busy storming parliament.

Oh, darling, you always do. You take on so much. Remember when you were little and you'd organise the neighbourhood Christmas play? You were barely eight! It’s in your blood, isn't it? The organisational gene. But don't burn yourself out, love. The carol concert sounds lovely, though. What songs are you thinking of? Mostly classics, you know. 'Silent Night', 'O Holy Night'. I'm trying to introduce a couple of modern ones, something a bit more relatable for the teenagers, but the headmaster is a traditionalist. He nearly had a fit when I suggested 'Mary, Did You Know?' Typical. Some people just can't move with the times. But at least you're trying! It's good to balance the old and the new. Speaking of moving on... how’s Liam doing? Still talking about opening that motorbike repair shop? He is! He's actually found a small unit just outside Newton Abbot. He's so excited, Mum. It’s terrifying, of course – it’s a huge risk, leaving a stable job to chase a dream – but he’s got that glint in his eye, you know? The one he gets when he's genuinely passionate about something. That's wonderful, dear. Really wonderful. A bit nerve-wracking for  us , naturally, but seeing him happy is all that matters. Has he told your Auntie Brenda yet? She’ll want to knit him a helmet cosy. Oh, she will. I haven't told her yet. I wanted to wait until he'd actually signed the lease. It feels a bit premature until then. Honestly, Mum, it's all happening so fast. One minute he's complaining about his awful boss, the next he's negotiating a business loan! Life rarely moves at a sensible pace, does it? It’s like a rollercoaster. Speaking of pace, have you thought about Christmas itself yet? Are we doing the big family gathering at yours again this year? That’s what I wanted to talk to you about. Honestly, the thought of hosting everyone – Dad, you, Liam, Sophie and her boyfriend… it’s just too much. My kitchen gets taken over, the house looks like a bomb’s hit it, and I end up spending Christmas Day cleaning up. I know the feeling. It  is  a lot. What about we do it at mine this year? I've been wanting to rearrange the furniture anyway.

…and then, honestly, he just  looked  at her, deadpan, and said, "Well, you're the one who left the biscuit crumbs on the sofa!" I nearly choked on my pint. Proper Yorkshire grit, that lad, Liam. Never backs down from a crumb-related argument. Aye, sounds like Liam, alright. You’ve got some characters up in Leeds, haven’t ya? Proper mad. Madder than your cousin, Barry, trying to parallel park a van, I reckon. Remember that, Sarah? The whole street was blocked! Don’t remind me! I spent half an hour talking him down from a panic attack, didn’t I? He genuinely thought he’d ruined everyone’s day. Oh, and speaking of ruining days… has anyone heard from Josh lately? He’s been quiet on the group chat. Nah, not really. He's been a bit off for a few weeks, actually. Said he was stressed with his dissertation, but he’s always stressed with something. Remember when he used to get stressed about Waterfields' custard tarts? He’d spend ages debating which ones were “peak tartness”. Oh, god, yes! He'd get properly intense about it. Worth every penny, though, weren't they? Better than any supermarket one. I’m proper craving one now. Waterfields are the best. Honestly, they do the best Richmond sausages too. My grandad swears by ‘em. Says they’re the only ones that taste like proper sausages. My grandma does, as well! She’s always saying, "Get some Waterfields, lad, you won’t get better anywhere else!" It’s a family motto, practically. More like a threat. You’d get a right telling off if you came home with any other brand. Right! Anyway, Josh. I'm worried about him. He hasn’t been returning my calls. And last night... I swear I heard him snoring through the wall! Snoring? Josh? He’s usually so energetic! That’s not a good sign. Stress, definitely. I know! Snoring usually means you're completely knackered. Like my flatmate, Mark. The man sounds like a walrus with a head cold. It’s horrendous. I've had to resort to earplugs. Awful! My dad used to snore like a freight train. You could hear him three houses down. Mum used to threaten to move him into the shed. My dad used to do that too! Mum’d be shaking the bed frame, shouting, “Albert! Stop causing an earthquake!”

Honestly, Dad, that was just what I needed. Proper country air. My lungs feel brand new after being stuck in London all week. Aye, weren't it grand? Good to get you outta that concrete jungle for a bit. You were lookin' a bit peaky, love. Didn't think you were eatin' properly either, all that project stuff keepin' you on the go. It is. It’s manic. This new client, Thorne & Davies, they want everything yesterday. I swear, if I have to look at another Gantt chart… But, seriously, being at the farm felt like a proper reset. Did you manage to fix that fence in the north pasture? Nearly. Got most of it done, alright. Bit o' a struggle with the last post, though. Ground's gone right hard, you know? Needed a good watering, but we haven't had a drop all week. Ruth's been keepin' an eye on the sheep, bless her. Said they're lookin' a bit restless too. Restless sheep! Sounds like a drama. You should livestream it. "Sheepwatch UK." Could be a thing! You’re daft, you are. Livestreamin’ sheep. Still, good for a laugh. Ruth did say old Agnes tried to climb the tractor. Don’t know what got into her. Ages. Agnes sounds like a rebel. I wish I’d had more time to help you and Mum in the garden. Everything looked so beautiful. Those roses... Aye, the roses were summat special this year. Ruth's been workin' her fingers to the bone on 'em. She’s thinking of entering some in the village flower show. Oh, brilliant! She should! She’d win for sure. Any chance you used that new fertilizer she bought? The organic stuff? Course I did! Don't you worry. Ruth's got a list longer than my arm and I follow it. Keeps me right, she does. Said it’s all about the microbial life in the soil. Whatever that means… Seems like a load o’ fancy words to me. It’s science, Dad! Good science. It helps the plants grow. Anyway... did you see Eleanor and Mark? They seemed a bit…off, didn’t they? Aye, they did. Mark kept lookin' down at his boots. And Eleanor barely touched her pie. Somethin’s botherin' ‘em, I reckon. Not sayin' anything, though. They keep things close to themselves, those two. I thought so. I tried to ask them if everything was alright, but they just said they were tired.

"…and honestly, the paperwork alone! It's just relentless. You’d think teaching young minds would be the hardest part, but it's navigating the system these days," Sarah said, swirling the remains of her tea in her mug. "It's miles away from what I imagined when I signed up." "Tell me about it!" replied Emily , nodding emphatically. "The accountability measures are just…suffocating. They want us to jump through hoops about every little thing. At least with primary, you get a little more leeway to be creative, you know? Secondary’s got so much data focus." Sarah chuckled, "Exactly! I spend half my week compiling spreadsheets. It’s hardly inspiring a love of French, is it?" "No, it's not," Emily agreed, leaning forward. "Although, speaking of languages… how's your Italian progressing? You were talking about wanting to get fluent before you turned forty." "Oh, don't even ask!" Sarah groaned playfully. "Life got in the way, didn't it? Matthew’s football, the house renovations… you know the drill. I'm doing Duolingo sporadically. I’ve got a lovely tutor, Maria, too, but we haven’t had a proper lesson in months. I feel guilty about it. It’s so frustrating. I love the language, I really do, but finding the time… it’s proving tricky." Emily smiled sympathetically. "I know the feeling. I started learning Spanish a few years back, but it's fallen by the wayside. It's one of those things you  want  to do, but…" She trailed off. "Do you ever feel like your brain just…slows down as you get older? Like it’s harder to absorb information?" "Absolutely!" Sarah exclaimed. "I swear, remembering a phone number used to be automatic. Now, I’m writing everything down immediately. And learning new grammar rules… it takes so much longer than it used to. You’d think being a language teacher would give me an advantage!" "Well, you understand the principles, don't you? That's half the battle," Emily offered. "Maybe you need a language buddy? Someone to practice with? We could even have a virtual coffee and natter in Italian." "That's actually a brilliant idea, Em! Seriously. I’d love that. It's always more motivating to have someone to hold you accountable." Sarah perked up. "What about you and Spanish? Still any hope?" "I’m trying! I’m using Babbel now, which is a bit more engaging than Duolingo, I think.

Aye, he is, isn’t he, Marjorie? Bold as brass, that one. Remember when we put up that fancy, copper feeder? Thought it’d keep ‘em all happy, separated nicely. Didn't last two days. The squirrel got to it faster than you can blink. Nasty little blighter. Squirrels! Don’t even get me started. They’re like furry little bandits, aren’t they? Stealing everything in sight. Though, I do find them rather amusing, in a frustrating kind of way. Did you see the nest the blue tits are building in the honeysuckle? It’s ever so pretty, all snug and neat. Honeysuckle’s gone a bit leggy this year, Marjorie. Needs a good trim. Used to be proper thick, you know. Covered the whole fence. Mind you, back then we didn't have all these feathered fiends about. Fewer birds in them days. Less competition, you mean, Arthur. Don’t go blaming the birds for your dodgy memory! Dodgy memory? I remember things just fine. I remember when you tried to convince Doris to let you build a miniature railway in her allotment. Now  that’s  a memory! Oh, don't remind me! Doris nearly had a fit! She said it’d attract all sorts of undesirables. That Doris always did have a bee in ‘er bonnet. Anyway, back to the birds… I was thinking of getting a proper wren feeder. Little house-shaped thing, just for 'em. That’s a lovely idea, Peter. They are darling little creatures. Speaking of lovely things… did you taste the Victoria sponge? I think it's rather good, even if I do say so myself. Made it especially for you both. It  is  rather nice, Marjorie. A bit sweet for me, mind. Reminds me of me mother’s baking. Though hers always had a bit more lemon. It's perfect, Marjorie. Thank you. Just what I needed. You know, all this sittin’ about, not doin' much… it plays havoc with the blood sugar. The doctor's been on at me again. Says I need to be careful. Peter, love, you know you need to. You promised me you wouldn’t be sneaking biscuits in the shed. Alright, alright. Just thinking out loud. It’s all these old folk, isn’t it? Seems like every other thing is related to joints and blood sugar and… well, you know. Don't we all know it!

Right then, Penelope. I’m thinking the kleftiko. Looks rather promising, doesn’t it? Though, to be honest, after yesterday’s grilled octopus, I'm slightly hesitant to be adventurous again. My stomach wasn't entirely pleased with me this morning. You and your delicate constitution, Richard! I’m leaning towards the moussaka. It’s comfort food, isn't it? Especially when you’ve been battling the Cypriot sun all morning. Are you still finding that the hearing aids are coping okay out here? The humidity must be dreadful for them. They're... managing. Just occasionally a bit of a buzz. Not as bad as that dreadful carnival in Brighton, though. Remember that, Penelope? The noise! I thought I’d go completely deaf. It’s infuriating, really. All that flashing and booming... I felt like a startled rabbit. Anyway, about the hearing, I spoke to that audiologist again, you know. He still insists I get them 'cleaned' more frequently. As if I  have  time! I can imagine. Between you and your environmental campaigns, you're hardly idle. Speaking of busy, have you heard from young Thomas? He’s been awfully quiet. Is he still grappling with his mother’s… situation? Yes, poor lad. It's rough, isn't it? The lymphoma… it’s just swept through her so quickly. He’s trying to be strong for his sister, Elsie, but you can see it weighing on him. He mentioned yesterday, said he was talking to a rather interesting woman about… well, it sounds a bit out there, to be honest. Apparently, she’s a shaman, here in Northern Cyprus. Doing readings, healing… A shaman? In Northern Cyprus? Goodness. I hope he's being sensible. Elsie's only eight, she needs a stable environment. Though, I suppose, if it's bringing him some peace… That's what he said. He also said she talked about 'destiny' and 'the alignment of energies.' Honestly, Penelope, it sounds like something out of a particularly eccentric magazine. Still, he seemed… lighter after the conversation. You know, reminds me of Aunt Millie and her dowsing rods. Oh, don’t remind me! Remember that time she tried to find our lost cat, Winston, using those rods in your garden? Ended up trying to convince you there was a massive water vein running under the patio! Winston was perched on the fence, the cheeky thing, the whole time! Do you recall Old Mr. Henderson, who used to come in here every Tuesday?

Lovely to see you both, honestly. It’s been a mad week at school, you wouldn't believe the panic about those GCSE results. Little Timmy Perkins nearly fainted when he saw his maths mark! Such a drama queen. Oh, bless him! Exams are always stressful, though, aren’t they? It’s nice to just…decompress, really. This house is always so calming. The smell of Mum’s roast dinner alone is therapeutic. Therapeutic and filling, that's what it is. Speaking of filling, how’s the project going, love? Still drowning in spreadsheets? Pretty much! We’re nearing the end of Phase One, thankfully, which is the big one. It’s just… relentless. The new client wants everything yesterday, even though we've warned them about timescales. They're a bit... demanding. Happens all the time, doesn't it? People think you can magic things. You've got to stand your ground, love. Remember what your Grandad used to say? "A watched pot never boils, and a pressured project never delivers." Oh, Grandad! I’ll never forget him. He always had the best sayings. I miss him. Speaking of missing people, have you heard from Sarah and Ben recently? Saw Ben last week at the rugby club. Birmingham Bulls played a good game, actually, finally! A bit rough around the edges, but showed some grit. He was talking about a weekend away to the Lake District – something about hiking and escaping the city. Oh, that sounds lovely! They deserve a break. Sarah’s been working incredibly hard at the hospital. She’s practically living there at the moment. We should all try to get together soon. Maybe for Christmas? Definitely. Christmas would be perfect. We need to start thinking about presents. I was thinking about getting Mum that nice cashmere scarf she was admiring in the window. Good idea, that. She’ll appreciate something warm. I was thinking… now, don't tell her before she’s had her pudding… about getting the garden sorted out next spring. That old shed is practically falling apart, and the patio needs re-laying. Oh, seriously, John? That’s a big project! Are you thinking of tackling it yourself? Well, I'm not getting any younger! I'd probably need to get some quotes, see if it’s feasible. It would be nice to have a proper outdoor space again, a place to sit and enjoy the sunshine.

Right, so then she sent him a picture, supposedly of 'herself' sunbathing in Majorca. Proper idyllic, innit? And he just…fell for it hook, line, and sinker. Honestly, you'd think he'd be a bit suspicious after all the red flags, wouldn't ya? You’re talking about Liam's cousin, Mark, yeah? The one obsessed with finding love online? Honestly, it's like a repeat cycle. This is, what, the third time he’s got himself properly hoodwinked? Typical. It's like watching a disaster unfold in slow motion. It's just sad, isn't it? I mean, you see these stories, and you think, "How can anyone be that naive?" Remember that Jeremy Kyle episode last year? The one where the fella thought he was in love with a woman who, spoiler alert, was actually a bloke in drag? It's horrifying! Aye, that was somethin’ else, that. Proper shocking. You felt for 'em, didn't ya? Even though you knew they were daft. But this Mark lad…he’s got to take some responsibility. He’s not exactly a genius, is he? I mean, the girl’s profile said she was a ‘professional wrestler’ and lived in Monaco. Come on! I know! And he sent her  money ! Loads of it, apparently. My sister told me he was bragging about how he’d invested in her 'business ventures'. What business ventures do professional wrestlers living in Monaco have that need funding from a bloke in Wigan? Good point. It's the desperation, isn't it? Everyone wants to feel loved, to feel wanted. Online, it's so easy to create this perfect persona, this fantasy version of yourself. People genuinely believe they’re connecting with something real, even when it’s completely fabricated. Like…like a really elaborate puppet show. Exactly! And it’s the validation, isn’t it? They get all these likes and comments and messages… it feeds their ego. Even though it’s all fake. Makes you wonder what’s real anymore, doesn't it? It's like the whole internet's become one big Jeremy Kyle show. Don’t say that! I try to forget Jeremy Kyle exists. It was just…so depressing. These people were genuinely hurting, and they were exposing themselves to public humiliation for a chance at a tiny bit of happiness. Yeah, but at least on Jeremy Kyle, they  knew  they were being filmed.

Right, so Professor Davies is  still  on about using a new coding language for the AI project. Python’s perfectly serviceable, innit? Why change it just for the sake of it? Honestly, feels like he's flexing more than teaching. Oh, academics. They love their complexities. A bit like trying to explain the shading in a Klimt painting using only geometry. Impossible, really. Though, Python sounds…modern. Was it well-suited for the project? Yeah, totally. It’s versatile, loads of libraries, well-documented… the whole shebang. It’s just… frustrating. Especially when the deadline's looming. Speaking of looming, remember how stressful applying for uni was? Feels like yesterday. Vienna felt even longer ago. Though the stress was different, wasn't it? Different kind of pressure. My father always wanted me to be a concert pianist. Me, with clumsy fingers and a terrible ear for music! Imagine. Blimey, what did you do then? I ran. Figuratively, of course. I ended up studying Classics at the University of Vienna. Latin and Greek… surprisingly liberating, after the piano. They call it the language of the gods. Did you study Classics at all, darling? Nah, not for me. Went full STEM. More my speed, you know? Though I wish I'd paid more attention in French lessons at school. Trying to order a croissant in Paris last year was a disaster. All I managed was "Bonjour… uh… pain au chocolat?" They looked at me like I'd grown a second head. Oh, the French! So very particular. My dear grandmother, she was Austrian, but escaped to Italy during the war. She could speak three languages fluently, you know. Italian, German, and French. It was all so natural for her. I tried to learn German, properly, and I just… floundered. I can manage a few phrases, "Bitte," "Danke," you know, the essentials. My German’s shocking. My friend, Ben, he's German. Says I mangle the grammar something awful. He keeps trying to correct me, but honestly, sometimes I just tune him out. That’s understandable. Language learning requires dedication. But it opens up such incredible worlds. Remember that trip we took to Italy? Florence was magical. And the bees! I was fascinated by the bees in Tuscany. They were so busy, buzzing amongst the olive groves… You were obsessed with them, weren’t you? Took like a million photos. I'm still trying to figure out how to sort them all out on my computer.

Honestly, Dad, you were tailgating that lorry! It was terrifying. I nearly had a heart attack. Tailgating? I was maintaining a suitable distance. That lorry wasn't going anywhere fast, love. Needed a nudge, that's what. Bit of encouragement, you see. Gets 'em moving. A nudge? Robert, you were practically breathing down its bumper! You know your eyesight isn't what it used to be. And young Chloe’s right to be worried. Dorset’s lovely, but not worth a near-miss for. Exactly! It’s pouring down too. Visibility’s awful. Shouldn't you be relying a bit more on the Sat Nav, Dad? It’s shouting directions at you. Sat Nav! Chimera! Useless thing. Took us the long way around last year, didn't it, Chloe? Ended up in some dreadful little town. Can't even remember the name. All grey stone and chip shops. A right depressing place. It was Nether Wallop, Robert. And it wasn’t  all  grey stone. It had a lovely little pub, didn’t it? The Red Lion? We had a nice pint. Pint’s the only good thing about practically any town these days. Course, I was feeling a bit better after the pint. Standing room only though; half the place was over 70! You wouldn’t get a seat in most pubs now, Dad. It's all about clever design and exposed brick. Speaking of which, Aunt Susan's finally decided to have that extension built. Costs a fortune, apparently. Paying solicitors something ridiculous just to draw up the plans. Oh, Susan. She always was a stickler for doing things properly. Remember when she tried to argue with the builders about the type of slate they were using? Claimed it didn’t match the original house. Slate? Pah! Give me corrugated iron any day. Sturdy stuff. Used to be everything was built to last. Not like this flimsy furniture they sell nowadays. Fell apart just looking at it. Remember that sideboard your Nan bought in the '60s, Chloe? Solid as a rock. I do! Still have it, actually. Just need to get around to polishing it. It’s a project. I've been so swamped with essays, honestly. This Victorian Literature module is killing me. Dickens' social commentary is fascinating, but writing about it... You need a good day off, love. A real one. Not just a few hours dashing about trying to fit everything in.

Honestly, Arthur, I'm just saying, it’s a bit much, isn't it? Another one? Three ceramic hedgehogs already! What are we going to  do  with them all? Now, Elsie, don't you go gettin’ yer knickers in a twist. They’re lovely, these. Reminds me of Mrs. Miggins’ garden, back in Costessey. She had a right passion for hedgehogs, she did. Painted ‘em all different colours, she did. Painted hedgehogs? Arthur, that’s precisely my point. We're accumulating a collection that's… well, let's just say it's becoming rather  extensive . She’d have called it a hoard, probably. And Mrs. Miggins, bless her soul, was a tad eccentric. Eccentric is just a fancy word for havin’ good taste, Elsie. And these weren’t exactly cheap, mind. Doreen at the market said they were hand-painted, you know. Proper artisan stuff. Worth every penny, I reckon. Doreen exaggerates everything, Arthur. You know that. She told me last week that Mr. Henderson’s cat was teaching squirrels to play chess. It’s Doreen, isn’t it? It's always Doreen. But honestly, are we really needing more ceramic animals? We've got the ducks, the squirrels, the… oh, good heavens, the porcelain badgers! Remember those? Well, the badgers were a bargain! And they do look rather distinguished, don’t they? Besides, it's nice to have somethin’ to look at. This place... it can feel a bit empty sometimes, can’t it? Since… you know… Since George passed, yes. I know, dear. I just... I worry about space, and clutter. It's just a thing I tend to think about. I don’t want us tripping over hedgehogs and badgers when we’re older. We're not  that  old, Elsie! Seventy-five and sixty-eight ain't ancient history. And we're both as fit as fiddles, aren't we? Still managing to potter round the garden, minding our own business. You are remarkably stubborn, you know that, Arthur? Honestly, you’d fill the house with ceramic sheep if I let you. Well, they do have a certain charm, don’t they? Think of it, Elsie! A whole flock of fluffy little ceramic sheep! We could line 'em up along the mantelpiece... Don’t you dare even suggest it! Look, let's compromise. No  more  hedgehogs. Or badgers. Or sheep. We'll focus on admiring the ones we have.

…and then, absolutely then, he started doing this caterwauling! It weren’t even singing, honestly. Just noise. Like a strangled cat trying to imitate Pavarotti. Sounds dreadful. Was it at the pub last night? You mentioned a work social. Aye, the pub. Poor Brenda from accounts nearly choked on her chips. Honestly, the man thought he were the next Ed Sheeran. He were more like... like a slightly tipsy badger. You’re ruthless. I’m sure he thought he was pretty good. People do, don’t they? It’s the confidence, I suppose. Reminds me of old Professor Davies in my department. Thinks his guitar playing is something special, but… well, let’s just say nobody encourages him to play during coffee breaks. Exactly! It's good to have a bit of confidence though, innit? Although, sometimes… …sometimes it needs a bit of controlling. This weather’s been doing the same thing! One minute it's sunshine, next minute you're battling hail the size of marbles. Seriously, the roses are battered this year. Tell me about it. My courgettes are looking decidedly glum. I’ve been trying to be all diligent and watering them, shielding them... Honestly, it's a full-time job. I was reading about companion planting – apparently, planting marigolds near courgettes deters some pests? Marigolds? Right. My Nana used to say clever things like that. Used to grow prize-winning tomatoes, she did. Said it were all about the soil and talking to them. Honestly, conversation with a tomato! It’s not completely ridiculous. People are discovering how important soil health is. It’s a whole ecosystem down there. Speaking of ecosystems, have you heard from Liam and Chloe recently? They were going to visit that wildlife sanctuary in Norfolk, weren't they? Aye, just yesterday! Sent me a load o' pictures. Apparently they spotted a bittern, which is reet rare! I’m dead chuffed for them. They deserve a good break. That whole graphic design business has been stressful for Chloe. It has. She's been putting in ridiculous hours. I keep telling her she needs to delegate more, but she's such a control freak. Like me with my research, I suppose. Hard to let go. You? Letting go? You're practically surgically attached to your data analysis. Well, someone needs to make sure the results are reliable! It’s my PhD, after all. This dissertation is looming over me like a particularly aggressive thunderstorm.

Right, so that’s it then. Rejection email. Another one. Honestly, I’m starting to think my CV is cursed. "While your experience is impressive..." Aye, well, impressive enough to get a polite 'thanks but no' for the last five jobs I’ve applied for, apparently. Five? Seriously? That’s rough, love. Which one was this? The one at the analytics firm? Aye, the big one. The one I was actually feeling good about. Had a decent interview, seemed like they were chuffed with my presentation. Then…poof. Gone. It’s just… frustrating. All those hours spent tweaking my CV, researching the company, practicing answers… For nothing. I know the feeling. Remember when I was applying for that research assistant position at UCL? Thought I'd nailed it, even had a second interview. Then got the standard ‘we went with someone with slightly more experience’ email. Still stings, even now. It does, doesn’t it? And the worst bit is, you start questioning yourself. Are I not good enough? Is my degree not good enough? Is something fundamentally wrong with me? Don’t go there, honestly. You're brilliant, Chloe. You’ve got a first-class honours, a Masters, and you ran that whole project at the university – a project everyone said was brilliant! It’s the market, isn’t it? It's a mess. Especially for research roles. Everyone and their dog is trying to get into data analytics these days. Easy for you to say, ya’re busy being a brainbox doing your PhD. At least you’ve got something to focus on, something that’s  yours . I’m just… adrift. And the student loans are laughing at me, I swear. Speaking of which... have you looked into any of those government schemes for graduates struggling to find work? Like, the ones that subsidize employers and things? Aye, a bit. Seems like a right faff, to be honest. Loads of paperwork. I’d rather just… disappear to somewhere warm and sunny and forget about it all. Tempting, definitely. Though I'd miss your sarcastic remarks. Look, maybe we can set aside some time tomorrow and have a proper look? Two heads are better than one, eh? And I've got a bit more time free now I've scrapped half the experiments that weren't working. That’d be good, thanks, Liam. Appreciate it. Honestly, sometimes just talking it through helps a bit.

Nah, it’s alright, Gran, but Liam wouldn’t  really  wrestle a badger, would he? He’s terrified of bugs, remember? Oh, you and your Liam. Always the realist, aren't you, Finn? It's a children’s book, love. A little imagination’s allowed. The badger's friendly, see? Look at his smile! I think it's lovely, Gran. It's charming. And Liam  does  have that cheeky glint in his eyes. He'd dress it up, wouldn’t you, sweetheart? Even if he was scared stiff. Maybe. But he’d probably just throw a biscuit at it. A biscuit, would he? My goodness, your lot are a peculiar bunch. Still, that’s what makes family, doesn't it? This is a good idea, though, Sarah. A story for the little ones, linking them to their heritage. Something to tell them about where they come from. That’s exactly what I was thinking. It’s important, isn’t it? Especially with… well, with everything. They need to know about their Scottish roots. And their Bristol roots too, with you, Finn. It’s all part of them. What about putting in pictures of Dad and Tom? They won't let me draw them properly, they keep moving around. Absolutely. We have loads of pictures. I’ll dig out some from when Tom was little. Remember that picture of him with the ridiculously oversized teddy bear? Oh, I do. He was a wee scamp, that one. Always getting into mischief. Just like his brother. Speaking of family trees, I've been thinking… perhaps we could include a simplified version in the back? Just the main branches and a few of the interesting characters. Could we put Uncle Rory in? The one who lives in Australia? Of course! He'd love that. Though getting a recent picture of him might be tricky. He's always gone for the wildlife shots, hasn't he? Koalas and kangaroos instead of family photos. It’s a funny thing, family. Spread out all over the world. My own children... scattered like leaves in the wind. I miss them dearly, you know. I know, Gran. You always say that. But they love you. And they call, don’t they? More often these days, I think. Aye, they do. It’s just… it’s not the same as having them here, is it? You know, your Liam… he reminds me so much of my youngest son, Alasdair.

…and then Mr. Davies  actually  said it was a 'career opportunity' to staple invoices to a laminated poster! A laminated poster, Chloe! Like I’m supposed to be getting excited about that. Honestly, I think they’re just keeping me busy so they don’t have to hire anyone proper. Oh my goodness, that's ridiculous! Stapling invoices to a laminated poster? Seriously? They’re taking the proverbial, aren’t they? Sounds like a nightmare. Still, at least you’re earning, right? What are you saving for anyway? Another holiday? Nah, not a holiday. More like, you know, a life. Eventually. I’m trying to build a deposit for somewhere that isn't a student house share. These houses are a right shambles. Damp everywhere, and the last tenant left a collection of novelty rubber ducks... A collection of rubber ducks? That  is  a bit eccentric. My flatmate left behind a single, very dusty pineapple. Still, at least it wasn't ducks. So, invoices and ducks. Exciting times! Changing the subject slightly...have you been doing… you know… the usual? "The usual"? What exactly constitutes "the usual" in our conversation, Chloe? Are we talking about the existential dread of late-stage capitalism, or… something else? No! Not  that  usual. I just meant... the leg maintenance. You know. The… shaving situation. Oh,  that  usual! Right, you’re onto something. The shaving situation, as you put it. Don't even get me started. It’s a constant battle, innit? I'm forever battling tiny, prickly hairs. And the ingrown ones! Don’t even mention ingrown ones. I know! It’s so unfair! Why do we have to do this? Honestly, I’ve been reading about this whole "body hair positivity" thing online… it’s making me question everything. Aye, it is. I’ve seen it too. It’s good, innit? Letting it grow wild and free. But then you go out and feel like everyone’s judging you, you know? Like you're a right scruff. Exactly! It's the societal pressure. My mum’s always going on about it. "Smooth legs are a sign of respectability," she says. As if respectability is tied to the absence of body hair. It’s bonkers. My nan used to say the same! "A proper lass keeps herself neat and tidy." But honestly, the time and effort! I tried going a few weeks without shaving once.

Aye, bottled it is. Could’ve gone either way, mind. But that was blatant. Pure blatant. Reckon he was daft enough to think he didn't see it? Well, you know how it is. Pressure, cameras… They get caught up in the moment. Though, letting Kane stay on the pitch probably influenced the whole game really. Did you see that tackle on Diaz? Woeful. Woeful doesn't even cover it, does it? Ridiculous challenge. And the way they cleared the pitch…gutting, eh? Absolutely. Shocking. It’s a constant problem, isn't it? Black players getting targeted. You’d think in 2024 we’d be further along, wouldn’t you? Aye, you’d hope so. But it's like, ingrained, innit? Always been there, haven’t it? Even when I were a kid watching Sunderland… the chants, the… it was always bubbling under the surface. Proper grim. It is. And the way these fan groups get away with it. These organised…things. It’s just terrifying the amount of hate that's out there. Aye. Makes you proper angry, doesn't it? I was reading summat about… what was it called… 'alphabet soup' policing? The way they're struggling to classify these hate crimes. Right, yeah! The growing complexity of identifying the motivations - the ‘alphabet soup’ of protected characteristics. It’s fascinating from a sociological perspective, but utterly depressing when you consider the human cost. I've been researching…well, it's tied into societal prejudice and how it manifests in online and offline spaces. Turns out, some of the underlying patterns are…well, unsettling. Unsettling how? Don’t go all academic on me now, love. I’m tryin’ to enjoy me pint. Sorry, sorry. Got carried away. Just… the way echo chambers reinforce pre-existing biases, the algorithms that amplify extremist content… it’s a whole system. It’s more than just a few bad apples. Aye, I get that. Feels like there’s more than just a few bad apples, doesn't there? Speaking of systems… fancy another one of these? It’s decent, actually. Strong, mind. Always, love. Another pint it is. So, back to football, then. You watch much boxing? I was thinking about seeing Fury fight Usyk. Boxing? Honestly, not really me, but Fury's entertaining, isn't he? All that bravado… makes you wonder what’s going on underneath, though, doesn’t it? The mental health struggles… Definitely.

Honestly, Penelope, the sheer volume of paperwork required for the St. Alphege restoration bid is quite frankly ludicrous. They want a five-year projection of costs, a detailed risk assessment – including potential pigeon infestation – and a full sustainability report! Pigeons! As if a 13th-century church wasn't already sustainably built. Oh, Beatrice, you’re telling me! I completely sympathize. The Diocese seems to have gotten a bit carried away with the funding guidelines. Five years is a lifetime in this industry. Things change. Damp metres shift, lead prices fluctuate… Exactly! And they’ve insisted on incorporating ‘community engagement’ metrics. Which, fine, important, but I’m not sure the villagers of Aston Clinton are going to be particularly engaged in the finer points of Norman tracery repairs. Community engagement is key, though. It's almost a prerequisite now. Have you considered something simple? A series of short talks, maybe, on the history of the building? Photos of the process, before and after? Even a little craft session for the children, making models of gargoyles? Gets everyone involved without drowning you in detail. A gargoyle craft session… That's… surprisingly appealing, actually. It’s certainly more practical than asking them to volunteer for lime rendering. I’ve bid for projects before, Penelope, and I’ve learned the hard way: show them you understand their needs, their community. It’s more than just technical expertise these days. Absolutely. And regarding the funding projections, are you using the Heritage Lottery Fund’s calculator? It’s quite clever, and adjusts for inflation and contingency. It won't be perfect, of course, but it can streamline the process considerably. I use it for almost every bid now. I’ve glanced at it, but to be honest, I found it a bit overwhelming. Always loved spreadsheets, used to build them for my late husband’s architectural practice. But this one looked like it had been designed by a committee. You and me both. It  has  been designed by a committee, I suspect. But persevere. It can save you hours of number-crunching. Have you started sketching out a business plan for the entire company, beyond this specific project, though? Not yet, no. I’ve been so consumed by individual projects, fire-fighting as it were. It’s always been enough to just keep busy, you know? Now, with the treasurer breathing down my neck about profitability… I realise I need a more structured approach.

Right, that’s tha sorted. Strong enough for us then, eh? You’re lookin' a bit peak, love. Long day in the lab? Yeah, you could say that. Struggling to get my Bayesian statistics to play nice with the corpus data. It's like they're actively arguing with each other. And Cambridge never stops raining, does it? Just adds to the gloom. Aye, tell me about it. This northeast weather’s got into me bones, even livin' down here. Though, Cambridge rain is a different beast, innit? It’s more… persistent. Less dramatic than a proper Sunderland shower. More of a damp sigh. A damp sigh. That's brilliantly put. You've got a knack for describing weather in the most concise way possible. So, how was your day? Did you make any progress on that phonological rule analysis? Aye, a bit. I’m gettin’ somewhere with the northern vowel shift, but it's a nightmare to disentangle from general dialectal variation. Everyone insists they don't  sound  different, but the data screams otherwise! It’s frustrating. You’d think after all these years, we’d’ve cracked it. I appreciate the struggle. It’s the same with my stuff. People's intuitions about language are often wildly inaccurate, especially when you start quantifying them. It's that classic disconnect between what we  think  we know and what the data actually  shows . Exactly! It’s like tryin’ to herd cats made of vowels. Tell me, that Bayesian stuff... what’s the advantage there? I’ve always preferred a good old hypothesis test, you know? Simple, straightforward. Well, with a massive corpus – and mine is  massive  – traditional methods can struggle to account for all the nuance and uncertainty. Bayesian statistics let you incorporate prior knowledge, which is crucial when dealing with things like word frequency or grammatical structure. It's less about declaring definitive judgements, and more about calculating probabilities and refining your understanding iteratively. Sounds complicated… like me head’ll explode just thinkin’ about it. So, no simple p-value then? Nope. No simple p-value. Just a posterior probability distribution, which is considerably less user-friendly, but, in theory, more accurate. It’s all about updating your beliefs in light of new evidence. Kind of like academic research overall, really. Aye, that’s true enough. So, listen, I was thinkin’... we've been a bit bogged down in work lately.

Honestly, you two, the feedback from school today was… something else. Apparently, half the class refused the shepherd's pie. Shepherd’s pie! It’s practically comfort food! I liked the shepherd's pie! It was yummy! Mine was too much mushy stuff. See? One of you liked it! But the others... they said it was "gloopy" and "not colourful enough." Honestly! What do they want? Rainbow-coloured mashed potatoes? Maybe they want dinosaurs made of peas? Dinosaurs made of peas. That's a good idea, actually. I'll mention it to Mrs. Peterson, the dinner lady. Though, I doubt she’ll be thrilled. Right, so, lunch money. I've topped up your cards, both of you. £10 each this week, okay? That should cover packed lunches too, just in case you don't fancy the school fare. Can I have some extra for the tennis tournament? Please? The tennis tournament? Oh, right! That’s on Saturday, isn’t it? You’re really keen on that, aren’t you, love? Yes! I want to win the bouncy ball prize! I want to win too! Can I play with Leo? We'll see, sweetheart. It depends on the teams, doesn't it? It's a doubles tournament, remember? Now, speaking of things that involve excitement and a bit of chaos… Granny mentioned wanting to hear all about your day at school over Sunday lunch. Granny makes the best apple crumble! And chips! Loads of chips! She does, doesn't she? Sunday lunch at Granny’s is a proper treat. But you two need to promise me you'll actually  tell  her about your day. Not just "it was good!" I want to know about your lessons, your friends… and whether anyone liked the shepherd's pie. I told Millie about the clown at assembly! He kept dropping his balloons. A clown? At assembly? What on earth was that about? Mr. Davies said it was to cheer everyone up. But the clown was silly. Silly clowns are often the best kind. Reminds me of that time I went to the circus with my dad. Remember how I told you about the lady who could balance on a ball? Yes! And the man with the stripy suit! Did the clown fall off the ball too? No, thankfully not! Though I think he tried to juggle with a rubber chicken at one point. It was mayhem, absolute mayhem.

That film was… startling, wasn’t it? The sheer bleakness of it all. Almost overwhelming. Bleakness is the order of the day, wouldn't you say? Film, politics, the news… all rather grey. Though, I did rather enjoy the cinematography. Reminded me a bit of something Stanley Kubrick might have done. Right, Dad. Kubrick. Always Kubrick. You and your classic films. Though I have to admit, the visuals were stunning. But really, it just felt… depressing. I need something lighter next time. Maybe a rom-com? Not the dress code, darling! A rom-com after  that ? You'll be questioning the very fabric of reality. Speaking of reality, did you hear about the debate in Cambridge last week? The one on teaching history? Vaguely. Something about moving away from a chronological approach, right? I saw a snippet online. Sounded quite heated. Heated is an understatement. It was a proper shouting match at times. The core argument seemed to be whether we should focus on ‘big themes’ - empire, industrial revolution – or individual narratives. I think I’m firmly in the latter camp. Those grand narratives often gloss over so much suffering, you know? Suffering is inherent in history, my dear. You can't sanitise it. Trying to tell history through individual stories… it becomes fragmented, loses the context. What's the point then? Just a collection of anecdotes. I think there's a balance, Dad. Individual stories  can  illuminate the larger themes. It makes it more relatable, more engaging for the kids. Especially with the national curriculum as it is now. So much to cram in, so little time. It feels like we’re teaching them dates and names for a test, not actually fostering an understanding of the past. Exactly! And the pressure! They’re being assessed on so much now. It’s squeezing the life out of everything. I wish they’d rethink the emphasis on exams at such a young age. I remember at my school, Dorchester Grammar, we did a fantastic project on local history in year nine. Really got us thinking. It wasn't a test, it was just… learning for the sake of learning. It's the same problem in other fields, isn't it? My team at work are constantly complaining about the academic world churning out graduates who are brilliant in theory but can’t apply anything they’ve learned to a real-world situation.

Cor blimey, Arthur. You always were one for a yarn, weren't you? Pigeons, indeed! Costessey pigeons used to just nick bits of bread off your doorstep, nothing more. Oh, Arthur, you magnificent fool! That’s brilliant! Where did this occur, by the way? It sounds like the peak of paranoia, Arthur. When was this supposed incident? You weren’t, ahem, indulging in a bit of… recreational gardening at the time, were you? Now, now, George. Don't you go implying things. It were just after the Falklands. Everyone were on edge. You’d read things in the paper about spies and… well, a chap felt he had to be vigilant! Remember the rationing, George? You didn’t! You were always off gallivanting already. Oh, leave him alone, George. Arthur's stories are precious. Remind me, Arthur, did your mum ever tell you about her great-uncle, the one who was a signalman in the Great War? Apparently, he used to talk about listening in on the German lines… Ah, now you're talking, Margaret. Uncle Barnaby. Aye, she did. Said he could pick up bits and pieces, enough to know they were planning something nasty. Kept it quiet, of course. Didn’t want to cause a panic. Good man, Uncle Barnaby. Solid Norfolk stock, he was. Never complained, even when the potatoes failed. Incredible. My grandfather, he rarely spoke of the War. Upper-middle-class family, you see. It was considered…unseemly. Vague mutterings about the Somme, a lost cousin... very understated. Far removed from a Norfolk signalman picking up German whispers, I can assure you! Interesting. The attitudes towards discussing conflict really varied, didn't they? My father, ran a small textile mill during the war, his focus was entirely on production and keeping families employed. Conflict was an economic pressure, not… a lived experience like it was for so many. Though he did have a rather remarkable collection of propaganda posters he kept tucked away in the attic. Speaking of attics and collections…George, are you still thinking about replacing this old armchair? It’s seen better days, I’ll admit, but it's so comfortable. It's been in the family for… well, ages. Margaret, darling, it's a veritable fire hazard. The springs are shot, the fabric is threadbare... It’s a testament to another era, certainly. But practically speaking? It needs going. We could get something rather lovely, something modern… Modern!

You know, this is… weird, isn’t it? Driving away from Mum’s for the last time. Feels like a proper end of an era. Yeah, it does. I’m glad we got to spend the weekend though. Sunday lunch was top-notch, as always. Though I might need to loosen my belt a notch or two. You always do. She spoils you, you know. More than she spoils me, and I'm her son! Blames it on me being the "sensible" one. Don't sell yourself short. You're incredibly reliable, Dad. Just… practical. She likes a bit of extravagance now and then. Speaking of which, have you sorted that paperwork for the mortgage on the new place? It felt a bit stressful last time we talked. Nearly there, lad. Just waiting on a few final details from the bank. It's a nightmare, honestly. All these fees, all these forms... greed, that’s what it is. Remember when we used to get a mortgage with a handshake and a smile? And a five-year fixed rate that felt like a lifetime away. Times have changed. Still, you're doing brilliantly. Proper step up for you and Sarah. Northamptonshire will be good. More space, closer to the grandkids. Exactly. Though I’m going to miss that little garden she’s got. Mum’s always growing something. Remember that time she tried to grow pumpkins? They were the size of your head! And tasted like… well, tasted like nothing much, to be honest. Vaguely. I was probably more interested in the football on the telly. Still, it was a good effort. Thinking about the move proper, are you worried about settling in? You’ve lived in Crayford your whole life. It’s the people, isn't it? Making new friends. You and Sarah have it easier, you're both young, got your careers... I’m just… an old customer service agent. What am I going to talk about? The joys of resolving billing disputes? Don’t be daft. You’re Dad. You’ve got a lifetime of stories. Remember Uncle Barry attempting to build a shed last summer? That was gold. And you’re a dab hand at the barbeque. That’ll win anyone over. Actually, Sarah mentioned her cousin, Fiona, lives nearby. She's into gardening like Mum. Fiona, eh? Good. Social interaction is vital for mental health, the doctor says.

Honestly, Mum, rearranging the cupboards  again ? You know Grandma's going to get completely baffled. She can barely remember what day it is, let alone where the teacups are now. I know, darling, but they were a complete disaster! The baking tins were blocking everything. I just want to make it a bit more efficient. It’s just… logistics, really. And besides, we need to think about the meal. Have you got any inspiration? Inspiration? Well, we could always do the Yorkshire puddings. Grandma loves a good Yorkshire pudding. And roast beef, obviously. Classic. Yes, beef is good. She does enjoy it. But it’s a bit… heavy, isn't it? Perhaps for a summer birthday a lighter option? Maybe salmon? We could get some nice fresh fish from that place down by the river. They get it in daily. Salmon? Hmm. She’s a bit fussy about fish, isn’t she? Remember that time we tried to get her to eat cod? The look on her face... I do. We’ll stick to salmon then. With Dauphinoise potatoes and some asparagus. Sounds nice, doesn't it? What about dessert? Definitely cake. A proper cake. Not one of those fancy, layered monstrosities. Something straightforward. Victoria sponge? Perfect! Victoria sponge it is. I’ll get the best raspberries I can find. And strawberries, of course. We'll need candles. Plenty of candles. And a nice tablecloth. I’ve got that cream one she likes… Wait, where did I put it…? Mum! Focus! Tables? Have we even thought about where everyone’s going to sit? Aunt Susan always wants to sit next to Uncle David and argue about politics. And poor Cousin Emily is terrified of Susan. Right, the table plan. That’s crucial. Okay, you're right about Susan and David. They’ll go at opposite ends of the table. Emily can sit next to me. And then… where does that leave poor Geoffrey? He’s a bit quiet, isn’t he? Geoffrey can have the seat next to Emily if Susan’s far enough away! Honestly, Mum, you’d think planning a dinner party was like negotiating international peace. It feels like it sometimes! It's not just about the food, is it? It’s about making sure everyone feels comfortable and happy. Especially Grandma. It's getting a bit tougher, isn't it? This… forgetting things… Yeah. It is. It’s hard seeing her like that.

Right, so, they’ve finally managed to prise ‘em out. All four. Feels like I’ve been to the dentist more times this year than I have in my whole life. Dramatic as ever, Maisie! Four wisdom teeth? You’re a hero. Mine were a piece of cake, honestly. Just two, and the anaesthetic wore off before I even got home. I was biting my tongue raw. Cake?! Love, you’ve never had a Yorkshire dentist. They take a  personal  interest in your mouth. Like they’re trying to win some sort of excavation competition. He kept muttering about "perfect anatomical excavation" - sounded proper creepy, reyt? And the swelling… I look like a chipmunk. Oh, that doesn’t sound pleasant at all. Are you in a lot of pain? You should have called your mum. She’d have been on the next Eurostar with a hot water bottle and some chicken soup. Aye, I thought about it. But she'd be halfway up the walls worrying, and Dad would be trying to diagnose me with some rare tropical disease he read about online. He's proper good at that, he is. Remember when I had a cold and he was convinced I'd picked up something from the pigeons in the park? Oh, God, yes! He was researching avian flu for hours! Your parents are… unique. My parents are just quietly disappointed I'm not a lawyer. Which, to be fair, feels fairly constant. Well, at least you’ve got options! I’m stuck between trying to scrape together the deposit for a flat and finishing this blasted degree. It's a right pickle, it is. Any progress on your moving situation? You were saying something about needing to find somewhere near your uni, weren’t you? It’s moving  very  slowly. London housing is… insane. I've looked at about fifty places online and most of them are either the size of a postage stamp or cost more than my student loan for the year. I'm seriously considering living in a cupboard under the stairs. I can imagine. Moving back to Doncaster isn’t exactly appealing, mind, but at least the rent’s reasonable. Honestly, sometimes I feel like chucking it all in and opening a bakery. Muffins and scones, that's where my true calling lies. You? A baker? I can see it! You’d be famous! "Maisie's Marvelous Muffins" – catchy, right?

Right, so the recipe for the lactose-free chocolate chip cookies is  almost  perfected. Just need to tweak the baking time a bit, I think. They came out a bit crumbly last time. But the cakes are a success! Honestly, sometimes I think these dietary restrictions are a good thing, it's forced me to be more creative. Can I have a cookie, Mummy? Even if they're a little crumbly? Of course, sweetheart! But let's finish this discussion first. We were talking about random acts of kindness, weren’t we? Not just the usual 'hold the door open' sort of things. Like... giving money to a homeless person? Exactly, Leo! That's a wonderful one. But what else? Something small, something we could do easily. Grandma suggested leaving a little bag of dog treats on a neighbour’s doorstep if they have a dog. Ooh! We could draw pictures for the nurses at the hospital! They look tired sometimes. That's brilliant, darling! Absolutely brilliant. We could do that this weekend. Leo, what about you? Got any ideas? We could…we could use these! Use the chess pieces? What on earth do you mean? To give to people! Like, if someone looks sad, we can give them a chess piece. It's like... lucky. Lucky chess! That’s… incredibly imaginative, Leo. A  very  generous offer, giving away your chess pieces! But you know, it's actually a lovely idea. Maybe not the pieces themselves, but the  thought  behind it. Like a small token of kindness. You could give someone a sticker or a drawing instead. But chess pieces are good! Daddy uses them! Daddy uses them to  pretend  they're money! Remember? When we play shops? That’s right! Pretend money. We could even make our own little "Kindness Coins" from paper. We'll decorate them with happy faces and give them to people who need a little cheering up. Can we decorate them with glitter? Please? Absolutely glitter! Loads of glitter. Now, about Chinese New Year... it's just around the corner, isn't it? It’s the year of the Dragon this year. Do you know what animal you are? I’m a rabbit! Because I was born last year! I think I'm a… a sheep! Clever clogs! Right, so we need to get some red envelopes. And maybe make some paper lanterns? We could even attempt some dumplings.
