"Honestly, Chloe? They're the worst, aren't they? Proper little thugs with wings." "They absolutely are. You've been out and about, then? You look… sun-kissed. Did you go to the beach all day?” "Yeah, with Liam. We went to the De La Warr Quarter, got some ice cream. He's really into theatre at the moment, you know. Said he wants to be an actor. A serious one." "Oh? Really? That's lovely! What sort of things does he enjoy acting? Anything specific?" "Mostly Shakespeare, actually. Bit pretentious, maybe. He was talking about  Hamlet  the other day. Said it was ‘a searing exploration of existential dread.’ I just wanted a flake in my 99.” "Well, that  is  a bit much for a Tuesday afternoon. Anything else interesting happen?" "Well… it’s a bit awkward to talk about. Remember I told you I was meeting Sarah and Josh? Near the seafront?” “Of course. To discuss the costume for the school play. What happened?” "There was… an accident. A car accident. Nothing too serious, thankfully. But Sarah’s mum, you know, Mrs. Davies? She… hit a lamppost. She’s okay, just a bit shaken up.” "Oh, Chloe, that's awful! Is Sarah alright? And Mrs. Davies?" "Yeah, Sarah's fine. She was really worried about her mum, obviously. Mrs. Davies had a bit of a scratch on her arm, a proper nasty one actually. It’s… quite visible. And Sarah was saying how she keeps getting anxious about her mum driving now. It's… brought up a lot." "I can imagine. Scars, visible ones especially… they trigger things, don't they? Memories. Feelings. I remember when I was younger, I fell off my bike and scraped my knee really badly. It ended up needing stitches, you know. I hated it. I felt… broken. And the scar… it was a reminder of the fall, of the pain." "Did it ever go?" "It faded considerably. But sometimes, when the light hits it just right, I can still feel it. A little twinge. It’s funny, isn't it? How the body remembers." "Yeah. So, anyway, the costume discussion… It's  Alice in Wonderland . You know I volunteered to help." "Really? That’s brilliant, darling! You always were partial to a bit of fancy dress." "I know! I'm thinking of suggesting we do a modern Alice. Like, ripped fishnets, Doc Martens, maybe a neon pink Cheshire Cat.

…and so, Margaret, they were utterly relying on this vague assertion of ‘local benefit.’ Benefit to whom, I asked! Benefit to the shareholders of Green Horizon Energy, more likely. Honestly, it’s infuriating. Just like last night with the SolarBright people. Same story, different shiny object. A remarkably consistent tactic, isn't it? The gloss of sustainability plastered over a distinctly profit-driven operation. I told them, young Colin and his wife, emphasizing the importance of meticulously scrutinizing the environmental impact assessment. Did they even  challenge  the baseline data? Baseline data! A lovely way of putting it. More like a carefully curated fiction. I’ve seen it time and again, even in my corporate days. Spin, spin, spin. You’ve got to dismantle it brick by brick. With facts, mind you, not just outrage. Precisely. Last night, I suggested they focus on the cumulative impact. They're proposing three separate solar farms within a five-mile radius. Individually, they might seem manageable, but together… it’s a significant alteration to the landscape, and a loss of agricultural land. The council representative just brushed it off as ‘progress.’ The local council… a necessary evil, wouldn't you say? I was at the Development Control Committee meeting last month. Mon Dieu! The sway of those energy company lobbyists is terrifying. And the councillors, nodding along like trained seals. Aye, and don’t forget the Planning Appeal stage. That's where the real money comes into play. They’ll hire the best barristers, the slickest consultants… you need to be prepared for that. We need a unified front. Are these groups willing to pool resources, share research? That’s the challenge, isn’t it? Everyone's so passionate, so convinced they're right, they end up working at cross-purposes. I keep telling them, a well-researched, legally sound challenge is far more effective than shouting slogans at a planning meeting. It’s about understanding the framework, exploiting the loopholes… Loopholes! A fascinating word. And precisely what they rely on. Did you mention the regulations regarding shadow flicker with the solar farm people? It can be a surprisingly effective sticking point. Speaking of energy, you know, it’s not just about fighting  against  these developments. We need to be thinking about alternatives. Tidal energy, for example. Properly harnessed, that could be a game changer. But the investment… where is it? That’s what I find so infuriating.

Honestly, Dad, I’ve been reading through these insurance quotes and it's just… bewildering. How much can it  really  cost to insure a little Fiat 500? Well, love, it all depends, don't it? Your age, your driving history - which you don't have yet, thankfully - the car itself, where you live… It’s a whole system, a right layered one. Back in my day, you just went to the local agent and paid what they told you. Simple as that. Oh, don't start, Arthur. Simple it certainly wasn’t! Remember when your Ford Cortina was practically half your monthly wage in insurance? You nearly had a heart attack! That was different, Brenda. That was a proper car! And the roads were more dangerous then. Less traffic calming, you see. These modern things... they want to charge you an arm and a leg for a tiny bit of metal. Exactly! Some of these are over a thousand pounds a year! I was hoping for something closer to £600. I’m trying to save for that trip to Italy, remember? Italy! Oh, that sounds lovely. Are you thinking about Rome again, darling? Yes! I found a really cute little Airbnb in Trastevere, near the river. Just picture it – pasta, gelato, ancient ruins… everything. But it all depends on managing to get insured and passing my test! Which, to be honest, feels like a monumental task at the moment. Mrs. Peterson keeps marking me down for observation at roundabouts. Roundabouts are tricky things, they are. You’ve got to anticipate, see what’s coming from all sides. It's all about spatial awareness, really. And a bit of luck. Don’t let her get you down. You're a smart girl, Eliza. You’ll pass. Are you doing your hazard perception test regularly? Yes, every other day. It’s strangely addictive… watching those cyclists pop out! It's terrifying in real life, I imagine. Bless her. It’s good you’re taking it seriously. Remember when I first tried to learn, Arthur? I stalled the car three times in a row at the traffic lights! Nearly caused a pile-up. You did, didn't you? And you blamed the clutch! Said it was defective. It  felt  defective! My knees weren't used to all that effort. Anyway, your trip to Italy sounds wonderful, Eliza. Are you going with Mark? Yes, we’re planning to go for two weeks in September.

Honestly, Dad, parking in Brighton is a nightmare. Absolutely mental. I spent twenty minutes circling just to find a space the other day. Twenty minutes! And then it was, like, £4.50 for an hour. Ridiculous. Brighton. Always was a bit… flash, that place. Remember your mum saying it was all ‘show’ when we used to visit for day trips? Not much real substance, she’d reckon. Nowadays, though, it’s even worse, isn’t it? All those fancy cars clogging up the roads. Exactly! I’m trying to think of ways around it. Walking a bit more, maybe. Or getting a bike, but then you have to find somewhere to lock it up that isn’t going to get nicked. This whole self-employed freelance thing is a lot harder than I thought it would be. You’re doing well, though, love. Gotta admire you for having a go. When I was younger… well, things were different. Opportunities… didn’t exactly grow on trees, did they? Remember that fella, Derek? From the betting shop? Always had a system for the horses. Oh, Derek! The man who swore he could predict the outcome based on the colour of the jockey's silks. Did he ever get it right? Occasionally. More often than not, he was singing a different tune come Saturday afternoon. But he was having a bit of luck last week, apparently. Won a few quid on that long shot, ‘Thunderclap’ or something. Proper value, he said. Value! That’s what everyone says. I dabble a bit, you know. Just a small bet now and then. Mainly for the excitement. Speaking of excitement, did you see that article about the food banks? It’s just… heartbreaking. It is. Awful. You read about people struggling, and then you see the politicians on the telly, arguing about… well, about nothing, really. They haven’t a clue what it's like. Back in the fifties, you know, we had rationing. That was hard. Real hard. But you knew where you stood. You looked after your neighbours. Everyone helped each other. That's what I keep saying. The sense of community has completely disappeared. It’s all so individualistic now. And people are being judged for needing help. It’s mad. I've been thinking about volunteering at a local food bank, actually. Do you think Mum would have liked that? Your Mum… she’d have been right there, rolling her sleeves up.

…and then Mr. Davies, bless his cotton socks, just stares at me, deadpan, and says, "Mr. Thompson, are you suggesting I  fashioned  the marketing plan out of thin air?" The whole lecture hall erupted. I nearly died of embarrassment, but honestly, it was brilliant. Oh, Davies! He’s legendary for his dryness. Reminds me of my grandfather, only with worse comb-over potential. Honestly, the sheer awkwardness of that situation... Did you get marked down? Thankfully, no! He actually ended up giving me a bit of extra credit for, apparently, “challenging the status quo.” Though I suspect he just wanted the room to stop laughing. It’s classic Shakespearean irony, isn't it? The misunderstanding, the subtle jabs… Shakespeare, eh? You're still on that tangent. I thought we were talking about humiliating experiences in marketing workshops, not Elizabethan drama. Everything is Elizabethan drama, Finn! Come on, you know you think so too. It's just a matter of spotting it. Like, think about your attempts at learning golf. That’s pure Lear, isn’t it? The overreaching ambition, the inevitable fall… Don’t remind me. I’ve spent more money on golf lessons than I have on textbooks. And I'm still consistently horrible. It’s infuriating. I’m determined to at least break 100 though, you know, just to… win something. Even if it’s just against myself. Winning, is it? That's rather your default mode, isn't it? It's always about beating someone, somehow. Remember when you tried to win that village bake-off with a shop-bought Victoria sponge? It was a  really  good Victoria sponge! And it was technically 'baked,' I just... delegated the initial stages. Skill learning is all about smart delegation, you know. Leveraging resources. Think of it as Agile marketing, but with cake. Agile cake marketing. I'm putting that on my CV. Seriously though, it’s the competitive streak. You’d try to win a staring contest. Perhaps. My surname does that to a person, I think. Wainwright. It just  sounds  like someone who should be scaling mountains and winning gold medals. Makes you feel like you have to live up to some grand, historical narrative. What about Thompson? Does bearing the Thompson name inspire great deeds in you? Thompson? Nope. Mostly just inspires people to call me ‘Thommo.’ Which is significantly less impressive. My mum’s side of the family are all Thompsons.

Aye, you get that sometimes, don't ya? Gotta be prepared for a right shambles, that's conference organising for ya. My nan always said, “Plan for the worst, hope for the best, lass.” Sounds wise. Though I’m not sure disasters involving mini quiches are really on my radar. I spent most of today wrestling a skip into place. Not exactly the same level of stress. A skip? Really, Liam? Sounds… strenuous. I had a relatively calm day, actually. Just finalising the production schedule for next month’s launch. Though, Sarah did spend the morning complaining about the lack of almond milk in the staff kitchen. Almond milk! That’s a right first world problem, innit? Back home, we're more worried about getting a decent pork pie. Seriously, though, Sarah complaining about almond milk? You’re surrounded by posh folk! She  is  particularly fussy. It’s endlessly amusing, and occasionally exhausting. It’s part of the charm, I suppose. Anyway, what about you, Chloe? Still stuck with the same hotel chain? Yup. Same old, same old. Trying to negotiate a slightly better rate, but they’re holding firm. It’s like pulling teeth. I'm thinking of trying to convince my boss we need to diversify. Maybe a boutique hotel in York next time? Something with a bit more… character. Less beige carpet, you know? A boutique hotel in York? Sounds lovely. Might have to swing by if you get it. Although, I'm pretty booked up for weekends at the moment. My mum's making me help her clear out the attic. Apparently, it's full of "heirlooms" that I need to "appreciate." Oh dear. That sounds… intense. My mum’s being far more reasonable. She’s hinting heavily that I should move closer to her, you know, settle down a bit. Settlement, eh? Are you getting the full-on guilt trip? My mum’s been on at me about finding a “nice young man” since I was sixteen. It’s more subtle than that. Just a constant stream of suggestions about suitable neighbourhoods and how much she misses me. You know, the casual, everyday reminders. My mum just straight-up asks if I’m seeing anyone. No beating around the bush with her. Pretty terrifying, actually. She’s already picked out names for my hypothetical children. Oh, that’s brilliant! What names has she got? Something about a Reginald and a Penelope.

Cor, look at you, Arthur! Your picture’s all wobbly again. What’s this internet doing to you? Feels like I’m looking at a picture in a heat haze. Sorry, George, sorry about that. Wi-Fi's being a bit temperamental today. The wind's picked up something fierce, you know. Nearly blew the shed door clean off! Right, let me get this sorted... There! Better? Much better, Arthur. It's lovely to see you both. George, you’re looking particularly rosy-cheeked. Did you have a nice walk earlier? Aye, a bit of a wander 'round the garden. Right mess it is, isn't it, Arthur? Needs a good tidy up. Especially with that eclipse coming. Don't want the neighbours complaining, do we? About the eclipse, George? Well, I’ve been reading up on it. Apparently, it’ll be quite spectacular. Total solar eclipse. Can you imagine? The sun disappearing completely for a few minutes. It is extraordinary, isn't it? I’ve ordered special glasses, though. Wouldn’t want to damage my eyes. Are you getting them, you two? Glasses? Pah! Never needed glasses for anything in my life, and I’m not starting now over a bit of shadow. George, be sensible. It’s not just a ‘bit of shadow’. It's a celestial event! Think about the beginnings of space, the cosmos… black holes even! It’s all connected. Arthur, you and your science! You’ll have him calculating the gravitational pull of the moon before you know it. Anyway, I wanted to show you what I've been up to. I’ve repainted that little watercolour scene I was telling you about. Want to see? Oh, that's lovely, Mary! Really lovely. The light on the cottage is… it’s just right. Looks a bit bland to me. Needs a bit more oomph. More grey! Everything needs a bit more grey. Always the critic, George! Oh, speaking of needing more, have you been eating well, both of you? I worry, you know. Especially with the bills going up. The TV licence nearly broke me this month. We’re managing, Mary. Trying to. Been putting down some bamboo in the garden, a bit of a screen to block out Mrs. Henderson’s dreadful fencing. She's put up that new mesh stuff, it’s awful, proper eyesore. Eyesore is right! Looks like a prison fence.

Honestly, this road is a nightmare. Sat in a queue for ages. Should’ve taken the bus. Aye, tell me about it. Buses are better, even though they’re always late. At least they don't involve this… this glacial progress. Did you see that sign for Alnwick? Fancy stopping for a bite there? Alnwick? Isn't that… really far out of the way? And I’m starving. Something a bit closer would be preferable. There’s that little Italian place in Morpeth, isn’t there? Bella Notte? I’ve heard good things. Bella Notte? Oh, aye, I’ve been there once or twice. It's alright, decent pasta. Bit pricey for what it is, mind. I was thinking more along the lines of that new place that opened up in Ponteland. 'The Hearthstone'? Heard their Sunday roast is dead good. Ponteland? I didn’t even know there  was  much in Ponteland. It always just seemed like a load of new build estates to me. All identical houses, lined up like little soldiers. No character at all. That's Ponteland in a nutshell, innit? But the pub there is lovely, really cosy. And their roast, apparently, is champion. Proper Yorkshire puddings. We’ve been driving around for ages, you're thinking about pudding now? Yorkshire puddings are essential. Fine, Ponteland it is then. Though, I still think we should have considered the bus. I’m starting to worry about the environmental impact of all this driving. My mum would have a field day. Your mum has a field day about everything, love. Remember when she started lecturing me about compostable coffee cups? Anyway, it’s only a short drive. And we’re seeing your Auntie Carol, so needs must. Did you remember to get her that lavender soap she likes? Blast! I completely forgot. I was so focussed on avoiding traffic. Typical. I’ll just quickly order some online when we get to her. She lives in that gorgeous Victorian house, doesn't she? Always loved the stained-glass windows. Reminds me of that cathedral in Salisbury, actually. Huge and impressive. Aye, Auntie Carol’s house is lovely. Proper old-fashioned, with all the nooks and crannies. Reckon it’s got a secret room somewhere. It’s a world away from those identikit boxes in Ponteland, that’s for sure. Salisbury Cathedral…never been, actually. Is it as big as York Minster?

Aye, they’re bold, aren't they? Especially now spring’s properly kickin' in. Him and his missus, always squabblin’ over the best spots. I reckon they’ve got a territory dispute goin' on with the blue tits. Did you get owt decent in your garden this mornin', Diane? Not much as plump as that robin, no. I had a lovely chaffinch though, singing away. I'm trying to get better at identifying them, you know. You're so much better than I am, Margaret. You can tell them just by the song. Years o' listenin', love. You pick it up. I had a right panic the other day, thought I’d heard a cuckoo. Turned out to be a blackbird just mimickin’ it. Blackbirds are clever buggers. Speaking of panicked, me alarm clock went off half an hour too early this morning. Gave me a right fright! Sent me jumpin’ halfway up the bed. Oh dear! That’s dreadful. I’m so reliant on my alarm. It's awful if it malfunctions. Reminds me, I need to get that hearing test booked in. Being an EFL teacher, I really need to hear everything - even the shyest student whispering. Aye, hearing's a grand thing. My brother, Peter, he's been complainin' about his tinnitus somethin' awful. Keeps him up at night. I had a bit of nosebleed last week, though. Proper gusher it was. Dreadful feeling, right? Oh, goodness! Nosebleeds are the worst. Are you taking anything for it? My aunt Mildred had terrible nosebleeds all the time, put down to the dry air in the house. She was a tiny woman, though. Like a little sparrow. Just keepin' an eye on it. Doctor says it's likely the air conditioning drying things out. Speaking of doctors... dentist's appointment next week. Dreadin' it, I am. Just want to get it over and done with. You still seein' Dr. Ellis? No, sadly. Dr. Ellis retired last year. I’m now seeing this young dentist – very efficient, but not quite the same as old Ellis. He kept a box of Werther's Originals in his waiting room, you see. A true gentleman. Werther's Originals! That’s a proper sign of a good dentist. My mate, Brenda – you remember Brenda from the WI? – she's convinced she's got throat cancer. She’s been readin’ all sorts online. Proper frettin' she is.

…and honestly, Sarah, the paperwork alone for this latest case is enough to drive a person bonkers. Three different assessments, endless referrals… it’s a constant treadmill. How's teaching going? Still battling teenagers and curriculum changes? You have no idea! They’re testing me, Sarah, really testing me. Year 11s are particularly… vibrant this year. But yes, the changes are relentless. They want us to incorporate mindfulness exercises now, can you believe it? It feels a bit…forced, somehow. Mindfulness? See, that’s something I’ve been meaning to try. I’m so stressed, I’m practically vibrating all the time. You do yoga, don't you? Is it any good? It's brilliant, actually. I started about six months ago. Changed my life, really. Before, I'd come home, collapse on the sofa, and just feel utterly drained. Now, even a short session helps me de-stress, clear my head. It’s amazing for both the body and the mind. You should give it a go. There’s a really good studio near you, I can send you the details. I might just do that. I feel like I'm constantly firefighting, and I desperately need some sort of grounding. Speaking of firefighting… how's Leo? Still the little tornado you described him as? He is, definitely. Full of energy. He's a whirlwind, but a lovely one. You know, being a single parent is…hard. Really hard. But also, the most rewarding thing I've ever done. I wouldn’t trade it for anything. I can only imagine. It takes such strength. Remember when we were younger, dreaming about partners, weddings, the whole nine yards? Life throws you some curveballs, doesn’t it? I’m still single, you know. Although, I wouldn’t put it past my mother to start aggressively matchmaking me at Christmas again. Oh, I’m sure she will. Listen, I wanted to ask you something… it’s a bit silly, really. I'm trying to write a book. A book! Seriously? That's fantastic! What's it about? It's… well, it’s semi-autobiographical. About my IVF journey, and then becoming a single mum. It's been surprisingly therapeutic, dredging all that up. The IVF was such a difficult time. It took five attempts, and the emotional toll… it’s something I don’t think a lot of people truly understand. And then, after all that, deciding to go it alone.

"Tell me about it. I teach French, and you’d think it’d be all beautiful grammar and romantic poetry, but no. It’s battling parents who insist their child  definitely  understands the subjunctive mood even though they’ve only been exposed to it twice. They all want their little ones to be accelerated, you know?" "Accelerated! That’s a good word for it. Used to be, it was all about a decent education, a bit of manners, and not getting into trouble. Now it's all about the rankings and the Oxbridge obsession. Blimey. Remember when we were at university, Anya? Didn't even  think  about Oxbridge. Just wanted to pass!" "Exactly! It’s a completely different landscape. It puts so much pressure on the kids, too. I had a little boy in Year 7 burst into tears the other day because he got a B+ on a maths test. A B+! He said his parents were going to be ‘disappointed’." "Disappointed! Lord love us. Kids these days. I tell you what, though, it wasn't all roses back then either. I remember my sister, Margaret, absolutely desperate to get into a good grammar school. Nearly drove our mother mad with the worry. She got in, of course, bright as a button she was. Became a pharmacist, you know." "That’s wonderful. My mum worked in Boots for years. Always said it was a steady job, but not terribly exciting. Do you see your sister much?" "Not as much as I'd like. Lives up in Manchester now, with her family. Three grandkids. I send her cards, she sends me biscuits. The usual. You got family nearby, Anya?" “My parents still live in Hitchin. It’s a bit of a trek, but I try to get home every few weeks. My brother’s out in Australia, which is a bit more complicated. He’s got two kids, so video calls are a must.” “Australia! Fancy that. Always wanted to go, you know. Never had the opportunity, though. Retirement's a funny thing. You think you'll be bursting with energy to do everything you've ever dreamt of, and… well, my knees aren't what they used to be.” ”Bad arthritis. Doctor wants me on something a bit stronger than paracetamol now. Dread the thought.” "Oh, that's awful. My grandma had terrible arthritis too. It’s just relentlessly painful, isn't it?

Honestly, I still can’t believe you guys managed to burn toast  twice  this morning. You’d think grown adults, engineers no less, would know how to operate a toaster. Aye, well, it were a tricky toaster, weren't it? New electrics, fiddly settings. And I were trying to get bacon crispy enough for you, lass! You’re always moaning it’s too soft. Crispy bacon and charcoal toast. A well-balanced breakfast. You're becoming quite the chef, Liam. A culinary genius, more like. I think we should be entering him into a competition. "Most Efficient Toast-Deconstruction." Right. Anyway, what's with all the indie music blaring? Sounds like something from a vintage record shop. Nah, it's The Harlequins. Proper good lads. Got a gig in Leeds next month, you should come. The Harlequins? Never heard of 'em. What's their sound like? They're kind of... post-punk revival, I guess? Think early Joy Division crossed with a bit of Interpol. It’s actually quite good, surprisingly. I've been listening to them a lot lately. Yes, I’ve checked them out. Solid. Though, a bit… earnest, perhaps? I prefer something a little more… polished. Earnest is good! It’s proper music, not all that autotuned rubbish you lot listen to. Oh, I wouldn't say  all  autotuned rubbish. There’s some genuinely impressive electronic music out there. But yes, I do gravitate towards a cleaner production sound. You wouldn't be into anything like Gorillaz, would you, Liam? Gorillaz? Don’t reckon so. Sound a bit… chaotic. I like meself a good guitar riff, somethin' you can feel in your bones. Speaking of feeling things… Anyone seen anything good at the cinema recently? I’m desperate for a night out. "Annihilation" is still on a few screens. Absolutely brilliant. Visually stunning and genuinely unsettling. Ooh, I’ve heard good things about that one. Sci-fi's not usually my thing, but I'm willing to give it a go. I saw 'Bohemian Rhapsody' last week. Surprisingly enjoyable. Freddie Mercury was captivating, obviously. The Queen stuff is just iconic. Bit cheesy, innit? All that singing and waving around. Cheesy, perhaps, but undeniably brilliant. And the portrayal of their recording sessions was remarkably insightful. The dedication... incredible. I think I'd prefer  Annihilation . Space blobs are always more exciting than dodgy wigs. Fair point. So, movie night it is then?

It makes all the difference. It does. You should put that in a jar and sell it, honestly. The whole family loves it. Yeah, even Finn likes it. He just smears it all over his face. Speaking of Finn, he seemed restless earlier. Thinking of a swim tomorrow?

Right, that was brilliant! Honestly, you two ate more than I thought possible. Little tornadoes, you are. Pizza good! More pizza? I want another slice! Pleeease, Mummy? Another one? You’ll be bouncing off the walls! Alright, alright, just one more small slice for you both. But then, absolutely no more until dinner. Deal? Speaker_2 & 3: Deal! Good. So, we were talking about… well, about a lot of things, weren't we? We went from pizza to handstands to party clothes, all in about ten minutes. Honestly, sometimes I feel like I’m conducting a particularly chaotic orchestra. I showed you my handstand! I was almost doing it! You were! You were wonderfully wobbly. You almost touched the ceiling! We should practice more. It’s good for your core strength too. You know, like Nessie’s! Nessie? Loch Ness monster? Yes! Remember we were reading about her this morning? A giant, mysterious creature living in a Scottish loch. Isn’t it amazing? Is she really big? Bigger than a bus? Probably bigger than a whole school bus! Maybe even bigger than our house! Imagine having a monster living in a lake nearby. What do you think she likes to eat? Fish! She eats lots of fish! Maybe she eats…pizza! Well, that would be convenient for her, wouldn’t it? Though I doubt there are many pizza delivery services in Loch Ness. Now, about communicating with Nessie... Do you reckon she understands us? Maybe she understands feelings! Like happy and sad. That’s a lovely thought. Perhaps she can feel our happy thoughts reaching her all the way from here. It's like when you're really concentrating on something and you just  know  it's right, even if you can't quite explain it. It's a sort of feeling-communication, isn't it? Like when I know you're hiding the biscuits! Oh, do you now? How on earth did you deduce  that ? Because you're smiling when you say it! And you’re looking at the biscuit tin! You're a very clever detective, you are! Right, moving swiftly on. Back to Nessie. If we  could  communicate with her, what would you ask her? I’d ask her name! Is her name Nessie? That’s a very good question! Maybe Nessie is just a nickname. Perhaps her real name is something wonderfully long and Scottish. Like… Fiona Morag Elizabeth!

“Elodie, love, you’re making me work up an appetite all over again! I had a lovely sea bass, but these croquettes... you're selling it hard, lass.” "Croquettes, eh? Sounds alright. I had the pizza. Standard.” "Standard pizza in Istria? That's a crime! You should have tried the truffle pasta, Liam. This region is renowned for its truffles.” “Liam’s still in his 'teenager refusing good food' phase, Dad. He’ll come around eventually. Anyway, about Istria... did you see those wild boar roaming near Pula yesterday? Absolutely massive!” “Aye, I did! Reminded me of our walks around Pike’s Lane back in the day, just without the Mediterranean sun. Speaking of which, this weather's been glorious, hasn’t it? Beats a Bolton drizzle any day.” “It certainly has. Though I’m noticing a slight shift. Feels like autumn's trying to nudge its way in. Thinking about a trip to Rovinj tomorrow? The old town is picture postcard perfect, and I fancy getting some shots for my Instagram.” "Ooh, that sounds lovely. Can we swim in the pool first though? I spent ages lounging by it this afternoon, finally finished that book I’ve been trying to get through. It was about Steve Jobs, proper fascinating. All about how they innovated – reminds me a bit of that food technology stuff we're doing at school, you know, lab-grown meat and all that." "Lab-grown meat? That's mental. Like, science gone mad. I’d rather have a proper burger.” “Don’t you start, Liam! There's no harm in exploring new technologies. Imagine, curing world hunger with lab-grown protein! It's something to think about. Though, speaking of things to think about, did you hear anything more about that Ebola outbreak in Africa on the news?" “Briefly. They seem to be containing it. More pressing for me are the immigration officers at the airport on the way here. Absolutely relentless with their forms and questions. Reminded me of dealing with overly bureaucratic clients. Everything must be triple-checked, signed in triplicate… It’s exhausting." “Tell me about it! They asked me about my grandad’s address – like, seriously? What does that have to do with anything? It’s giving me the 'ick'. But then, thinking about travel… I was reading about Japan. I’d love to go there, especially Kyoto, all those beautiful temples.” "Japan?

PPI, eh? Still going on, is it? Never thought I’d see the back of it, to be honest. Should’ve just ignored it all, like I usually do. These letters…get everywhere, don’t they? Absolutely, Arthur. They’re relentless. Though, David did say that sometimes you can get a decent payout. Remember that article in "Good Housekeeping"? About the woman who got… what was it… five thousand pounds back? "Good Housekeeping"? Maureen, you're reading  Good Housekeeping ? I thought you were more of an "Architectural Digest" type. Don't be silly, David. I like a bit of everything. It had a lovely spread on rose gardening as well, actually. Reminded me of your mother’s garden, didn’t it, Charles? All those rambling climbers… Yes, very fond memories. Though, mum was always muttering about the aphids. Speaking of gardens, how are those new runner bean seeds doing, Arthur? You said you’d ordered some of those extra-long ones. Oh, they're coming along nicely! Put 'em in last week. Proper little fellas, pushing their way through. Hope they get as big as I remember. Used to grow 'em as a boy, you know. Mountains of beans! Made a right mess of the compost heap, we did. And we’ll need some for the party, won’t we? You promised to make that lovely bean salad. Wouldn't miss it for the world. Though, I do get a bit tired these days, standing about in the kitchen… We'll help, Arthur. Plenty of hands. And speaking of the party, have you sorted out the music? We need something a bit more lively than your usual hymns. Hymns are perfectly respectable! Wonderful harmonies. Used to love singing in the Abbey choir, when I was a young man. Proper choir, that was. Not like some of the racket you hear these days. You always say that, Arthur. But I agree, the Abbey choir was something special. You had a beautiful tenor voice, you know. He still does, Charles! Though he’ll deny it. Come on, Arthur, sing us a little something. Don't be daft, Maureen. My voice ain’t what it used to be. Besides, I nearly had a fright the other day, driving up to the shops… What happened? Had a bit of a wobble, I did. Didn't see a car pulling out. Gave me a proper jolt.

Honestly, love, another day, another deluge of petty squabbles. You wouldn't believe the things people argue about these days. A parking space, a misplaced bin… it's exhausting. I can imagine! It must be draining dealing with that all day. It’s certainly a far cry from trying to teach French verbs to teenagers. Though,  they  can be pretty draining too, in their own way. Teenagers, eh? At least they're learning something, aren't they? This court… it's often just reinforcing bad habits. I sometimes wonder if we're actually doing any good. I understand that feeling. There's a frustration, isn’t there, when you see people repeatedly making the same mistakes, and you wish you could just… explain things more clearly. Like, preventative education, you know? Exactly! My granddaughter, Maisie, she's doing a citizenship course at school. Good on them for teaching that, really. Makes you think, shouldn’t they be doing more of this stuff earlier on? Before people end up in front of a magistrate. Absolutely. Life skills, really. And financial literacy. I swear, half the problems we see stem from money worries. Speaking of which, have you been watching petrol prices lately? They’re ridiculous! Don’t even  start  me on petrol. I drive in from Tamworth, you know. It’s not a short hop. Used to be I could manage on a twenty pound note, now? Forget about it. They should have invested more in public transport. A decent bus service would be a godsend. I agree completely. The trains around here are also patchy, and so expensive. Makes you think about just… staying put, doesn't it? I've been toying with the idea of a holiday, but the cost of flights is just putting me off. Oh, I know that feeling. I used to love going back up to Scotland, Insch is my birthplace, you see. But the flights... and the accommodation... it’s all become so prohibitive. Although, my sister Elsie went last year. Said the scenery was still as stunning as ever. Scotland’s always been on my list. The landscapes look incredible. I read an article the other day about how climate change is impacting the Highlands, though. Glacier melt and all that – it’s worrying. Aye, it is. The weather's been so strange lately, hasn't it? Hot summers, wet winters… not like when I was a girl.

…and so, if you finish your porridge, we can look for ladybirds in the garden, yes? It's such a lovely day. Makes you feel happy, doesn't it? Ladybirds! Red ones? Red ones, yes! With little spots. They're very lucky, you know. They bring good things. Like happiness! Happy’s like… like a bouncy ball! Boing, boing, boing! That’s a brilliant way to describe it, darling. Happy  is  a bit like a bouncy ball – all full of energy and fun! Do you know what rhymes with happy? …Puppy! Absolutely! Puppy! That’s a super one. What else? Think, think! Nappy! Oh, you little rascal! Yes, nappy rhymes too! Clever boy. But let's try and think of something a bit… less about needing changing! Daddy! That’s a very good one! Daddy rhymes with happy. Now, let's talk about something a bit different. Imagine you had a giant bag… a  really  giant bag… full of money. What would you buy? A pony! And a castle! A pink castle! With a slide! A digger! A big, yellow digger that can dig  really  deep! And a robot to help me dig! A pink castle and a digger and a robot! That’s quite a shopping list. But even with all that money, would it make you truly happy? Mmm… maybe. But I’d still want ladybirds. I'd want lots of biscuits. And to build a really,  really  tall tower! See? Happiness is more than just having lots of toys, or a castle, or even biscuits. It's about things like ladybirds, and building towers, and… well, it's about being together, isn’t it? I love ladybirds with you! Me too! And building with you! Towers are better with you! That's the best thing of all, isn't it? More valuable than all the money in the world. It’s about laughter and games and silly rhymes… and feeling safe and loved. That's what makes you happy. He’s happy when he builds! And you’re happy when you read us stories! I am. You both make me incredibly happy. You know what rhymes with happy, happy? Speaker_2 & Snappy! You're such clever little monkeys! Now, who wants to go and find those lucky ladybirds? And perhaps, just perhaps, we’ll find a tiny little treasure, too. A clover, maybe? Four leaves instead of three! That's really lucky, you know.

Honestly, Mr. Davies was droning on about quadratic equations  again . Like, when are we ever going to need to solve for 'x' in the real world? Probably when we’re inventing something, Liam. You know, need to calculate trajectories or something. Inventing? You and your inventing! You’re still obsessed with that self-watering plant pot thing, aren’t you? It’s got potential! I’ve been thinking about adding a solar panel to power the pump. Imagine, a completely self-sufficient little ecosystem. Patent-worthy, I reckon. Patent-worthy? You’re dreaming, Finn. My cousin’s mate tried to patent a special kind of bottle opener – shaped like a shark. Didn't get anywhere. It’s a nightmare, apparently. All those forms and lawyers… But that's different. A shark bottle opener is just a gimmick. This is a genuine solution to a problem – saving water and simplifying gardening. Think about the environmental impact! Okay, okay, Mr. Eco-Warrior. Still seems like a lot of effort for a glorified plant pot. What about something actually useful? Like... teleportation? Teleportation? Seriously? That’s a bit ambitious, even for me. Although, if we could crack that... think of the implications! No more traffic jams, instant travel... Exactly! And the investment opportunities! Imagine the stock market when teleportation becomes a reality. Everyone would be snapping up shares in the company that made it. It's crazy to think. My dad was talking about China the other day, how their tech industry is exploding. They’re investing huge amounts in AI and robotics. It's kind of scary, actually. Scary how? Scary in terms of global power, I guess. They’re developing technology at an insane pace. Think about it - they could be the ones to invent teleportation first! Or, even worse, automate  everything . What happens to all the jobs? That’s the thing, isn't it? My mum says it’s all about adapting. Learn new skills, be prepared to change careers multiple times. She's trying to invest in some renewable energy companies – reckons that’s a good bet. Renewable energy’s definitely a smart move. It's got to be, right? Fossil fuels aren’t going to last forever. My grandma’s always going on about the importance of investing responsibly. She's got a few shares in a company that builds wind turbines. My mum’s skeptical about investment in general.

Honestly, Sarah, this is exactly what I needed. Just…peace. And sunshine. And ridiculously good Bulgarian red wine. Sutton Coldfield in February just doesn’t compare, does it? Absolutely not, Claire. Sutton Coldfield in February is grey, damp, and filled with the mournful sounds of people scraping ice off their car windows. This… this is vibrant. Did you see the view from the top of the mountain today? Breathtaking. Though, I must say, my legs are screaming. You are being far too modest. You were absolutely  flying  down that black run! I’m sticking to the blues, thank you very much. My knees aren’t what they used to be. Though, I did manage to avoid falling over, which is always a win. Progress! Remember last time we went skiing, in France? You spent more time on your bottom than on your feet. Don't remind me. That was a humbling experience. I think I single-handedly kept the ski patrol in business that week. Seriously though, how’s Mum doing? She seemed a bit under the weather when we spoke last week. She’s… fine. As fine as she can be, I suppose. She’s being her usual self, complaining about the price of everything and reminding me to eat my vegetables. I told her I was having a mountain of salad, so that should keep her happy for a while. She misses you, though. She keeps asking if you’re working too hard. I am, a bit. Proofreading’s been particularly frantic lately. So many adverts needing last-minute tweaks. It pays the bills, though, and I enjoy it, mostly. It’s just… tiring. I should really delegate more. You need to, Claire. You always take on too much. You wouldn’t let a freelancer touch your work, though, would you? You’re too much of a control freak. Guilty as charged. I just like things done  right . But seriously, maybe I will look into getting someone part-time. It would free up some time to actually, you know,  enjoy  these holidays. Speaking of which, have you decided about tomorrow? We could try that long blue run towards the other side of the mountain? I'm tempted. I did fancy a bit more of a challenge. But… I think I’ll stick with something a bit less strenuous. My thighs are protesting violently. I was thinking we could take the gondola up and just enjoy the views.

Honestly, Harold, this is the third one this week. They’re snapping like dry spaghetti. What are we going to  do ? It’s putting people off coming back to our little racket repair service. Well, Penelope, we’ve established that the original string isn’t up to the job. It’s far too thin for the tension we’re putting on it. Remember Mrs. Higgins complaining about the vibrations? Yes, yes, I remember. But thicker string is more expensive. We're barely breaking even as it is, aren't we? And where are we going to  find  a suitable replacement? It needs to be strong, flexible… and not cost the earth. I was thinking… cable ties. Cable ties, Harold? You’re joking! People will think we’re mad. Badminton rackets, held together with plastic ties? Hear me out! We'd need some strong ones, naturally. The thicker, industrial kind. Not your garden variety. And we’d weave them through the existing string holes, crisscrossing them for support. It’s essentially a reinforcing matrix. A reinforcing matrix...sounds awfully technical for a badminton racket repair. But the cost... you’re right, it would be significantly cheaper. What about the dimensions? Can we get them long enough? And the weight… it won’t add too much, will it? Players are very sensitive about weight. We can get them long enough, definitely. And if we strategically position them, spreading the weight throughout the frame rather than concentrating it in one spot, it shouldn’t be noticeable. Think of a suspension bridge, Penelope – lots of cables, but the bridge itself feels sturdy. A suspension bridge! That's quite the comparison, Harold. And you’re suddenly an engineer? You know, using "fleet" the other day… I thought you were referring to a group of birds. Turns out you meant a  collection  of rackets! Guilty as charged. I’ve always mixed up my metaphors. It’s important to get a ‘fleet’ of rackets repaired, though, isn't it? Keeps the money coming in. Though, I must admit, thinking of the sheer number needed makes me slightly dizzy. Speaking of dizzy, look at this! I've completely messed up ANON's hair. I meant to just trim the earlobes, but… well, look at that stripe! It's like a bizarre zebra pattern. Clearly, Penelope, your focus was momentarily compromised by our discussion of cable ties and suspension bridges.

I’m still trying to wrap my head around this whole neo-expressionism thing, honestly. It feels… deliberately chaotic, doesn't it? Like someone spilled a box of crayons and decided that was profound. Well, dear, everything's chaotic in its own way, innit? Life’s a bit of a splatter, if you ask me. And art, it just reflects that. Don't get bogged down in labels, love. Look at the feeling it gives you. Does it move you? That's what really matters. Rothko… now, there’s a fella who knew a thing or two about feeling. Didn't need no fancy explanations. Just blocks of colour. Made you think, he did. Powerful stuff. Reminded me of the sunsets back ‘ome in Costessey. Big, proper skies. That’s precisely it, Dad. Rothko wasn't  about  something. It  was  something. An experience. Neo-expressionism, though, it often feels like it's trying too hard to be angry or edgy. Basquiat, for instance… undeniably important culturally, but I’m not always convinced by the technical skill. I was reading about Basquiat, actually. The sheer speed of his creation, the urgency… it's compelling. But the execution… it almost feels subconscious. Like he wasn’t consciously composing, but just letting it flow. Let it flow, that's good advice, isn't it? My little ones used to do that with finger painting. They’d just smear it all about, bright colours everywhere. And sometimes, you'd look at it and think, ‘Well, that’s rather lovely, isn't it?’ Not neat, mind you, not tidy at all. But full of life. There's a difference between joyful spontaneity and deliberate messiness, though, isn’t there? I think some neo-expressionists mistake the latter for the former. It's like they're actively trying  not  to be good painters, which is… perplexing. You young 'uns and your fancy words. When I were a lad, art were about things y’could understand. Landscapes, portraits… somethin’ you could recognise. Not splodges and scribbles. Though, I did like that Monet fella. Water lilies, eh? Now  that  were art. Peaceful. But Dad, isn’t that partly because you grew up in a different era, with different aesthetic expectations? Art has  always  evolved. Impressionism was radical in its time, too. It was seen as unfinished, sloppy. She’s right, Dad. Art reflects the society it's created in. The anxieties, the aspirations… the chaos.

Honestly, Chloe, I’m starting to think Zara actively  tries  to be irritating. Did you see her face when I pointed out the discrepancy in the patient notes? Like I’d personally insulted her mother. Zara, huh? Yeah, I’ve noticed. A bit much, isn’t she? Though, to be fair, being a mental health nurse sounds properly stressful. You're probably just picking up on her general… intensity. Intensity? That’s a generous word. It’s full-blown drama. And then she tries to play the victim! "Oh, I'm just so overworked and emotionally drained." Yeah, well, so are we all, love. Just not actively stirring the pot. It's exhausting. Tell me about it. I had a mini meltdown with Gemma at the office today. Apparently, sending an email at 7pm isn’t "standard practice" even though the deadline was technically midnight. Honestly, these corporate rules are ridiculous. Reminds me of that weird grammar thing I was reading – apparently, the word "literally" is now used to mean figuratively. It’s driving me mad! Don’t even get me started. The English language is imploding, I swear. They’re going to teach kids "literally means not literally" in school soon. It’s a linguistic tragedy! Anyway, back to Zara… Did you finish cleaning your room yet? Nope. Procrastinating, obviously. It's a skill, honestly. It's an art form. I’ve got a rather impressive collection of things I  should  be doing. Laundry mountain, dust bunnies the size of small rodents… you know the drill. You are unbelievable. We’re having people over on Saturday, Chloe! It can’t just be a chaotic mess of discarded clothes and empty pizza boxes. I’m not rescuing you again. Rescuing? You secretly enjoy rescuing. You get a little thrill out of folding my socks. Don't be absurd. It’s just…basic hygiene. Look, could you at least do the dishes? They're breeding. I swear I saw a new species of mould growing on that pasta pot. Fine, fine. But you owe me. Big time. Then, to compensate for the mental drain of being around Zara, we’re ordering takeaway and watching trashy TV. Deal? Deal. But if I find one more sock on the floor abandoned on Saturday, you're scrubbing the bathroom. And speaking of trashy TV, did you see that weird documentary about the pigeon racing community?

Honestly, another day, another avalanche of emails. Mr. Davies really needs to learn to delegate better. It’s exhausting being his right hand, you know? Sounds familiar. My client, Henderson & Sons, are obsessed with micro-managing every single pixel on their new website. Drives me mad. You’d think after twenty years in this business, people would trust my judgment. Twenty years! You’re practically a dinosaur in the tech world. Though, you always were clever, weren’t you? Even at school. Remember that time you built that radio from scratch? Ancient history. Not clever, just… practical. Common sense, really. I suppose that's what separates a lot of people. Folks with intelligence, but no common sense. They overthink everything. Absolutely. It's a shame, isn't it? There's this tendency to equate intelligence with knowing obscure facts, but the genuinely smart people are the ones who can figure things out, adapt, you know? Like… knowing when to duck when a storm’s coming. Precisely. And knowing when to enjoy a nice pint after a stressful day. Speaking of which, want one? I’ve got a decent pale ale in. Tempting. Very tempting. But I really shouldn't. I’m trying to cut down. Though... Just a small one. It was a particularly awful afternoon. Mr. Davies spent twenty minutes complaining about the font size on a memo. Twenty minutes! Only you could be subjected to that level of bureaucracy. You know, Sarah was asking me the other day about that article she read on, what was it, intersectional feminism? Something about how Western feminist ideals don't always translate well to other cultures. Oh, yeah, I saw something similar. It's a really important point, isn't it? Like, expecting women in, say, rural India, to prioritize the same things as women in London is just… ridiculous. Their struggles are different, their priorities are different. Exactly. She was arguing that imposing a Western feminist framework can be patronising and even damaging. It's not as simple as just saying "everyone should be equal." The context matters. It made me think about Mum and Dad, really. They’d never have considered themselves feminists, but they gave me and my sister so much independence. They just… did it. Without the labels. My Nan was like that. Strong as an ox, stubbornly independent. Wouldn't have called herself a feminist, but she worked incredibly hard her whole life, mostly to keep her family afloat.

Right, well, that was quite the day, wasn’t it? Absolute chaos, but a good kind of chaos. Honestly, I think the kids are finally properly worn out. Farm! Tractor! Piggy! Oink, oink! Sheep! Baaa! And... and the bouncy castle was the BEST! It certainly was, wasn't it, darling? You two were bouncing non-stop. Poppy, you nearly bounced into the duck pond! Honestly, I was panicking for a minute. Leo, you were glued to the tractor display. Not moving an inch! I saw a fluffy sheep! And it ate grass! The man let me sit in the tractor! A real one! With a big seat! He did, bless him. He was lovely. Said you were a natural farmer. Though, I think the enthusiasm outweighed the actual knowledge! How was school today, both of you? Mrs. Peterson said Poppy was a little… distracted. Distracted? I was learning about letters! With Miss Emily! "A" is for apple! That’s right, love. But Mrs. Peterson said you kept wandering off to look at the window. There was a bird! A blue one! Leo didn't get into any trouble! I helped Thomas with his sums! That's wonderful, Leo! That's a very kind thing to do. See, Poppy? Leo's being helpful. You could try being helpful too! But the bird was shiny! Shiny birds are lovely, darling, but you need to concentrate when you're learning. It’s important. We talked about it, remember? Focus, then bird watching. Right? Can we watch Dinosaur Train now? Please? Please? Alright, alright. Dinosaur Train it is. But only one episode. We need to get you both showered and into your pyjamas. It was a long day, even for me. I'm absolutely aching. Shower! Bubble bath! Can I have the dinosaur bath bomb? The green one! Yes, you can have the green one, sweetie. Now, did you have any favourites at the farm, apart from the bouncy castle and the shiny birds? The piglets! They were pink and muddy! I liked the cows! They were big! And they mooed really loud! They did! I thought I was going to lose my hearing at one point! Honestly, the noise was incredible. Maybe we should have brought earplugs! Though, it was lovely to see you both so happy. It’s been a bit… stressful lately, with school reports and everything. What's "stressful?" It just means things have been a little busy and a bit worrying sometimes.

Right, that’s tha sorted. Strong enough for us then, eh? Honestly, this British tea… it's the only thing that gets me through research proposals. They’re a right nightmare, aren't they? Absolutely. Though, I did make a bit of headway on mine earlier. Found a promising angle on the interaction of quantum entanglement and… well, you don’t want the details. It’ll put you to sleep faster than counting sheep. Aye, I reckon it would. Quantum entanglement? Sounds a bit complicated even for me. I’m still trying to get my head around the best colour scheme for this fairisle I’m knitting. It’s for me mam’s birthday, see? She's always wanted a proper Northumbrian fairisle. A fairisle? That's lovely! You're really getting into knitting, aren’t you? You mentioned last time you weren't sure if you’d stick with it. Nah, I’m hooked! It’s so relaxing, you know? So different from staring at data all day. Plus, it’s a proper skill. Me grandma used to knit these incredible things. Scarves longer than a car, jackets bright enough to blind ya… Proper works of art, they were. That's wonderful. Art, actually. Have you been to see that Hockney exhibition at the Fitzwilliam? I went last week. No, not yet! Been meaning to, though. Is it as good as everyone says? I saw summat about it online, looked proper vibrant. I’m a big fan of vibrant, especially when everything else feels a bit grey and drizzly. It's fantastic. Really captures the light, you know? He’s got this incredible way of making the ordinary look extraordinary. Reminds me a bit of Turner, actually. Turner, aye. Fancy. Speaking of things that are extraordinary, did you see the Olympics opening ceremony? Proper spectacle, that was. Freddie Mercury hologram! Mad! Absolutely mad! Brilliant, though. I thought the Queen’s cameo was genius. Honestly, nobody expected that. And the performances… wow. Aye, wow is right. Makes you feel proper proud to be British, doesn’t it? Even when we’re losing in, like, everything. But seriously, it's been a good bit of cheering up after all the doom and gloom about the economy. Definitely. A welcome distraction. So, how's the Easter planning going? Are you coming down for Easter Sunday? My mum's been hinting at a particularly ambitious chocolate cake this year.

Cor, this Tube’s packed tighter than sardines, innit? I swear, they cram more people on these trains than they did back in the war. And the smell... don't even get me started on the smell. It’s Sunday afternoon, Margaret. What do you expect? Everyone's flooding into the city. At least we managed to get a seat, eh? Though it  is  a bit close. Reminds me of the rush hour on the Northern line back in the day. Used to be unbearable. Unbearable is puttin' it mildly, Arthur. Back in me day, a body could breathe a bit! This new fancy stuff, though... this 'accessibility' they're on about. Makes it even worse. More people can squeeze in, see? But there’s no room to properly  move . Are you sure this is the right platform for the British Museum? I thought it was the next one. Nope, this is it. Platform 3. British Museum’s a short walk from here, about ten minutes. Remember what I said? We’re going there first. Need to see that Rosetta Stone before it vanishes in a puff of smoke and historical revisions. Historical revisions… that’s all the youngsters are on about these days. Always revising history. It’s just history, Arthur! Anyway, I’m proper knackered. This walkin's takin’ it out o' me. You remembered to get those mobility cards sorted last week, yeah? Of course I did, Margaret. Don’t you start worrying. They’re in my wallet, right here. Honestly, you’d think I was completely incompetent. And speaking of memories... remember that IMAX cinema down by the South Bank? The one with the massive screen? We went to see 'Contact' there. Extraordinary experience. Really felt like you were  in  space. 'Contact'! Oh, I loved that film! Jodie Foster was brilliant. It  was  a good experience, that IMAX. …and then, honestly, he just  stared  at me. Like I’d personally offended him by offering him a sourdough loaf. Said it was “too crusty.” Too crusty! It’s sourdough, Liam, that's the whole point! That would be amazing, Liam! Thank you! I’d really appreciate it. Just, like, clean, modern, welcoming... and definitely not floral. Avoid floral at all costs. No floral! Got it. Speaking of welcoming, I was thinking about a little getaway. I’m feeling burnt out with the baking, it’s just…constant. Where were you thinking of going? Margate. Remember we talked about it, ages ago? Just a few days by the sea, bit of fish and chips, breathe some salty air.

Speaker_1 exclaimed, waving her fork for emphasis. "Oisin's a rascal!" "Raspberries are good, though. I had some in my smoothie this morning." “They  are  lovely. It’s been a bit chaotic since Oisin decided he’s a gerbil whisperer. He’s been sneaking them bits of his dinner, you know. Bread crusts and… raspberries." "He’s got them spoiled rotten!

Honestly, Patricia, the price of everything at Tesco’s this week! It's scandalous. A punnet of strawberries? Nearly four quid! I swear, they’re having a laugh. I noticed, didn’t I? Seems a bit of a racket, doesn't it?

Honestly, this weaning business is a minefield, isn't it? I remember reading all these books, all these opinions… pure overwhelm. I felt like I was failing him every time he rejected a new puree. Remember to make sure he's sitting upright, and offer just tiny, tiny pieces. And don't panic, even if he does gag. It’s a natural reflex. Right, speaking of different ways… Sarah was asking yesterday if we could all get together next week. She’s got that new Italian place she’s been wanting to try. Oh, lovely! Tuesday? Apparently, they’re planning a big ramble along the coast, with a picnic. Sounds bracing. Mark’s Mum is determined his father will carry the picnic blanket. He's not thrilled. Classic! My dad would be the same. Alright, Wednesday BBQ it is with Sarah and the family.

Honestly, this is… restorative. London feels a million miles away. I forgot what proper quiet sounds like. Just the sheep, the wind… and your occasionally pointed commentary. Pointed commentary? I’m merely appreciating the subtle beauty, David. You’re the one who started complaining about the lack of decent coffee shops five minutes in. That’s a valid point! A decent flat white is a basic human right. Though, I will concede, these views  are  spectacular. This little rise… it’s really quite something, isn't it? For Norfolk. We're not exactly known for our dramatic topography, are we? Not like the Lake District, obviously. No, quite. It’s a gentle rise, not a hill in the traditional sense. More of a…pronounced hump, really. But yes, it offers a lovely panorama. Look at the way the light catches the thatched roofs of Little Brampton down there. Little Brampton… Is that the one they brag about having the oldest pub in the county? The Ploughshare or something? The Ploughman’s Arms, yes. And technically, “oldest” is a bit of a stretch. Their claim rests on the original building being a medieval hall, repurposed as a pub later. There's a fascinating article in the Norfolk Archaeology journal about it, if you’re interested. Oh, please no. Not a lecture while we’re supposed to be relaxing. I’ll stick to appreciating the aesthetic, thank you very much. Though, I would be interested in a pint at that pub later. Do they do decent food as well? I believe so. Traditional pub fare, nothing fancy. It’s more about the atmosphere. And the local beer, of course. You know, the way these villages cling to the landscape… it’s utterly charming. So resistant to change. Resistant is putting it mildly. My aunt lives in Wicken Green, you know. Trying to get them to install a village-wide broadband connection has been an exercise in futility. They're terrified it’ll “attract the wrong sort.” That’s Norfolk for you. A beautiful, stubbornly traditional county. It’s what draws me back, I think. Even though I grumble about the lack of decent museums sometimes. See? Pointed commentary! You can't help yourself. Though, I get it. It's not about  wanting  things, is it? It’s about preserving what’s already here. The way the fields slope down to the river… the way the hedgerows are dense with wildflowers… It’s a very particular kind of beauty.

Honestly, I still can’t believe how many cyclists there were on that road. It was like a peloton had decided to hold a race through rush hour. Aye, well, they’ve got a right to be there, haven't they? Roads are for everyone. Though I did nearly clip one earlier; he was weaving all over the place. Proper dodgy. Dodgy is an understatement. One of them actually  slowed  as I was trying to overtake. Do they not teach road awareness? I've got a degree in engineering, you know. Basic physics dictates… Oh, here we go. The lecture. Just because you’ve got a fancy postgraduate degree doesn't mean you know everything about cyclist behaviour, Finn. Some of 'em are just tryin' to get their exercise in. I’m not saying I know everything, Maisie, just applying logic! It’s just… frustrating. It slows everything down. Speaking of frustrating, how's sorting out the corpus going? Still wrestling with ambiguous pronouns? Don’t even  start  on the pronouns. It’s endless. And the slang! Trying to get the AI to understand “reeet”? Nearly broke the system. Honestly, some of the phrases people use… it’s like a whole different language. At least it's challenging, keepin' me on my toes. It's a far cry from what I thought I’d be doing after uni, eh? Definitely. I remember you saying you wanted to be a journalist, didn’t you? Traveling the world, writing captivating stories… Aye, well, the world can wait. At least I’m doin’ something useful. And the pay’s alright. Better than deliverin’ pizzas, that’s for sure. Did you hear back from Sarah about that promotion at all? Last I heard she was interviewing for the senior project management role. I did! Just spoke to her actually. She got it! Apparently, they were really impressed with the Breckenridge bridge project. She's over the moon. Properly deserves it, she’s worked incredibly hard. Champion! That’s brilliant news! She'll be earning proper money now, then. She always was clever, that lass. Remember when we were kids and she built that working model of the Tyne Bridge out of Lego? Absolutely bonkers. I do! You tried to recreate the Angel of the North with marshmallows, if I recall correctly. That went spectacularly badly. It did, didn't it? Marshmallows aren't exactly structurally sound.

“Right, that’s officially the most sunshine I’ve seen in weeks. Feels… restorative, doesn't it? Though I’m starting to regret those new boots. Blisters already, I think.” "Serves you right for prioritising style over practicality, darling. Honestly, you'd think a lecturer would have better sense. They look lovely though, I’ll grant you that. And yes, restorative is exactly the word. My brain feels like it’s been wading through mud for the last month with the Peterson paper. Just… overwhelming.” "Peterson? Still battling with that post-structuralist hogwash? Honestly, sometimes I think you actively  seek  out the impenetrable. Have you considered just… abandoning it?” "Abandoning it? Absolutely not! It’s crucial for my research on linguistic shifts in post-colonial literature. Think, the way Creole languages have absorbed and adapted colonial terminology… it’s fascinating! But he's so dense. He uses a sentence structure that requires a degree in applied logic to decipher. Remember that lecture last year where half the students walked out?" "Oh, I remember. Sounded like a mass exodus. Though, to be fair, you weren’t exactly selling it. You looked like you were wrestling a particularly stubborn badger. What about that new economic model Professor Davies was talking about, the one with the focus on localised cash crops and sustainable farming? Might be a more enjoyable intellectual pursuit." "Davies? Interesting, but it’s less directly relevant. It's tempting, though. The Norfolk landscape is perfect for it, isn't it? Imagine, entire communities built around growing heritage varieties of barley or flax. Self-sufficiency, local markets… it addresses a lot of global instability, doesn’t it?" She bends down, examining a wildflower. "Look at this. A common cornflower. They used to be everywhere, you know. Now you’re lucky to see a handful.” "It’s a tragedy, isn’t it? All this monoculture. Maximising yield at the expense of everything else. Reminds me of the Premier League frankly. All about the money, the spectacle, and utterly devoid of any real artistic merit. Speaking of which, did you catch the Chelsea game on Saturday?" “Don’t even start. It was a disaster. They’re so reliant on that one striker. No creativity, no tactical flexibility. Just… hoofing it upfield. It's predictable, and ultimately boring. Unlike analysing the subtle nuances of Derrida, of course." She winks. "You’re impossible. Always finding a metaphor for football in literary theory.

Right, so, parking at Wimbledon is still utter chaos. I managed to snag a spot three blocks away, blessedly, but getting back after match point… well, that’s another story. …and honestly, the way Rebekah Vardy's legal team handled things! It was just… chaotic. Didn't stand a chance against Coleen's meticulous planning, did she? Well, dear, I can't say I follow all that celebrity fuss, can I? It all seems a bit much to me. All that money spent arguing over social media. Seems a bit silly, don't it? Honestly, Chloe, I'm just…stuck. Completely and utterly stuck. Stuck how, Liv? Still stressing about that promotion at Apex? I thought you were making good headway. I  was . I really was. Well, he sounds like he’s giving you good advice. Positioning is key, isn’t it? Remember what your grandad used to say about anticipating the play… My rugby coach says the same! Anticipation is everything. Got a proper thrashing the other day, though. Our scrum was rubbish. Oh, that’s a shame, Tom. Don’t let it get you down, though. These things happen. We’ll get you practicing your scrumming this weekend, shall we? Maybe we can find a park with some space. I might be able to sneak away for an hour on Saturday. It’d be good for them both to get some exercise. Speaking of which, I need to look into booking those tickets for the Korea vs. Germany match. It's in Seoul in November. Seriously? You’re still planning that trip? It’s going to be freezing! It'll be a little nippy, yes. But it's the World Cup qualifying match! I have to see it. I was thinking Sarah and the kids could come with us. It would be an adventure for Jamie and Tom. Seoul? Seriously?! Like,  Korea  Korea? Massive! Can we go to a K-Pop concert? Yeah! And a waterpark! Do they have huge waterparks in Korea? Hold your horses, you two! It’s still a maybe. Your dad needs to actually book the tickets and sort out visas. And it's a long way to go, especially with school.

Honestly, I think I've permanently ingrained the smell of pine into my nostrils. It's… a lot. A  lot  of pine. You say that like you weren't practically squealing with excitement when we first saw those giant trees. Remember? You kept calling them ‘nature's skyscrapers’ and wanting to stop every five minutes to take a picture. Well, they  are  spectacular! It’s just… sustained exposure really changes things. It felt different being amongst them, you know? This constant, concentrated pine scent is… overwhelming. And are we  sure  this is the scenic route? I feel like we’ve been driving through a green tunnel for three hours. It is the scenic route! And it’s beautiful. I deliberately booked this drive. You wanted to experience California, didn't you? This is California. Untouched wilderness. Think of the Instagram likes! Instagram likes won’t cure my pine-induced headache, I'm afraid. Did you hear from Aunt Carol lately? She seemed a bit down when we last spoke. Actually, yes! I spoke to her just last week. She’s… well, still going on about the garden slugs, of course. But she did say the new puppy, Winston, is really bringing some light into the house. Apparently, he tries to steal her slippers. Winston, eh? A proper name for a proper puppy. She deserves some joy. I feel bad we haven’t been able to visit. Remember when she tried to teach me how to make proper Victoria sponge? I completely ruined it. The meringue was like concrete. Oh, goodness, yes! You tried to whip it with a fork! She was so patient, though. She just calmly took it away and started again. She’s always been like that - unflappable, even when faced with culinary disasters. She is, isn’t she? I should really call her. I keep meaning to. It’s just… life gets so busy. And frankly, constant updates on slug infestations aren’t exactly a priority when you’re trekking through Californian forests. Speaking of busy, how's the editing work going? You seemed a little stressed about that museum catalogue before we left. It’s… progressing. The museum was initially thrilled with the translations, which is good, but now they've decided they want everything re-worded to be “more accessible” for a wider audience. Apparently, referencing 18th-century Parisian salons is “too niche.” Oh, the  nerve !

These Chicken Kievs are brilliant, Dad! Honestly, better than Mum's. No offence, Mum. Oh, right you are, aren’t you? Suddenly you're a culinary expert. Your mum spends ages making them! And they’re proper, homemade Kievs, not that… that processed nonsense you get in the supermarket. Now, now, ladies. Let's not start a Kiev war at the dinner table. He’s just being a lad. And they  are  good, Sarah. I've got to give you that. The garlic butter is perfectly balanced. See! Dad agrees! And Granny would love them. Should we take some when we go to see her next week? Perhaps. Though she mainly lives on digestive biscuits and tea, doesn’t she? Remember last time? She ate half a packet and said, “Lovely, dear, but I could do with a bit more.” She’s a character, our Granny. I'm looking forward to seeing her too. How’s your headache, Sarah? You seemed a bit out of sorts earlier. It’s easing up, thankfully. Just one of those things, isn’t it? Toddler life, practically a guarantee of headaches. Little Leo’s been a whirlwind today. Threw his mashed potatoes at the dog. Again. Leo's a legend! He tried to steal my Lego earlier. I had to wrestle it back. Wrestling Lego, eh? Sounds like a lively afternoon then. Did you catch any of that rugby match today, Finn? The Ireland game? Yeah, Dad! It was mental! That try in the second half was… wow. Best game I’ve seen in ages. Though, I thought the ref was a bit dodgy. Definitely a Wallie. A what, now? You know, Mum! A Wallie! A rubbish ref. Someone who's clearly biased. Ah, bringing the Northern Irish terminology to Bristol, are you? Good man. It's no good to call them names, though, Finn. Just say they made some questionable decisions. He’s learning the language of frustration, dear. Speaking of frustration, I need to sort out some photos for Granny. I was thinking of putting them on Flickr, but I'm not sure it's the safest. Do you think Dropbox would be better, Liam? Dropbox is probably a safer bet, love. More secure, better control over who can access them. I can set it up for you tonight if you like. Just send me the folder. And, Sarah, don't send  too  many pictures of Leo throwing food.

Honestly, David, you won’t  believe  what I managed to snag on eBay this afternoon. Let me guess. Another set of floral china? Your collection is threatening to take over the dining room, love. It’s a bit more special than just ‘floral’ this time. It’s Shelley, darling. Shelley! A quartet, all matching, with this tiny little violet design and gilt edging. Practically pristine. I got them for a song, too. Fifty quid, including postage. Fifty quid? For Shelley? You’ve got a good eye, then. My aunt Elsie used to collect Shelley. She'd have fainted at that price. Though, knowing Elsie, she’d probably have accused you of robbing the poor seller. Exactly! Elsie would have had something to say. Right, are you nearly done with those carrots? I’m thinking buckwheat bread with a simple mushroom sauce tonight. Sound alright? Buckwheat bread? You’re getting adventurous. I thought we were settled on sourdough. I know, but I saw a recipe – proper hearty, you know? And it felt…right. Different. Besides, we need to use up that buckwheat flour I bought for Agnes. Remember, she was practically begging me for some at the market last week. Ah, the market. That’s another thing - are we going this weekend? The apple stall has been looking promising. Definitely! I promised Agnes I’d bring her back some of the spiced apple chutney they do. Though honestly, the last time I went I spent more time chatting to Mrs. Peterson about her prize-winning dahlias than actually buying anything! You and Mrs. Peterson. A match made in horticultural heaven. Speaking of which, how’s your herb garden doing? You were saying the rosemary wasn't happy. It’s…recovered. Sort of. I think moving it slightly helped. But I'm still worried. Anyway, back to the market. We should also check out that new cheesemonger. Apparently, he does a phenomenal Lincolnshire Poacher. Excellent. Food is always a good reason to brave the crowds. More importantly, have you heard anything new about Mark's leaving do? He was awfully quiet about it. Oh, yes! I was chatting to Sarah in accounts, and apparently it’s at The Old Mill on Friday. They're doing a buffet and a DJ. She says it’s going to be quite the affair. The Old Mill? That’s a bit fancy for Mark. He usually prefers a quiet pint.

Speaker_2 trailed off, swirling the remaining wine in her glass. The Parisian bistro hummed around them, oblivious to the clandestine discussion. “Layering? Sounds dead complicated, honestly. Like, I can barely work out my student loan statement, never mind international finance.” She chuckled nervously. "You're actually doing this, then, Liv? Properly?” "It's necessary, El. To protect…assets. And yes, properly. It’s a complex business, but incredibly rewarding. It’s vital to have the right contacts, the right advisors. Think of it as a very intricate game of chess, El. One wrong move and..." she let the sentence hang, a subtle warning in her tone. “Right, well, sounds a bit risky, doesn’t it? Wouldn’t want any of those French police sniffing around, would we?” He glanced around the bistro, then lowered his voice. “Mark, honestly. You’d think you were discussing selling dodgy cigarettes down the market, not legitimate international finance. Liv knows what she’s doing. She’s got a head for this sort of thing. Better than any of us, frankly.” “But what if you get caught? What about the kids, Liv? Little Maisie and Finn... They wouldn’t understand.” Her voice was laced with genuine concern. “Exactly why I’m so careful, Ella. It’s for them, ultimately. To give them a future, a security I never had. Don’t worry about me getting caught. It simply won’t happen. David here,” she gestured towards her partner and Speaker_4, “has helped set everything up. We've got contingencies for  everything ." “Contingencies indeed. Remember that fine I had a couple of years back? Discrepancy with a VAT return, ages ago. Pain in the backside, that was. But I learned from it. Proper record keeping, meticulous attention to detail; it’s crucial in  any  business, let alone…this kind.” He took a sip of his beer. “Speaking of fines, remember when Grandad got done for that dodgy car boot sale deal? Said he didn't know those watches were counterfeit. Honestly, the man...” He shook his head, chuckling. "He was lucky to get away with just the fine. Could have been a lot worse." "It’s all about perception, Mark. Appearing legitimate is half the battle. Banks are very particular. If they see anything…unusual, they flag it. And that’s when you get the auditors poking around. The key is to make it  look  like a normal business transaction.”

Honestly, this weather is just bonkers, isn't it? Sunshine one minute, drizzle the next. Feels like autumn already, and it’s barely September. Tell me about it, love. Absolutely ludicrous. My washing line's had more action than a roundabout this week. You’d think summer would have lasted a bit longer, wouldn't you? Well, classic British weather, that’s all. You never know what you’re going to get. Least it's not snow. Don't want a repeat of last Christmas, do we? Remember trying to get that frozen turkey in the car? Oh god, yes! That was chaotic. You were slipping and sliding everywhere, Dad! And Mum was shouting at you to be careful. Someone had to keep a level head! Anyway, how was school, Chloe? Did the little ones behave themselves today? It was… eventful. Little Leo decided he’s a pirate and refused to take off his eye patch all afternoon. And Mia painted her face entirely blue. Apparently, she was a mermaid. Bless them. But it’s rewarding, you know? They’re just so full of imagination. Sounds fun! Sometimes managing a shop feels less…creative, to be honest. Constant stock takes and dealing with returns. Still, pays the bills, doesn’t it? Exactly. Gotta keep everything ticking over. So, Chloe, are you still thinking about that sign language class? I told Mrs. Peterson at the fundraising gala, she said it’s brilliant for working with children. Yes, I am! I signed up for the introductory session next week.
