Still, we are talking about putting that fence up soon aren't we? That's going to require some serious savings. Got any of those loyalty points from Superdrug racking up? I’m having to tighten my belt. These rising electricity bills are a killer. Dad, you always complain about the electricity bills. It’s not our fault if the weather’s been rubbish and we’ve had the heating on all the time! Speaking of budgets, remember that referendum? Remember all that fuss? Still can’t believe they voted to leave. It was a difficult time. And the impact is still being felt. I’m finding it harder to send money home… the exchange rate is just awful. Affects everyone, doesn’t it? Still, it’s calmer now, I suppose. Less shouting on the news. Calmer? It's just simmering, love. Always simmering. They’re talking about another vote, aren’t they? Political turmoil… gives me a headache just thinking about it. I'm more worried about the chickens. The foxes have been particularly cheeky lately. Little blighters are eyeing them up. Oh, Dad. You and your chickens! You’d think they were royalty.

It’s looking a bit sparse, isn’t it, Mum? Like a sad little pine tree lost in the woods. Well, you know what they say, Elsie. Rome wasn’t built in a day. And neither is a proper Christmas tree. I’m still battling with these ruddy lights. Keeps flickering, it does. Think it’s a dodgy bulb. Honestly, modern technology… Let me have a look. You know, I’ve been thinking about getting one of those pre-lit trees next year. Less hassle. Less hassle, less  charm , I say! Where’s the fun in that? This one's been with us for years. You remember when you were little and you insisted on putting every single bauble on backwards? Oh god, yes! And Dad had to spend an hour just re-hanging them all. He pretended to be thoroughly annoyed, but he was secretly finding it hilarious. Speaking of Dad, has he finished putting up those ridiculous reindeer lights on the shed again? He’s halfway through. Said something about needing to brighten up Mrs. Higgins’ winter days. She's been a bit down since her cat, Whiskers, went. Poor dear. Sometimes I think she's more bothered about the lack of feline company than anything else. She really loved that cat. It’s awful. Did you manage to finally get that appointment at the clinic for Buster? Yes, I did! Tuesday morning. He’s been scratching at the furniture something awful lately. Reckon he's got fleas. Dreadful little critters, fleas. Reminds me of my childhood, growing up in Kent. My mum used to slather us in flea powder every weekend. Smelled like a dusty lavender farm, it did. Sounds…pleasant. Anyway, work’s been pretty chaotic. The client wanted a whole new campaign for a dog biscuit brand, and the creative director wants everything to scream “German heritage.” Can you believe it? German? What's German about dog biscuits? Apparently, Germany has a rich history of dog breeding and… I don’t know, artisanal animal treats? It's ridiculous. I had to do a mini-research project on Bavarian dog breeds. It’s all very… intense. I’ve basically become a semi-expert on Dachshunds. You and your posh words! Dachshunds, eh? Little sausage dogs? Always did look a bit grumpy to me. My neighbour, Doreen, has a couple. Absolute terrors, they are. Chasing the postman every day.

Right, so, this is it. Sussex. Feels… a bit bare, doesn't it? Like a particularly optimistic waiting room. It will. Give it a week, and you’ll be complaining about how cluttered it is. It's a big improvement from your student halls, though, isn't it? Actual space! True, true. The halls were… compact. Though I miss the constant background hum of 200 stressed-out teenagers. This is just… quiet. Almost  too  quiet. And where are we going to put all my plants? They won’t survive on neglect. We'll figure it out. We've got that balcony – plenty of sun for your leafy friends. First things first, though, is getting the internet sorted. I called Virgin earlier, they said a technician can come tomorrow afternoon. Brilliant. Because honestly, I’m going to go slowly insane without a decent Wi-Fi signal. I’ve got online tutorials and lectures to catch up on. And, you know, Instagram. Of course. Priorities. Speaking of which, I managed to grab some groceries while you were wrestling that sofa through the door. Found some lovely courgettes and tomatoes at the Farmer’s Market. Figured we could do a ratatouille tonight? Oh, you’re a star! Ratatouille sounds amazing. I’m starving. Did you manage to find out about the rubbish collection? I’m dreading accidentally putting the wrong bin out. I did that once in Gillingham and got a proper telling off from Mrs. Higgins. She was  fierce . I read the council website. Tuesdays for recycling, Fridays for general waste. Easy peasy. Though, apparently, there's a strict policy on how much cardboard you can put out. We might need to flatten a LOT of boxes. Fantastic. Cardboard flattening. Another essential life skill. Okay, so, what's the state of the kitchen? Any sign of life beyond my rumbling stomach? It’s… functional. Found some basic pots and pans, but no actual cooking utensils. We’ll need to hit up a shop tomorrow. I was thinking maybe Argos? They do decent, budget-friendly stuff. Argos it is. Honestly, I feel a bit bad relying on you to sort everything out. I'm still trying to get my head around banking here. Do I need to change my address with the bank right away? Yeah, you should do that. And you've still got that lingering smoke smell on your clothes, don’t you?

Thirty's not that old, Chloe! My Nan was still dancing the night away at sixty. And your mum, bless her, just wants you to be happy, doesn't she? Is she still fussing over the garden? Last time I saw her, the roses were absolutely blooming. Oh, the garden is her life. She’s got some new hybrid thing going on now, apparently it needs constant pruning and feeding. She's got a spreadsheet for it, honestly! It’s a full-time job, the gardening. But yeah, she just means well. It’s just…the pressure, you know? Everyone seems to have a five-year plan, a house, a partner… I feel like I'm still figuring out what I want for dinner! I know exactly what you mean! My parents are similar. They keep asking about "potential suitors." Like I'm some dating project they're overseeing. It's a bit cringe, to be honest. But at least you have a settled-down project co-ordinator job. What’s new there? Still managing that massive rebrand for Riverside Tech? Ugh, don’t remind me. It’s relentless. Honestly, I feel like I’m living on caffeine and spreadsheets. We’re just in the final stages now, the launch is next month. It’s been a complete rollercoaster, but at least it'll be over soon. What about you? How's the placement going? Still with Miller & Sons? Yeah, still with them. It’s...interesting. It's a proper family business, you know? Three generations all working under one roof. It's brilliant in some ways, really supportive, but also incredibly chaotic. Yesterday, I spent an hour trying to track down Mr. Miller Sr.'s reading glasses, which were apparently balanced on a stack of invoices. That sounds like a sitcom waiting to happen! So, are you enjoying it though? Is there a chance of it turning into something permanent? Honestly, I'm not sure yet. The experience is amazing, I'm learning a ton about logistics and supply chain management... things I barely understood back at Uni. But the company culture is… well, let’s just say it’s very traditional. Lots of hierarchy, not a huge amount of flexibility. I’m trying to navigate it. They keep hinting at a possible junior position, but it’s all very vague. You deserve something great, honestly. You worked so hard at Uni.

…so, honestly, the archives at Birmingham Uni are a nightmare. Just mountains and mountains of papers. It's fascinating, don't get me wrong, but sifting through it all… it’s a slow burn. You wouldn't believe the number of pamphlets on the history of Birmingham brass bands. Brass bands? Seriously? Who cares that much about brass bands? Aside from, like, brass band enthusiasts, obviously. Sounds well dull, love. You'd be happier back up North, watching a proper football match and getting some fresh air. It’s for the research! It’s tied into broader industrial social history, you see… The banding culture was intrinsically linked to the factories… Oh, never mind. You'd probably just say it's a load of cobblers. Cobblers is right. Cambridge is lovely, mind. Nicer than Birmingham, definitely. But you’re missing out on a decent parmo, that's for sure. I had one the other day that nearly brought a tear to me eye. Proper chippy parmo, not one of those fancy gastropub things. A parmo? Is that… a potato thing? A potato thing? No! Don’t you dare insult the parmo! It’s breaded chicken or pork, smothered in cheese sauce and chips, served on a massive slab of chips. It’s basically a heart attack on a plate, but it’s the best thing you’ll ever taste. You absolutely  have  to try one when you come up to Sunderland. Right. Noted. Sounds... intense. Speaking of intense, my supervisor's been on at me about getting a revised methodology proposal to him by next week. He's a bit of a stickler for detail. Aye, bosses are all the same, aren’t they? Mine’s breathing down my neck about the Baker report. Apparently, the board wants it presented before the end of the month. Pressure's on, eh? At least my research is a bit more… dynamic than brass bands. It's all about consumer behaviour in the green energy sector. Not exactly thrilling, but at least it feels relevant. Relevant and, presumably, involving less sifting through faded Victorian pamphlets. So, you’re still into that Arctic Monkeys album then? The one you kept playing non-stop on the train when I came down to visit last month? ‘AM’? Oh, absolutely. It’s proper good, innit? Always had a soft spot for Sheffield bands, I have. Something about the grit.

Right, Gran, so, this new thing with Starmer… what’s all the fuss about? Seems like everyone's having a right go at him. Fuss? Aye, lad, there’s always a fuss. Politics is nothing but fuss, innit? Starmer… now he's a curious one. Lot of talk about him trying to be ‘serious’. Acting like he’s got all the answers. But Dad was saying he's being too… wishy-washy? Not taking a strong enough stance on things. Like, that thing about the strikes. Wishy-washy, eh? Your dad's got a good head on his shoulders. Remember Harold Wilson? Now  he  knew how to dance around a tricky situation. Kept folks guessing. Starmer's trying to be too upfront, like he thinks he can just tell everyone what to do. Doesn’t always work, does it? I dunno. Feels like you need to be clear sometimes. Especially when people are struggling, like with the cost of living and all that. Dad keeps muttering about energy prices. Says we’re all getting rinsed. Rinsed is right! They are, lad. They are. I remember rationing. Not quite the same, mind, but knowing every penny counted… it makes you appreciate things. They keep telling us things will get better, but I've heard that tune before. Politicians always promise things. Your grandad, God rest his soul, used to say, “Never trust a politician who promises you the moon, lad. They’ll sell you the cow to get it.” That's a good one, Gran. So, you reckon Starmer’s just another one selling the cow? Well, I wouldn’t be so quick to write him off entirely. He’s trying, I think. But he doesn't seem to understand the… the grit of it all, you know? The everyday struggles. He's surrounded by people who tell him what he wants to hear. It’s the same wherever you look. Remember Thatcher? She came to Darlington once, waving and smiling. Said she was there for the people. My neighbour, Elsie, she spat at her. Said she was ruining the country! Elsie spat at Thatcher? Really? Aye, really. Elsie was a fiery one. Didn’t suffer fools gladly. And Thatcher... well, she closed the mines didn’t she? So many folk lost their livelihoods. That's why you have to be careful, lad. When someone promises you easy answers, they’re usually hiding something.

Ugh, these peas are like, tiny green bullets. And they’re cold! Jaysus, Liam, would ya stop yer whinin’? Your Granny cooked a lovely dinner. Show a bit o' respect, alright? It's not every day we all get together like this. Don't listen to him, love. He’s just being a teenager. Granny makes the best stew. And peas  are  good for you! You need your greens to grow big and strong. Grow big and strong? He's a gangly lad already, Fiona! Can’t fault the sentiment, though. And Liam, honestly. Remember what your mother taught you about thanking the cook? Sorry, Granny. They're still like, cold bullets. See? He apologised! Now, eat yer dinner. We were talkin' about the blood moon earlier. Did you see it last night, Granny? Aye, I did. A bonny sight it was. A deep, rich colour. Reminded me of old copper kettles. Used to see them in the cottages back in Glasgow. Superstition, of course, but it always seemed a bit… otherworldly. People used to say it brought bad luck. Bad luck? Really? I thought it was just a cool astronomical event. Something about the Earth's shadow falling on the moon. That's right, Fiona. A bit o' science to go with the folklore. Although, I wouldn’t be sayin’ no to a wee bit o’ magic myself these days. Keepin’ the servers runnin’ smoothly feels like magic sometimes, let me tell you. Is there going to be another one soon? Can we, like, go somewhere to see it properly? Like Fitzgeralds Park? Fitzgeralds Park is a grand spot, Liam. Open space, not too much light pollution. We could definitely do that. We'll check the dates. Looks like there might be another one in a few months. That sounds lovely. It would be nice to get out. Little Thomas has been a bit restless lately. He’s been clingy, probably missing you, Daniel. I miss him too, darlin'. Things have been hectic at work. I was thinking, could Granny maybe take him for a few hours next Saturday? Just to give us a bit of a breather? Oh, I’d love to, Daniel. Thomas is a wee treasure. He calls me ‘Granny Scotland’ now, which I find particularly charming. Though he does pull my hair sometimes. Granny Scotland! That’s a funny name. Can I go with you and Thomas?

Honestly, Arthur, the whole thing with the Scottish referendum… it’s just left me feeling a bit… unsettled. I mean, I understand the arguments, of course, but the potential ramifications… it’s a lot to take in. Aye, it is, Bernard. It is. Though I must say, I never thought I’d see the day. Growing up in Hove, we always just assumed Scotland was… well, part of the Union. Never questioned it, really. Bit of a shocker, wasn't it? For an old buffer like me. A shocker indeed. And the misinformation swirling about! Trying to sift through it all is a nightmare. Reminds me a bit of the Brexit debates, if you recall. Same kind of passionate arguments, same amount of… well, frankly, nonsense. You're not wrong, Bernard. Though I reckon this is a bit more… significant. Brexit, we’ll muddle through, somehow. This could rearrange the map, couldn't it? Still, one thing’s for sure, my nephew in Edinburgh's beside himself with excitement – either way. Says it’s history in the making. He’s right, of course. History. Speaking of history... Did I tell you about young Thomas Henderson? The new candidate for the History post at the school? Had the interview yesterday. No, you didn’t. How did it go? Henderson… rings a bell. Seemed bright enough when I met him at the Christmas do last year, clever lad. Bright, yes. Enthusiastic. But… lacking a certain gravitas, I’d say. He spoke at length about incorporating gaming into the curriculum – which, don’t get me wrong, I’m not against – but when I asked him about the long-term impact of the Industrial Revolution on social structures, he just… stammered. Stammered, did he? That’s not ideal for a History teacher, is it? Sounds a bit light on the substance. Reminds me of running a business sometimes – you need the spark of enthusiasm, but you also need a solid foundation. Can't just be all sizzle and no sausage, as they say! Precisely! And then there’s Mrs. Abernathy. Honestly, Arthur, the woman is a nightmare. Been with the school forever, a good teacher in her day, I'm sure, but now... Just resistant to  everything . I suggested incorporating some primary source analysis into the syllabus, and she practically accused me of undermining her authority! Oh, Mrs. Abernathy! I remember her from when my daughter, Emily, was at the school.

Right then, nearly there. Just gotta navigate this roundabout. Aaron, are you alright in the back? Ann, you doing okay? Bit of a squeeze, innit? Yeah, alright, Dad. Just… a bit dusty back here, if I'm honest. All this cardboard, you know? I’m starving though. Properly starving. Lunch feels like a lifetime ago. Tell me about it, love. That cheese and pickle sandwich wasn't exactly a feast. Though, it was better than nothing after the morning we’ve had packing up the kitchen! Honestly, Gordon would have a fit. Gordon, the cat? He's going to be lost without his favourite sunbeam spot on the windowsill. We'll have to find him a new favourite, won’t we? Speaking of which, have you two thought about what we're going to have for dinner tonight? Moving house works up an appetite. We could do a proper roast! Something easy, like chicken with roast potatoes and veg. Comfort food. I'm feeling the stress of the move, too. Speaking of stress, did you see that article about tuition fees rising again? It's ridiculous! Seriously, Jamie! It's daylight robbery. I'm already terrified about paying them back. I’ll probably be doing it until I’m your age, Dad. Well, you've got to think about things, haven't you? Pensions, savings… It's all part of being an adult. Though I’ll admit, the whole thing’s a bit frightening. Remember when pensions were straightforward? Now it's all ISAs and… things I don’t understand. Oh, don’t get me started on pensions! I was reading about someone who set a world record for collecting stamps – apparently, it’s a brilliant way to try and secure one. A bit niche, admittedly! Though less stressful than investing, probably. A stamp collection? Actually, that's… kind of cool. My grandpa used to have one. Said he'd learned a lot about history from it. You know, connected to the countries and the people… Speaking of countries, I saw a bloke on YouTube the other day who’d travelled to every country in the world. Apparently his secret was finding really cheap flights. Maybe when I'm not drowning in debt... Right, deep breaths everyone. Roundabout approaching. Ann, are you thinking about popping down to Asda tomorrow? We need milk, bread, and something to make a decent cup of tea.

This road’s a right mess, isn’t it? All these little twists and turns. Makes a body feel a bit queasy, it does. Used to be able to navigate anywhere blindfolded, back in the day. Knowing the routes 'round Manchester like the back of me hand, I did. Aye, it's a bit winding, Grandad. But ANON’s doing a grand job, aren't you, love? It’s quicker than the main road, honestly. You were saying it’s really bustling down there near the motorway? It definitely is, Elara. Traffic was a nightmare. This route avoids all that, though. And look – sheep! On the verge. Sheep! Bless 'em. Proper Lancashire whites, I reckon. Always were good sheep, Lancashire whites. Strong and hardy. Reminds me of old Mr. Hargreaves’ flock. He had a prize ram once, called Bartholomew. Showed him at the county fair. Bartholomew the ram? That’s brilliant, Grandad. You always have the best stories. What happened to Bartholomew? Oh, he did well, he did. Won the ‘Best in Show’ ribbon, he did! But he had a temper, that one. Tried to headbutt the judge, he did. Had to be wrestled to the ground. Good times, good times. Do you ever think about how differently the world was back then? Fewer cars, more fields… It's certainly a contrast. My project involves optimising resource allocation on precision farming operations, increasingly reliant on automation and data analytics. We’re seeing a massive shift - moving away from traditional grazing patterns towards monitored and controlled environments. It's incredibly efficient, but… there’s something to be said for the simplicity of a flock like Mr. Hargreaves’. Aye. It's good to keep a bit of tradition going, innit? I saw a farmer on the telly the other day trying to teach a pig to play fetch. It were cracking! A pig! Playing fetch! That’s a new one. Pigs aren't known for their obedience, are they? We had a sow once, Bessie, who used to raid the vegetable patch. My mum used to chase her 'round the garden with a broom. Best carrots in the village, though, after Bessie'd been at them. Gave 'em a lovely sweetness. I suppose even rogue pigs can contribute to quality control in their own way. Modern farming aims to minimise that kind of… variability. Optimisation, you see. You and your optimisation, Finn! You sound like a robot sometimes.

Right then, Nan, tuck in. I think this is a proper champion pie, even if I do say so myself. Dad’s been bragging about his mashed potato technique all week. Champion indeed, love. It  is  delightful. Though, your father did make a frightful mess of the kitchen getting it just so. A veritable flour blizzard! Reminds me a bit of when I used to try and bake for the school fairs… never quite had his flair, did I? Flair and a complete disregard for tidiness. It’s a Midland thing, Nan. We're all a bit… artistic in the kitchen. She’d have you believing I cleared up though, wouldn’t she? Well, you  helped , Dad. Briefly. Mostly you supervised and offered commentary. "Needs more pepper, John. Or a pinch of nutmeg. Definitely more nutmeg.” He’s always been a man of strong opinions. Remember when little Emily was convinced she hated broccoli? Your father swore he could convert her. Forced her to eat a tiny floret every day! Don’t remind me! I'm still recovering from childhood broccoli trauma. Though, thankfully, I've learned to appreciate it now. So, Mum, how’s the choir going? You seemed really enthusiastic about the new pieces they’re tackling. Oh, it’s wonderful, dear. Absolutely wonderful. We're doing a medley of folk songs this term. It’s bringing back memories of singing in the church choir as a child back in Dublin. It’s such a lovely, supportive group. And the conductor, Mr. Davies, he’s a dear. A bit… particular about tempo, mind you. Has to be  exactly  right, or he’ll stop and start again. Sound like some teachers I knew. Precise, demanding… and rarely appreciated. The oil industry wasn't much different, you know. Everything needed to adhere to rigid protocols. Less room for artistic interpretation, thankfully. That’s fascinating, Dad. You never really talked much about your work. You always seemed… reluctant. It was a long time ago, love. A different life, in a different world. Not one I particularly miss. Easier to enjoy a shepherd's pie and a glass of red these days. Now, about Christmas… have you booked the theatre tickets, Sarah? Not yet, Dad. Been meaning to. Is it the panto again this year? Emily  insists  on seeing Cinderella. The poor dear! She’s obsessed. But it’s lovely to see her so excited.

Right, so Mrs. Davies thinks Leo’s really struggling with fractions. Says he gets completely flustered and just shuts down. Fractions are silly, Mummy. Why do we need to split things up? Because you need to share fairly, Rosie! Like when we were playing with the dinosaurs and you had three and I only had one. That wasn’t fair. Exactly, Leo! That's fractions in action. But clearly, he's not seeing it that way. She also suggested maybe he’s feeling anxious about Maths in general. Anxious? Why would I be anxious? Maths is just… numbers. Well, sometimes numbers can be tricky, darling. It’s okay to feel a bit nervous. Leo, you weren’t being very chatty about it at all. Did you tell Mrs. Davies anything? She asked me loads and loads of questions! I got confused. Oh, poor love. Well, I told her we’d work on it at home. I was thinking maybe some games? Something less formal than the worksheets she’s sending. Can we play that game with the Lego? Where we build towers and count the bricks? We could! That's a brilliant idea, Rosie. See, Leo? Rosie gets it. We can make Maths fun! Although, having said that, Mrs. Peterson – you remember, from nursery? – she told me the  weirdest  thing. What? Did she see a dinosaur? No, silly. She said her nephew, who’s studying forensic science, told her about a case they were working on… apparently, cooking human flesh smells like burnt almonds. Bleugh! Almonds are yucky anyway. Burnt almonds? Gross! That's even worse than Brussels sprouts! I know, right? Where do people come up with this stuff? Completely bizarre topic to bring up at parent’s evening. It just kind of… popped out. Anyway, back to more pressing matters. I also need to look at your World Book Day costume plans, you two. I’m still being Goldilocks! I’ve got the bears ready. I’m going to be Captain Flinn! I found this amazing pirate hat at the charity shop. Look! . It  is  brilliant, darling! You look very dashing. Right, after school on Thursday, I’m picking you both up and then we’re heading to that circus, remember? The one we booked ages ago. Ooh, the lions! Will there be lions? Probably, love. Although, hopefully, they'll be treated really well. Speaking of books, have you both been reading your Character Analysis books?

…and he’s telling me he’s going to be Treasurer of the garages! At five years old! Imagine that, a wee accountant. Where does he get these notions, Moira? He gets them from his Da, doesn't he, Liam? You’re the one who filled his head with numbers and spreadsheets when he was a baby. Though, I must say, he IS remarkably good at counting. He was sorting his Lego by colour and quantity earlier. Ach, don’t be giving me all the credit, love. He's a clever wee lad, that's all. It’s pure natural. Still, a Treasurer! He'll be running the whole country before you know it. Oisin, stop shoving spaghetti up your nose! 'Tatoes! He’s trying to say “potatoes.” He still mumbles a bit, doesn’t he, Liam? It’s so cute. Like he's speaking a secret language. He has a lovely way of talking, he does. A little bit...Scottish, almost, sometimes. It’s a funny combination of both of your accents. He gets a bit of everything, he does. Confuses the life out of the neighbours. Speaking of neighbours, have you confirmed Mrs. O’Connell about the bouncy castle for Oisin’s birthday? I called her earlier. She’s happy to let us use her garden, but reminded me that little Tommy is a menace with a football, so we need to keep an eye on him. Said he nearly took out her prize-winning roses last week. Right, right. Keep the young scallywag away from the roses. Better that than a broken nose. What about the cake? Did you order it yet? I did! Chocolate fudge, his favourite. And I got those little plastic rugby players to put on top. He’s obsessed with rugby at the moment. Keeps shouting “try!” at the television. He’ll be playing for Ireland one day, you mark my words. I could get tickets for the Leinster match next Saturday, you fancy going? Oh, I would love to! But... I don’t know, Liam. With Oisin… it might be a bit much. All that noise and crowds. He gets overwhelmed easily. We'll keep him close. I can manage him. It'll be a nice change, getting out for a few hours. And you deserve it, love. You’ve been carrying the brunt of things lately. It’s very kind of you, Liam.

Right, okay, so I'm genuinely stumped. "Flibbertigibbet." You’re telling me that’s a  real  word? And it means… a flighty, talkative person? Seriously? Aye, dead serious! Look it up! It's been around for hundreds of years. My Gran used to call Auntie Brenda a flibbertigibbet. Always gossiping and fluttering about. Aye, she was. You're winding him up, aren’t you, Chloe? He’s giving you a perfect opening. Honestly, Liam, you’re far too serious sometimes. It  is  a real word. She’s right. And a brilliant one, at that. I just… it feels so utterly ridiculous. It’s like something out of a Victorian novel! I've been through like, five dictionaries. And I’m a consultant engineer! I deal with stress analysis and finite element modelling - I should know words! Well, maybe you need a bit o’ flibbertigibbet in your life, Liam! Loosen up a bit! It’s a right good word, innit? Makes you smile just saying it. "Flibbertigibbet!" Try it. Go on. Flibber… tigibbet. It feels like I'm trying to pronounce a sneeze. See? You’re already exhibiting the characteristics! Lighthearted, whimsical… a bit of a nonsense word enthusiast! Nonsense is the operative word! So, moving on. What about this one: "petrichor"? Petrichor... that's a good one. I reckon I've heard that somewhere. Let me think... It's got something to do with… rain? It's the earthy scent produced when rain falls on dry ground. Specifically, it’s caused by plant oils and a bacteria called Actinomycetes. Aha! I knew you’d know, Ben! Chloe was completely blanking! I was thinking! It's a fancy word! We don’t use words like that in Sunderland, do we? We just say "smells lovely after the rain!" It's more straightforward, isn’t it? Straightforward is good, but petrichor is far more evocative, Chloe. It encapsulates the whole sensory experience. Exactly! Okay, next one – and this is a tricky one. “Agastopia.” Right, now you're just being mean. That sounds… Greek. It is. It means a fondness for a particular part of your own body. Seriously?! Someone coined a word for liking their own thighs?! Absolutely bonkers. Who needs a word for that? "I like my legs!" is perfectly adequate. This is why I stick to simpler words. Words about proper things. Like… crisps. A perfectly valid and important area of vocabulary, Chloe.

…and then Kev just  face-planted  into the birthday cake! Full on! Chocolate everywhere. Honestly, I thought he’d broken something. Kev? Face-planting into a cake? That sounds peak Kev. Where was that, again? Liam’s 21st? Aye, Liam’s 21st. Remember how much he moaned about the buffet beforehand? Said it were "tragic" and “didn't deserve to be fed.” Then Kev goes and provides the entertainment. It's on my phone somewhere… let me just… Don't bother, I've seen it a million times. Still makes me snort. Speaking of tragic, I’m absolutely knackered. Didn't get a wink of sleep last night. Seriously? What happened? Didn't you have that deadline for the history essay? Had it ages ago. Nah, it was Fiona. Next door’s dog, you know, the little yappy thing? It’s decided my fence is its personal chew toy. Barking and scratching all night. I swear, I was contemplating setting up a motion-sensor sprinkler just to soak the poor little beast. Oh, that’s awful! Poor you. You look like you’ve been dragged through a hedge backwards. Fancy a nap after this? I’m proper tempted myself. University’s absolutely draining me this term. A nap sounds heaven. Seriously. Maybe we should just bail on Jamie and Chloe tonight then? They were saying something about going to Peel last minute for a bonfire. Ooh, Peel! But... that's ages. Jamie was raving about this band playing, “Static Bloom,” apparently they're right good. Indie-rockish? Indie-rockish? Sounds like my kind of nap deterrent. Honestly, I’m drawing a blank trying to recall the last time I properly appreciated indie-rockish music. It’s just…noise. Don't be like that! It's not just noise! Static Bloom have a wicked guitarist. You’d probably like them. They’re not full-on, shouty guitar stuff. More… atmospheric. Atmospheric? So, pretentious then? No! Just… layered, yeah. You’re deliberately trying to wind me up. Remember when you claimed Oasis were "overrated shepherds”? That was a dark time. But they  were ! Look, I'm just saying a comfy sofa and a duvet would be a more appealing soundtrack tonight. Alright, alright. Point taken. But we’re going next weekend, whether you like it or not. I’ve been wanting to get out of Warrington for ages. Fine, fine. But  you’re  driving.

Right, so, the feedback from Mrs. Higgins was... robust, wasn’t it? "Lacks a clear narrative arc," she said. Honestly! It’s a planning application for a solar farm, not a Victorian novel. Robust is putting it mildly, darling. She practically accused us of trying to turn the village into a science fiction landscape. Though, I suppose the potential visuals  are  a bit dramatic if you don't grasp the benefits. Did she mention the aesthetic impact report specifically? That's the really key bit to address. She glossed over it, said it was "adequate but unconvincing." I think she's fundamentally against anything modern near the village green. It's infuriating. We've done the modelling, demonstrated minimal visual impact from the higher ground… it’s a solid report. Right. Well, we need to bolster that. Less technical language, more relatable arguments. Less "spectral reflectance analysis," more "preserving the rural character while embracing sustainable energy." You know, softening the edges. And we absolutely need David on board for the presentation. He’s got that ability to charm even the most staunch NIMBY. David’s away this week though, remember? Sailing in the Hebrides. Stranded with me and a worried planning committee. Brilliant. So, we’re solo. Look, I think the biggest problem is the sheer number of objections. All those anonymous letters… Probably a few stirred up by Higgins’ initial campaign. We need to acknowledge their concerns, but without validating them. Something like, "We've received several valid inquiries regarding…" and then systematically address each one in the presentation. The water table concerns, the impact on local wildlife… Agreed. And we  have  addressed them adequately, haven’t we? The borehole analysis was impeccable. And we're offering a significant biodiversity offset scheme – planting native hedgerows, creating a new wetland area… Absolutely. We need to highlight that. People react better to proactive solutions than vague promises. Okay, so, presentation structure. I’m thinking: Start with the context – the national need for renewable energy, the council’s commitment to sustainability... then showcase the site's suitability. Emphasize the minimal impact, the biodiversity benefits, the economic opportunities... finally, a clear Q&A. What do you think? That sounds decent, but we’re going to be on the defensive the whole time. I was thinking maybe flipping it. Start with the community benefits - jobs created, local investment, increased energy security... Lead with the positives. Hook them in  before  we hit them with the technical stuff.

Honestly, the queues at Sainsbury's were  ridiculous  today. I spent nearly an hour just grabbing milk and bread! You wouldn’t believe the drama unfolding at the checkout – a full-blown argument over a loyalty card. Tell me about it. My day hasn't exactly been a picnic either. The Peterson report is due on Friday, and half the data is missing. Management are breathing down my neck. Need a cuppa? I’m making some. Please! Strong, Yorkshire Tea, two sugars. Sounds amazing. So, the Peterson report… still giving you grief? You looked properly frazzled earlier. Is Mark still… being Mark? Don't even. He’s convinced he knows better than everyone else, naturally. Keeps pinging me emails at 10pm with 'minor adjustments' that completely derail everything. I swear, he just enjoys the chaos. Classic Mark. Remember in sixth form when he tried to convince Mr. Harrison that Shakespeare was actually written by a team of squirrels? Oh my god, yes! He stood there, completely serious, arguing about nut-burying patterns and Elizabethan rodent colonies. Mr. Harrison practically choked on his tea. Good times. Speaking of good times, have you heard from Chloe and Liam? I wonder what they're up to. I saw Chloe’s Instagram post – they’re finally going to Cornwall! About time. They've been planning that trip for ages. Remember how obsessed Liam was with surfing? He'd be terrible, though. All elbows and splashing. He would be! He'd probably wipe out within five seconds. I’m jealous, though. A proper beach holiday sounds lovely. We should actually do something like that, don't you think? Instead of just Netflix and takeaways, like we always do. I'm in! Somewhere sunny and with decent cocktails. What about Brighton? We haven't been in ages. Or even the New Forest – a bit of hiking, a pub lunch… That actually sounds really nice. I need a break from spreadsheets and passive-aggressive emails. Right, tea's ready. So, speaking of drama… have you seen Mrs. Henderson’s new garden gnome? Don't even start. It's hideous. A truly offensive shade of pink. And it’s wearing a tiny tutu. What is she  thinking ? I know! She's gone full eccentric, hasn't she? It’s like she’s been replaced by a rogue garden centre display. Remember when she used to bake us those amazing lemon drizzle cakes?

Honestly, Liam, you’re glued to that thing. The poor puffins are struggling and you’re looking at… what  is  that, another cat video? Nah, it’s a car boot sale near St Helens. Loads of vintage vinyl. Might be worth a look, eh? Could pick up some stuff for the school. They’re always wantin’ classic records for music lessons. A car boot sale? Really? You'd brave those crowds? I'd rather order everything online. It's just so much easier. Easier, aye, but where's the adventure in that, love? Besides, you never know what treasures you’ll find. Found a first edition of 'The Hobbit' for a quid once at one of them! You and your treasures. Reminds me of that awful advert I saw earlier - for those slimming pills. Honestly, it was just manipulative. "Lose ten pounds in a week!" It felt so… predatory. Advertising these days, innit? They’ll sell ya anything. Remember that one for the electric toothbrush that made you feel like you were personally responsible for climate change if you used a normal one? Exactly! And the subliminal messaging… it’s terrifying. I was reading about NLP – Neuro-Linguistic Programming - the other day, and how advertisers use it to subconsciously influence our buying habits. It's proper clever, but a bit creepy. NLP, eh? That’s a bit beyond me, la. Me brain’s full enough tryin’ to explain present perfect tense to a room full of teenagers. Still, used to watch those crime documentaries, y’know, the ones that explain how they get confessions. That’s all psychological levers, isn’t it? It is. It’s fascinating, but also highlights how easily people can be misled. Speaking of which, have you seen that article in the  Echo  about the spate of burglaries in Oxton? Aye, wicked, wasn't it? Gotta be more careful, I reckon. Makes you think. You lockin’ up tight enough tonight? Always. Honestly, it's made me think about getting an alarm system. Though, that's another expense. Speaking of which, I need to do some online shopping. My running shoes are on their last legs. Running shoes? You’re still running? After that disastrous attempt at a 5k last month? It was a  challenging  5k, Liam. And yes, I’m persevering. I’m determined to get back into shape. Maybe I should try that new keto diet everyone’s on.

Oh, really? I'm a language teacher, you know. I feel like I  should  be on top of these apps, but I've been so busy marking essays, I haven’t really explored them. Which language are you learning? Mandarin. Absolutely mental. My company's expanding into China, and well, I thought I’d give it a go. It’s… challenging, to say the least. Unlike you, Sarah, I haven't got a clue about tones. Feel like I'm just shouting at my phone half the time. Mandarin! That’s ambitious, James. Proper respect. I’m trying to get back into Italian. Used to be pretty decent, you know, back in uni. Now, I can barely order a pizza without butchering the pronunciation. Speaking of pizza… Anon, this lasagna is amazing! Seriously, you need to put this on your restaurant review blog. Seriously. I’ve been trying to find a decent Italian in Brum, and this is already beating everything I’ve tried. Aye, that’s proper good lasagna, Chloe. Anon, you’ve outdone yourself! Better than my nan’s even, and that’s saying something. She’d kill me if she heard me say that, mind. It  is  fantastic, Anon. And you made it? I’m impressed! I attempted a paella last week. Let’s just say it involved a lot of rice and not a lot of flavour. See, that’s what I’m talking about. I was thinking of doing a house renovation project, trying my hand at tiling… suddenly, learning Mandarin seems a lot less daunting. Don't even  think  about it, James. Remember what happened to Uncle Barry and his disastrous attempt at wallpapering? We're still finding bits of that floral monstrosity. Oh, god, the Barry wallpaper incident. Legendary. Speaking of disastrous attempts… I'm trying to write a novel. It's going… slowly. Really slowly. I’ve got the first chapter, and it’s basically just a description of a coffee shop. Coffee shops are good starting points! Get the atmosphere right, build the world. Don't beat yourself up about it. I’m trying to write a radio drama, and I'm stuck on the sound design. Too much rain, apparently, according to my producer. Says it sounds like the Yorkshire Dales all the time, even when the scene is set in London. That’s a good point, though. Sound design is everything.

...and honestly, the sheer  lack  of central heating in that little cottage! Rain came right through the windows. Martha nearly froze solid the first winter. We were romanticising rural life, you see, forgetting the realities. Oh, I know exactly what you mean. We were all so keen to escape the city, weren’t we? Almondsbury seemed so idyllic on paper. The reality was a bit… damp. Remember when we first moved here, David? Finding somewhere to rent was a nightmare. Every tiny, draughty room seemed to be occupied by a family of six. Absolutely. Ramsgate was bursting at the seams then. Everyone wanted to escape London, and the South Coast became a magnet. The rentals were appalling. I ended up sharing a tiny bedsit with a taxidermist for six months! A very quiet, rather dusty gentleman, he was. Didn't say much at all. A taxidermist! Good heavens, David! You’ve certainly had some interesting lodgers. Manchester was a different story. More student accommodation, thankfully. Though my landlady, Mrs. Higgins, insisted on playing polka music at full volume every morning. It nearly drove me mad preparing for lectures. Speaking of lectures... I had a particularly memorable trip for my postgraduate course in Athens. 1967. Honestly, you wouldn't believe it. We’d just arrived, all bright-eyed dental students ready to immerse ourselves in ancient Greek dentistry , and on the very first day, the military coup happened. Tanks rolling through the streets! Oh, my goodness! That’s extraordinary! Were you frightened? Absolutely terrified! The time difference didn't help either. We were completely disoriented. Imagine trying to learn about fillings while a revolution unfolds around you. The university shut down immediately, of course. We had to find our way back to the airport. It took days, and we nearly missed our flight. And trying to explain to the customs officials what had happened… utter chaos! That’s incredible. I can just picture it. I remember bringing Margaret over here in the early 70s. We met at Canterbury College, you know. She was doing her PGCE. Absolutely charming girl. Trying to introduce her to the local pub scene...that was an adventure in itself! Canterbury’s a lovely place. I always admired the cathedral. I met Geoffrey at Bristol University, though it was during a summer school focused on phonology. Dreadful stuff, phonology. Not remotely appealing compared to his smile. To smiles, then!

Oh, yes, it is, isn't it, dear? You've a painter's eye, I’d wager. I wish I’d taken more time to really  look , you know? Running the gallery, dealing with estate sales… it was all so rushed. Never did feel I had enough peace to properly appreciate it. Though, I did have a lovely little watercolour of Glastonbury Tor I was quite chuffed with. Do you paint, Penelope? Not really, Marion. Never had the inclination, I’m afraid. I always admired it, though. My mother dabbled a bit, a bit of watercolour, mostly landscapes, but nothing serious. She was a teacher, you see. Very practical, my mother. All about sensible things. My father, though, he was a hopeless romantic. Always talking about finding the perfect beach, the perfect view… he even tried to write poetry once. Dreadful poetry, really. Oh, fathers! Mine was a farmer. Didn't say much, but he had a good eye for the land. Taught me a lot about colours, funny enough. The different shades of the soil, the way the wheat turned golden in the late afternoon sun… things a proper art school wouldn't teach you, d'you know? My mother, bless her, she was a Welsh speaker. Used to sing to me in Welsh when I was little. I can remember a few phrases, but the grammar’s all gone, sadly. That’s fascinating! I’ve always been intrigued by Welsh. Such a beautiful, ancient language. My grandmother on my mother's side – she was Irish, from County Clare. Always a touch of melancholy about her, she was. Storyteller, though. Oh, she could weave a tale! I remember one about a selkie, a seal woman who could shed her skin and walk on land… I used to be terrified of the sea after hearing that one! Selkies… yes, there are Celtic echoes everywhere here, in Somerset too. Ancient things bubbling under the surface. It's what draws me to the land, I suppose. Makes you feel connected to something bigger. Being a speech therapist… that must have been a very rewarding job. Did you see many children struggling with particularly difficult things? It was, Marion, very rewarding. Heartbreaking at times, too, of course. Mostly it was a question of helping them find their voice, literally and figuratively. One little boy, Thomas, comes to mind. Completely withdrawn, wouldn’t speak a word when he first came to me.

Right, so, I’m thinking butternut squash risotto for tonight. Fancy, innit? A bit of a step up from beans on toast, yeah? Sounds lovely, Liam. Butternut squash is peak autumn. Good choice. You dealing with the parmesan then? Because last time, you sprinkled enough on to snow the kitchen. Fair point. Lesson learned. Light hand on the cheese this time. Seriously though, feeling a bit festive. Getting into the Christmas spirit, you know? You are? Already? It’s barely November! You’re going full-blown Christmas elf, aren't you? Nah, not  full  elf. Just… the lights are putting me in a mood. Saw a shop in Camden with the most incredible fairy lights. All vintage-looking, like tiny little lanterns. Thought about getting some. Camden, eh? Expensive as anything there. My shop could definitely use some fairy lights. Always wanting to make it look more cosy, especially when it's freezing outside. Do you think I should go for the warm white or the multicoloured ones? Warm white, definitely. Multicoloured’s a bit… overwhelming. You want cosy, not a rave. Speaking of which, the gingerbread men need decorating. Got those candy eyes and sprinkles yesterday. Ooh, exciting! They look terrifying half-finished. Like tiny, doughy monsters. I'm gonna have to pop round and sample the goods later, for quality control purposes, naturally. Right on cue. That’ll be Sarah. Come in! Sorry I’m late! The traffic was brutal. But I brought reinforcements! Christmas decorations, glorious Christmas decorations. Managed to snag a few genuine vintage ones from an antique stall in Brum. You're a legend, Sarah! Show us what you got! Ta-da! Look at these! Hand-painted baubles, proper old-fashioned ones, not the plastic rubbish you get everywhere. And some paper chains, remember those? We used to make them as kids. Oh my god, those are amazing! They’re so… nostalgic. Much better than anything I can buy. Where did you find them? Antique market near the Bullring. They were practically giving them away. I also got a ridiculous amount of tinsel. Because, you know, it wouldn't be Christmas without tinsel. Tinsel is vital! Although, I’m thinking this year, less tinsel, more understated elegance. Maybe some pine cones and cinnamon sticks. Liam, you’re scaring me with your 'understated elegance'. Christmas needs sparkle! Think of the children! Think of the cake! Speaking of cake… I’m planning on doing a yule log this year.

Honestly, Mum, I'm still reeling. Getting that offer from Oxford… it's mental, innit? Mental in a good way, I hope, darling? It's a phenomenal opportunity, Liam. Your thesis was exceptional. They recognised that. Yeah, yeah, it’s good. Obviously. But it's... intense. Cambridge was stressful enough, you know? This feels like a whole other level. And the politics… I’ve heard Oxford's a right viper’s nest. Every institution has its challenges, Liam. It’s about navigating them. Besides, you're brilliant at that. Remember that debacle with Professor Harding and the citation error? You handled that like a diplomat. Yeah, but that was just one grumpy old guy. Oxford will be a whole department full of 'em. And what about…everything else? Like, where am I going to  live ? Well, that’s what we need to figure out. Your current room in Cambridge isn't exactly suitable for a permanent move, is it? Too small, too far from everything. We could look at something in Oxford, of course. A small flat, perhaps, shared with someone. Shared? Nah, Mum. I need peace. Seriously. After three years of student digs with… questionable roommates, I need my own space. Even if it’s just a tiny box. Alright, alright. A tiny box then. There are student houses, Liam. Slightly older, a bit rundown sometimes, but…characterful. And significantly more private. We could scour Rightmove when we get back to London. Rightmove. It’s terrifying, isn’t it? Everything’s so expensive. You wouldn't believe the prices for even the most basic places around Oxford. It feels a bit… grim, facing that reality. It  is  a reality. But we'll manage. We always do. Look, about the finances… I know things are tight with your Dad's work at the moment, but we'll sort it out. Don't you worry about that. Thanks, Mum. Seriously. You're the best. But… have you thought about moving? Like, permanently? Moving? Moving where? I don't know. Somewhere outside London. Somewhere nicer. Maybe near Cambridge? You could get a lovely little cottage. Think about it – peace, quiet, a garden… No more rush hour, no more council tax nightmares. You’re trying to recruit me to be your Oxford support system, aren’t you? A grand plan to control your movements from a quaint village cottage. Maybe. Wouldn’t that be amazing?

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork involved in just  getting  permission to excavate felt disproportionate to the potential historical significance. It's a frustrating part of the job, isn’t it? Tell me about it! I'm coordinating language research now, which, on the surface, seems less… literal digging. But the grant applications, the ethics protocols… it’s still a mountain of documentation. Though, I suppose the stakes are different. We’re dealing with potentially sensitive linguistic data, preserving dialects and languages. Less about finding pottery shards, more about documenting living voices. Living voices are just as important, my dear. Perhaps more so. Pottery shards tell us about a civilization’s material culture; language reveals their very soul. I’ve spent years lecturing on the influence of Arabic on medieval European dialects – astonishing how much flowed across those cultural boundaries. And it all started with a shared capacity for language. That’s fascinating! I didn’t realize just how interwoven those histories were. I’ve always been drawn to the Roman influence in Britain, the way their language and building techniques fundamentally altered the landscape. It's incredible, isn’t it? Thinking about the layers of history beneath our feet. Have you ever travelled much, then, to see these places firsthand? I'm a bit of a history geek myself. A little. I went to Italy a few years ago, mostly Rome and Florence. It was overwhelming – the sheer density of historical monuments. It did give me a deeper appreciation for the scale of the Roman Empire. You? Loads! I spent six months backpacking around Southeast Asia after uni. That really broadened my perspective. I tried learning Mandarin, but... let’s just say my pronunciation was appalling. . The tonal nature of the language completely baffled me. Mandarin is a beast! I attempted Japanese decades ago, for a research project on early Sino-Japanese trade. Gave up after six months. The written characters alone require a lifetime of dedication. Though, the similarities between many Chinese dialects and some ancient Turkic languages are quite remarkable. Have you encountered that in your research? Indirectly, yes. We've been looking at the evolution of Romani dialects, and there are fascinating linguistic connections to Indic languages. It’s that feeling of trying to trace a linguistic family tree across continents and millennia – it’s breathtaking. What kind of lecturing have you been doing, Professor…? Sorry, I don't think I caught your name.

Blimey, have you seen this one? It’s this bloke, right? Trying to make a latte art swan. Absolute disaster. It looks like a…a melted blob with a beak. It's gone viral. Let me guess, another TikTok fail? They breed like rabbits, don't they? I saw one earlier with someone trying to build a cake using only marshmallows. Catastrophe. Though, I have to admit, the comments are funnier than the videos themselves. Tell me about it. Running a café these days is half dealing with customers and half curating the ‘most ridiculous thing I saw on the internet’ conversation. It's exhausting, honestly. Especially when you’re trying to actually  run  a business. You know, it's funny. These viral videos, they're a symptom of something bigger, I reckon. Everyone wanting fifteen minutes of fame, sharing everything. It's fascinating from a production point of view, though. The speed at which things spread…it changes everything we do in film. Yeah, but it’s also a bit depressing, innit? Like, everyone’s desperately chasing likes. Remember when ‘going viral’ was, like, a fluke thing? Now it’s a whole strategy. Exactly! And it puts so much pressure on young people. They feel like they  have  to be constantly creating content, to be relevant. It's tough. I see it with my younger cousin, he's glued to his phone, agonizing over what to post. It’s the education system’s fault, too, to a degree. We're pushing everyone down the same narrow academic track, stressing over grades, and not nurturing creativity or practical skills. My staff, a lot of them, they wouldn’t have even considered starting their own business if they hadn't felt disillusioned with the traditional route. I agree. There’s a real disconnect. I worked with a brilliant young photographer last year. Absolutely incredible talent, but riddled with self-doubt. Turns out he was diagnosed with dyslexia as a child, but it was never properly addressed. He felt like he was failing because he struggled with the paperwork, not because he lacked artistic ability. Honestly, that's rough, man. Schools are supposed to support kids with that, aren't they? My mate, Liam, he really struggled at uni with dyslexia. Got accused of plagiarism once because his brain just processes stuff differently. It was a nightmare. Ended up dropping out. Now he’s doing well, teaching music to underprivileged kids, but it shouldn't have been that hard.

Honestly, David, I'm just…exhausted. Not just tired, but  deeply  exhausted. It's more than the marking, you know? More than the marking? That alone sounds draining. The essays this year have been particularly…creative, haven’t they? I swear, half of them are arguing that Shakespeare invented TikTok. Exactly! But no, it’s the constant stream of information. Students needing to know where they stand  right now , wanting feedback on every paragraph, feeling like they're entitled to a perfect grade just for showing up. It's relentless. And then the university's constant demands…the impact assessments, the research grants… it's just never-ending. I hear you. Academia’s become a performance, hasn't it? Less about the joy of learning and more about ticking boxes. My department’s pushing for that collaborative project on sustainable tourism again. It’s dreary, and I suspect it’s more about reputation than actual impact. Don’t even get me started on the politics. Did you see what Johnson’s successor is proposing about student loans? It’s utter madness. It’ll only deter students from lower-income backgrounds. We’re practically creating a two-tier education system. It's disgusting, isn’t it? The short-sightedness is unbelievable. And the irony! They’re promising to ‘level up’ the country while simultaneously making education less accessible. I think they genuinely believe the clever ones will somehow just  know  how to navigate the system. They do. And it’s infuriating. I spent half an hour this morning explaining to a student the nuances of the loan system. He looked utterly bewildered. It shouldn't be this complicated! You’re doing a brilliant job, you know. You always go above and beyond for your students. Don’t let the bureaucracy grind you down. I’m trying. But it's impacting my health, I think. I haven’t slept properly in weeks. Everything aches. And I'm snapping at you, which is completely unfair. You're allowed to be stressed. We all are. The cost of living is terrifying. Have you looked at our energy bills? They’re going to be astronomical this winter. Don't remind me. I was trying to work that out last night. We need to seriously cut back. I'm thinking about cancelling that subscription to…what's it called…that streaming service with all the period dramas?

Honestly, Auntie Penelope, this is divine. You've really outdone yourself with this lemon and dill dressing. It's just… summery. Oh, you think so, dear? It's a very old recipe, actually. My mother used to make it every year for our summer picnics. We'd all pile out to Alderley Edge, armed with sandwiches and cricket bats... Cricket bats and wasps, more like! I remember one year, your Uncle Arthur got stung something awful. Face swelled up like a prize pumpkin! Oh, Arthur! He’s always been a magnet for those pesky things. He blamed the lavender, you know. Said it attracted them. Nonsense, of course. Did anyone film it? Imagine the TikTok! "Uncle Arthur vs. the Wasps – A Summer Classic." TikTok? What on earth is that? You youngsters and your… inventions. It all sounds frightfully distracting. I’m quite content with a good book, thank you very much. It’s a video-sharing app, Penelope. Loads of short clips. Quite addictive, apparently. Your granddaughter, Emily, showed it to me. She’s obsessed with it. Emily’s always been… enthusiastic. Remember when she tried to build a birdhouse out of teacups? Oh my goodness, I do! It was a complete disaster. But bless her heart, she was so proud of it. I sent her a kit for her birthday last year. Proper wood, properly glued. Speaking of birthdays, has anyone heard from young Thomas? His birthday's next week, innit? Not a peep. He’s probably gallivanting around somewhere, doing whatever it is young scientists do. Climbing mountains and discovering new species, no doubt. He did mention he was working on a really exciting project – something involving bioluminescence in deep-sea creatures. Apparently, it’s revolutionary. Bioluminescence? Sounds like something out of a science fiction film. Although, I suppose science  is  increasingly like fiction these days. Remember when they said we’d never travel to the moon? Now look! True, true. The world's changed beyond recognition. I used to teach about the dinosaurs and now they're finding feathers on 'em! Blows your mind, it does. It’s incredible, isn’t it? The sheer pace of discovery. I’m working on a manuscript right now about the latest advancements in quantum physics. My head spins just trying to comprehend it. Quantum… whatsit? All this modern science. Makes my head ache. I much preferred teaching Shakespeare. At least I understood that!

Speaker_1 chuckled, a dry, rattling sound. "Proper picture, it was. Reminded me of that Constable painting, you know, 'The Hay Wain'?" Speaker_3 sighed good-naturedly. "A car is more than just a metal box, Brenda. It’s a symbol of freedom! Of the open road! Imagine Constable painting the Volvo... chasing the setting sun..." Chloe and Maisie simultaneously groaned. "Grandad!" Chloe exclaimed. "Seriously!" "He's incorrigible," Maisie added, grinning. “So, Maisie's not the only one thinking about horses, then?” Chloe asked, turning to Peter. “Mum said she saw a new exhibition at the gallery. Apparently, it’s all horse portraits!” "Oh, really?" Peter seemed genuinely interested. “I might pop along.

…and then Brenda, bless her, tries to explain NFTs to Margaret! Margaret just stares at her, completely blank, and finally says, "Is that something to do with gardening, dear?" I nearly choked on my tea. Oh, Brenda! She's a whirlwind, isn’t she? Always leaping onto the latest bandwagon. Honestly, Dave, sometimes I think she makes things up just to have something to talk about. Though Margaret's response  is  brilliant. Gardening NFTs! Imagine. Woah, what’s all the laughter about? Sounds like Brenda’s been causing trouble again. Is that curry I smell? Please tell me it's curry. I'm starving. It is, love. Your favourite, chicken madras. Thought you’d appreciate a proper meal after that freelance deadline you were wrestling with. You’re the best, Dad! Seriously, I was pulling my hair out trying to finish that campaign for "Bloom & Brew" – coffee shop, florist combo. So niche, but apparently very lucrative. Bloom & Brew? Sounds rather lovely. Are they doing well? They are! Which is good because they were on the brink, you know? Proper small business, run by a lovely couple. Sometimes I feel guilty charging them what I do, but hey, gotta pay the rent! Don't you fret about that, sweetheart. You’re worth every penny. And good on you for supporting small businesses like that. Anyway, back to Brenda and her digital gardening… She was trying to convince me I should invest. Said it was the future! I told her I was quite happy with my roses, thank you very much. Though, thinking about it, Rupert's birthday is next week... He's been moaning about needing a new set of weeding tools. Weeding tools? Seriously? That’s your birthday present idea? He’s nearly 50, Mum! Surely he deserves something a little more… exciting. He'd appreciate good quality weeding tools! He’s a practical man. Plus, I've already spent a fortune on that new projector he wanted. The projector was a good shout. Remember how he was complaining about not being able to see the football properly? That’ll come in handy. Although, I'm still thinking he needs something… splashier. Maybe a trip? Somewhere warm? Ooh, a trip! Now you’re talking! Somewhere with cocktails and sunshine. He'd love that. But it’s a bit much, isn’t it? For just weeding tools? It's not  just  weeding tools!

"Well, Arthur, I reckon it's a bit more than 'not the end of the world' when it's your best friend's marriage we're talkin' about. Poor Geoffrey seemed right gutted, bless 'im. He’s always been a decent chap, Geoffrey. Goes to church every Sunday, volunteers at the animal shelter…” "Arthur, you're being remarkably blasé. Patricia flaunting it all over social media! Honestly, the audacity! And did you  see  the dress she wore to the garden party? Scarlet red, practically screaming 'look at me!' Geoffrey's always been a bit… sensitive, hasn't he?" "Margaret, with all due respect, Patricia derives a clear and demonstrable pleasure from disruption. It's a well-established pattern. Geoffrey is, as you say, sensitive, but he’s also a man who prefers a quiet life. A scandal like this... it’s debilitating for him." He takes a sip of his tea. "Though, publicly, he maintains a dignified silence. Good for him, really." "Dignified silence? Sounds a bit stiff, doesn't it? Geoffrey needs to have a proper word with Patricia. A good, strong confrontation. Though, I suppose, after all these years…" He trails off, shaking his head. "Speaking of confrontations, did you see Big Brother last night? That young lad, Jamie? Right drama queen!" "Big Brother? Don't get me started on that nonsense. All shoutin' and screamin’ for nowt. Give me a good nature programme any day. Watchin' them dogs, chasin' rabbits… now that’s entertainment." He chuckles. “Though, I do miss a bit o' power on telly. Makes you feel like you’re at least…participatin’ in somethin’.” "You're always missin' somethin', Arthur. It's your default setting. Remember when we went shopping last week? You practically mourned the loss of electricity for an hour while we were in that little antique shop with no lighting!" "Well, it's hard to appreciate a nice piece o' pottery when you can't  see  it, innit? And the cold! Goodness me, the cold! Thankfully, the heating's back on now. Bit of a fright that was, though, bein' without it." "The energy crisis is a genuine problem, Margaret. It’s impacting small businesses significantly. I’m seeing increased operating costs across the board.” "Speaking of impact, Patricia's antics have certainly impacted Geoffrey’s social circle. I spoke to Penelope from the WI – she's actively avoiding Patricia at the moment.

Speaker_1 chuckled, stirring a pot of pasta sauce with gusto. Speaker_2 laughed, leaning back against the kitchen counter. "You're kidding! A pigeon attack? You're always having the most random things happen, Bronte. Cambridge's wildlife is clearly more aggressive than Doncaster's." Bronte huffed playfully. "Don't you go starting on Cambridge. Doncaster’s got its charm. Besides, it was a particularly grumpy-looking pigeon. I think it disapproved of my choice of window box flowers." Imogen shook her head, smiling. "Right. A discerning pigeon. So, how's the sauce coming along? Smells amazing, as usual. You've got a knack for this cooking lark, you know." "Cheers, love. Just needs a bit more basil. Right, Anon's got the film ready, hasn't he?" Bronte glanced towards the living room where a faint glow emanated. "He said he picked something proper brilliant." “He did. Apparently, it’s a new French arthouse film. Something about a lighthouse keeper and existential dread.” Imogen wrinkled her nose slightly. “Sounds… intense.” Bronte grinned. "Sounds right up Anon's street, doesn't it? He's been going on about ‘atmospheric cinematography’ for weeks.” She tested the sauce with a spoon. “But hey, at least it’ll give us something to talk about afterwards. It wouldn't be a proper Anon film night without at least one bewildered expression." Imogen laughed. "True. Remember that Danish film about the smuggling rings and the sheep? We were all utterly lost. My mum still asks me what it was about." Bronte snorted. "Oh my god, yes! My Nan was proper baffled. She kept asking if the sheep were escaped from a farm. It's a miracle she didn't fall asleep." She paused. "Speaking of family, are your folks alright? Did you manage to get through to your mum yesterday?" “Yeah, I did. She's… she’s still a bit down about the flat sale, you know? It's been her home for thirty years. She keeps saying she doesn’t want to move to Surrey, but Dad’s insisting. Retirement village, apparently.” Imogen sighed, swirling the pasta around in her bowl. “That’s rough, innit?” Bronte offered sympathetically. “Big changes are always hard to swallow. Though, Surrey does sound a bit… beige.” “Tell me about it. She says she’ll be surrounded by beige people doing beige things. She wants to stay in Lewisham, keep going to the market, you know?

Aye, Ethan, you're pickin' up on it, aren't ya? It’s massively problematic. I marked it on the marking scheme, see? Just like with exam papers - secure chain of custody is paramount. And postal votes...well, they're a loophole the size of Yorkshire. But Mum, they say it’s to make it easier for people to vote, especially those living far away, or who have disabilities. Easier, yes. Secure? Absolutely not. Remember old Mrs. Grimshaw down the street? She nearly voted twice last election! Her grandson was tryin' to “help” her, bless 'im, but she got all confused. Had to spend an hour explaining the whole thing to her. And think of the potential for coercion, Ethan. A family member pushin' someone one way or another... it’s a worry, a real worry. I read an article this morning about the demographics. Younger people are more likely to support independence, and most of them will be voting by post. Doesn’t that skew the results? It could, aye, it could. It’s why I’m worried about this referendum. It’s not just about whether Scotland wants to be independent – it’s about  how  that decision is made. It needs to be fair, solid, above reproach, don't it? Like exam marking. It's all about integrity. My history teacher, Mr. Davies, reckons the SNP are pushing for it because they’re struggling with other policy issues. He said they’re hoping independence will be a distraction. Politicians, eh? Always lookin' for a quick fix. Mind you, I can see why some folks up there feel disillusioned with Westminster. The government's been a bit of a shambles lately, hasn't it? Although, breakin' away… it’s a big decision. Affects everyone in the UK, not just Scotland. My grandad used to work in a shipyard in Glasgow. He always said Scotland was better off in the Union, security and all that. But he also said the Union hasn't always been fair to Scotland. It's complicated. Aye, it is complicated. Your grandad's right on both counts, lad. There’s a real history there, a long and tangled one. My uncle, bless his soul, used to be a miner. Worked in a pit in South Yorkshire. Strong Labour man. He was dead against independence, said it would weaken the mining communities and make us all vulnerable.

Honestly, tha’s reet mingin', innit? Look at ‘er, blubberin’ over some bloke’s DNA. Jeremy Kyle, bless ‘im, he’s got a job, haven't he? Proper entertainment. Entertainment? It's a train wreck, Chloe! A proper shambles. Like watchin’ a bunch of seagulls fightin’ over a chip. And the accents... honestly, it's layered. You get the Geordie, the Mancunian, the Londoner... it’s a linguistic nightmare! I find it fascinatin’, actually. The way they drop all their ‘g’s. "Going' to the shops," becomes "goin' to the shops.” Proper elision, it is. Makes you think about how language evolves. Ee, Gill, you’re proper academic about it! They’re just tryin’ to sound tough, aren't they? Like they're somethin' they're not. And listen to that fella, he’s practically swallowin’ half his words. Makes it hard to understand what he’s on about. Aye, an’ look at the mum. Proper dramatic, wasn't she? "He says he ain't tha' faaather!" Like she’s in a soap opera. Faatha'? Official, that is! You only hear “faatha” round ‘ere, don't ya? It's like a Yorkshire trademark. I wish I could get away with sayin' it at uni. They'd think I was takin' the mickey. I could get away with it, probably. I mean, I’ve got a strong Scouse accent. It covers a multitude of sins. It hides all my linguistic shortcomings. You lot with your… flattened vowels… it's a bit drier, isn’t it? Drier? We're practical! Precise! We don’t waste no time on unnecessary fluff. It's efficiency. Unlike some people I know who drawl every single word out. Oh, comin’ from Miss "Proper Elision," that's rich! You’re basically describin' your own accent, Gill. Alright, alright, point taken. But at least I can be understood! Listen to that woman. "I wuz gonna…" Wuz? Who says “wuz”? She did! Oh, my days! She’s butchering the Queen's English, she is! It’s a crime against language! Rest o’ us aren’t doin' much better tha', are we? Droppin' g’s and sayin’ "faatha." It's all a bit chaotic, innit? Although... I do like sayin' "faatha." It just feels… right. It's home. It's a comfort thing, isn’t it? Rooted in where you’re from. I wouldn’t change my Scouse accent for the world.

Right, right. He’s makin’ a right mess o’ it, innit? That pass was awful. Honestly, you’d think he’d learned by now. He’s having an off day, Liv. Everyone does. Don’t be too harsh. If we’re ever lucky enough to have a wee one, that is. Speaking of wee ones, have you given any more thought to names? Actually, that's a good image. Makes me think of the Olympics, a bit. All that speed and agility! The Olympics have been fantastic so far, haven’t they? Got the whole country shoutin' at the telly. I remember gettin’ a free pint down the pub when he won that first gold. Best pint I ever tasted, mind you, even though it was probably lukewarm. Damp and dodgy wiring...

Honestly, this parking situation is ridiculous. I swear, finding a space near the clinic feels like winning the lottery these days. I circled for twenty minutes! Aye, tell me about it. Try finding a spot on Sefton Street after five! You've got better luck finding a unicorn. You’d think with all the new developments they'd have sorted parking out properly. Exactly! And it’s always the same people taking up two spaces with their massive SUVs. You know, I’m really hoping that Masters interview goes well. I need something to compensate for the everyday stresses, like battling for a parking space. The Masters? How did it go? I thought you were nervous about it. It was… okay. The panel were a bit intimidating, but I think I answered their questions alright. They seemed interested in my research proposal, thankfully. Fingers crossed! Did you manage to get that new batch of teaching materials? The ones Mrs. Davies wanted for the Year 7s? Sorted 'em! Headed into town earlier, just after you left. Managed to grab a quick look at the Walker Art Gallery while I was there. They've got that new photography exhibition on. It’s dead good, actually. You'd like it. Proper powerful images. Reminded me a bit of that documentary we watched about the Merseyrail tunnels. Ooh, photography! I’m in, definitely. Need a bit of culture after dealing with anxious teenagers all day. Speaking of culture, your Mum keeps asking about the wedding. She wants to know if we’ve booked the photographer yet. Don't remind me. Wedding planning is turning into a second job. Keep telling her we're still looking, but it’s a nightmare finding someone decent within budget. She’s got a specific vision, you know – "romantic, airy, natural light…" Sounds expensive! Tell her we're prioritizing a decent buffet. That's the real key to a successful wedding. Food, Liam. Food! You’re right. I’ll mention the buffet. Anyway, I was thinking… about moving. Moving? Where to? Back to Wirral? Nah, not the Wirral. I was thinking… maybe further out in South Liverpool? Something with a bit of a garden. You know, somewhere we could actually get a dog. Little Freddie needs a garden. Freddie? You haven't even got a dog yet! But…a garden  would  be nice. And a bit more space. We are cramped in here.

Honestly, this pizza’s doing  nothing  for me today. It’s like…cardboard with tomato sauce. Tell me about it! I thought the canteen was supposed to be getting better. Remember last week when they had that proper lasagna? That was dreamy. Dreamy is the word! This is just…beige. Anyway, did you see Liam Hemsworth's post on Insta? He’s in Australia, looking all… rugged. Oh my god! Yeah! Proper heart eyes emoji territory that. Bit annoying, innit? Like, he knows exactly what he’s doing. Playing the handsome Aussie card. He  is  handsome, though. And I’m obsessed with that new show, “Wednesday.” You seen it? Yeah, proper dark, yeah? Loved it! Jenna Ortega is amazing. Though, I’m still gutted about Tim Burton not directing the whole thing. Feels like it lost a bit of that… creepy magic towards the end. I know! It did. My Nan keeps asking me about it, though. She’s really into anything spooky. She’s obsessed with Disney now too! Can you imagine? My gran, practically 70, watching “Encanto” for the fifth time this month. Honestly, my little cousin’s the same. Non-stop "We Don't Talk About Bruno” even though you've heard it a million times. It gets stuck in your head, doesn’t it? Like a cartoon earworm. Speaking of cartoons, did you ever watch "Recess" growing up? "Recess"? Vaguely. I was more of a "Powerpuff Girls" girl, myself. Remember Dexter’s Laboratory? My brother was obsessed. He wanted a lab coat and everything. Proper mental! Anyway, less cartoons, more serious stuff. How’s uni going? You sounded stressed last week. It’s…a lot. The history essays are killing me. I spent last night re-reading one chapter about the Victorian workhouses. Seriously depressing stuff. I need a weekend full of sunshine and something other than dust and poverty. You do. I was thinking, there's that new little cafe down by the canal - "The Rusty Mug," they call it. Apparently, they have amazing pancakes. We could go Saturday morning? Ooh, pancakes! Actually, that sounds perfect. Could Mia and Chloe join us? I haven’t seen them properly in ages. Yeah, definitely. I’ll text them. What are you doing Saturday night, though? Thinking of heading to that club, "Neon Nights." Sarah's going. "Neon Nights"? Ugh, the music's always so loud. And it's always packed.

Ugh, this is good, Mum. Really good. But seriously, did you see Charizard’s new Tera Type? It's absolutely mental! Electric/Dragon. Electric  and  Dragon! It is lovely, isn't it, love? And yes, I did see. Your Grandad showed me. He's obsessed with Pokémon Go again. Said he caught a shiny Snorlax yesterday. Apparently, it’s very rare. Dada! Yeah, yeah, Oisin. You want some pasta. Hold on, hold on. So, the Electric/Dragon Charizard... I’m thinking of using it in my raid team. You reckon it's a good shout? I’m struggling to beat Melmetal. Well, your Grandad says you should build a good team around it. Strategically, of course. Not just chucking your favourite Pokémon in. He’s been giving you lessons, hasn't he? Yeah, but he keeps going on about type advantages and weaknesses. It’s a bit much sometimes. He’s like, “Liam, you need to consider the inherent vulnerability of a Flying-type Pokémon against a Rock-type opponent!” Like, chill out, Grandad, it's a game. He just wants to help, love. And it  is  a strategic game, you know. Remember when you were gutted because your Blastoise was destroyed by a single Leaf Blade? Okay, point taken. It was a bit embarrassing. But still! I was thinking later, could we Skype Nana and Uncle Mark? I haven't seen them in ages. Of course, darling. Let me finish clearing up this dinner mess first. Oisin’s making a proper production of things, as you can see. He’s got your Uncle Mark’s stubbornness, that one. He really does! Hey, I was also thinking… maybe we could go to that Ramen place in town next week? The one we talked about? Oh, yes! That sounds lovely. When are you free? And if we go, Oisin can have a little bowl of noodles, won't he? Don’t tell him they’re not  proper  Ramen. He'll have a meltdown. Deal. He can have all the noodles he wants. So, about my team… I'm also thinking of a new guitar. The one I’ve got is… well, it’s seen better days. Dad said he might be able to get me a used one. A new guitar? That's wonderful! What kind were you thinking of? Acoustic or electric? Probably electric. I want to learn some proper riffs.

Honestly, this gnome is hideous. Where did  this  even come from? It’s been lurking in here for decades, I swear. Probably from that charity shop trip we took in ’98. Remember?
